Since "they establish the prayer and give the zakat" describes something renewed and not continuous through all time, the relative clause was expressed with a verb. Since belief in the Hereafter is, in their view, a settled and enduring matter, the clause was expressed as a nominal sentence, and the subject was emphasized by repeating it, so that it says: ﴿they are certain﴾. The predicate of the subject-predicate sentence is a verb, to indicate permanence. It is also possible that the clause is a new statement (*istinaf*, a resumptive sentence, one that begins a new thought). Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is possible that the relative clause is complete at His saying, 'and they' (*wa-hum*). The clause would then be parenthetical (*i'tirādiyya*), as if it were said: 'And these who believe and do righteous deeds, through establishing the prayer and giving the zakat, are the ones certain of the Hereafter.' This is the preferred view, and it is supported by the fact that he formed an independent nominal clause and repeated in it the subject, which is 'they', until its meaning became: 'None are certain of the Hereafter with true certainty except these who combine faith and righteous action, for the fear of the consequence drives them to bear hardships.'" End of quotation. His saying "the clause would be parenthetical" is not in accordance with the grammarians' usage of the parenthetical clause (*jumla i'tirāḍiyya*), which they define as occurring only between two things that are related to one another, such as its occurrence between a relative clause and its relative pronoun, between the two parts of a predication, between a condition and its response, between an adjective and its noun, or between an oath and what is sworn to. Here it does not occur between any of the things mentioned, and his saying "until its meaning became..." contains a trace of Mu'tazilite (*i'tizāl*, the rationalist school) doctrine. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Zakat here may be understood as not the obligatory zakat, since the surah is an early Meccan surah; it may also be understood as the obligatory zakat without further explanation. It has also been said that zakat here means purity from defects and constant adherence to noble character." End of quotation.

When Allah mentioned the believers who are certain of the resurrection, He mentioned the deniers. The reference is to the Quraysh and those who follow their path in denying the resurrection. The deeds may be either deeds of goodness and monotheism, which it was incumbent upon them to make their deeds, but they were blind to them, hesitated and were bewildered. This view is attributed to al-Hasan al-Basri. Or the deeds may be deeds of disbelief and misguidance, in which case Allah has made these appealing to them and adorned them by creating them within their souls, so that they saw those ugly deeds as good. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If it is asked: how did He attribute the adornment of their deeds to His own Self, while He attributed it to Satan in His saying, ﴿And Satan made their deeds appealing to them﴾ [An-Naml: 24]? I answer: there is a difference between the two attributions. Attributing it to Satan is literal, while attributing it to Allah, exalted is He, (p-54) is figurative (*majāz*). In the science of rhetoric (*'ilm al-bayān*) it has two ways. The first is that it belongs to the figurative speech called metaphor (*isti'āra*). The second is that it belongs to the figurative speech called the figure of attribution (*majāz al-maḥkī*, the figure in which the attribution is to the agent who is the cause of the action).

As for the first way: since He gave them long life and abundant provision, and they took Allah's bounty and beneficence toward them as a means to follow their desires and their insolence, and to prefer ease, and to shun whatever demands difficult obligations and wearying hardships, then it is as if He adorned their deeds for them through this. To this refers the angels' saying: ﴿But You gave them and their fathers enjoyment until they forgot the Reminder﴾ [Al-Furqan: 18].

As for the second way: Allah's granting Satan respite and leaving him free until he makes the deeds appealing is a clear involvement in the adornment, so the attribution was made to Allah because He is the one who chooses, and this is the figure reported through one of its involvements." End of quotation. This is an interpretation along Mu'tazilite lines.

*Ulā'ika* ("those") refers to the deniers of the resurrection. *Sū' al-'adhāb* ("the evil of punishment") is apparently not restricted to this world; rather they have it both in this world and in the Hereafter. It has been said that the meaning is in this world, and it was explained as what befell them on the day of Badr of killing, capture, and plunder. It has also been said that it is what they will encounter at death and after it, including the punishment of the grave. *Sū' al-'adhāb* means its severity and magnitude.

The apparent meaning is that *al-akhsarūn* ("the greatest losers") is the elative form (*af'al al-tafḍīl*, the comparative/superlative), because the disbeliever has lost this world and the Hereafter, as Allah, exalted is He, informed of, and in the Hereafter his loss is greater, since his end is a lasting punishment. As for in this world, when a trial befalls him, it may leave him and be removed. Thus the greater and increased loss is his in the Hereafter. The comparative may also be applied even when the subject is one in relation to time, place, condition, or other things that admit of increase. Al-Kirmani said: "The form *af'al* here is for emphasis, not for sharing (*lil-mubālagha lā lil-shirka*), as if he is saying: the believer has no loss at all, such that the disbeliever would share it with him and exceed him in it. We have explained how the sharing works with respect to this world and the Hereafter." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "*Al-akhsarūn* is the plural of *akhsar*, because *af'al* as an adjective is not pluralized except when it is made genitive (*idāfa*), so its rank in nouns is strengthened. There is room for examination in this." End of quotation. There is no problem with it being pluralized in both the sound plural and the broken plural when it has the definite article *al-*. Rather, in that case, nothing else is permitted, when there precedes it something that agrees with it in plurality, so one says: *al-Zaydūna hum al-afḍalūna* and *al-afāḍil*, and *al-Hindāt hunna al-fuḍliyyāt* and *al-fuḍl*. As for his saying that it is not pluralized except when made genitive, the pluralization is not then necessarily determined. Rather, when it is made genitive to an indefinite noun, its pluralization is not permitted, while if it is made genitive to a definite noun, both pluralization and singularity are permitted, as established in the books of grammar.

When He said earlier: ﴿These are the verses of the Qur'an﴾, He addressed His Prophet with His saying: ﴿And indeed you﴾, meaning: this Qur'an which you received is from Allah, exalted is He, and He is the All-Wise, the All-Knowing, not as the polytheists claimed, that it is a lie, fables, soothsaying, or poetry, and other such fabrications. The verb is in the passive voice and the agent is omitted, and it is Gabriel, upon him be peace, to indicate him in His saying: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara': 193]. *Laqqā* is transitive to one object, and the doubling in it is for making transitive, so it is made transitive to two objects, and it is as if he was absent from it, then met it and received it (*talaqqāhu*). Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Its meaning is 'given,' as He said: ﴿And none receives it except one of great fortune﴾ [Fussilat: 35]." Al-Hasan said: "The meaning is: indeed you are receiving the Qur'an." It has also been said: its meaning is "you are taught it." Wisdom (*ḥikma*) is knowledge of practical matters, and knowledge is more general than it, since it may be practical or theoretical. The perfection of knowledge is its relation to all knowables and its persistence protected from every change, and this is not but for Allah, exalted is He. This verse is a preparation for what he informs of the unseen matters and the explanation of the stories of the earlier nations, which indicates that he received this from Allah, and His informing him of His subtle wisdom and His precise knowledge, exalted is He. It has been said: *idh* ("when") is governed by a suppressed "remember" (*udhkur*), or by *'alīm* ("All-Knowing"). Its being governed by *'alīm* is not clear, since then the description would be restricted by the object.

A portion of the story of Moses, upon him be peace, has already been mentioned, in his journey with his family from Midian, in Surah Ta-Ha. The apparent meaning of "his family" is plural, given His saying: ﴿I will bring you﴾ and ﴿so that you may warm yourselves﴾. It has been narrated that he had with him only his wife. It has also been said that she had given birth to a child for him while he was with Shu'ayb, so the child was with his mother. If this report is sound, then it is from the usage of the plural in address as a form of honor and reverence. The road had become unclear to him, the weather was cold, and the journey was at night, so his soul longed, when he saw the fire, for an end to what had afflicted him from losing the way and the severity of the cold, and he said: ﴿I will bring you from it news﴾, meaning from its fire, news that indicates the way, (p-55) ﴿or I will bring you a burning brand﴾, meaning if there is no one there to give information, then I will bring with me what you may warm yourselves by from it. This alternation with "or" is clear, because his first aim was to find someone at the fire who would tell him the way, since he was a traveler and not a resident. If there was no one, then he was a resident, and they would need to repel the harm of the cold, which means that he would bring them what they could warm themselves by. He was therefore not in need of both things together, but of one of them: news, if he found someone to inform him so that he could continue on, or warmth, if he did not find anyone and stayed. So his aim was either guidance to the road or taking a brand of fire, and this is the meaning of His saying: ﴿Perhaps I will bring you from it a brand, or find at the fire guidance﴾ [Ta-Ha: 10].

Here it says: ﴿I will bring you from it news﴾, and it is news. In Ta-Ha it says: ﴿Perhaps I will bring you from it a brand﴾ [Ta-Ha: 10], and in Al-Qasas it says: ﴿Perhaps I will bring you from it news﴾ [Al-Qasas: 29]. The second is an expression of hope, and the meaning of hope is different from the meaning of news. But when hope is strong, it is permitted for the one hoping to report it, even if disappointment may occur. He used the future particle *sa-* ("I will"), either because the distance was great, or because he may be delayed by what he anticipated might hold him back. A *shihāb* is a flame, and a *qabas* is fire that has been kindled, on the pattern *fa'al* in the sense of *maf'ūl*, and it is a piece of fire on a stick or otherwise, as was mentioned in Ta-Ha. The Kufans read *bi-shihābin* with tanwin, so *qabasin* is either an apposition or an adjective, since it has the meaning of "that which is kindled." The rest of the seven readers read it with the genitive construction (*idāfa*), and this is the reading of al-Hasan. Al-Zamakhshari said: "He made *shihāb* genitive to *qabas* because it may be a kindled fire or other than a kindled fire, and he followed Abu al-Hasan in this." Abu al-Hasan said: "The genitive construction is better and more common in recitation, as you say: *dār ājurr* ("a house of brick") and *siwār dhahab* ("a bracelet of gold")."

The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in *jā'ahā* ("when he came to it") refers to the fire. It was also said it refers to the tree, since he had seen it in a *samur* tree (an acacia). It was also said: a *'alīq* tree, which does not burn it, and whenever he approached it, it moved away. The passive verb *nūdiya* ("he was called") has as its unnamed agent the pronoun referring to Moses, upon him be peace. On this view, *anna* may be explanatory, because the conditions of an explanatory particle are present in it, and it may also be the verbal *anna* (the "that" introducing a clause). As for the binary *anna* which governs the imperfect verb, *būrika* ("blessed") is its complement, and the original is the preposition, meaning "that there is blessing," and *būrika* is the predicate. As for the lightened form of the heavy *anna*, its origin is the preposition. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If it is asked: may the lightened form of the heavy *anna* be used here, with the sense 'that he was blessed,' and the pronoun being the pronoun of the matter and the story? I answer: no, because it requires *qad*. If it is asked: then with it suppressed? I answer: that is not correct, because it is a sign and is not deleted." End of quotation. It is also permitted that it be the lightened form of the heavy *anna*, with *būrika* as a verb of supplication, as one says: *bārak Allāhu fīk* ("may Allah bless you"). When it is a supplication, it is not permitted for *qad* to precede it, so it is like His saying: ﴿And the fifth [that the wrath of Allah be upon her]﴾ [An-Nur: 9], in the reading of the one who made it a past verb, and like the Arabs' saying: *immā an jazāka Allāhu khayran, wa-immā an yaghfira Allāhu lak* ("either may Allah reward you with good, or may Allah forgive you"). Al-Zamakhshari had based this on the view that *būrika* is a statement and not a supplication, which is why he did not permit it to be the lightened form of the heavy *anna*. Al-Zajjaj permitted that *anna būrika* be in the position of the unnamed object, and it is by dropping the preposition, meaning: he was called with *anna būrika*, just as one says: *nūdiya bi-l-rukhas* ("he was called with cheapness"). It is also permitted that *anna* be the binary or the lightened form of the heavy, and then *būrika* is a supplication. It has been said that the unnamed object is the pronoun of the call, meaning: he was called it, that is the calling, and then it was explained by what follows it. The meaning of *būrika* is: it was sanctified, purified, and its good increased. One says: *bārakaka Allāh*, *bārak fīk*, *bārak 'alayk*, and *bārak lak*. The poet said:

*fa-būrikta mawlūdan wa-būrikta nāshi'an*
*wa-būrikta 'inda al-shaybi idh anta ashyabu*

And another said:

*būrika al-mayyitu al-gharību kamā*
*būrika nab'u al-rummāni wa-al-zaytūni*

And 'Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr said:

*fa-būrika fī banīka wa-fī banīhim*
*idhā dhukirū wa-naḥnu laka al-fidā'*

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 27, verses 1–14 (part 3 of 4):

"Man" (مَن): The well-known view is that it refers to one who has knowledge. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan and others said: God, exalted is He, meant by "whoever is in the fire" His Own Essence. Some of them expressed this in offensive terms that are rejected as applied to God, exalted is He. If this is established from Ibn 'Abbas and those he mentioned, then the first reading involves an ellipsis, meaning: Blessed is the One whose power and authority are in the fire. It was also said that it was said to Moses, peace be upon him: Blessed is whoever is in the place or the direction in which the fire appeared to him. Al-Suddi said: "man" refers to the angels appointed over it. It was also said: "man" may refer to what does not have intellect. Ibn 'Abbas said: it means the light. It was said: it means the tree in which the fire blazes.

It was said: the apparent meaning of "and those around it" (﴿ومَن حَوْلَها﴾) is that it refers to those who have knowledge, and its explanation is "O Moses," and it was explained as referring to the angels. This is supported by the reading of Ubayy, as transmitted by Abu 'Amr al-Dani, and Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and 'Ikrima: "and those around it of the angels." This reading is to be taken as an explanation, because it contradicts the consonantal text of the Mushaf (sawad al-mushaf), on which there is consensus. It was also explained as referring to Moses and the angels together, peace be upon them. It was said: it may refer to what does not have intellect, and it was explained as referring to the places around the fire. It is fitting that the one within it and those around it be blessed, since a great matter occurred, namely God's speaking to Moses, peace be upon him. His being informed and opened with the call of blessing is glad tidings to Moses, a comfort to him, and an introduction to his intimate conversation with God.

The apparent view is that His saying "And glory be to God, Lord of the worlds" (﴿وسُبْحانَ اللَّهِ رَبِّ العالَمِينَ﴾) falls under His saying "was called" (﴿نُودِيَ﴾). When he was called with the blessing of the one mentioned, he was also called with something that indicates transcendence and freedom from the attributes of created things, from whatever might occur to the mind. This is especially so if "whoever is in the fire" is understood according to Ibn 'Abbas's interpretation that "whoever" refers to God, exalted is He, for that implies a location, so the verse brings what necessitates transcendence (tanzih). Al-Suddi said: it is from the speech of Moses. When he heard the call, he said: "And glory be to God, Lord of the worlds," declaring God, exalted is He, free from the marks of created things. Ibn Shajara said: it is from the speech of God, and its meaning is: "Blessed is whoever glorifies God." This is far from the indication of the wording. It was said: "And glory be to God, Lord of the worlds" is an address to Muhammad, peace be upon him, and it is a parenthetical statement between the two speeches, its purpose being transcendence.

When God, exalted is He, comforted him, He called him and turned toward him, saying: "O Moses, indeed it is I, God, the Mighty, the Wise" (﴿يامُوسى إنَّهُ أنا اللَّهُ العَزِيزُ الحَكِيمُ﴾). The apparent view is that the pronoun in "innahu" is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n), "I am God" is a clause in the position of the predicate, and "the Mighty, the Wise" are two attributes. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that the pronoun in "innahu" refers back to what is indicated by what precedes it, meaning: "Indeed the one speaking to you is I, and God is an explanation of 'I,' and 'the Mighty, the Wise' are two attributes of the explanation." End of quotation. When the agent is omitted and the verb is put in the passive form, the pronoun cannot refer back to that omitted agent, since the verb has been changed from being built for it and it has been resolved that it is not what is spoken of. Referring the pronoun back to it contradicts that, for it would become the intended and emphasized subject. This call, this turning toward him, and this address are a preparation for what God, exalted is He, wished to manifest through his hand of miracles (al-mu'jiz, the miracle that proves prophethood), meaning: I am the Strong, the Capable of what is far-fetched in the imagination, the One who does what I do with wisdom.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: upon what does His saying 'And throw down your staff' (﴿وألْقِ عَصاكَ﴾) depend grammatically? I answer: upon 'blessed,' because the meaning is: 'He was called that whoever is in the fire is blessed,' and it was said to him: 'Throw down your staff.' The evidence for this is His saying: 'And that throw down your staff' (﴿وأنْ ألْقِ عَصاكَ﴾) [al-Qasas: 31] after His saying: 'That O Moses, indeed I am God' (﴿أنْ يا مُوسى إنِّي أنا اللَّهُ﴾) [al-Qasas: 30], with the repetition of the explanatory particle, just as you say: 'I wrote to him that perform hajj and 'umra,' and if you wish: 'that perform hajj and that perform 'umra.'" End of quotation. His saying "innahu" (إنَّهُ) coordinated with "blessed" contradicts its being a predicate. It was said that "throw down" is coordinated with "blessed," but this is not a clause whose part is what it is. It was said: it is coordinated with "blessed," and a supposition was needed. It was said: "throw down your staff" so that the clause would be informative and suit the informative clause it is coordinated with, as if he saw in coordination the agreement of the two coordinated elements. The correct view is that this is not required. Rather, His saying "And throw down your staff" is coordinated with His saying "Indeed it is I, God, the Mighty, the Wise," coordinating an imperative clause with an informative clause. Sibawayh permitted: "Zayd came and 'Amr was with him" (jā'a Zaydun wa-man 'Amrun).

"So when he saw it moving" (﴿فَلَمّا رَآها تَهْتَزُّ﴾): there is an omitted element here, its supposition being: "so he threw it from his hand." Al-Hasan, al-Zuhri and 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd read "ja'n" (جَأْنٌ) with a hamza in place of the alif, as if he fled from the meeting of two unvocalized letters. The discussion of such things has already preceded in His saying "wa-lā al-ḍāl'īn" with the hamza in the reading of 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd. And it came: "then behold, it was a snake" (﴿فَإذا هي حَيَّةٌ﴾) [Ta-Ha: 20], "then behold, it was a manifest serpent" (﴿فَإذا هي ثُعْبانٌ مُبِينٌ﴾) [al-A'raf: 107]. This is God's report of its transformation and the change of its attributes and accidents, not the annihilation of its essence and its creation as a snake or serpent. Rather, that is a change of attributes, not a change of essence. Here He likened it, in the state of its movement, to the jann, and it was said: they are the small snakes, He likening it to them in the speed of its agitation and movement, together with the greatness of its bulk.

When Moses saw this terrible matter, "he turned back fleeing and did not return" (﴿ولّى مُدْبِرًا ولَمْ يُعَقِّبْ﴾). Mujahid said: he did not return. Al-Suddi said: he did not linger. Qatada said: he did not look back. It is said: "'aqqaba al-rajul" means he turned toward something he had turned away from, as if he turned back on his heels. From this is "'aqqaba al-muqatil," when a fighter charges again after fleeing. The poet said:

They turned back when it was said: "Is there any who will return?" and they did not stop at the place of dread.

What befalls human nature befell him, when a person sees a thing extremely terrifying, namely seeing the staff transform into a snake running swiftly, and no reassurance had preceded it at the sight of it. Al-Zamakhshari said: he was averse only because he assumed that this was for a matter intended for him, and this is shown by: "Indeed the messengers do not fear in My presence" (﴿إنِّي لا يَخافُ لَدَيَّ المُرْسَلُونَ﴾). End of quotation. Ibn 'Atiyya said: God, exalted is He, called him, comforting him and strengthening him for the matter: "O Moses, do not fear" (﴿يا مُوسى لا تَخَفْ﴾), for My messengers whom I have chosen for prophethood fear none but Me. Moses, peace be upon him, then took the snake, and it returned to being a staff, and then it became his habit. End of quotation. It was said: the meaning is that the messengers do not fear in the place where revelation is sent to them, though they are the most fearful of people toward God. It was said: when I command them to display a miracle, they should not fear in what relates to displaying it, for the messenger certainly fears God. End of quotation.

The more evident view is that His saying "except one who has done wrong" (﴿إلّا مَن ظَلَمَ﴾) is a disjunctive exception (istithnā' munqaṭi'), and the meaning is: "but rather, whoever among others has done wrong." This was stated by al-Farra' and a group, since prophets are protected from committing the wrong that others commit. From al-Farra': it is a connected exception (istithnā' muttaṣil) from omitted clauses, and the supposition is: "Rather, others fear, except one who has done wrong." Al-Nahhas rejected this and said: an exception from an omitted element is impossible. If this were permitted, it would be permitted to say: "I do not strike the people except Zayd," meaning: "Rather, I strike others except Zayd." This is the opposite of clarity and of bringing something whose meaning is not known. End of quotation. A group said: "illā" here has the meaning of "wa" (and), the supposition being: "nor one who has done wrong." This is worthless, because the meaning of "illā" is greatly distinct from the meaning of "wa," since "wa" is for inclusion and "illā" is for exclusion, so it is not possible for one to take the place of the other. It was narrated from al-Hasan, Muqatil, Ibn Jurayj and al-Dahhak what indicates that it is a connected exception.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: The scholars have agreed that prophets, peace be upon them, are protected from the major sins and from those minor sins that are base vices, and it has been disputed concerning what lies beyond that. Perhaps al-Hasan and Ibn Jurayj were pointing to what is beyond that. End of quotation. Al-Zamakhshari said: "illā" here has the meaning of "but rather," because when he absolutely negated fear from the messenger, that would be a cause for harm and suspicion, so it was corrected. The meaning is: "But rather, whoever among them has done wrong," that is, a minor lapse occurred from them of what is not permitted for prophets, like what occurred from Adam, Jonah, David, Solomon, the brothers of Joseph, and from Moses in striking the Copt. It is likely that this allusion is aimed at what came from Moses, and it is among the allusions whose meaning is subtle. He called it wrongdoing, as Moses said: "My Lord, indeed I have wronged myself, so forgive me" (﴿رَبِّ إنِّي ظَلَمْتُ نَفْسِي فاغْفِرْ لِي﴾) [al-Qasas: 16]. End of quotation.

Abu Ja'far and Zayd ibn Aslam read "alā man ẓalama" (ألا مَن ظَلَمَ), with a fatha on the hamza and the lam lightened, as the interrogative particle of opening (ḥarf istiftāḥ). "Man" is conditional. "Al-husn" is the goodness of repentance, and "al-sū'" is the wrong that he committed. The majority read "ḥusnan" with a ḍamma on the ḥā' and a sukūn on the sīn, with tanwīn. Muhammad ibn 'Isa al-Isbahani read "kadhalika" but without tanwīn, making it fu'lā, so it is not declined. Ibn Miqsam read it with a ḍamma on the ḥā' and the sīn, with tanwīn. Mujahid, Abu Hayawa, Ibn Abi Layla, al-A'mash, Abu 'Amr in the transmission of al-Ju'fi, Abu Zayd, 'Isma, 'Abd al-Warith, Harun and 'Ayyash read it with fatha on both, with tanwīn.

"And insert" (﴿وأدْخِلْ﴾) is a command with what follows from it, namely the appearance of the great miracle. When He showed him a miracle in something other than himself, which is the staff, He showed him a miracle in himself, which is the brilliance of his hand as if it were a piece of light, when he did what he was commanded. The apparent answer to the command is "it will come out" (تَخْرُجْ), because its coming out follows from its insertion. It was said: there is an omitted element in the speech, its supposition being: "Insert your hand into your pocket and it will enter, and bring it out and it will come out," so the first omitted what its counterpart is stated in the second, and the second omitted what its counterpart is stated in the first. Qatada said: "in your pocket" (﴿فِي جَيْبِكَ﴾) means your shirt. He had a woolen tunic without sleeves. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: its sleeve reached part of his hand. Al-Suddi said: "in your pocket" means under your armpit.

The apparent view is that His saying "among nine signs to Pharaoh" (﴿فِي تِسْعِ آياتٍ إلى فِرْعَوْنَ﴾) is connected to an omitted element, its supposition being: "Go with these two signs among nine signs to Pharaoh." This is shown by His saying afterward: "But when Our signs came to them, visible" (﴿فَلَمّا جاءَتْهم آياتُنا مُبْصِرَةً﴾). This omission is like the poet's words:

They came to my fire, and I said: "Are you humans?" They said: "Jinn." I said: "Stay, be dark!"

And I said: "To the food," and from them one group envies the humans the food.

The estimate: "Come to the food." Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also possible that the meaning is: "Cast your staff and put your hand [into your garment], among nine signs", i.e., among the total of nine signs. One may object: the signs were eleven, two of which are the hand and the staff, and the nine are: the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, the obliteration, the drought in their desert regions, and the shortfall in their crops. End of quotation. According to the first view, the staff and the hand are included among the nine. According to the second, the preposition *fi* (in) carries the meaning of *ma'a* (with), i.e., "with nine signs." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "*Among nine signs*" is connected to his words "cast" and "put in," and there is an abbreviation and an omission in it. Its estimate is: "That is made smooth and made easy for you within the total of nine signs," which are: the staff, the hand, the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, the obliteration, and the stone. There is disagreement about the last two, and the meaning is: he brings them to Pharaoh and his people. Al-Zajjaj said: "*Among nine signs*" means "from nine signs," just as you say: "Take for me ten camels, among which are two stallions," i.e., from them, to Pharaoh, i.e., sent to Pharaoh. End of quotation.

*Mubsiran* (clear, visible) is in the accusative as a *hal* (circumstantial clause), meaning: clear and evident. The seeing is attributed to them metaphorically (*majaz*): since it is by them that one sees, they are described as "seeing"; or because seeing and clarity accompany them. It was said: it is because they make people into seers, from your saying "abṣartuhu," the transitive form made with the hamza of transference from *baṣara*. It was also said: it is an active participle with the meaning of a passive, as in *ma' dafiq* (gushing water). Qatada and 'Ali ibn al-Husayn read *mabṣarah*, with a fatha on the *mim* and the *ṣad*, which is a verbal noun (*masdar*), as you say: "The child is a source of cowardice" (*majbanah*). It is used in place of the noun, and it is also in the accusative as a *hal*. This pattern is frequent in descriptions of places, as in: "a land abounding in lions" (*arḍun masba'ah*) and "a place abounding in marshes" (*makānun maḍabbah*). Al-Zamakhshari said: i.e., a place where much seeing occurs. End of quotation.

The most eloquent reading of ﴿واسْتَيْقَنَتْها﴾ ("though their souls were certain of them") is that the *waw* is the *waw* of the *hal* clause, meaning: they denied them and rejected them outwardly, while inwardly their souls were certain that they were signs from God, but they were obstinate and called them magic. God the Exalted said, relating about Moses in his dialogue with Pharaoh: ﴿He said: "You certainly know that none sent these down but the Lord of the heavens and the earth, as clear proofs."﴾ [al-Isra: 102].

*Zulman* (in wrongdoing) means exceeding the limit, and *'uluwwan* (in arrogance) means haughtiness and pride, rising above faith. Both are in the accusative as verbal nouns in the position of a *hal*, meaning: wronging and exalting themselves. Or they are objects of purpose (*maf'ulan min ajlihima*), meaning: because of their wrongdoing and their arrogance, i.e., what drove them to denial and rejection, while being certain that these were signs from God, was wrongdoing and arrogance. The form *istaf'ala* here carries the meaning of *tafa''ala*, as *istakbara* means *takabbara* (to be arrogant).

'Abdullah, Ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, Talhah, and Aban ibn Taghlib, and "Iliyyan" read it with the *waw* changed to *ya'*, with a kasra on the *'ayn* and the *lam*. Its original form is *fu'ul*, but they made the *'ayn* a kasra for harmonization (*ittiba'*). It is also narrated that its *ḍamma* (vowel) was read by Ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, and Talhah. The disagreement has already been mentioned concerning obstinate disbelief (*kufr al-'inad*): is it possible for it to occur or not?

The "consequence" (*'aqibah*) is what the people of Pharaoh came to, of evil outcome, and what is prepared for them in the Hereafter is worse. In this there is an example for the disbelievers of Quraysh, since they were corrupters and haughty, and a warning to them that there may befall them the like of what befell those who were before them.

(سُورَةُ النَّمْلِ وهي خَمْسٌ وتِسْعُونَ آيَةً مَكِّيَّةً)
(Surat an-Naml, which has ninety-five verses, is Meccan.)

(بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمَنِ الرَّحِيمِ)
(In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.)

﴿طس﴾ ﴿تِلْكَ آياتُ القُرْآنِ وكِتابٍ مُبِينٍ﴾ ﴿هُدًى وبُشْرى لِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ ﴿الَّذِينَ يُقِيمُونَ الصَّلاةَ ويُؤْتُونَ الزَّكاةَ وهم بِالآخِرَةِ هم يُوقِنُونَ﴾ ﴿إنَّ الَّذِينَ لا يُؤْمِنُونَ بِالآخِرَةِ زَيَّنّا لَهم أعْمالَهم فَهم يَعْمَهُونَ﴾ ﴿أُولَئِكَ الَّذِينَ لَهم سُوءُ العَذابِ وهم في الآخِرَةِ هُمُ الأخْسَرُونَ﴾ ﴿وإنَّكَ لَتُلَقّى القُرْآنَ مِن لَدُنْ حَكِيمٍ عَلِيمٍ﴾ ﴿إذْ قالَ مُوسى لِأهْلِهِ إنِّي آنَسْتُ نارًا سَآتِيكم مِنها بِخَبَرٍ أوْ آتِيكم بِشِهابٍ قَبَسٍ لَعَلَّكم تَصْطَلُونَ﴾ ﴿فَلَمّا جاءَها نُودِيَ أنْ بُورِكَ مَن في النّارِ ومَن حَوْلَها وسُبْحانَ اللَّهِ رَبِّ العالَمِينَ﴾ ﴿يامُوسى إنَّهُ أنا اللَّهُ العَزِيزُ الحَكِيمُ﴾ ﴿وألْقِ عَصاكَ فَلَمّا رَآها تَهْتَزُّ كَأنَّها جانٌّ ولّى مُدْبِرًا ولَمْ يُعَقِّبْ يامُوسى لا تَخَفْ إنِّي لا يَخافُ لَدَيَّ المُرْسَلُونَ﴾ ﴿إلّا مَن ظَلَمَ ثُمَّ بَدَّلَ حُسْنًا بَعْدَ سُوءٍ فَإنِّي غَفُورٌ رَحِيمٌ﴾ ﴿وأدْخِلْ يَدَكَ في جَيْبِكَ تَخْرُجْ بَيْضاءَ مِن غَيْرِ سُوءٍ في تِسْعِ آياتٍ إلى فِرْعَوْنَ وقَوْمِهِ إنَّهم كانُوا قَوْمًا فاسِقِينَ﴾ ﴿فَلَمّا جاءَتْهم آياتُنا مُبْصِرَةً قالُوا هَذا سِحْرٌ مُبِينٌ﴾ ﴿وجَحَدُوا بِها واسْتَيْقَنَتْها أنْفُسُهم ظُلْمًا وعُلُوًّا فانْظُرْ كَيْفَ كانَ عاقِبَةُ المُفْسِدِينَ﴾ ﴿ولَقَدْ آتَيْنا داوُدَ وسُلَيْمانَ عِلْمًا وقالا الحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ الَّذِي فَضَّلَنا عَلى كَثِيرٍ مِن عِبادِهِ المُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ [النمل: ١٥] ﴿ووَرِثَ سُلَيْمانُ داوُدَ وقالَ ياأيُّها النّاسُ عُلِّمْنا مَنطِقَ الطَّيْرِ وأُوتِينا مِن كُلِّ شَيْءٍ إنَّ هَذا لَهو الفَضْلُ المُبِينُ﴾ [النمل: ١٦] ﴿وحُشِرَ لِسُلَيْمانَ جُنُودُهُ مِنَ الجِنِّ والإنْسِ والطَّيْرِ فَهم يُوزَعُونَ﴾ [النمل: ١٧] ﴿حَتّى إذا أتَوْا عَلى وادِي النَّمْلِ قالَتْ نَمْلَةٌ ياأيُّها النَّمْلُ ادْخُلُوا مَساكِنَكم لا يَحْطِمَنَّكم سُلَيْمانُ وجُنُودُهُ وهم لا يَشْعُرُونَ﴾ [النمل: ١٨] ﴿فَتَبَسَّمَ ضاحِكًا مِن قَوْلِها وقالَ رَبِّ أوْزِعْنِي أنْ أشْكُرَ نِعْمَتَكَ الَّتِي أنْعَمْتَ عَلَيَّ وعَلى والِدَيَّ وأنْ أعْمَلَ صالِحًا تَرْضاهُ وأدْخِلْنِي بِرَحْمَتِكَ في عِبادِكَ الصّالِحِينَ﴾ [النمل: ١٩] ﴿وتَفَقَّدَ الطَّيْرَ فَقالَ ما لِيَ لا أرى الهُدْهُدَ أمْ كانَ مِنَ الغائِبِينَ﴾ [النمل: ٢٠] ﴿لَأُعَذِّبَنَّهُ عَذابًا شَدِيدًا أوْ لَأذْبَحَنَّهُ أوْ لَيَأْتِيَنِّي بِسُلْطانٍ مُبِينٍ﴾ [النمل: ٢١] ﴿فَمَكَثَ غَيْرَ بَعِيدٍ فَقالَ أحَطتُ بِما لَمْ تُحِطْ بِهِ وجِئْتُكَ مِن سَبَإٍ بِنَبَإٍ يَقِينٍ﴾ [النمل: ٢٢] ﴿إنِّي وجَدْتُ امْرَأةً تَمْلِكُهم وأُوتِيَتْ مِن كُلِّ شَيْءٍ ولَها عَرْشٌ عَظِيمٌ﴾ [النمل: ٢٣] ﴿وجَدْتُها وقَوْمَها يَسْجُدُونَ لِلشَّمْسِ مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ وزَيَّنَ لَهُمُ الشَّيْطانُ أعْمالَهم فَصَدَّهم عَنِ السَّبِيلِ فَهم لا يَهْتَدُونَ﴾ [النمل: ٢٤] ألّا يَسْجُدُوا لِلَّهِ الَّذِي يُخْرِجُ الخَبْءَ في السَّماواتِ والأرْضِ ويَعْلَمُ ما تُخْفُونَ وما تُعْلِنُونَ ﴿اللَّهُ لا إلَهَ إلّا هو رَبُّ العَرْشِ العَظِيمِ﴾ [النمل: ٢٦] ﴿قالَ سَنَنْظُرُ أصَدَقْتَ أمْ كُنْتَ مِنَ الكاذِبِينَ﴾ [النمل: ٢٧] ﴿اذْهَبْ بِكِتابِي هَذا فَألْقِهِ إلَيْهِمْ ثُمَّ تَوَلَّ عَنْهم فانْظُرْ ماذا يَرْجِعُونَ﴾ [النمل: ٢٨] ﴿قالَتْ ياأيُّها المَلَأُ إنِّي أُلْقِيَ إلَيَّ كِتابٌ كَرِيمٌ﴾ [النمل: ٢٩] ﴿إنَّهُ مِن سُلَيْمانَ وإنَّهُ بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمَنِ الرَّحِيمِ﴾ [النمل: ٣٠] ﴿ألّا تَعْلُوا عَلَيَّ وأْتُونِي مُسْلِمِينَ﴾ [النمل: ٣١] ﴿قالَتْ ياأيُّها المَلَأُ أفْتُونِي في أمْرِي ما كُنْتُ قاطِعَةً أمْرًا حَتّى تَشْهَدُونِ﴾ [النمل: ٣٢] ﴿قالُوا نَحْنُ أُولُو قُوَّةٍ وأُولُو بَأْسٍ شَدِيدٍ والأمْرُ إلَيْكِ فانْظُرِي ماذا تَأْمُرِينَ﴾ [النمل: ٣٣] ﴿قالَتْ إنَّ المُلُوكَ إذا دَخَلُوا قَرْيَةً أفْسَدُوها وجَعَلُوا أعِزَّةَ أهْلِها أذِلَّةً وكَذَلِكَ يَفْعَلُونَ﴾ [النمل: ٣٤] ﴿وإنِّي مُرْسِلَةٌ إلَيْهِمْ بِهَدِيَّةٍ فَناظِرَةٌ بِمَ يَرْجِعُ المُرْسَلُونَ﴾ [النمل: ٣٥] ﴿فَلَمّا جاءَ سُلَيْمانَ قالَ أتُمِدُّونَنِ بِمالٍ فَما آتانِيَ اللَّهُ خَيْرٌ مِمّا آتاكم بَلْ أنْتُمْ بِهَدِيَّتِكم تَفْرَحُونَ﴾ [النمل: ٣٦] ﴿ارْجِعْ إلَيْهِمْ فَلَنَأْتِيَنَّهم بِجُنُودٍ لا قِبَلَ لَهم بِها ولَنُخْرِجَنَّهم مِنها أذِلَّةً وهم صاغِرُونَ﴾ [النمل: ٣٧] ﴿قالَ ياأيُّها المَلَأُ أيُّكم يَأْتِينِي بِعَرْشِها قَبْلَ أنْ يَأْتُونِي مُسْلِمِينَ﴾ [النمل: ٣٨] ﴿قالَ عِفْريتٌ مِنَ الجِنِّ أنا آتِيكَ بِهِ قَبْلَ أنْ تَقُومَ مِن مَقامِكَ وإنِّي عَلَيْهِ لَقَوِيٌّ أمِينٌ﴾ [النمل: ٣٩] ﴿قالَ الَّذِي عِنْدَهُ عِلْمٌ مِنَ الكِتابِ أنا آتِيكَ بِهِ قَبْلَ أنْ يَرْتَدَّ إلَيْكَ طَرْفُكَ فَلَمّا رَآهُ مُسْتَقِرًّا عِنْدَهُ قالَ هَذا مِن فَضْلِ رَبِّي لِيَبْلُوَنِي أأشْكُرُ أمْ أكْفُرُ ومَن شَكَرَ فَإنَّما يَشْكُرُ لِنَفْسِهِ ومَن كَفَرَ فَإنَّ رَبِّي غَنِيٌّ كَرِيمٌ﴾ [النمل: ٤٠] ﴿قالَ نَكِّرُوا لَها عَرْشَها نَنْظُرْ أتَهْتَدِي أمْ تَكُونُ مِنَ الَّذِينَ لا يَهْتَدُونَ﴾ [النمل: ٤١] ﴿فَلَمّا جاءَتْ قِيلَ أهَكَذا عَرْشُكِ قالَتْ كَأنَّهُ هو وأُوتِينا العِلْمَ مِن قَبْلِها وكُنّا مُسْلِمِينَ﴾ [النمل: ٤٢] ﴿وصَدَّها ما كانَتْ تَعْبُدُ مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ إنَّها كانَتْ مِن قَوْمٍ كافِرِينَ﴾ [النمل: ٤٣] ﴿قِيلَ لَها ادْخُلِي الصَّرْحَ فَلَمّا رَأتْهُ حَسِبَتْهُ لُجَّةً وكَشَفَتْ عَنْ ساقَيْها قالَ إنَّهُ صَرْحٌ مُمَرَّدٌ مِن قَوارِيرَ﴾ [النمل: ٤٤] ﴿قالَتْ رَبِّ إنِّي ظَلَمْتُ نَفْسِي وأسْلَمْتُ مَعَ سُلَيْمانَ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ العالَمِينَ﴾ [النمل: ٤٤]

(p-٥١)Al-waz‘ (restraint, holding back): its root meaning is restraining and preventing. One says *wazaʿahu yazaʿuhu*. From this is the saying of ʿUthman, may Allah be pleased with him: "The ruler restrains more than the Qur'an restrains." And the saying of al-Hasan: "The judge must have enforcers (wazaʿah)." And the words of the poet:

Whoever is not restrained by his intellect and his modesty,
Then there is no restrainer for him from the whiteness of his temples.

An-naml (ants): a collective noun whose singular is *namlah*. It is also said with a *ḍamma* on the *mīm* in both forms, and with a *ḍamma* on the *nūn* together with a *ḍamma* on the *mīm*. It was named so because of its frequent movement (*tanammul*), which is its motion. Al-ḥaṭm: breaking, as stated by al-Naḥḥas. At-tabassum: the beginning of laughter; the form *tafaʿʿala* here carries the meaning of the bare form, which is *basama*. The poet said:

And she smiles, showing teeth like a bright flower, 
Set among the fine sand, a mound with dew upon it.

Another said:

He bared his molars, not in a smile.

At-tafaqqud: seeking what you have lost and what has become absent from you. Al-hudhud: a well-known bird; its diminutive by analogy is *hudayhid*, though some claim its *yāʾ* was changed to an *alif* in the diminutive, so it is said *hudāhid*. The poet said:

Like a hoopoe whose wing the archers have broken,

just as they said *dūbbah* and *shūbbah*, meaning *duwaybbah* and *shuwaybbah*. Saba': he is Saba' ibn Yashjub ibn Yaʿrub ibn Qahtan. It is declined and not declined when it becomes the name of a people or tribe, or of the region called Maʾrib, named after the man. Al-khabʾ: the hidden thing, from *khabaʾtu al-shayʾ khabʾan*, meaning I concealed the thing; the passive object is named by the verbal noun. Al-hadiyyah (gift): what is brought to a person of what is presented as an honour. Al-ʿifrit, al-ʿifr, al-ʿifriyyah, and al-ʿufariyyah: among men, the wicked and reprehensible one who throws down his peers; among devils, the wicked rebellious one. The poet said:

As if it were a star following a demon,
Shot down in the darkness of the night, sent flying.

Aṣ-ṣarḥ: a palace, or the courtyard of a house, or its open space, or a pool, or a pavement made of glass; these opinions will come in the commentary. As-sāq (shin/leg): well known; its plural in the paucal is *aswuq*, and in the plural of abundance *suwwuq* and *suwq*; its hamza is a dialect form. Al-mumarrad: smooth, polished, and from it comes *al-amrad* (the beardless), and a *shajarah marda'* is a tree with no leaves on it. Al-qawarir: the plural of *qarurah* (glass bottle/flask).

* *

(p-٥٢)﴿طس تِلْكَ آياتُ القُرْآنِ وكِتابٍ مُبِينٍ﴾ ﴿هُدًى وبُشْرى لِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ ﴿الَّذِينَ يُقِيمُونَ الصَّلاةَ ويُؤْتُونَ الزَّكاةَ وهم بِالآخِرَةِ هم يُوقِنُونَ﴾ ﴿إنَّ الَّذِينَ لا يُؤْمِنُونَ بِالآخِرَةِ زَيَّنّا لَهم أعْمالَهم فَهم يَعْمَهُونَ﴾ ﴿أُولَئِكَ الَّذِينَ لَهم سُوءُ العَذابِ وهم في الآخِرَةِ هُمُ الأخْسَرُونَ﴾ ﴿وإنَّكَ لَتُلَقّى القُرْآنَ مِن لَدُنْ حَكِيمٍ عَلِيمٍ﴾ ﴿إذْ قالَ مُوسى لِأهْلِهِ إنِّي آنَسْتُ نارًا سَآتِيكم مِنها بِخَبَرٍ أوْ آتِيكم بِشِهابٍ قَبَسٍ لَعَلَّكم تَصْطَلُونَ﴾ ﴿فَلَمّا جاءَها نُودِيَ أنْ بُورِكَ مَن في النّارِ ومَن حَوْلَها وسُبْحانَ اللَّهِ رَبِّ العالَمِينَ﴾ ﴿يامُوسى إنَّهُ أنا اللَّهُ العَزِيزُ الحَكِيمُ﴾ ﴿وألْقِ عَصاكَ فَلَمّا رَآها تَهْتَزُّ كَأنَّها جانٌّ ولّى مُدْبِرًا ولَمْ يُعَقِّبْ يامُوسى لا تَخَفْ إنِّي لا يَخافُ لَدَيَّ المُرْسَلُونَ﴾ ﴿إلّا مَن ظَلَمَ ثُمَّ بَدَّلَ حُسْنًا بَعْدَ سُوءٍ فَإنِّي غَفُورٌ رَحِيمٌ﴾ ﴿وأدْخِلْ يَدَكَ في جَيْبِكَ تَخْرُجْ بَيْضاءَ مِن غَيْرِ سُوءٍ في تِسْعِ آياتٍ إلى فِرْعَوْنَ وقَوْمِهِ إنَّهم كانُوا قَوْمًا فاسِقِينَ﴾ ﴿فَلَمّا جاءَتْهم آياتُنا مُبْصِرَةً قالُوا هَذا سِحْرٌ مُبِينٌ﴾ ﴿وجَحَدُوا بِها واسْتَيْقَنَتْها أنْفُسُهم ظُلْمًا وعُلُوًّا فانْظُرْ كَيْفَ كانَ عاقِبَةُ المُفْسِدِينَ﴾ .
This surah is Meccan without disagreement. The connection of the beginning of the surah with what precedes it is clear, for He said: ﴿And the devils did not bring it down﴾ [al-Shuʿara': 210], and before it: ﴿And indeed it is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shuʿara': 192], and here He says: ﴿Ta-Sin. These are the verses of the Qur'an﴾, meaning the one which is the revelation of the Lord of the worlds. He attributed the verses to the Qur'an and to the Clear Book in a manner of magnifying and glorifying them, because what is attributed to the Great is great. As for "the Clear Book", it may be the Preserved Tablet, and its clarity is that everything that will exist has been inscribed in it, so it makes it clear to observers; or it may be the surah; or it may be the Qur'an, and the clarity of both is that they make clear the knowledge, wisdom and laws deposited in them; and their miraculous nature is apparent and manifest. It was made indefinite.
﴿And a Clear Book﴾: it is indefinite so that it is left unspecified, which makes it more majestic for it, like His saying: ﴿In a seat of truth﴾ [al-Qamar: 55]. If by it the Qur'an is meant, then its conjunction is the conjunction of one of the two attributes to the other, because they differ in what each attribute indicates: the indication of "Qur'an" is gathering (*ijtimaʿ*), and the indication of "Kitab" is writing. It has been said that "al-Qur'an" and "al-Kitab" are two proper names for what was sent down to Muhammad (ﷺ); so wherever it comes with the definite form, it is the proper name, and wherever it comes in the form of an indefinite description, it is the attribute. It has been said that they operate like "al-ʿAbbas" and "ʿAbbas", so it is in both cases a proper noun. End of quote. This is an error, for if its status were that it had been stripped of being a proper noun, it would not be permissible for it to be described by an indefinite. Do you not see His saying: ﴿And a Clear Book﴾ and ﴿and a Clear Qur'an﴾ [al-Hijr: 1]? And you do not say: "I passed by ʿAbbas standing," meaning by it the attribute? Ibn Abi ʿAbla read "wa kitabun mubin" with both nouns in the nominative, the estimate being: "and the verses of a book," so the genitive noun was deleted and the noun in the genitive was put in its place, and it took its case. Here the Qur'an is mentioned before the Book, and in al-Hijr the reverse, and no distinction appears; this is like coordinated nouns in such as: "Zayd and ʿAmr did not come." Sometimes a preference appears, as in His saying: ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no god but Him, and the angels and those of knowledge﴾ [Aal ʿImran: 18], and sometimes it does not appear, as in His saying: ﴿And say, "Hittah," and enter the gate prostrating﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 161].
Yahya ibn Sallam said: "guidance" (*hudan*) to Paradise, and "good tidings" (*bushra*) of reward. Al-Shaʿbi said: guidance from error, and good tidings of Paradise. *Hudan* and *bushra* are in the form of the unextended (*maqsur*); it is possible that both are accusative as circumstantial states, meaning "guiding" and "bringing good tidings." It has been said: the operator of the circumstantial state is the meaning of indication in "those" (*tilka*). It is possible that both are verbal nouns (*masdar*), and both may be nominative by supposing an omitted subject, meaning: "it is guidance and good tidings"; or as an apposition to "verses"; or as a predicate after a predicate, meaning: it has combined being verses, guidance, and good tidings. The meaning of its being guidance for the believers is the increase of their guidance. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿As for those who believed, it has increased them in faith, and they rejoice﴾ [al-Tawbah: 124]. It has been said: it is guidance for all creation, and "guidance" here carries the meaning of indication, direction and clarification, not the meaning of attaining guidance, which is the opposite of error.
﴿And good tidings for the believers﴾ specifically. It has been said: it is guidance for the believers and good tidings for the believers, and He singled them out for mention because they benefit from it.

And they are certain of the Hereafter. This clause may be coordinated with the relative clause (*alladhīna*, "those who"). Since "they establish the prayer and give the zakat" describes something renewed and not continuous through all time, the relative clause was expressed with a verb. Since belief in the Hereafter is, in their view, a settled and enduring matter, the clause was expressed as a nominal sentence, and the subject was emphasized by repeating it, so that it says: ﴿they are certain﴾. The predicate of the subject-predicate sentence is a verb, to indicate permanence. It is also possible that the clause is a new statement (*istinaf*, a resumptive sentence, one that begins a new thought). Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is possible that the relative clause is complete at His saying, 'and they' (*wa-hum*). The clause would then be parenthetical (*i'tirādiyya*), as if it were said: 'And these who believe and do righteous deeds, through establishing the prayer and giving the zakat, are the ones certain of the Hereafter.' This is the preferred view, and it is supported by the fact that he formed an independent nominal clause and repeated in it the subject, which is 'they', until its meaning became: 'None are certain of the Hereafter with true certainty except these who combine faith and righteous action, for the fear of the consequence drives them to bear hardships.'" End of quotation. His saying "the clause would be parenthetical" is not in accordance with the grammarians' usage of the parenthetical clause (*jumla i'tirāḍiyya*), which they define as occurring only between two things that are related to one another, such as its occurrence between a relative clause and its relative pronoun, between the two parts of a predication, between a condition and its response, between an adjective and its noun, or between an oath and what is sworn to. Here it does not occur between any of the things mentioned, and his saying "until its meaning became..." contains a trace of Mu'tazilite (*i'tizāl*, the rationalist school) doctrine. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Zakat here may be understood as not the obligatory zakat, since the surah is an early Meccan surah; it may also be understood as the obligatory zakat without further explanation. It has also been said that zakat here means purity from defects and constant adherence to noble character." End of quotation.

When Allah mentioned the believers who are certain of the resurrection, He mentioned the deniers. The reference is to the Quraysh and those who follow their path in denying the resurrection. The deeds may be either deeds of goodness and monotheism, which it was incumbent upon them to make their deeds, but they were blind to them, hesitated and were bewildered. This view is attributed to al-Hasan al-Basri. Or the deeds may be deeds of disbelief and misguidance, in which case Allah has made these appealing to them and adorned them by creating them within their souls, so that they saw those ugly deeds as good. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If it is asked: how did He attribute the adornment of their deeds to His own Self, while He attributed it to Satan in His saying, ﴿And Satan made their deeds appealing to them﴾ [An-Naml: 24]? I answer: there is a difference between the two attributions. Attributing it to Satan is literal, while attributing it to Allah, exalted is He, (p-54) is figurative (*majāz*). In the science of rhetoric (*'ilm al-bayān*) it has two ways. The first is that it belongs to the figurative speech called metaphor (*isti'āra*). The second is that it belongs to the figurative speech called the figure of attribution (*majāz al-maḥkī*, the figure in which the attribution is to the agent who is the cause of the action).

As for the first way: since He gave them long life and abundant provision, and they took Allah's bounty and beneficence toward them as a means to follow their desires and their insolence, and to prefer ease, and to shun whatever demands difficult obligations and wearying hardships, then it is as if He adorned their deeds for them through this. To this refers the angels' saying: ﴿But You gave them and their fathers enjoyment until they forgot the Reminder﴾ [Al-Furqan: 18].

As for the second way: Allah's granting Satan respite and leaving him free until he makes the deeds appealing is a clear involvement in the adornment, so the attribution was made to Allah because He is the one who chooses, and this is the figure reported through one of its involvements." End of quotation. This is an interpretation along Mu'tazilite lines.

*Ulā'ika* ("those") refers to the deniers of the resurrection. *Sū' al-'adhāb* ("the evil of punishment") is apparently not restricted to this world; rather they have it both in this world and in the Hereafter. It has been said that the meaning is in this world, and it was explained as what befell them on the day of Badr of killing, capture, and plunder. It has also been said that it is what they will encounter at death and after it, including the punishment of the grave. *Sū' al-'adhāb* means its severity and magnitude.

The apparent meaning is that *al-akhsarūn* ("the greatest losers") is the elative form (*af'al al-tafḍīl*, the comparative/superlative), because the disbeliever has lost this world and the Hereafter, as Allah, exalted is He, informed of, and in the Hereafter his loss is greater, since his end is a lasting punishment. As for in this world, when a trial befalls him, it may leave him and be removed. Thus the greater and increased loss is his in the Hereafter. The comparative may also be applied even when the subject is one in relation to time, place, condition, or other things that admit of increase. Al-Kirmani said: "The form *af'al* here is for emphasis, not for sharing (*lil-mubālagha lā lil-shirka*), as if he is saying: the believer has no loss at all, such that the disbeliever would share it with him and exceed him in it. We have explained how the sharing works with respect to this world and the Hereafter." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "*Al-akhsarūn* is the plural of *akhsar*, because *af'al* as an adjective is not pluralized except when it is made genitive (*idāfa*), so its rank in nouns is strengthened. There is room for examination in this." End of quotation. There is no problem with it being pluralized in both the sound plural and the broken plural when it has the definite article *al-*. Rather, in that case, nothing else is permitted, when there precedes it something that agrees with it in plurality, so one says: *al-Zaydūna hum al-afḍalūna* and *al-afāḍil*, and *al-Hindāt hunna al-fuḍliyyāt* and *al-fuḍl*. As for his saying that it is not pluralized except when made genitive, the pluralization is not then necessarily determined. Rather, when it is made genitive to an indefinite noun, its pluralization is not permitted, while if it is made genitive to a definite noun, both pluralization and singularity are permitted, as established in the books of grammar.

When He said earlier: ﴿These are the verses of the Qur'an﴾, He addressed His Prophet with His saying: ﴿And indeed you﴾, meaning: this Qur'an which you received is from Allah, exalted is He, and He is the All-Wise, the All-Knowing, not as the polytheists claimed, that it is a lie, fables, soothsaying, or poetry, and other such fabrications. The verb is in the passive voice and the agent is omitted, and it is Gabriel, upon him be peace, to indicate him in His saying: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara': 193]. *Laqqā* is transitive to one object, and the doubling in it is for making transitive, so it is made transitive to two objects, and it is as if he was absent from it, then met it and received it (*talaqqāhu*). Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Its meaning is 'given,' as He said: ﴿And none receives it except one of great fortune﴾ [Fussilat: 35]." Al-Hasan said: "The meaning is: indeed you are receiving the Qur'an." It has also been said: its meaning is "you are taught it." Wisdom (*ḥikma*) is knowledge of practical matters, and knowledge is more general than it, since it may be practical or theoretical. The perfection of knowledge is its relation to all knowables and its persistence protected from every change, and this is not but for Allah, exalted is He. This verse is a preparation for what he informs of the unseen matters and the explanation of the stories of the earlier nations, which indicates that he received this from Allah, and His informing him of His subtle wisdom and His precise knowledge, exalted is He. It has been said: *idh* ("when") is governed by a suppressed "remember" (*udhkur*), or by *'alīm* ("All-Knowing"). Its being governed by *'alīm* is not clear, since then the description would be restricted by the object.

A portion of the story of Moses, upon him be peace, has already been mentioned, in his journey with his family from Midian, in Surah Ta-Ha. The apparent meaning of "his family" is plural, given His saying: ﴿I will bring you﴾ and ﴿so that you may warm yourselves﴾. It has been narrated that he had with him only his wife. It has also been said that she had given birth to a child for him while he was with Shu'ayb, so the child was with his mother. If this report is sound, then it is from the usage of the plural in address as a form of honor and reverence. The road had become unclear to him, the weather was cold, and the journey was at night, so his soul longed, when he saw the fire, for an end to what had afflicted him from losing the way and the severity of the cold, and he said: ﴿I will bring you from it news﴾, meaning from its fire, news that indicates the way, (p-55) ﴿or I will bring you a burning brand﴾, meaning if there is no one there to give information, then I will bring with me what you may warm yourselves by from it. This alternation with "or" is clear, because his first aim was to find someone at the fire who would tell him the way, since he was a traveler and not a resident. If there was no one, then he was a resident, and they would need to repel the harm of the cold, which means that he would bring them what they could warm themselves by. He was therefore not in need of both things together, but of one of them: news, if he found someone to inform him so that he could continue on, or warmth, if he did not find anyone and stayed. So his aim was either guidance to the road or taking a brand of fire, and this is the meaning of His saying: ﴿Perhaps I will bring you from it a brand, or find at the fire guidance﴾ [Ta-Ha: 10].

Here it says: ﴿I will bring you from it news﴾, and it is news. In Ta-Ha it says: ﴿Perhaps I will bring you from it a brand﴾ [Ta-Ha: 10], and in Al-Qasas it says: ﴿Perhaps I will bring you from it news﴾ [Al-Qasas: 29]. The second is an expression of hope, and the meaning of hope is different from the meaning of news. But when hope is strong, it is permitted for the one hoping to report it, even if disappointment may occur. He used the future particle *sa-* ("I will"), either because the distance was great, or because he may be delayed by what he anticipated might hold him back. A *shihāb* is a flame, and a *qabas* is fire that has been kindled, on the pattern *fa'al* in the sense of *maf'ūl*, and it is a piece of fire on a stick or otherwise, as was mentioned in Ta-Ha. The Kufans read *bi-shihābin* with tanwin, so *qabasin* is either an apposition or an adjective, since it has the meaning of "that which is kindled." The rest of the seven readers read it with the genitive construction (*idāfa*), and this is the reading of al-Hasan. Al-Zamakhshari said: "He made *shihāb* genitive to *qabas* because it may be a kindled fire or other than a kindled fire, and he followed Abu al-Hasan in this." Abu al-Hasan said: "The genitive construction is better and more common in recitation, as you say: *dār ājurr* ("a house of brick") and *siwār dhahab* ("a bracelet of gold")."

The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in *jā'ahā* ("when he came to it") refers to the fire. It was also said it refers to the tree, since he had seen it in a *samur* tree (an acacia). It was also said: a *'alīq* tree, which does not burn it, and whenever he approached it, it moved away. The passive verb *nūdiya* ("he was called") has as its unnamed agent the pronoun referring to Moses, upon him be peace. On this view, *anna* may be explanatory, because the conditions of an explanatory particle are present in it, and it may also be the verbal *anna* (the "that" introducing a clause). As for the binary *anna* which governs the imperfect verb, *būrika* ("blessed") is its complement, and the original is the preposition, meaning "that there is blessing," and *būrika* is the predicate. As for the lightened form of the heavy *anna*, its origin is the preposition. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If it is asked: may the lightened form of the heavy *anna* be used here, with the sense 'that he was blessed,' and the pronoun being the pronoun of the matter and the story? I answer: no, because it requires *qad*. If it is asked: then with it suppressed? I answer: that is not correct, because it is a sign and is not deleted." End of quotation. It is also permitted that it be the lightened form of the heavy *anna*, with *būrika* as a verb of supplication, as one says: *bārak Allāhu fīk* ("may Allah bless you"). When it is a supplication, it is not permitted for *qad* to precede it, so it is like His saying: ﴿And the fifth [that the wrath of Allah be upon her]﴾ [An-Nur: 9], in the reading of the one who made it a past verb, and like the Arabs' saying: *immā an jazāka Allāhu khayran, wa-immā an yaghfira Allāhu lak* ("either may Allah reward you with good, or may Allah forgive you"). Al-Zamakhshari had based this on the view that *būrika* is a statement and not a supplication, which is why he did not permit it to be the lightened form of the heavy *anna*. Al-Zajjaj permitted that *anna būrika* be in the position of the unnamed object, and it is by dropping the preposition, meaning: he was called with *anna būrika*, just as one says: *nūdiya bi-l-rukhas* ("he was called with cheapness"). It is also permitted that *anna* be the binary or the lightened form of the heavy, and then *būrika* is a supplication. It has been said that the unnamed object is the pronoun of the call, meaning: he was called it, that is the calling, and then it was explained by what follows it. The meaning of *būrika* is: it was sanctified, purified, and its good increased. One says: *bārakaka Allāh*, *bārak fīk*, *bārak 'alayk*, and *bārak lak*. The poet said:

*fa-būrikta mawlūdan wa-būrikta nāshi'an*
*wa-būrikta 'inda al-shaybi idh anta ashyabu*

And another said:

*būrika al-mayyitu al-gharību kamā*
*būrika nab'u al-rummāni wa-al-zaytūni*

And 'Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr said:

*fa-būrika fī banīka wa-fī banīhim*
*idhā dhukirū wa-naḥnu laka al-fidā'*

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 27, verses 1–14 (part 3 of 4):

"Man" (مَن): The well-known view is that it refers to one who has knowledge. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan and others said: God, exalted is He, meant by "whoever is in the fire" His Own Essence. Some of them expressed this in offensive terms that are rejected as applied to God, exalted is He. If this is established from Ibn 'Abbas and those he mentioned, then the first reading involves an ellipsis, meaning: Blessed is the One whose power and authority are in the fire. It was also said that it was said to Moses, peace be upon him: Blessed is whoever is in the place or the direction in which the fire appeared to him. Al-Suddi said: "man" refers to the angels appointed over it. It was also said: "man" may refer to what does not have intellect. Ibn 'Abbas said: it means the light. It was said: it means the tree in which the fire blazes.

It was said: the apparent meaning of "and those around it" (﴿ومَن حَوْلَها﴾) is that it refers to those who have knowledge, and its explanation is "O Moses," and it was explained as referring to the angels. This is supported by the reading of Ubayy, as transmitted by Abu 'Amr al-Dani, and Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and 'Ikrima: "and those around it of the angels." This reading is to be taken as an explanation, because it contradicts the consonantal text of the Mushaf (sawad al-mushaf), on which there is consensus. It was also explained as referring to Moses and the angels together, peace be upon them. It was said: it may refer to what does not have intellect, and it was explained as referring to the places around the fire. It is fitting that the one within it and those around it be blessed, since a great matter occurred, namely God's speaking to Moses, peace be upon him. His being informed and opened with the call of blessing is glad tidings to Moses, a comfort to him, and an introduction to his intimate conversation with God.

The apparent view is that His saying "And glory be to God, Lord of the worlds" (﴿وسُبْحانَ اللَّهِ رَبِّ العالَمِينَ﴾) falls under His saying "was called" (﴿نُودِيَ﴾). When he was called with the blessing of the one mentioned, he was also called with something that indicates transcendence and freedom from the attributes of created things, from whatever might occur to the mind. This is especially so if "whoever is in the fire" is understood according to Ibn 'Abbas's interpretation that "whoever" refers to God, exalted is He, for that implies a location, so the verse brings what necessitates transcendence (tanzih). Al-Suddi said: it is from the speech of Moses. When he heard the call, he said: "And glory be to God, Lord of the worlds," declaring God, exalted is He, free from the marks of created things. Ibn Shajara said: it is from the speech of God, and its meaning is: "Blessed is whoever glorifies God." This is far from the indication of the wording. It was said: "And glory be to God, Lord of the worlds" is an address to Muhammad, peace be upon him, and it is a parenthetical statement between the two speeches, its purpose being transcendence.

When God, exalted is He, comforted him, He called him and turned toward him, saying: "O Moses, indeed it is I, God, the Mighty, the Wise" (﴿يامُوسى إنَّهُ أنا اللَّهُ العَزِيزُ الحَكِيمُ﴾). The apparent view is that the pronoun in "innahu" is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n), "I am God" is a clause in the position of the predicate, and "the Mighty, the Wise" are two attributes. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that the pronoun in "innahu" refers back to what is indicated by what precedes it, meaning: "Indeed the one speaking to you is I, and God is an explanation of 'I,' and 'the Mighty, the Wise' are two attributes of the explanation." End of quotation. When the agent is omitted and the verb is put in the passive form, the pronoun cannot refer back to that omitted agent, since the verb has been changed from being built for it and it has been resolved that it is not what is spoken of. Referring the pronoun back to it contradicts that, for it would become the intended and emphasized subject. This call, this turning toward him, and this address are a preparation for what God, exalted is He, wished to manifest through his hand of miracles (al-mu'jiz, the miracle that proves prophethood), meaning: I am the Strong, the Capable of what is far-fetched in the imagination, the One who does what I do with wisdom.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: upon what does His saying 'And throw down your staff' (﴿وألْقِ عَصاكَ﴾) depend grammatically? I answer: upon 'blessed,' because the meaning is: 'He was called that whoever is in the fire is blessed,' and it was said to him: 'Throw down your staff.' The evidence for this is His saying: 'And that throw down your staff' (﴿وأنْ ألْقِ عَصاكَ﴾) [al-Qasas: 31] after His saying: 'That O Moses, indeed I am God' (﴿أنْ يا مُوسى إنِّي أنا اللَّهُ﴾) [al-Qasas: 30], with the repetition of the explanatory particle, just as you say: 'I wrote to him that perform hajj and 'umra,' and if you wish: 'that perform hajj and that perform 'umra.'" End of quotation. His saying "innahu" (إنَّهُ) coordinated with "blessed" contradicts its being a predicate. It was said that "throw down" is coordinated with "blessed," but this is not a clause whose part is what it is. It was said: it is coordinated with "blessed," and a supposition was needed. It was said: "throw down your staff" so that the clause would be informative and suit the informative clause it is coordinated with, as if he saw in coordination the agreement of the two coordinated elements. The correct view is that this is not required. Rather, His saying "And throw down your staff" is coordinated with His saying "Indeed it is I, God, the Mighty, the Wise," coordinating an imperative clause with an informative clause. Sibawayh permitted: "Zayd came and 'Amr was with him" (jā'a Zaydun wa-man 'Amrun).

"So when he saw it moving" (﴿فَلَمّا رَآها تَهْتَزُّ﴾): there is an omitted element here, its supposition being: "so he threw it from his hand." Al-Hasan, al-Zuhri and 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd read "ja'n" (جَأْنٌ) with a hamza in place of the alif, as if he fled from the meeting of two unvocalized letters. The discussion of such things has already preceded in His saying "wa-lā al-ḍāl'īn" with the hamza in the reading of 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd. And it came: "then behold, it was a snake" (﴿فَإذا هي حَيَّةٌ﴾) [Ta-Ha: 20], "then behold, it was a manifest serpent" (﴿فَإذا هي ثُعْبانٌ مُبِينٌ﴾) [al-A'raf: 107]. This is God's report of its transformation and the change of its attributes and accidents, not the annihilation of its essence and its creation as a snake or serpent. Rather, that is a change of attributes, not a change of essence. Here He likened it, in the state of its movement, to the jann, and it was said: they are the small snakes, He likening it to them in the speed of its agitation and movement, together with the greatness of its bulk.

When Moses saw this terrible matter, "he turned back fleeing and did not return" (﴿ولّى مُدْبِرًا ولَمْ يُعَقِّبْ﴾). Mujahid said: he did not return. Al-Suddi said: he did not linger. Qatada said: he did not look back. It is said: "'aqqaba al-rajul" means he turned toward something he had turned away from, as if he turned back on his heels. From this is "'aqqaba al-muqatil," when a fighter charges again after fleeing. The poet said:

They turned back when it was said: "Is there any who will return?" and they did not stop at the place of dread.

What befalls human nature befell him, when a person sees a thing extremely terrifying, namely seeing the staff transform into a snake running swiftly, and no reassurance had preceded it at the sight of it. Al-Zamakhshari said: he was averse only because he assumed that this was for a matter intended for him, and this is shown by: "Indeed the messengers do not fear in My presence" (﴿إنِّي لا يَخافُ لَدَيَّ المُرْسَلُونَ﴾). End of quotation. Ibn 'Atiyya said: God, exalted is He, called him, comforting him and strengthening him for the matter: "O Moses, do not fear" (﴿يا مُوسى لا تَخَفْ﴾), for My messengers whom I have chosen for prophethood fear none but Me. Moses, peace be upon him, then took the snake, and it returned to being a staff, and then it became his habit. End of quotation. It was said: the meaning is that the messengers do not fear in the place where revelation is sent to them, though they are the most fearful of people toward God. It was said: when I command them to display a miracle, they should not fear in what relates to displaying it, for the messenger certainly fears God. End of quotation.

The more evident view is that His saying "except one who has done wrong" (﴿إلّا مَن ظَلَمَ﴾) is a disjunctive exception (istithnā' munqaṭi'), and the meaning is: "but rather, whoever among others has done wrong." This was stated by al-Farra' and a group, since prophets are protected from committing the wrong that others commit. From al-Farra': it is a connected exception (istithnā' muttaṣil) from omitted clauses, and the supposition is: "Rather, others fear, except one who has done wrong." Al-Nahhas rejected this and said: an exception from an omitted element is impossible. If this were permitted, it would be permitted to say: "I do not strike the people except Zayd," meaning: "Rather, I strike others except Zayd." This is the opposite of clarity and of bringing something whose meaning is not known. End of quotation. A group said: "illā" here has the meaning of "wa" (and), the supposition being: "nor one who has done wrong." This is worthless, because the meaning of "illā" is greatly distinct from the meaning of "wa," since "wa" is for inclusion and "illā" is for exclusion, so it is not possible for one to take the place of the other. It was narrated from al-Hasan, Muqatil, Ibn Jurayj and al-Dahhak what indicates that it is a connected exception.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: The scholars have agreed that prophets, peace be upon them, are protected from the major sins and from those minor sins that are base vices, and it has been disputed concerning what lies beyond that. Perhaps al-Hasan and Ibn Jurayj were pointing to what is beyond that. End of quotation. Al-Zamakhshari said: "illā" here has the meaning of "but rather," because when he absolutely negated fear from the messenger, that would be a cause for harm and suspicion, so it was corrected. The meaning is: "But rather, whoever among them has done wrong," that is, a minor lapse occurred from them of what is not permitted for prophets, like what occurred from Adam, Jonah, David, Solomon, the brothers of Joseph, and from Moses in striking the Copt. It is likely that this allusion is aimed at what came from Moses, and it is among the allusions whose meaning is subtle. He called it wrongdoing, as Moses said: "My Lord, indeed I have wronged myself, so forgive me" (﴿رَبِّ إنِّي ظَلَمْتُ نَفْسِي فاغْفِرْ لِي﴾) [al-Qasas: 16]. End of quotation.

Abu Ja'far and Zayd ibn Aslam read "alā man ẓalama" (ألا مَن ظَلَمَ), with a fatha on the hamza and the lam lightened, as the interrogative particle of opening (ḥarf istiftāḥ). "Man" is conditional. "Al-husn" is the goodness of repentance, and "al-sū'" is the wrong that he committed. The majority read "ḥusnan" with a ḍamma on the ḥā' and a sukūn on the sīn, with tanwīn. Muhammad ibn 'Isa al-Isbahani read "kadhalika" but without tanwīn, making it fu'lā, so it is not declined. Ibn Miqsam read it with a ḍamma on the ḥā' and the sīn, with tanwīn. Mujahid, Abu Hayawa, Ibn Abi Layla, al-A'mash, Abu 'Amr in the transmission of al-Ju'fi, Abu Zayd, 'Isma, 'Abd al-Warith, Harun and 'Ayyash read it with fatha on both, with tanwīn.

"And insert" (﴿وأدْخِلْ﴾) is a command with what follows from it, namely the appearance of the great miracle. When He showed him a miracle in something other than himself, which is the staff, He showed him a miracle in himself, which is the brilliance of his hand as if it were a piece of light, when he did what he was commanded. The apparent answer to the command is "it will come out" (تَخْرُجْ), because its coming out follows from its insertion. It was said: there is an omitted element in the speech, its supposition being: "Insert your hand into your pocket and it will enter, and bring it out and it will come out," so the first omitted what its counterpart is stated in the second, and the second omitted what its counterpart is stated in the first. Qatada said: "in your pocket" (﴿فِي جَيْبِكَ﴾) means your shirt. He had a woolen tunic without sleeves. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: its sleeve reached part of his hand. Al-Suddi said: "in your pocket" means under your armpit.

The apparent view is that His saying "among nine signs to Pharaoh" (﴿فِي تِسْعِ آياتٍ إلى فِرْعَوْنَ﴾) is connected to an omitted element, its supposition being: "Go with these two signs among nine signs to Pharaoh." This is shown by His saying afterward: "But when Our signs came to them, visible" (﴿فَلَمّا جاءَتْهم آياتُنا مُبْصِرَةً﴾). This omission is like the poet's words:

They came to my fire, and I said: "Are you humans?" They said: "Jinn." I said: "Stay, be dark!"

And I said: "To the food," and from them one group envies the humans the food.

The estimate: "Come to the food." Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also possible that the meaning is: "Cast your staff and put your hand [into your garment], among nine signs", i.e., among the total of nine signs. One may object: the signs were eleven, two of which are the hand and the staff, and the nine are: the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, the obliteration, the drought in their desert regions, and the shortfall in their crops. End of quotation. According to the first view, the staff and the hand are included among the nine. According to the second, the preposition *fi* (in) carries the meaning of *ma'a* (with), i.e., "with nine signs." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "*Among nine signs*" is connected to his words "cast" and "put in," and there is an abbreviation and an omission in it. Its estimate is: "That is made smooth and made easy for you within the total of nine signs," which are: the staff, the hand, the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, the obliteration, and the stone. There is disagreement about the last two, and the meaning is: he brings them to Pharaoh and his people. Al-Zajjaj said: "*Among nine signs*" means "from nine signs," just as you say: "Take for me ten camels, among which are two stallions," i.e., from them, to Pharaoh, i.e., sent to Pharaoh. End of quotation.

*Mubsiran* (clear, visible) is in the accusative as a *hal* (circumstantial clause), meaning: clear and evident. The seeing is attributed to them metaphorically (*majaz*): since it is by them that one sees, they are described as "seeing"; or because seeing and clarity accompany them. It was said: it is because they make people into seers, from your saying "abṣartuhu," the transitive form made with the hamza of transference from *baṣara*. It was also said: it is an active participle with the meaning of a passive, as in *ma' dafiq* (gushing water). Qatada and 'Ali ibn al-Husayn read *mabṣarah*, with a fatha on the *mim* and the *ṣad*, which is a verbal noun (*masdar*), as you say: "The child is a source of cowardice" (*majbanah*). It is used in place of the noun, and it is also in the accusative as a *hal*. This pattern is frequent in descriptions of places, as in: "a land abounding in lions" (*arḍun masba'ah*) and "a place abounding in marshes" (*makānun maḍabbah*). Al-Zamakhshari said: i.e., a place where much seeing occurs. End of quotation.

The most eloquent reading of ﴿واسْتَيْقَنَتْها﴾ ("though their souls were certain of them") is that the *waw* is the *waw* of the *hal* clause, meaning: they denied them and rejected them outwardly, while inwardly their souls were certain that they were signs from God, but they were obstinate and called them magic. God the Exalted said, relating about Moses in his dialogue with Pharaoh: ﴿He said: "You certainly know that none sent these down but the Lord of the heavens and the earth, as clear proofs."﴾ [al-Isra: 102].

*Zulman* (in wrongdoing) means exceeding the limit, and *'uluwwan* (in arrogance) means haughtiness and pride, rising above faith. Both are in the accusative as verbal nouns in the position of a *hal*, meaning: wronging and exalting themselves. Or they are objects of purpose (*maf'ulan min ajlihima*), meaning: because of their wrongdoing and their arrogance, i.e., what drove them to denial and rejection, while being certain that these were signs from God, was wrongdoing and arrogance. The form *istaf'ala* here carries the meaning of *tafa''ala*, as *istakbara* means *takabbara* (to be arrogant).

'Abdullah, Ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, Talhah, and Aban ibn Taghlib, and "Iliyyan" read it with the *waw* changed to *ya'*, with a kasra on the *'ayn* and the *lam*. Its original form is *fu'ul*, but they made the *'ayn* a kasra for harmonization (*ittiba'*). It is also narrated that its *ḍamma* (vowel) was read by Ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, and Talhah. The disagreement has already been mentioned concerning obstinate disbelief (*kufr al-'inad*): is it possible for it to occur or not?

The "consequence" (*'aqibah*) is what the people of Pharaoh came to, of evil outcome, and what is prepared for them in the Hereafter is worse. In this there is an example for the disbelievers of Quraysh, since they were corrupters and haughty, and a warning to them that there may befall them the like of what befell those who were before them.

(p. 59) ﴿And We had certainly given David and Solomon knowledge, and they said: "Praise be to God, who has favoured us over many of His believing servants."﴾ ﴿And Solomon inherited from David, and he said: "O people, we have been taught the speech of the birds, and we have been given of everything. Indeed, this is surely the manifest bounty."﴾ ﴿And for Solomon were gathered his armies of the jinn and the humans and the birds, and they were marshalled.﴾ ﴿Until, when they came upon the valley of the ants, an ant said: "O ants, enter your dwellings, lest Solomon and his armies crush you while they do not perceive."﴾ ﴿So he smiled, laughing at her words, and said: "My Lord, inspire me to be grateful for Your blessing with which You have blessed me and my parents, and to do righteous deeds that You are pleased with, and admit me by Your mercy among Your righteous servants."﴾

This is the beginning of narratives and reports about unseen matters, lessons, and admonitions. [The word] "knowledge" (ʿilman) is indefinite because it is a portion of knowledge. Qatada said: "ʿilman" means understanding. Muqatil said: knowledge of judgement. Ibn ʿAtaʾ said: knowledge of God, exalted is He. Al-Zamakhshari said: or a lofty, mighty knowledge.

"And they said" (waqalā). He said: "If you say: Is this not a place for the particle fa' (then) rather than waw (and), as in your saying: 'I gave him and he thanked, and I withheld from him and he was patient'?" I say: Yes, but coordinating it with waw indicates that what they both said is part of what was produced in them: the giving of knowledge and something of its obligations. So it is implied, and then praise is coordinated with it, as if he said: "And We had certainly given them both knowledge, so they acted upon it and taught it, and they recognised the right of the blessing in it and its excellence, and they said: 'Praise be to God.'" The "many" who are preferred over (them) are those who have not been given knowledge, or who have not been given the like of their knowledge. In the verse there is evidence for the nobility of knowledge. End.
