*Alla ya islami ya dara Mayya ʿala al-bili* (Ah, O you, be safe, O abode of Mayya, against decay)

He said:

*Alla ya isqiyani qabla habli Abi Bakr* (Ah, O you two, give me drink before the rope of Abu Bakr)

*Fa-qalat alla ya isma' aʿizuka bi-khutbatin* ... *Fa-qultu sami'na fa-ntiqi wa-asībī* (She said: "Ah, O you, listen, I will admonish you with a sermon," and I said: "We have listened, so speak and be correct.")

He said:

*Alla ya islami ya Hind Hind Bani Badr* ... *wa-in kana jabanan ʿada akhira al-dahr* (Ah, O you, be safe, O Hind, Hind of the Banu Badr, even if he was a coward, he passed beyond the end of time)

And some Arabs were heard saying:

*Alla ya irhamuna alla tasaddaqu ʿalayna* (Ah, O you, have mercy on us, will you not give alms to us?)

Al-Kisai paused in this reading on "ya", then began with usjudu; this is a pause of choice, not of testing. What I hold is that in such a construction reported from the Arabs, "ya" is not a vocative particle, and the vocative is not omitted; because in my view the vocative cannot be omitted, since the verb governing the vocative has been omitted and its subject dropped along with it. If we omitted the vocative, that would mean omitting the whole vocative clause and omitting its complement, which is the vocative, and that would be a great defect. When we keep the vocative and do not omit it, that is evidence for the governing element in it, the vocative clause. The particle of calling is not a particle of response, like nam, la, bala, and ajal, after which clauses may be omitted by the indication of the preceding question. So "ya" in those constructions is, in my view, a particle of alerting, emphasized by which the "alla" that is for alerting, and this was permitted because the two particles differ, and for the purpose of intensifying emphasis. Since emphasis has been found in combining two differing particles that govern in the poet's saying:

*Fa-asbahna la yasʾalnani ʿamma bihi* (so they no longer ask me about what is with him)

and the two particles of the same form governing in his saying:

*Wa-la lilama bihim abadan dawaʾ* (and there is no cure for their ailments ever)

and this was permitted, even if they regard it as necessity or rarity, then combining non-governing particles, which differ in form, is permissible; and "ya" in his saying:

*Ya laʿnata Allahi wal-aqwami kullihim* (O curse of Allah and of all the peoples)

...ليس مِمّا حُذِفَ مِنهُ المُنادى لِما ذَكَرْناهُ. (Hmm, the passage continues:)

The particle is not a vocative particle (harf nida') in my view. Rather, it is a particle of alerting (harf tanbih), after which comes the subject (al-mubtada'), and it is not among those from which the vocative noun has been omitted, for the reason we have mentioned.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask:) Is the prostration of recitation (sujud al-tilawa, the prostration performed upon reciting a verse of prostration) obligatory in both readings together, or in only one of them? (I answer:) It is obligatory in both. One of the two readings is a command to prostrate, and the other is a rebuke of the one who abandons it. As for what al-Zajjaj mentioned, that prostration is obligatory with the lightened reading (al-takhfif) but not with the doubled reading (al-tashdid), it is not a view to be relied upon. End of quote.

Al-Khabʾ is a verbal noun (masdar) used for that which is hidden (al-makhbu'), namely rain, plants, and other things which Allah the Exalted has concealed among His unseen things. Al-Jumhur (the majority of readers) read al-khabʾ with a sukun on the ba' and the hamzah. Ubayy and Isa read it by transferring the vowel of the hamzah to the ba' and dropping the hamzah. Ikrima read it with an alif in place of the hamzah, so the letter before it had to be fathah. This is the reading of Abdullah and Malik ibn Dinar. It can be explained according to the dialect of those who say in pause: hadha al-khabw, marartu bi-l-khabi, ra'aytu al-khaba, and who apply the pronunciation of connection (al-wasl) as the pronunciation of pause. The Kufans permitted saying, of al-mar'ah and al-ka'mah: al-marah and al-kamah, so the hamzah is replaced by an alif and the letter before it is made fathah. According to their view, it is permissible for al-khaba' to derive from this. It has been said: this is a weak dialect, and applying the pronunciation of connection as that of pause is also rare and few. So the two explanations are balanced.

The transfer of the vowel to the ba' and the dropping of the hamzah were reported by Sibawayh from a people of Banu Tamim and Banu Asad. As for the reading al-khaba' with the alif, Abu Hatim criticised it and said: "It is not permissible in Arabic. For if he drops the hamzah he places its vowel on the ba' and says al-khab; and if he transfers it, he says al-khabyi, with a sukun on the ba' and a ya' after it." Al-Mubarrad said: Abu Hatim was below his companions in grammar and did not reach their level, but whenever he left his town, no one more learned than him was found.

The apparent meaning is that "fi al-samawat" (in the heavens) is connected to al-khabʾ, i.e. the thing hidden in the heavens. Al-Farra' said, concerning (the two words) yata'aqabani (succeed one another) in the saying of the Arabs: "La-astakhrijanna al-'ilma fikum" (I will surely extract the knowledge from among you), meaning "minkum" (from you). End of quote. According to this, it is connected to yukhriju, i.e. "min fi al-samawat" (out from the heavens).

(When the hoopoe had been given knowledge of water beneath the earth that no one else had been given, and Allah the Exalted inspired him with this, his description of his Lord the Exalted with this attribute, which is His saying: ﴿Who brings forth what is hidden﴾, was appropriate, since each one is distinguished by an attribute of knowledge or craft, and the signs of that attribute appear upon him in his bearing, his speech and his character. For this reason it has been transmitted: "No servant does a deed except that Allah casts over him the cloak of his deed.")

Al-Haramayn (the two sanctuaries, i.e. the readers of Makkah and Madinah) and the majority read ﴿ma yukhfuna wa ma (p-70) yu'linun﴾ (what they conceal and what they proclaim) with the third-person ya' (yaʾ al-ghaybah), the pronoun referring to the woman and her people. Al-Kisa'i and Hafs read it with the second-person ta' (ta' al-khitab). It is possible that this is an address to Sulayman, peace be upon him, and those present with him, since it is unlikely that the hoopoe's conversation was with Sulayman while no one else was with them. Just as it was permissible for him to address him with his saying ﴿I have encompassed what you have not encompassed﴾, it is permissible for him to address him and those present with him with his saying ﴿what you conceal and what you proclaim﴾. Indeed, his address with this does not reveal the same ardour as that other address.

The apparent meaning is that His saying ﴿that they do not prostrate ... the Mighty﴾ is part of the words of the hoopoe. It has been said that it is part of the words of Allah the Exalted addressed to the community of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Ibn 'Atiyya said: The reading with the ya' of absence indicates that the verse is part of the hoopoe's speech, while the reading with the ta' of address indicates that it is from the address of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, to the community of Muhammad (ﷺ).

The author of al-Ghunyan said: When the hoopoe mentioned the throne of Bilqis and described it as great, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, responded to him and made clear that His own throne is the one truly described with this attribute, since no throne apart from Him deserves to be described with greatness. It has been said that this is part of the hoopoe's speech, as if he corrected himself and returned the greatness from the throne of Bilqis to the Throne of Allah.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask:) How did the hoopoe make the throne of Bilqis equal to the Throne of Allah in describing it as great? (I answer:) There is a difference between the two descriptions, for describing her throne as great is an exaltation of it in relation to the thrones of the kings of her kind, while describing the Throne of Allah as great is an exaltation of it in relation to all that He has created of the heavens and the earth. End of quote.

Ibn Muhaysin and a group read al-'Azim (the Mighty) in the nominative (bi-l-raf'). It is possible that it is an adjective of al-'arsh (the throne), and it is a separate (qat') nominative by implied "huwa" (he is) for the purpose of praise; then its reading and the reading of the majority are the same in meaning. It is also possible that it is an adjective of the Lord, and the throne was singled out for mention because it is the greatest of created things, and all else is included within it.

When the hoopoe finished his speech, and presented his excuse for his absence, Sulayman postponed his command until it became clear to him whether his report was true or false. So he said: ﴿We shall see whether you have told the truth or were of the liars.﴾ Here "al-nazar" (looking) means reflection and examination. "Asadaqta" (have you told the truth) is a clause suspended from "sanazhur" (we shall see); it is in the position of an accusative, by dropping the preposition, because nazar in the sense of reflection and consideration only takes its object with the preposition "fi". He balanced the two clauses with "am" (or), and the composition was not "am kadhabta" (or did you lie), because his saying ﴿or were you of the liars﴾ is more emphatic in attributing lying to him; for his being "of the liars" indicates that he is known for lying, and this description preceded him before the report he gave. When the description of lying had already attached to him, he became suspect in what he reported, unlike one whose lying is only presumed initially regarding what he reports.

In the speech there is an ellipsis, whose estimate is: So he commanded that a letter be written to them, and that the hoopoe go as a messenger to them with the letter. Then he said: ﴿Go with this letter of mine﴾, i.e. the present one, now written.

﴿Then throw it to them, then turn away from them﴾, i.e. withdraw from them to a nearby place, such that you hear what comes from them and what some of them say to others.

In His saying ﴿Go with this letter of mine, then throw it to them﴾ there is evidence for the imam (leader) sending letters to polytheists, conveying the call to them and inviting them to Islam. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wrote to Khosrow, Caesar and others, the kings of the Arabs. Wahb said: His command to turn away is good manners, that he withdraw in the manner in which kings conduct themselves, meaning: and be near enough that you hear their exchanges. Ibn Zayd said: He commanded him to turn away in the sense of returning to him, i.e. throw it and return. He said: His saying ﴿then see what they return﴾ is in the sense of being placed before His saying ﴿then turn away from them﴾. End of quote. Abu 'Ali said this too, but there is no necessity to make a change of order; rather the apparent meaning is that looking follows the turning away from them.

In the Seven (al-Sab'a, the seven canonical readers) it is read ﴿fa-alqihi﴾ with a kasrah on the ha' and a ya' after it, with the kasrah stolen (ikhtilas), and with a sukun on the ha'. Muslim ibn Jundub read it with a dammah on the ha' and a waw after it. In His saying ﴿to them﴾ he used the plural, and the hoopoe said ﴿I found her and her people﴾. In the letter also there is the plural pronoun in His saying ﴿that you not exalt yourselves over me﴾, and the letter contained the call to Islam for Bilqis and her people.

The meaning of ﴿then see what they return﴾ is: reflect and bring it to your mind. It has been said its meaning is: then wait. If the meaning of "fa-anzur" is reflection by thought, then "unzur" is suspended, and "madha" is either an interrogative word in the position of an accusative, or "ma" is an interrogative and "dha" is a relative pronoun meaning "alladhi". On the first, "yarji'una" (they return) is the predicate of "madha"; on the second, "dha" is the predicate and "yarji'una" is the relative clause of "dha". If the meaning of "fa-anzur" is "fa-intazir" (then wait), it is not a verb of the heart so as to be suspended; rather "madha" entirely is a relative pronoun meaning "alladhi", i.e. "wait for what they return", and the meaning is: "look at what they return" until you bring back to me what they return of speech.

[p. 64] Apparently he inspected all the birds, which is what the care for the affairs of the kingdom and attention to his subjects would require. It is said that each kind of bird would come to him one at a time, and he did not see the hoopoe. It is also said that the birds would shade him from the sun, and the hoopoe would shield his right side, so the sun struck him, and he looked at the hoopoe's place and did not see it. It is narrated from Abdullah ibn Salam that Sulayman, peace be upon him, camped in a barren desert with no water. The hoopoe could see the surface of the earth and what lay beneath it, and he would inform Sulayman of this. The jinn would extract water for him by stripping the earth in an hour, as a sheep is skinned. So he asked about the hoopoe when they reached that desert, because they needed water. In His words ﴿And he inspected the birds﴾ there is evidence that a leader should inspect the conditions of his subjects and look after them. Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "If a young goat on the bank of the Euphrates were seized by a wolf, Umar would be questioned about it." There is an omission in the speech, meaning: he missed the hoopoe when he inspected the birds.

Ibn Atiyya said: His words ﴿What is wrong with me that I do not see the hoopoe?﴾ aim at the hoopoe. He was absent, but he took the necessary consequence of his absence, which is that he does not see him, and so he asked in the form of a reproach about that consequence. This is a kind of brevity, and the interrogative in His words "what is wrong with me" takes the place of the alif that "am" would normally accompany. End of quotation. The apparent meaning of this speech is that "am" is connected (muttasila, joined to the question), and that the interrogative in "mali" takes the place of the interrogative alif. Its meaning for him is: "Has he now gone out of my sight so that I did not see him during the inspection, or was he among those who were absent before and I did not notice his absence?"

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Am" here is the disconnected one (munqati'a, which introduces a new question). He looked at the hoopoe's place, did not see him, and said: ﴿What is wrong with me that I do not see the hoopoe?﴾ meaning: he does not see him although he is present, either because of a screen that hides him or for some other reason. Then it occurred to him that he was absent, so he turned away from that and began to say: "Is he absent?" As if he were asking whether what had occurred to him was correct. A similar expression is their saying: "Is it camels, or sheep?" End of quotation. The correct view is that "am" here is the disconnected one, because the condition for the connected "am" is that it be preceded by the interrogative hamza. If it is preceded by an interrogative particle other than the hamza, then "am" is disconnected. Here it is preceded by "ma," so the condition for the connected form is not met. It has also been said that it is possible that this is an inversion (maqlub, transposition of words), its intended sense being: "What is the matter with the hoopoe that I do not see him?" But there is no need to claim inversion.

In al-Kashshaf: When Sulayman completed the building of the Temple of Jerusalem, he prepared for the Pilgrimage, arrived at the Sacred Precinct, and stayed there as long as he wished. Then he resolved to set out for Yemen, and he left Mecca in the morning heading for Suhayl (a star), and reached Sanaa at midday. That journey is a month's march. He saw a beautiful land whose greenery pleased him, so he dismounted to eat and pray, but he found no water. The hoopoe used to come to him, and he could see water under the earth. It is mentioned that the jinn would strip the earth until the water appeared.

﴿A severe punishment﴾: He left the severe punishment unspecified. There are conflicting statements about what it was, and the best view is that these are examples. From Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and Ibn Jurayj: he would pluck out his feathers. Ibn Jurayj also said: all of his feathers. Yazid ibn Ruman said: his wing. Ibn Wahb said: he would cut off half and leave half. It was also said: plucking along with leaving him to the sun. It was said: he would be imprisoned in a cage. It was said: he would be smeared with tar and exposed to the sun. It was said: he would be plucked and thrown to the ants. It was said: he would be put together with a different species. It was said: he would be barred from serving Sulayman, peace be upon him. It was said: he would be separated from his mate. It was said: he would be bound to serve his wife. This statement from Sulayman was an expression of anger for the sake of Allah, since the prayer had come and he asked for water for ablution but did not find any. Allah permitted him to do this for the sake of the public good, just as He permitted animals and birds to be eaten, and just as He subjected the birds to him. So he was entitled to discipline the hoopoe if he did not do what he was subjected to do.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿أَوْ لَيَأْتِيَنِّي﴾ (or he will surely bring me) with a doubled nun followed by the first person ya; Ibn Kathir read it with a doubled nun followed by the nun of protection (nun al-wiqaya) after the ya; Isa ibn Umar read it with a doubled, fatha-vowelled nun without ya. ﴿A clear authority﴾ means proof and excuse. There is in this a proof of severity toward the disobedient and of punishing them. He began with the lighter of the two punishments, which is torment, then followed it with the more severe, which is ending life by slaughter. He swore to these two because they were his own actions. He swore to bringing the authority, which was not his own action, but when he arranged the three in the ruling with "or," it was as if he said: one of the three will certainly happen. The meaning is: if he brings the authority, there will be neither torment nor slaughter; otherwise one of them will occur. His oath to bringing him does not imply a claim of knowledge, since it is possible that his oath about the two actions was followed by a revelation from Allah that he would bring him an authority, so that his words ﴿or he will surely bring me a clear authority﴾ would be based on knowledge and certainty.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿فَمَكَثَ﴾ (then he stayed) with a damma on the kaf; Asim, Abu Amr in the narration of al-Ju'fi, Sahl, and Rawh read it with a damma. In the reading of Ubayy: "fa-yamkuth" (then he will stay), and then he said: in the reading of Abdullah: "fa-yamkuth," then he said. Both are in reality an explanation, not a reading, because that contradicts the consonantal text of the codex and what has been transmitted from them by sound transmission. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in "famakatha" refers to the hoopoe, i.e., he stayed for a short time, meaning soon. His staying is described as brief to show his speed, out of fear of Sulayman, and so that it may be known how the birds were subjected to him, and to demonstrate the miracle given to him, which indicates his prophethood and Allah's power. It has also been said: he stopped at a place not far from Sulayman. It is reported that when Sulayman descended, the hoopoe circled and saw another hoopoe, descended upon him, and described to him Sulayman's kingdom and everything subjected to him. His companion told him about the kingdom of Bilqis and exaggerated its greatness, and he went with him to see it, and did not return until after the afternoon. It has also been said that the pronoun in "famakatha" refers to Sulayman. It has also been said that it may refer to both Sulayman and the hoopoe, and there is an omission in the speech. If "not far" refers to time, the implied sense is: then Sulayman came and asked him: "What kept you away?" and he said: "I have encompassed." If it refers to place, the implied sense is: then he came and stood at a place near Sulayman, and Sulayman asked him: "What kept you away?" It was reported that he already knew what Sulayman had sworn about, so he hastened to answer him with something that would calm his anger: that his absence was due to a great matter that had come up for him. So he said: ﴿I have encompassed what you have not encompassed﴾. In this there is the boldness of one who possesses knowledge that no one else has, and his boasting about it, and his leaving it vague until the soul yearns to know what that vague matter is. The meaning of "encompassing" here is that he knew a knowledge that the prophet of Allah, Sulayman, did not have.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Allah inspired the hoopoe, and so he confronted Sulayman with these words, despite the fact that Sulayman had been given the excellence of prophethood, wisdom, numerous sciences, and encompassing of many known things. This was a trial for him regarding his knowledge, and an alert that among the lowest and weakest of His creatures there is one who has encompassed knowledge of what Sulayman did not encompass, so that his own soul would consider itself small and his knowledge would seem minor to him, and so that it would be a kindness to him in avoiding self-admiration (ujb), which is a trial for scholars, and how great a trial it is! The encompassing of a thing by knowledge means that it is known from all its aspects, so that no known thing is hidden from it. They said: In this there is evidence against the claim of the Rafidah (Rafidites) that "the imam has nothing hidden from him, and there is no one in his time more knowledgeable than him." End of quotation.

When he made it vague in His words ﴿what you have not encompassed﴾, he moved to something less vague, which is His words ﴿and I have come to you from Saba with a certain news﴾, for in it there is information about the place from which he came and that he had knowledge of a certain report that was established for him.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿مِن سَبَأٍ﴾ (from Saba) with tanwin (declined); Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr read it with a fatha on the hamza, without tanwin, in both this place and in ﴿Indeed there was for Saba﴾ [Saba 34:15]; Qunbul, through al-Nabbal, read it with a sukun on the hamza in both places. Whoever declined it made it the name of a tribe, a place, or a forefather, as in the hadith of Farwa ibn Musayk and others, from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "He is the name of a man who had ten children; six of them went to the right (tayammana), and four went to the left (tashaama)." The six are: Himyar, Kindah, al-Azd, Ash'ar, Khath'am, and Bajilah. The four are: Lakhm, Judham, Amilah, and Ghassan. Saba was a man from Qahtan whose name was Abd Shams. It has also been said: Amir. He was named Saba because he was the first to take captives (sabaa). Whoever did not decline it made it the name of the tribe or the region. They cited as evidence for declining:
"The ones who came and Tayyim are on the heights of Saba, the buffalo hide has bitten their necks."

As for whoever pronounced the hamza with a sukun, it is due to the succession of vowels in one who does not decline it, and to treat the connection like a pause. Makki said: pronouncing the sukun in connected speech is far-fetched, not preferred, and not strong. End of quotation. Al-A'mash read ﴿مِن سَبَأِ﴾ with a kasra on the hamza and no tanwin; Ibn Khalawayh and Ibn Atiyya related this from him, and its justification is weak. Ibn Kathir in one transmission read ﴿مِن سَبًا﴾ with tanwin on the ba, on the pattern of "raha," treating it as a declined word with a short alif. Abu Mu'adh reported that he read ﴿مِن سَبْأ﴾ with a sukun on the ba and an unvowelled open hamza without tanwin, treating it as the pattern fa'la, so it was not declined because of its obligatory feminine form. Ibn Habib reported from al-Yazidi: ﴿مِن سَبَأْ﴾ with a quiescent alif, like their saying: "They scattered every which way (aydi saba)." A group read ﴿بِنَبَا﴾ with an alif in place of the hamza, and this is probably the reading of whoever read ﴿سَبَا﴾ with alif, so that the two words would balance, just as they balance in the reading of whoever read both with a kasrah on the hamza and tanwin.

In al-Tahrir he said: this type in the science of badi' (rhetoric) is called al-tardid (repetition of an ending), and in the book al-Tafrif fi funun al-badi': tardid means returning the ends of verses to their beginnings, or returning a word from the first half to the second half, and it is also called al-tasdir (beginning with the repeated word). An example of the first is his saying:
"Swift to his paternal cousin, he mends his break,
but he is not swift to the summoner of obscenity."
An example of the second is his saying:
"The nights when you are far away are long,
and the nights when you are near are short."
He mentioned that something like ﴿مِن سَبَإٍ بِنَبَإٍ﴾ is called tajnis al-tasrif (paronomasia of inflection), and he said: it means that each of the two words is distinguished from the other by a single letter. Among examples of it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is because you used to rejoice in the land without right and because you used to exult﴾ [Ghafir 40:75], and what came in the hadith: "Good is bound to the foreheads of horses." The poet said:
"By Allah, what those veils and faces (al-ma'ajir wa-l-mahajir) have done to us!"

Al-Zamakhshari said: His saying ﴿from Saba' with news﴾ is of the kind of speech that the scholars of rhetoric call al-badi' (embellishment), and it is among the fine points of speech that relate to the wording, on condition that it comes naturally, or in a form that is aware of the essence of speech, by which the soundness and rightness of the meaning is preserved. Here it has come beyond mere soundness, so it is excellent and novel in both wording and meaning. Do you not see that if bi-nabaʾin were replaced by bi-khabar, the meaning would still be sound? And yet what came is more sound, because of the added nuance in nabaʾ that the description of the situation corresponds to. End of quotation. The nuance he pointed to is that a nabaʾ is only a report that has significance, whereas the word khabar is general, applying to what has significance and to what does not.

When the hoopoe first left things vague, and then left them vague a second time, short of that vagueness, he made explicit what he had left vague and said: ﴿I found a woman ruling over them﴾. His saying ﴿ruling over them﴾ does not indicate that it is permissible for a woman to be a ruler, because that was the practice of the people of Bilqis, who were unbelievers, so there is no proof in it. In the Sahih of al-Bukhari, from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas, when the Prophet (ﷺ) was informed that the people of Persia had made the daughter of Kisra their ruler, he said: "A people will never prosper who entrust their affairs to a woman." It is related from Muhammad ibn Jarir that it is permissible for a woman to be a judge, but this is not authentically transmitted from him. It is related from Abu Hanifa that she may judge in matters in which she is a witness, not absolutely, nor that a document be written for her stating that so-and-so is appointed over the judgment; rather that is only by way of delegation and deputization in a single case. The meaning of "I found" (wajadtu) here is "I came to know/I reached"; the pronoun in "ruling over them" refers to Saba', if by it is meant the tribe; if by it is meant the place, then there is an ellipsis, i.e. "and I have come to you from the people of Saba'."

The woman is Bilqis daughter of Sharahil. Her father was king of all Yemen, and he had no child other than her, so she gained control of the kingdom; she and her people were Magians who worshipped the sun. Its father's name has been disputed greatly. It is said that her mother was a jinn-woman called Rayhana daughter of al-Sakan, whom her father married, since in his greatness he did not think fit to marry any of the kings of his time; so Bilqis was born to him. They have extended their narratives about her with what is not established in the Qur'an or in sound hadith.

The hoopoe began by informing about her kingdom, that she had been given of everything, and this is by way of hyperbole; the meaning is: of everything she needed, or of everything in her land. Between the hoopoe's saying this and Sulayman's saying ﴿and we have been given of everything﴾ [al-Naml: 16] there is a difference: Sulayman's statement was joined to his saying ﴿we have been taught the speech of the birds﴾ [al-Naml: 16], which is a miracle, so it refers first to what he was given of prophethood, wisdom and the means of religion, and then to kingship and the means of this world; whereas the hoopoe's conjunction was to kingship, so he meant only what she had been given of the worldly means suitable to her condition.

﴿And she has a great throne﴾. Ibn Zayd said: it is her seat of sitting. Sufyan said: it is her chair, which was inlaid with jewels and had seven doors. They mentioned a number of things about the description of her throne; Allah alone knows the reality of that. The hoopoe's magnifying of her throne was either to belittle her situation, that she should have a throne like this, or because Sulayman did not have one like it, although he was great in dominion in every respect, since some regional governors may possess something that the king they serve under does not.

Since Allah had given Sulayman of everything, and he had a great throne, he informed him of this great news, since there was in the world someone who shared with him in things that approach this. Sulayman did not turn his attention to this, since he was turned away from worldly affairs. So the hoopoe moved on to informing about what relates to matters of religion. How excellent is the sequence of these reports after the hoopoe's threat and his knowledge of that: he first reported his having knowledge of what Sulayman had not known, thereby securing himself against punishment, by the adornment of the knowledge he had acquired, so the listener was eager to know that. Then he informed us a second time of the connection of that knowledge, namely that it is from Saba', and that it is a certain matter without doubt, so the listener's eagerness to hear that news increased. Then he informed a third time about the kingdom that a woman had been given; and Sulayman, peace be upon him, had asked Allah to give him a kingdom that would not befit anyone after him. Then he informed a fourth time of what outwardly indicates a shared condition between him and this woman, whom it is not in the nature of her or of women to rule over male men; and this is his saying ﴿and she has been given of everything﴾ and his saying ﴿and she has a great throne﴾. Sulayman had a carpet that had been made for him, and it was great. When Sulayman was not moved by the report of all this, since it is a worldly matter, he informed him fifthly of what would stir him to seek this queen and to call her to faith in Allah and to devoting worship to Him alone, so he said: ﴿I found her and her people prostrating to the sun instead of Allah﴾. It has already been stated that they were Magians who worshipped lights, and this is the saying of al-Hasan. It was also said that they were zindiqs.

These reports from the hoopoe were by way of excusing his absence from Sulayman; and he knew that Sulayman's aim was to call to the oneness of Allah and faith in Him, so this was a clear excuse that removed from him the punishment with which Sulayman had threatened him. This report stood in the place of certainty about the clear authority, since in his absence there was a benefit in informing Sulayman of what had been hidden from him, and its outcome was the faith of the queen and her people. The kingship of this woman and her place were hidden from Sulayman, even though the distance between them was short, just as the kingship of Yusuf was hidden from Yaqub; and that was for a matter which Allah the Exalted intended.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Among the foolish storytellers is one who pauses at His saying ﴿and she has a throne﴾ and then begins ﴿great, I found her﴾, meaning "a great matter, that I found her," fleeing from the hoopoe's magnifying of her throne, and so he fell into a grave error, which is the distortion of the Book of Allah. End of quotation. He also said: (If you say: from where did the hoopoe get the guidance to know Allah and the obligation of prostrating to Him, and the denial of prostrating to the sun, and its attribution to Satan and his adornment? I say: It is not far-fetched that Allah inspired him with that, just as He inspired him and others among the birds and the rest of the animals with subtle knowledge that intelligent people hardly come to know. Whoever wishes to investigate this, let him consult the book on animals, especially in the time of a prophet to whom the birds were subjected and who was taught their speech, and this was made a miracle for him.) End of quotation.

The adornment was attributed to Satan, since he was the one who caused it, by the decree of Allah the Exalted.

﴿So he barred them from the way﴾, i.e. Satan, or his adornment, from the way, which is faith in Allah and devoting worship to Him alone.

﴿So they are not guided﴾, i.e. to the truth. Ibn ʿAbbas, Abu Jaʿfar, al-Zuhri, al-Sulami, al-Hasan, Humayd and al-Kisai read: alla, with the lam of the alif lightened. According to this reading, one may pause at ﴿so they are not guided﴾ and begin at ﴿alla yasjudu﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: If he wishes, he may pause at alla and then begin with usjudu. The rest of the seven read it with the lam doubled, and according to this, His saying ﴿so they are not guided﴾ is connected with His saying ﴿alla yasjudu﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: In the reading of ʿAbd Allah, which is the reading of al-Aʿmash: halla and hala, with the two hamzas changed into a haʾ; and from ʿAbd Allah: hala yasjudun, meaning "why do you not prostrate", in address. In the reading of Ubayy: "Why do you not prostrate to Allah, who brings forth the hidden thing in the heavens and the earth, and knows what you conceal and what you disclose." End of quotation.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: al-Aʿmash read halla yasjudun; in the reading of ʿAbd Allah: alla hal tasjudun, with ta'; in the reading of Ubayy: alla tasjudun, also with ta'. As for the reading of those who keep the nun in yasjudun and read with ta' or ya', its explanation is clear. As for the reading of the rest of the seven, it is explained as follows: His saying ﴿alla yasjudu﴾ is in a position of accusative, as a substitute (badal) for His saying "their deeds" (aʿmalahum), meaning: Satan adorned for them that they should not prostrate. What lies between the substituted and the substitute is a parenthesis; or it is in a position of genitive, as a substitute for "the way", meaning: he barred them from not prostrating. According to this explanation, "la" is extra, meaning: he barred them from prostrating to Allah, and ﴿so they are not guided﴾ is a parenthesis between the substituted and the substitute, and the sense is: lest they prostrate. The lam is either connected to "adorned" or to "their intention", and the lam that enters upon "an" (that) is a lam of purpose; that is, the cause of Satan's adornment for them, or of his barring them from the way, is the absence of their prostrating to Allah, or for fear that they would prostrate to Allah. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible that "la" be extra, and the meaning would be: so they are not guided to prostrating. End of quotation. As for the reading of Ibn ʿAbbas and those who agree with him, it is explained as: "alla" is an interjection of opening, "ya" is a particle of calling, the vocative is omitted, and "usjudu" is an imperative verb; the alif of "ya" which is for calling is dropped, and the alif of connection in "usjudu" too, since the orthography of the Mushaf writes yasjudu without the two alifs; when they drop in pronunciation, they also drop in writing. Such a construction occurs in the speech of the Arabs. The poet said:

*Alla ya islami dhatal-damaliji wal-ʿiqdi* (Ah, O you, greet Dhat al-Damalij and the necklace)

He said:

*Alla ya isqiyani qabla ghaarati Sinjal* (Ah, O you two, give me drink before the raid of Sinjal)

(p-69) He said:

*Alla ya islami ya dara Mayya ʿala al-bili* (Ah, O you, be safe, O abode of Mayya, against decay)

He said:

*Alla ya isqiyani qabla habli Abi Bakr* (Ah, O you two, give me drink before the rope of Abu Bakr)

*Fa-qalat alla ya isma' aʿizuka bi-khutbatin* ... *Fa-qultu sami'na fa-ntiqi wa-asībī* (She said: "Ah, O you, listen, I will admonish you with a sermon," and I said: "We have listened, so speak and be correct.")

He said:

*Alla ya islami ya Hind Hind Bani Badr* ... *wa-in kana jabanan ʿada akhira al-dahr* (Ah, O you, be safe, O Hind, Hind of the Banu Badr, even if he was a coward, he passed beyond the end of time)

And some Arabs were heard saying:

*Alla ya irhamuna alla tasaddaqu ʿalayna* (Ah, O you, have mercy on us, will you not give alms to us?)

Al-Kisai paused in this reading on "ya", then began with usjudu; this is a pause of choice, not of testing. What I hold is that in such a construction reported from the Arabs, "ya" is not a vocative particle, and the vocative is not omitted; because in my view the vocative cannot be omitted, since the verb governing the vocative has been omitted and its subject dropped along with it. If we omitted the vocative, that would mean omitting the whole vocative clause and omitting its complement, which is the vocative, and that would be a great defect. When we keep the vocative and do not omit it, that is evidence for the governing element in it, the vocative clause. The particle of calling is not a particle of response, like nam, la, bala, and ajal, after which clauses may be omitted by the indication of the preceding question. So "ya" in those constructions is, in my view, a particle of alerting, emphasized by which the "alla" that is for alerting, and this was permitted because the two particles differ, and for the purpose of intensifying emphasis. Since emphasis has been found in combining two differing particles that govern in the poet's saying:

*Fa-asbahna la yasʾalnani ʿamma bihi* (so they no longer ask me about what is with him)

and the two particles of the same form governing in his saying:

*Wa-la lilama bihim abadan dawaʾ* (and there is no cure for their ailments ever)

and this was permitted, even if they regard it as necessity or rarity, then combining non-governing particles, which differ in form, is permissible; and "ya" in his saying:

*Ya laʿnata Allahi wal-aqwami kullihim* (O curse of Allah and of all the peoples)

...ليس مِمّا حُذِفَ مِنهُ المُنادى لِما ذَكَرْناهُ. (Hmm, the passage continues:)

The particle is not a vocative particle (harf nida') in my view. Rather, it is a particle of alerting (harf tanbih), after which comes the subject (al-mubtada'), and it is not among those from which the vocative noun has been omitted, for the reason we have mentioned.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask:) Is the prostration of recitation (sujud al-tilawa, the prostration performed upon reciting a verse of prostration) obligatory in both readings together, or in only one of them? (I answer:) It is obligatory in both. One of the two readings is a command to prostrate, and the other is a rebuke of the one who abandons it. As for what al-Zajjaj mentioned, that prostration is obligatory with the lightened reading (al-takhfif) but not with the doubled reading (al-tashdid), it is not a view to be relied upon. End of quote.

Al-Khabʾ is a verbal noun (masdar) used for that which is hidden (al-makhbu'), namely rain, plants, and other things which Allah the Exalted has concealed among His unseen things. Al-Jumhur (the majority of readers) read al-khabʾ with a sukun on the ba' and the hamzah. Ubayy and Isa read it by transferring the vowel of the hamzah to the ba' and dropping the hamzah. Ikrima read it with an alif in place of the hamzah, so the letter before it had to be fathah. This is the reading of Abdullah and Malik ibn Dinar. It can be explained according to the dialect of those who say in pause: hadha al-khabw, marartu bi-l-khabi, ra'aytu al-khaba, and who apply the pronunciation of connection (al-wasl) as the pronunciation of pause. The Kufans permitted saying, of al-mar'ah and al-ka'mah: al-marah and al-kamah, so the hamzah is replaced by an alif and the letter before it is made fathah. According to their view, it is permissible for al-khaba' to derive from this. It has been said: this is a weak dialect, and applying the pronunciation of connection as that of pause is also rare and few. So the two explanations are balanced.

The transfer of the vowel to the ba' and the dropping of the hamzah were reported by Sibawayh from a people of Banu Tamim and Banu Asad. As for the reading al-khaba' with the alif, Abu Hatim criticised it and said: "It is not permissible in Arabic. For if he drops the hamzah he places its vowel on the ba' and says al-khab; and if he transfers it, he says al-khabyi, with a sukun on the ba' and a ya' after it." Al-Mubarrad said: Abu Hatim was below his companions in grammar and did not reach their level, but whenever he left his town, no one more learned than him was found.

The apparent meaning is that "fi al-samawat" (in the heavens) is connected to al-khabʾ, i.e. the thing hidden in the heavens. Al-Farra' said, concerning (the two words) yata'aqabani (succeed one another) in the saying of the Arabs: "La-astakhrijanna al-'ilma fikum" (I will surely extract the knowledge from among you), meaning "minkum" (from you). End of quote. According to this, it is connected to yukhriju, i.e. "min fi al-samawat" (out from the heavens).

(When the hoopoe had been given knowledge of water beneath the earth that no one else had been given, and Allah the Exalted inspired him with this, his description of his Lord the Exalted with this attribute, which is His saying: ﴿Who brings forth what is hidden﴾, was appropriate, since each one is distinguished by an attribute of knowledge or craft, and the signs of that attribute appear upon him in his bearing, his speech and his character. For this reason it has been transmitted: "No servant does a deed except that Allah casts over him the cloak of his deed.")

Al-Haramayn (the two sanctuaries, i.e. the readers of Makkah and Madinah) and the majority read ﴿ma yukhfuna wa ma (p-70) yu'linun﴾ (what they conceal and what they proclaim) with the third-person ya' (yaʾ al-ghaybah), the pronoun referring to the woman and her people. Al-Kisa'i and Hafs read it with the second-person ta' (ta' al-khitab). It is possible that this is an address to Sulayman, peace be upon him, and those present with him, since it is unlikely that the hoopoe's conversation was with Sulayman while no one else was with them. Just as it was permissible for him to address him with his saying ﴿I have encompassed what you have not encompassed﴾, it is permissible for him to address him and those present with him with his saying ﴿what you conceal and what you proclaim﴾. Indeed, his address with this does not reveal the same ardour as that other address.

The apparent meaning is that His saying ﴿that they do not prostrate ... the Mighty﴾ is part of the words of the hoopoe. It has been said that it is part of the words of Allah the Exalted addressed to the community of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Ibn 'Atiyya said: The reading with the ya' of absence indicates that the verse is part of the hoopoe's speech, while the reading with the ta' of address indicates that it is from the address of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, to the community of Muhammad (ﷺ).

The author of al-Ghunyan said: When the hoopoe mentioned the throne of Bilqis and described it as great, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, responded to him and made clear that His own throne is the one truly described with this attribute, since no throne apart from Him deserves to be described with greatness. It has been said that this is part of the hoopoe's speech, as if he corrected himself and returned the greatness from the throne of Bilqis to the Throne of Allah.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask:) How did the hoopoe make the throne of Bilqis equal to the Throne of Allah in describing it as great? (I answer:) There is a difference between the two descriptions, for describing her throne as great is an exaltation of it in relation to the thrones of the kings of her kind, while describing the Throne of Allah as great is an exaltation of it in relation to all that He has created of the heavens and the earth. End of quote.

Ibn Muhaysin and a group read al-'Azim (the Mighty) in the nominative (bi-l-raf'). It is possible that it is an adjective of al-'arsh (the throne), and it is a separate (qat') nominative by implied "huwa" (he is) for the purpose of praise; then its reading and the reading of the majority are the same in meaning. It is also possible that it is an adjective of the Lord, and the throne was singled out for mention because it is the greatest of created things, and all else is included within it.

When the hoopoe finished his speech, and presented his excuse for his absence, Sulayman postponed his command until it became clear to him whether his report was true or false. So he said: ﴿We shall see whether you have told the truth or were of the liars.﴾ Here "al-nazar" (looking) means reflection and examination. "Asadaqta" (have you told the truth) is a clause suspended from "sanazhur" (we shall see); it is in the position of an accusative, by dropping the preposition, because nazar in the sense of reflection and consideration only takes its object with the preposition "fi". He balanced the two clauses with "am" (or), and the composition was not "am kadhabta" (or did you lie), because his saying ﴿or were you of the liars﴾ is more emphatic in attributing lying to him; for his being "of the liars" indicates that he is known for lying, and this description preceded him before the report he gave. When the description of lying had already attached to him, he became suspect in what he reported, unlike one whose lying is only presumed initially regarding what he reports.

In the speech there is an ellipsis, whose estimate is: So he commanded that a letter be written to them, and that the hoopoe go as a messenger to them with the letter. Then he said: ﴿Go with this letter of mine﴾, i.e. the present one, now written.

﴿Then throw it to them, then turn away from them﴾, i.e. withdraw from them to a nearby place, such that you hear what comes from them and what some of them say to others.

In His saying ﴿Go with this letter of mine, then throw it to them﴾ there is evidence for the imam (leader) sending letters to polytheists, conveying the call to them and inviting them to Islam. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wrote to Khosrow, Caesar and others, the kings of the Arabs. Wahb said: His command to turn away is good manners, that he withdraw in the manner in which kings conduct themselves, meaning: and be near enough that you hear their exchanges. Ibn Zayd said: He commanded him to turn away in the sense of returning to him, i.e. throw it and return. He said: His saying ﴿then see what they return﴾ is in the sense of being placed before His saying ﴿then turn away from them﴾. End of quote. Abu 'Ali said this too, but there is no necessity to make a change of order; rather the apparent meaning is that looking follows the turning away from them.

In the Seven (al-Sab'a, the seven canonical readers) it is read ﴿fa-alqihi﴾ with a kasrah on the ha' and a ya' after it, with the kasrah stolen (ikhtilas), and with a sukun on the ha'. Muslim ibn Jundub read it with a dammah on the ha' and a waw after it. In His saying ﴿to them﴾ he used the plural, and the hoopoe said ﴿I found her and her people﴾. In the letter also there is the plural pronoun in His saying ﴿that you not exalt yourselves over me﴾, and the letter contained the call to Islam for Bilqis and her people.

The meaning of ﴿then see what they return﴾ is: reflect and bring it to your mind. It has been said its meaning is: then wait. If the meaning of "fa-anzur" is reflection by thought, then "unzur" is suspended, and "madha" is either an interrogative word in the position of an accusative, or "ma" is an interrogative and "dha" is a relative pronoun meaning "alladhi". On the first, "yarji'una" (they return) is the predicate of "madha"; on the second, "dha" is the predicate and "yarji'una" is the relative clause of "dha". If the meaning of "fa-anzur" is "fa-intazir" (then wait), it is not a verb of the heart so as to be suspended; rather "madha" entirely is a relative pronoun meaning "alladhi", i.e. "wait for what they return", and the meaning is: "look at what they return" until you bring back to me what they return of speech.

[p. 64] Apparently he inspected all the birds, which is what the care for the affairs of the kingdom and attention to his subjects would require. It is said that each kind of bird would come to him one at a time, and he did not see the hoopoe. It is also said that the birds would shade him from the sun, and the hoopoe would shield his right side, so the sun struck him, and he looked at the hoopoe's place and did not see it. It is narrated from Abdullah ibn Salam that Sulayman, peace be upon him, camped in a barren desert with no water. The hoopoe could see the surface of the earth and what lay beneath it, and he would inform Sulayman of this. The jinn would extract water for him by stripping the earth in an hour, as a sheep is skinned. So he asked about the hoopoe when they reached that desert, because they needed water. In His words ﴿And he inspected the birds﴾ there is evidence that a leader should inspect the conditions of his subjects and look after them. Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "If a young goat on the bank of the Euphrates were seized by a wolf, Umar would be questioned about it." There is an omission in the speech, meaning: he missed the hoopoe when he inspected the birds.

Ibn Atiyya said: His words ﴿What is wrong with me that I do not see the hoopoe?﴾ aim at the hoopoe. He was absent, but he took the necessary consequence of his absence, which is that he does not see him, and so he asked in the form of a reproach about that consequence. This is a kind of brevity, and the interrogative in His words "what is wrong with me" takes the place of the alif that "am" would normally accompany. End of quotation. The apparent meaning of this speech is that "am" is connected (muttasila, joined to the question), and that the interrogative in "mali" takes the place of the interrogative alif. Its meaning for him is: "Has he now gone out of my sight so that I did not see him during the inspection, or was he among those who were absent before and I did not notice his absence?"

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Am" here is the disconnected one (munqati'a, which introduces a new question). He looked at the hoopoe's place, did not see him, and said: ﴿What is wrong with me that I do not see the hoopoe?﴾ meaning: he does not see him although he is present, either because of a screen that hides him or for some other reason. Then it occurred to him that he was absent, so he turned away from that and began to say: "Is he absent?" As if he were asking whether what had occurred to him was correct. A similar expression is their saying: "Is it camels, or sheep?" End of quotation. The correct view is that "am" here is the disconnected one, because the condition for the connected "am" is that it be preceded by the interrogative hamza. If it is preceded by an interrogative particle other than the hamza, then "am" is disconnected. Here it is preceded by "ma," so the condition for the connected form is not met. It has also been said that it is possible that this is an inversion (maqlub, transposition of words), its intended sense being: "What is the matter with the hoopoe that I do not see him?" But there is no need to claim inversion.

In al-Kashshaf: When Sulayman completed the building of the Temple of Jerusalem, he prepared for the Pilgrimage, arrived at the Sacred Precinct, and stayed there as long as he wished. Then he resolved to set out for Yemen, and he left Mecca in the morning heading for Suhayl (a star), and reached Sanaa at midday. That journey is a month's march. He saw a beautiful land whose greenery pleased him, so he dismounted to eat and pray, but he found no water. The hoopoe used to come to him, and he could see water under the earth. It is mentioned that the jinn would strip the earth until the water appeared.

﴿A severe punishment﴾: He left the severe punishment unspecified. There are conflicting statements about what it was, and the best view is that these are examples. From Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and Ibn Jurayj: he would pluck out his feathers. Ibn Jurayj also said: all of his feathers. Yazid ibn Ruman said: his wing. Ibn Wahb said: he would cut off half and leave half. It was also said: plucking along with leaving him to the sun. It was said: he would be imprisoned in a cage. It was said: he would be smeared with tar and exposed to the sun. It was said: he would be plucked and thrown to the ants. It was said: he would be put together with a different species. It was said: he would be barred from serving Sulayman, peace be upon him. It was said: he would be separated from his mate. It was said: he would be bound to serve his wife. This statement from Sulayman was an expression of anger for the sake of Allah, since the prayer had come and he asked for water for ablution but did not find any. Allah permitted him to do this for the sake of the public good, just as He permitted animals and birds to be eaten, and just as He subjected the birds to him. So he was entitled to discipline the hoopoe if he did not do what he was subjected to do.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿أَوْ لَيَأْتِيَنِّي﴾ (or he will surely bring me) with a doubled nun followed by the first person ya; Ibn Kathir read it with a doubled nun followed by the nun of protection (nun al-wiqaya) after the ya; Isa ibn Umar read it with a doubled, fatha-vowelled nun without ya. ﴿A clear authority﴾ means proof and excuse. There is in this a proof of severity toward the disobedient and of punishing them. He began with the lighter of the two punishments, which is torment, then followed it with the more severe, which is ending life by slaughter. He swore to these two because they were his own actions. He swore to bringing the authority, which was not his own action, but when he arranged the three in the ruling with "or," it was as if he said: one of the three will certainly happen. The meaning is: if he brings the authority, there will be neither torment nor slaughter; otherwise one of them will occur. His oath to bringing him does not imply a claim of knowledge, since it is possible that his oath about the two actions was followed by a revelation from Allah that he would bring him an authority, so that his words ﴿or he will surely bring me a clear authority﴾ would be based on knowledge and certainty.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿فَمَكَثَ﴾ (then he stayed) with a damma on the kaf; Asim, Abu Amr in the narration of al-Ju'fi, Sahl, and Rawh read it with a damma. In the reading of Ubayy: "fa-yamkuth" (then he will stay), and then he said: in the reading of Abdullah: "fa-yamkuth," then he said. Both are in reality an explanation, not a reading, because that contradicts the consonantal text of the codex and what has been transmitted from them by sound transmission. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in "famakatha" refers to the hoopoe, i.e., he stayed for a short time, meaning soon. His staying is described as brief to show his speed, out of fear of Sulayman, and so that it may be known how the birds were subjected to him, and to demonstrate the miracle given to him, which indicates his prophethood and Allah's power. It has also been said: he stopped at a place not far from Sulayman. It is reported that when Sulayman descended, the hoopoe circled and saw another hoopoe, descended upon him, and described to him Sulayman's kingdom and everything subjected to him. His companion told him about the kingdom of Bilqis and exaggerated its greatness, and he went with him to see it, and did not return until after the afternoon. It has also been said that the pronoun in "famakatha" refers to Sulayman. It has also been said that it may refer to both Sulayman and the hoopoe, and there is an omission in the speech. If "not far" refers to time, the implied sense is: then Sulayman came and asked him: "What kept you away?" and he said: "I have encompassed." If it refers to place, the implied sense is: then he came and stood at a place near Sulayman, and Sulayman asked him: "What kept you away?" It was reported that he already knew what Sulayman had sworn about, so he hastened to answer him with something that would calm his anger: that his absence was due to a great matter that had come up for him. So he said: ﴿I have encompassed what you have not encompassed﴾. In this there is the boldness of one who possesses knowledge that no one else has, and his boasting about it, and his leaving it vague until the soul yearns to know what that vague matter is. The meaning of "encompassing" here is that he knew a knowledge that the prophet of Allah, Sulayman, did not have.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Allah inspired the hoopoe, and so he confronted Sulayman with these words, despite the fact that Sulayman had been given the excellence of prophethood, wisdom, numerous sciences, and encompassing of many known things. This was a trial for him regarding his knowledge, and an alert that among the lowest and weakest of His creatures there is one who has encompassed knowledge of what Sulayman did not encompass, so that his own soul would consider itself small and his knowledge would seem minor to him, and so that it would be a kindness to him in avoiding self-admiration (ujb), which is a trial for scholars, and how great a trial it is! The encompassing of a thing by knowledge means that it is known from all its aspects, so that no known thing is hidden from it. They said: In this there is evidence against the claim of the Rafidah (Rafidites) that "the imam has nothing hidden from him, and there is no one in his time more knowledgeable than him." End of quotation.

When he made it vague in His words ﴿what you have not encompassed﴾, he moved to something less vague, which is His words ﴿and I have come to you from Saba with a certain news﴾, for in it there is information about the place from which he came and that he had knowledge of a certain report that was established for him.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿مِن سَبَأٍ﴾ (from Saba) with tanwin (declined); Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr read it with a fatha on the hamza, without tanwin, in both this place and in ﴿Indeed there was for Saba﴾ [Saba 34:15]; Qunbul, through al-Nabbal, read it with a sukun on the hamza in both places. Whoever declined it made it the name of a tribe, a place, or a forefather, as in the hadith of Farwa ibn Musayk and others, from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "He is the name of a man who had ten children; six of them went to the right (tayammana), and four went to the left (tashaama)." The six are: Himyar, Kindah, al-Azd, Ash'ar, Khath'am, and Bajilah. The four are: Lakhm, Judham, Amilah, and Ghassan. Saba was a man from Qahtan whose name was Abd Shams. It has also been said: Amir. He was named Saba because he was the first to take captives (sabaa). Whoever did not decline it made it the name of the tribe or the region. They cited as evidence for declining:
"The ones who came and Tayyim are on the heights of Saba, the buffalo hide has bitten their necks."

As for whoever pronounced the hamza with a sukun, it is due to the succession of vowels in one who does not decline it, and to treat the connection like a pause. Makki said: pronouncing the sukun in connected speech is far-fetched, not preferred, and not strong. End of quotation. Al-A'mash read ﴿مِن سَبَأِ﴾ with a kasra on the hamza and no tanwin; Ibn Khalawayh and Ibn Atiyya related this from him, and its justification is weak. Ibn Kathir in one transmission read ﴿مِن سَبًا﴾ with tanwin on the ba, on the pattern of "raha," treating it as a declined word with a short alif. Abu Mu'adh reported that he read ﴿مِن سَبْأ﴾ with a sukun on the ba and an unvowelled open hamza without tanwin, treating it as the pattern fa'la, so it was not declined because of its obligatory feminine form. Ibn Habib reported from al-Yazidi: ﴿مِن سَبَأْ﴾ with a quiescent alif, like their saying: "They scattered every which way (aydi saba)." A group read ﴿بِنَبَا﴾ with an alif in place of the hamza, and this is probably the reading of whoever read ﴿سَبَا﴾ with alif, so that the two words would balance, just as they balance in the reading of whoever read both with a kasrah on the hamza and tanwin.

In al-Tahrir he said: this type in the science of badi' (rhetoric) is called al-tardid (repetition of an ending), and in the book al-Tafrif fi funun al-badi': tardid means returning the ends of verses to their beginnings, or returning a word from the first half to the second half, and it is also called al-tasdir (beginning with the repeated word). An example of the first is his saying:
"Swift to his paternal cousin, he mends his break,
but he is not swift to the summoner of obscenity."
An example of the second is his saying:
"The nights when you are far away are long,
and the nights when you are near are short."
He mentioned that something like ﴿مِن سَبَإٍ بِنَبَإٍ﴾ is called tajnis al-tasrif (paronomasia of inflection), and he said: it means that each of the two words is distinguished from the other by a single letter. Among examples of it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is because you used to rejoice in the land without right and because you used to exult﴾ [Ghafir 40:75], and what came in the hadith: "Good is bound to the foreheads of horses." The poet said:
"By Allah, what those veils and faces (al-ma'ajir wa-l-mahajir) have done to us!"

Al-Zamakhshari said: His saying ﴿from Saba' with news﴾ is of the kind of speech that the scholars of rhetoric call al-badi' (embellishment), and it is among the fine points of speech that relate to the wording, on condition that it comes naturally, or in a form that is aware of the essence of speech, by which the soundness and rightness of the meaning is preserved. Here it has come beyond mere soundness, so it is excellent and novel in both wording and meaning. Do you not see that if bi-nabaʾin were replaced by bi-khabar, the meaning would still be sound? And yet what came is more sound, because of the added nuance in nabaʾ that the description of the situation corresponds to. End of quotation. The nuance he pointed to is that a nabaʾ is only a report that has significance, whereas the word khabar is general, applying to what has significance and to what does not.

When the hoopoe first left things vague, and then left them vague a second time, short of that vagueness, he made explicit what he had left vague and said: ﴿I found a woman ruling over them﴾. His saying ﴿ruling over them﴾ does not indicate that it is permissible for a woman to be a ruler, because that was the practice of the people of Bilqis, who were unbelievers, so there is no proof in it. In the Sahih of al-Bukhari, from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas, when the Prophet (ﷺ) was informed that the people of Persia had made the daughter of Kisra their ruler, he said: "A people will never prosper who entrust their affairs to a woman." It is related from Muhammad ibn Jarir that it is permissible for a woman to be a judge, but this is not authentically transmitted from him. It is related from Abu Hanifa that she may judge in matters in which she is a witness, not absolutely, nor that a document be written for her stating that so-and-so is appointed over the judgment; rather that is only by way of delegation and deputization in a single case. The meaning of "I found" (wajadtu) here is "I came to know/I reached"; the pronoun in "ruling over them" refers to Saba', if by it is meant the tribe; if by it is meant the place, then there is an ellipsis, i.e. "and I have come to you from the people of Saba'."

The woman is Bilqis daughter of Sharahil. Her father was king of all Yemen, and he had no child other than her, so she gained control of the kingdom; she and her people were Magians who worshipped the sun. Its father's name has been disputed greatly. It is said that her mother was a jinn-woman called Rayhana daughter of al-Sakan, whom her father married, since in his greatness he did not think fit to marry any of the kings of his time; so Bilqis was born to him. They have extended their narratives about her with what is not established in the Qur'an or in sound hadith.

The hoopoe began by informing about her kingdom, that she had been given of everything, and this is by way of hyperbole; the meaning is: of everything she needed, or of everything in her land. Between the hoopoe's saying this and Sulayman's saying ﴿and we have been given of everything﴾ [al-Naml: 16] there is a difference: Sulayman's statement was joined to his saying ﴿we have been taught the speech of the birds﴾ [al-Naml: 16], which is a miracle, so it refers first to what he was given of prophethood, wisdom and the means of religion, and then to kingship and the means of this world; whereas the hoopoe's conjunction was to kingship, so he meant only what she had been given of the worldly means suitable to her condition.

﴿And she has a great throne﴾. Ibn Zayd said: it is her seat of sitting. Sufyan said: it is her chair, which was inlaid with jewels and had seven doors. They mentioned a number of things about the description of her throne; Allah alone knows the reality of that. The hoopoe's magnifying of her throne was either to belittle her situation, that she should have a throne like this, or because Sulayman did not have one like it, although he was great in dominion in every respect, since some regional governors may possess something that the king they serve under does not.

Since Allah had given Sulayman of everything, and he had a great throne, he informed him of this great news, since there was in the world someone who shared with him in things that approach this. Sulayman did not turn his attention to this, since he was turned away from worldly affairs. So the hoopoe moved on to informing about what relates to matters of religion. How excellent is the sequence of these reports after the hoopoe's threat and his knowledge of that: he first reported his having knowledge of what Sulayman had not known, thereby securing himself against punishment, by the adornment of the knowledge he had acquired, so the listener was eager to know that. Then he informed us a second time of the connection of that knowledge, namely that it is from Saba', and that it is a certain matter without doubt, so the listener's eagerness to hear that news increased. Then he informed a third time about the kingdom that a woman had been given; and Sulayman, peace be upon him, had asked Allah to give him a kingdom that would not befit anyone after him. Then he informed a fourth time of what outwardly indicates a shared condition between him and this woman, whom it is not in the nature of her or of women to rule over male men; and this is his saying ﴿and she has been given of everything﴾ and his saying ﴿and she has a great throne﴾. Sulayman had a carpet that had been made for him, and it was great. When Sulayman was not moved by the report of all this, since it is a worldly matter, he informed him fifthly of what would stir him to seek this queen and to call her to faith in Allah and to devoting worship to Him alone, so he said: ﴿I found her and her people prostrating to the sun instead of Allah﴾. It has already been stated that they were Magians who worshipped lights, and this is the saying of al-Hasan. It was also said that they were zindiqs.

These reports from the hoopoe were by way of excusing his absence from Sulayman; and he knew that Sulayman's aim was to call to the oneness of Allah and faith in Him, so this was a clear excuse that removed from him the punishment with which Sulayman had threatened him. This report stood in the place of certainty about the clear authority, since in his absence there was a benefit in informing Sulayman of what had been hidden from him, and its outcome was the faith of the queen and her people. The kingship of this woman and her place were hidden from Sulayman, even though the distance between them was short, just as the kingship of Yusuf was hidden from Yaqub; and that was for a matter which Allah the Exalted intended.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Among the foolish storytellers is one who pauses at His saying ﴿and she has a throne﴾ and then begins ﴿great, I found her﴾, meaning "a great matter, that I found her," fleeing from the hoopoe's magnifying of her throne, and so he fell into a grave error, which is the distortion of the Book of Allah. End of quotation. He also said: (If you say: from where did the hoopoe get the guidance to know Allah and the obligation of prostrating to Him, and the denial of prostrating to the sun, and its attribution to Satan and his adornment? I say: It is not far-fetched that Allah inspired him with that, just as He inspired him and others among the birds and the rest of the animals with subtle knowledge that intelligent people hardly come to know. Whoever wishes to investigate this, let him consult the book on animals, especially in the time of a prophet to whom the birds were subjected and who was taught their speech, and this was made a miracle for him.) End of quotation.

The adornment was attributed to Satan, since he was the one who caused it, by the decree of Allah the Exalted.

﴿So he barred them from the way﴾, i.e. Satan, or his adornment, from the way, which is faith in Allah and devoting worship to Him alone.

﴿So they are not guided﴾, i.e. to the truth. Ibn ʿAbbas, Abu Jaʿfar, al-Zuhri, al-Sulami, al-Hasan, Humayd and al-Kisai read: alla, with the lam of the alif lightened. According to this reading, one may pause at ﴿so they are not guided﴾ and begin at ﴿alla yasjudu﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: If he wishes, he may pause at alla and then begin with usjudu. The rest of the seven read it with the lam doubled, and according to this, His saying ﴿so they are not guided﴾ is connected with His saying ﴿alla yasjudu﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: In the reading of ʿAbd Allah, which is the reading of al-Aʿmash: halla and hala, with the two hamzas changed into a haʾ; and from ʿAbd Allah: hala yasjudun, meaning "why do you not prostrate", in address. In the reading of Ubayy: "Why do you not prostrate to Allah, who brings forth the hidden thing in the heavens and the earth, and knows what you conceal and what you disclose." End of quotation.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: al-Aʿmash read halla yasjudun; in the reading of ʿAbd Allah: alla hal tasjudun, with ta'; in the reading of Ubayy: alla tasjudun, also with ta'. As for the reading of those who keep the nun in yasjudun and read with ta' or ya', its explanation is clear. As for the reading of the rest of the seven, it is explained as follows: His saying ﴿alla yasjudu﴾ is in a position of accusative, as a substitute (badal) for His saying "their deeds" (aʿmalahum), meaning: Satan adorned for them that they should not prostrate. What lies between the substituted and the substitute is a parenthesis; or it is in a position of genitive, as a substitute for "the way", meaning: he barred them from not prostrating. According to this explanation, "la" is extra, meaning: he barred them from prostrating to Allah, and ﴿so they are not guided﴾ is a parenthesis between the substituted and the substitute, and the sense is: lest they prostrate. The lam is either connected to "adorned" or to "their intention", and the lam that enters upon "an" (that) is a lam of purpose; that is, the cause of Satan's adornment for them, or of his barring them from the way, is the absence of their prostrating to Allah, or for fear that they would prostrate to Allah. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible that "la" be extra, and the meaning would be: so they are not guided to prostrating. End of quotation. As for the reading of Ibn ʿAbbas and those who agree with him, it is explained as: "alla" is an interjection of opening, "ya" is a particle of calling, the vocative is omitted, and "usjudu" is an imperative verb; the alif of "ya" which is for calling is dropped, and the alif of connection in "usjudu" too, since the orthography of the Mushaf writes yasjudu without the two alifs; when they drop in pronunciation, they also drop in writing. Such a construction occurs in the speech of the Arabs. The poet said:

*Alla ya islami dhatal-damaliji wal-ʿiqdi* (Ah, O you, greet Dhat al-Damalij and the necklace)

He said:

*Alla ya isqiyani qabla ghaarati Sinjal* (Ah, O you two, give me drink before the raid of Sinjal)

(p-69) He said:

*Alla ya islami ya dara Mayya ʿala al-bili* (Ah, O you, be safe, O abode of Mayya, against decay)

He said:

*Alla ya isqiyani qabla habli Abi Bakr* (Ah, O you two, give me drink before the rope of Abu Bakr)

*Fa-qalat alla ya isma' aʿizuka bi-khutbatin* ... *Fa-qultu sami'na fa-ntiqi wa-asībī* (She said: "Ah, O you, listen, I will admonish you with a sermon," and I said: "We have listened, so speak and be correct.")

He said:

*Alla ya islami ya Hind Hind Bani Badr* ... *wa-in kana jabanan ʿada akhira al-dahr* (Ah, O you, be safe, O Hind, Hind of the Banu Badr, even if he was a coward, he passed beyond the end of time)

And some Arabs were heard saying:

*Alla ya irhamuna alla tasaddaqu ʿalayna* (Ah, O you, have mercy on us, will you not give alms to us?)

Al-Kisai paused in this reading on "ya", then began with usjudu; this is a pause of choice, not of testing. What I hold is that in such a construction reported from the Arabs, "ya" is not a vocative particle, and the vocative is not omitted; because in my view the vocative cannot be omitted, since the verb governing the vocative has been omitted and its subject dropped along with it. If we omitted the vocative, that would mean omitting the whole vocative clause and omitting its complement, which is the vocative, and that would be a great defect. When we keep the vocative and do not omit it, that is evidence for the governing element in it, the vocative clause. The particle of calling is not a particle of response, like nam, la, bala, and ajal, after which clauses may be omitted by the indication of the preceding question. So "ya" in those constructions is, in my view, a particle of alerting, emphasized by which the "alla" that is for alerting, and this was permitted because the two particles differ, and for the purpose of intensifying emphasis. Since emphasis has been found in combining two differing particles that govern in the poet's saying:

*Fa-asbahna la yasʾalnani ʿamma bihi* (so they no longer ask me about what is with him)

and the two particles of the same form governing in his saying:

*Wa-la lilama bihim abadan dawaʾ* (and there is no cure for their ailments ever)

and this was permitted, even if they regard it as necessity or rarity, then combining non-governing particles, which differ in form, is permissible; and "ya" in his saying:

*Ya laʿnata Allahi wal-aqwami kullihim* (O curse of Allah and of all the peoples)

...ليس مِمّا حُذِفَ مِنهُ المُنادى لِما ذَكَرْناهُ. (Hmm, the passage continues:)

The particle is not a vocative particle (harf nida') in my view. Rather, it is a particle of alerting (harf tanbih), after which comes the subject (al-mubtada'), and it is not among those from which the vocative noun has been omitted, for the reason we have mentioned.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask:) Is the prostration of recitation (sujud al-tilawa, the prostration performed upon reciting a verse of prostration) obligatory in both readings together, or in only one of them? (I answer:) It is obligatory in both. One of the two readings is a command to prostrate, and the other is a rebuke of the one who abandons it. As for what al-Zajjaj mentioned, that prostration is obligatory with the lightened reading (al-takhfif) but not with the doubled reading (al-tashdid), it is not a view to be relied upon. End of quote.

Al-Khabʾ is a verbal noun (masdar) used for that which is hidden (al-makhbu'), namely rain, plants, and other things which Allah the Exalted has concealed among His unseen things. Al-Jumhur (the majority of readers) read al-khabʾ with a sukun on the ba' and the hamzah. Ubayy and Isa read it by transferring the vowel of the hamzah to the ba' and dropping the hamzah. Ikrima read it with an alif in place of the hamzah, so the letter before it had to be fathah. This is the reading of Abdullah and Malik ibn Dinar. It can be explained according to the dialect of those who say in pause: hadha al-khabw, marartu bi-l-khabi, ra'aytu al-khaba, and who apply the pronunciation of connection (al-wasl) as the pronunciation of pause. The Kufans permitted saying, of al-mar'ah and al-ka'mah: al-marah and al-kamah, so the hamzah is replaced by an alif and the letter before it is made fathah. According to their view, it is permissible for al-khaba' to derive from this. It has been said: this is a weak dialect, and applying the pronunciation of connection as that of pause is also rare and few. So the two explanations are balanced.

The transfer of the vowel to the ba' and the dropping of the hamzah were reported by Sibawayh from a people of Banu Tamim and Banu Asad. As for the reading al-khaba' with the alif, Abu Hatim criticised it and said: "It is not permissible in Arabic. For if he drops the hamzah he places its vowel on the ba' and says al-khab; and if he transfers it, he says al-khabyi, with a sukun on the ba' and a ya' after it." Al-Mubarrad said: Abu Hatim was below his companions in grammar and did not reach their level, but whenever he left his town, no one more learned than him was found.

The apparent meaning is that "fi al-samawat" (in the heavens) is connected to al-khabʾ, i.e. the thing hidden in the heavens. Al-Farra' said, concerning (the two words) yata'aqabani (succeed one another) in the saying of the Arabs: "La-astakhrijanna al-'ilma fikum" (I will surely extract the knowledge from among you), meaning "minkum" (from you). End of quote. According to this, it is connected to yukhriju, i.e. "min fi al-samawat" (out from the heavens).

(When the hoopoe had been given knowledge of water beneath the earth that no one else had been given, and Allah the Exalted inspired him with this, his description of his Lord the Exalted with this attribute, which is His saying: ﴿Who brings forth what is hidden﴾, was appropriate, since each one is distinguished by an attribute of knowledge or craft, and the signs of that attribute appear upon him in his bearing, his speech and his character. For this reason it has been transmitted: "No servant does a deed except that Allah casts over him the cloak of his deed.")
