It is also said that he dropped it from a window and then hid himself there.

So she took the letter and called out to the nobles of her people: ﴿She said, "O chiefs."﴾ The letter was honored because it was sealed with a signet ring; there is a saying in a hadith: "The nobility of a letter is in its sealing." Or it was honored because it came from Sulayman, and she knew of his kingdom. Or because the bearer was a bird, so she assumed it was a heavenly writing. Or because it contained gentleness and softness, not abuse, nor anything that would disturb the soul. Or because it began with the name of Allah. These are the views. Then she informed them, saying: ﴿"It is from Sulayman,"﴾ as if she had been asked: From whom is the letter, and what is it? So she said: ﴿"It is from Sulayman,"﴾ and that it contains such and such. She first left it vague, then explained it. In the construction ﴿أُلْقِيَ﴾ ("was delivered") in the passive voice, there is an indication that she did not know who delivered it, since she omitted the agent. Or it was in order to belittle him, since he was a bird, if she had seen him.

It is possible that "From Sulayman" came before "In the name of Allah," which is the apparent meaning; and he put it first because of the possibility that something unbecoming might come from her, since she was an unbeliever, so his name would serve as a shield for the name of Allah, exalted is He. Or it was a heading on the outside of the letter, while inside it was "In the name of Allah" and so on. It is also possible that it was written after "In the name of Allah," even if the letter began with the name of Allah. And when she read it to them after having read it to herself, she placed "From Sulayman" first in her narration, even though it was not placed first in the writing.

Or the meaning is that the implied sense is "because it..." as if she gave the reason for the nobility of the letter: that it was from Sulayman and began with "In the name of Allah." What Sulayman wrote is in the utmost brevity and eloquence, and so are the letters of the prophets.

The apparent meaning is that (p-73) the letter is only what Allah has explicitly stated. It is also possible that it was in the language Sulayman used to speak, and she had someone with her who translated for her, since she herself knew that language. To proceed: do not exalt yourselves over me, and come to me in submission." The letters of the prophets were short sentences, neither prolix nor verbose. When she read the letter to the chiefs, and they saw what it contained of the demand that she move over to Sulayman, she consulted them about her affair. Qatadah said: Her counselors numbered three hundred and twelve; and from him: thirteen; each man among them had command over ten thousand. She was in the land of Ma'rib, three days from San'a'. Something greater and more numerous than this about her army has been mentioned, and Allah knows best.

The intended meaning here is: advise me with what you have of sound opinion and planning concerning what has happened to her. By their consultation she intended to explore their opinions, to win them over, and to make them content, so that they would support her and stand with her.

﴿"I would not decide an affair"﴾ meaning: I would not finalize and settle an affair ﴿"until you are present"﴾ meaning: until you attend before me, so that I do not act alone in any matter, but you will be present with me. In the recitation of Abdullah it reads: "I would not judge an affair (qadiya)," meaning: I would not conclude except with you present with me. "I would not decide an affair" is general to every affair, meaning: if this is my custom with you, how then would I not consult you in this great event, which is leaving the kingdom, entering into obedience to another and becoming a follower? So the chiefs answered her with what gladdened her eye, saying that they are ﴿"people of strength"﴾ meaning: strength in numbers and equipment, ﴿"and of great military might"﴾ meaning: possessors of courage and valor. They displayed the external strength first, then the inherent strength, meaning: we are prepared for war and for repelling this event. Then they said: ﴿"but the command is yours, so consider what you will command."﴾ This is from the good manner of their discourse, since they entrusted the matter to her, which is evidence of excessive obedience. That is, we have mentioned what we are, and yet the matter is entrusted to you. It is as though they had first recommended war to her, or meant: we are the sons of war, not the sons of consultation, and you are the one of sound opinion and good planning. Consider what you will command, and we will return to you and follow your opinion. "Consider" (fa-nzuri) is from contemplation and reflection, and "what" (madha) is the second object of "you command" (ta'murina); the first object is omitted because the meaning is understood, meaning: you command us. The clause is suspended from "consider" (unzuri), so it is in the position of an object of "consider" after the interrogative particle has dropped its preposition.

When Sulayman's letter reached her, not through the hand of a man but through a bird, she greatly esteemed Sulayman's kingdom and knew that one to whom birds are subjected, so that he sends them with a specific command to a specific person enclosed behind locked doors, is not unable to subdue the earth and its kings. So she informed them of the state of kings and inclined toward gifts and reconciliation, and she said: ﴿"Indeed, when kings enter a town"﴾ meaning: they overcome it, ﴿"they ruin it"﴾ meaning: they lay it waste by demolition, burning and cutting, and they humiliate the honored of its people by killing, plundering and capturing. Her saying here is a discrediting of their opinions regarding war, a warning for them, a protection of them, and an exaltation of Sulayman's kingdom. The apparent meaning is that ﴿"And thus do they act"﴾ is part of her speech, meaning: this is the unceasing custom of kings, of corruption and abasement. This was rooted in the house of kingship, so she saw and heard it. She mentioned it to reinforce what she had said about the state of kings. It is also said that it is part of Allah's speech, informing His Messenger (ﷺ) and his community, and confirming her report about kings when they overcome.

Since the custom of kings is to accept gifts, and since accepting them indicates satisfaction and affection, she said: ﴿"But I am sending them"﴾ meaning: to Sulayman and those with him, messengers with a ﴿"gift"﴾. The word "gift" came unspecified. They have mentioned various and conflicting views about what it was, and they have mentioned some of her stratagems and the state of Sulayman when the gift reached him and his conversation with her messengers, which only Allah knows. ﴿"Will wait to see"﴾ is coordinated with ﴿"sending"﴾. ﴿"What"﴾ (bima) is connected to ﴿"return"﴾ (yarji'u). Al-Hawfi held that the preposition (ba') is connected to "waiting to see" (nazira), and this is a gross error, and the "looking" here is also suspended. The clause is in the position of an object. This indicates that she did not trust that the gift would be accepted, but allowed for its rejection, and by this she wanted Sulayman's purpose to become clear to her. A "gift" (hadiyya) is a noun for what is given as a present, just as "bounty" (atiyya) is a noun for what is given. It is reported that she said to her people: If he is a worldly king, wealth will satisfy him, and we will deal with him accordingly; but if he is a prophet, wealth will not please him, and we should follow him in his religion. In the speech there is an omission, whose implied sense is: So she sent the gift; then when the messenger came to Sulayman, the messenger being the genus rather than the singular form. The pronoun in ﴿"return" (irji')﴾ and "the messenger" apply to the plural and singular, masculine and feminine alike. Abdullah read: ﴿"When they came"﴾ and read ﴿"return" (irji'u)﴾, making it refer to the word ﴿"the messengers"﴾.

﴿"Would you provide me with wealth?"﴾ is an interrogative of denial and disparagement, and in this there is an indication of his detachment from this world and that his heart was not attached to it, upon him be prayer and peace.

---

Then he mentioned God's blessing upon him, and that what God had given him of prophethood and vast dominion is better than what He had given you. "Rather, you are, in your gift that is presented to you, rejoicing, because you love this world." The word hadiyyah (gift) may be construed as annexed to the one who gives it or to the one to whom it is given, and here it is annexed to the recipient, which is the apparent reading. It is also permissible that it be annexed to the giver, meaning: "Rather, you are, in this gift of yours which you have sent, rejoicing with the joy of boasting over the kings, since you were able to send the like of it." It is also permissible that it be an expression of rejection, as if he said: "Rather, it is your right to take back your gift and rejoice in it."

The majority of the Seven Readers read ﴿أتُمِدُّونَنِي﴾ with two nuns, while some read it with the yā' (أتُمِدُّونَنِي with yā'). Hamzah read it by assimilating the nun of rafʿ (nūn al-rafʿ) into the nun of protection (nūn al-wiqāyah) and affirming the yā' of the speaker. Al-Musayyabi, on the authority of Nafi', read it with a single light nun.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: what is the difference between your saying, 'Will you aid me with wealth when I am richer than you?' and his saying it with the fā' (fa-)? I answer: If you say it with the wāw (wa-), you have made your addressee aware of my surplus over him in wealth, and yet he aids me with wealth. But if you say it with the fā', you have made him one from whom my condition is hidden, and I am informing him right now of what makes his aid unnecessary to me, as if I were saying to him: 'I reject what you have done, for I am independent of it.'" On this is revealed His saying: ﴿فَما آتانِيَ اللَّهُ﴾. If you ask: what is the aspect of the idrāb (the turning away/transition)? I answer: When he denied them the aid and gave a reason for his denial, he turned away from that to explaining the cause that moved them to it, which is that they do not know the cause of contentment or joy except that some portion of this world, which they know no other than, be given to them. End.

﴿ارْجِعْ إلَيْهِمْ﴾ is an address to the messenger who brought the gift, and he is al-Mundhir ibn ʿAmr, the leader of the delegation. The meaning: "Return to them with their gift." The reading of ʿAbdullah (Ibn Masʿud) was previously mentioned: ﴿ارْجِعُوا إلَيْهِمْ﴾ (ir-ji'u ilayhim, plural). Here ﴿ارْجِعُوا﴾ is intransitive, meaning: turn back and go away to them. It was also said that the address in "ir-ji' (return)" is to the hoopoe, carrying another letter.

Then Sulayman swore and said: ﴿فَلَنَأْتِيَنَّهم بِجُنُودٍ﴾ ("We shall surely come to them with armies"), threatening them, and there is an ellipsis in it, meaning: if they do not come to me submitting. This threat indicates that they were disbelievers, remaining upon disbelief at that time.

The pronoun in ﴿بِها﴾ ("with them") refers to the armies, which is a broken (collective) plural, so the pronoun may refer to it as it refers to the singular, as the Arabs say: "al-rijālu wa-aʿḍāduhā" (the men and their limbs). ʿAbdullah read ﴿بِهِمْ﴾ (with them). The meaning of ﴿لا قِبَلَ﴾ ("no power to resist") is "no strength," and the true meaning of qibal is confrontation and facing, i.e., you will not be able to confront them. The pronoun in ﴿مِنها﴾ ("from it") refers to Saba', which is the land of Bilqis and her people. ﴿أذِلَّةً﴾ ("humbled") is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl).

﴿وهم صاغِرُونَ﴾ ("while they are abased") is another circumstantial state. Dhull (humiliation) is the departure of the honour they were in, and ṣaghār (abasement) is their falling into captivity and servitude; it is not limited to their returning as commoners after having been kings. The coming of these two states is evidence for the permissibility of a single governing verb taking two states for one bearer of the state, which is a matter of scholarly disagreement. It may be said that the second here came as an emphasis of ﴿أذِلَّةً﴾, so that they are together as one state.

Al-Hawfi held that the preposition (ba') is connected to "waiting to see" (nazira), and this is a gross error, and the "looking" here is also suspended. The clause is in the position of an object. This indicates that she did not trust that the gift would be accepted, but allowed for its rejection, and by this she wanted Sulayman's purpose to become clear to her. A "gift" (hadiyya) is a noun for what is given as a present, just as "bounty" (atiyya) is a noun for what is given. It is reported that she said to her people: If he is a worldly king, wealth will satisfy him, and we will deal with him accordingly; but if he is a prophet, wealth will not please him, and we should follow him in his religion. In the speech there is an omission, whose implied sense is: So she sent the gift; then when the messenger came to Sulayman, the messenger being the genus rather than the singular form. The pronoun in ﴿"return" (irji')﴾ and "the messenger" apply to the plural and singular, masculine and feminine alike. Abdullah read: ﴿"When they came"﴾ and read ﴿"return" (irji'u)﴾, making it refer to the word ﴿"the messengers"﴾.

Then he mentioned God's blessing upon him, and that what God had given him of prophethood and vast dominion is better than what He had given you. The word hadiyyah (gift) may be construed as annexed to the one who gives it or to the one to whom it is given, and here it is annexed to the recipient, which is the apparent reading. It is also permissible that it be annexed to the giver, meaning: "Rather, you are, in this gift of yours which you have sent, rejoicing with the joy of boasting over the kings, since you were able to send the like of it." It is also permissible that it be an expression of rejection, as if he said: "Rather, it is your right to take back your gift and rejoice in it."

The majority of the Seven Readers read ﴿أتُمِدُّونَنِي﴾ with two nuns, while some read it with the yā' (أتُمِدُّونَنِي with yā'). Hamzah read it by assimilating the nun of rafʿ (nūn al-rafʿ) into the nun of protection (nūn al-wiqāyah) and affirming the yā' of the speaker. Al-Musayyabi, on the authority of Nafi', read it with a single light nun.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: what is the difference between your saying, 'Will you aid me with wealth when I am richer than you?' and his saying it with the fā' (fa-)? End.

Then Sulayman swore and said: ﴿فَلَنَأْتِيَنَّهم بِجُنُودٍ﴾ ("We shall surely come to them with armies"), threatening them, and there is an ellipsis in it, meaning: if they do not come to me submitting. This threat indicates that they were disbelievers, remaining upon disbelief at that time.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 27, verses 29–37 (part 1 of 2):**

I would not decide an affair until you are present with me."﴾ ﴿They said, "We are people of strength and of great military might, but the command is yours, so consider what you will command."﴾ ﴿She said, "Indeed, when kings enter a town, they ruin it and make the honored of its people humiliated. What Allah has given me is better than what He has given you. Rather, it is you who rejoice in your gift."﴾ ﴿"Return to them. It is also said that she was in her palace, had locked the doors, and was lying on her bed asleep, and he dropped the letter onto her chest. It is also said that there was a window in the room through which the sun fell every day; whenever she looked at it, she would prostrate to it. The hoopoe came and blocked it with his wing. She saw this and rose toward him, and he dropped the letter to her. She was a literate Arab woman from the people of Tubba'. It is also said that he dropped it from a window and then hid himself there.

Or because it contained gentleness and softness, not abuse, nor anything that would disturb the soul. Or because it began with the name of Allah. These are the views. It is also possible that it was written after "In the name of Allah," even if the letter began with the name of Allah. And when she read it to them after having read it to herself, she placed "From Sulayman" first in her narration, even though it was not placed first in the writing.

"In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful" is a noble opening, of excellent meaning, with which books begin in every language and every religious law.

Abu al-Baqa' allowed that the implied sense is "an la ta'lu," making it the predicate of an omitted subject.

The meaning of "la ta'lu" is: do not be arrogant, as kings do. Ibn Abbas, in the transmission of Wahb ibn Munabbih and al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli, read ﴿أَنْ لا تَغْلُوا﴾ with a ghayn (with a dot), meaning: do not exceed the limit, from ghuluww (excess). The apparent meaning is that he asked them to come to him as Muslims, having abandoned disbelief and the worship of the sun. It is also said that the meaning is: submitting, surrendering, yielding in obedience and entering into submission. What Sulayman wrote is in the utmost brevity and eloquence, and so are the letters of the prophets.

The apparent meaning is that (p-73) the letter is only what Allah has explicitly stated. It is possible that it was written in Arabic, since kings have translators in several languages; so he wrote in Arabic script and in the Arabic wording, because she was Arab, from the descendants of Tubba' ibn Sharahil al-Himyari. It is also possible that it was in the language Sulayman used to speak, and she had someone with her who translated for her, since she herself knew that language. It is reported that the text of the letter from the servant of Allah, Sulayman son of Dawud, to Bilqis, queen of Saba', was: "Peace upon whoever follows guidance. To proceed: do not exalt yourselves over me, and come to me in submission." The letters of the prophets were short sentences, neither prolix nor verbose. The letter was sealed with musk, and he stamped it with his signet ring. It is reported that no one wrote "In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful" before Sulayman. When she read the letter to the chiefs, and they saw what it contained of the demand that she move over to Sulayman, she consulted them about her affair. Qatadah said: Her counselors numbered three hundred and twelve; and from him: thirteen; each man among them had command over ten thousand. She was in the land of Ma'rib, three days from San'a'. Something greater and more numerous than this about her army has been mentioned, and Allah knows best.

The intended meaning here is: advise me with what you have of sound opinion and planning concerning what has happened to her. They displayed the external strength first, then the inherent strength, meaning: we are prepared for war and for repelling this event. Then they said: ﴿"but the command is yours, so consider what you will command."﴾ This is from the good manner of their discourse, since they entrusted the matter to her, which is evidence of excessive obedience. That is, we have mentioned what we are, and yet the matter is entrusted to you. Consider what you will command, and we will return to you and follow your opinion. The clause is suspended from "consider" (unzuri), so it is in the position of an object of "consider" after the interrogative particle has dropped its preposition.

It is possible that "From Sulayman" came before "In the name of Allah," which is the apparent meaning; and he put it first because of the possibility that something unbecoming might come from her, since she was an unbeliever, so his name would serve as a shield for the name of Allah, exalted is He. Or it was a heading on the outside of the letter, while inside it was "In the name of Allah" and so on. It is also possible that it was written after "In the name of Allah," even if the letter began with the name of Allah. And when she read it to them after having read it to herself, she placed "From Sulayman" first in her narration, even though it was not placed first in the writing.

Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said: When the messengers of earlier times wrote a letter, they began with themselves: "From so-and-so to so-and-so." This is also what the indication (in this verse) conveys. From Anas: No one was more esteemed than the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and his companions, when they wrote to him, began with themselves. Abu al-Layth said in his book "Kitab al-Bustan": If one began with the addressee, it is permissible, because the Community (ummah) has agreed upon it and has done it.

The majority of reciters (al-Jumhur, meaning the majority of Qur'anic reciters) read ﴿إنَّهُ مِن سُلَيْمانَ وإنَّهُ﴾ with a kasra on the hamza in both places. Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud) read ﴿وإنَّهُ مِن سُلَيْمانَ﴾ with the addition of a waw, as a conjunction to ﴿إنِّي أُلْقِيَ إلَيَّ﴾. Ikrimah and Ibn Abi 'Abla read them with a fatha on both: this is explained as an apposition (badal) to "kitab" (letter), meaning: "It was delivered to me that it..." Or the meaning is that the implied sense is "because it..." as if she gave the reason for the nobility of the letter: that it was from Sulayman and began with "In the name of Allah." Ubayy read ﴿أنْ مِن سُلَيْمانَ وأنْ بِسْمِ اللَّهِ﴾ with a fatha on the hamza and a silent nun, and this is explained as "an" being the explanatory "an," since a clause containing the sense of saying had preceded it; or as the lightened form of the heavy "anna," with the pronoun omitted.

"In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful" is a noble opening, of excellent meaning, with which books begin in every language and every religious law.

As for "an" in His saying ﴿أَلَّا تَعْلُوا﴾ ("Do not exalt yourselves"): it is said to be in the nominative position as an apposition to "kitab." It is also said to be in the accusative position, in the sense of "that you do not exalt yourselves." On these two interpretations, "an" governs the verb. Az-Zamakhshari said: "An" in ﴿أَلَّا تَعْلُوا عَلَيَّ﴾ is explanatory, so "la" in "la ta'lu" is for prohibition. This is good, because it matches the conjunction of the command after it. Abu al-Baqa' allowed that the implied sense is "an la ta'lu," making it the predicate of an omitted subject.

The meaning of "la ta'lu" is: do not be arrogant, as kings do. Ibn Abbas, in the transmission of Wahb ibn Munabbih and al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli, read ﴿أَنْ لا تَغْلُوا﴾ with a ghayn (with a dot), meaning: do not exceed the limit, from ghuluww (excess). The apparent meaning is that he asked them to come to him as Muslims, having abandoned disbelief and the worship of the sun. It is also said that the meaning is: submitting, surrendering, yielding in obedience and entering into submission. What Sulayman wrote is in the utmost brevity and eloquence, and so are the letters of the prophets.

The apparent meaning is that (p-73) the letter is only what Allah has explicitly stated. It is possible that it was written in Arabic, since kings have translators in several languages; so he wrote in Arabic script and in the Arabic wording, because she was Arab, from the descendants of Tubba' ibn Sharahil al-Himyari. It is also possible that it was in the language Sulayman used to speak, and she had someone with her who translated for her, since she herself knew that language. It is reported that the text of the letter from the servant of Allah, Sulayman son of Dawud, to Bilqis, queen of Saba', was: "Peace upon whoever follows guidance. To proceed: do not exalt yourselves over me, and come to me in submission." The letters of the prophets were short sentences, neither prolix nor verbose. The letter was sealed with musk, and he stamped it with his signet ring. It is reported that no one wrote "In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful" before Sulayman. When she read the letter to the chiefs, and they saw what it contained of the demand that she move over to Sulayman, she consulted them about her affair. Qatadah said: Her counselors numbered three hundred and twelve; and from him: thirteen; each man among them had command over ten thousand. She was in the land of Ma'rib, three days from San'a'. Something greater and more numerous than this about her army has been mentioned, and Allah knows best.

The discussion of "fatwa" (legal opinion, here meaning counsel) has been mentioned in the surah of Yusuf. The intended meaning here is: advise me with what you have of sound opinion and planning concerning what has happened to her. By their consultation she intended to explore their opinions, to win them over, and to make them content, so that they would support her and stand with her.

﴿"I would not decide an affair"﴾ meaning: I would not finalize and settle an affair ﴿"until you are present"﴾ meaning: until you attend before me, so that I do not act alone in any matter, but you will be present with me. In the recitation of Abdullah it reads: "I would not judge an affair (qadiya)," meaning: I would not conclude except with you present with me. "I would not decide an affair" is general to every affair, meaning: if this is my custom with you, how then would I not consult you in this great event, which is leaving the kingdom, entering into obedience to another and becoming a follower? So the chiefs answered her with what gladdened her eye, saying that they are ﴿"people of strength"﴾ meaning: strength in numbers and equipment, ﴿"and of great military might"﴾ meaning: possessors of courage and valor. They displayed the external strength first, then the inherent strength, meaning: we are prepared for war and for repelling this event. Then they said: ﴿"but the command is yours, so consider what you will command."﴾ This is from the good manner of their discourse, since they entrusted the matter to her, which is evidence of excessive obedience. That is, we have mentioned what we are, and yet the matter is entrusted to you. It is as though they had first recommended war to her, or meant: we are the sons of war, not the sons of consultation, and you are the one of sound opinion and good planning. Consider what you will command, and we will return to you and follow your opinion. "Consider" (fa-nzuri) is from contemplation and reflection, and "what" (madha) is the second object of "you command" (ta'murina); the first object is omitted because the meaning is understood, meaning: you command us. The clause is suspended from "consider" (unzuri), so it is in the position of an object of "consider" after the interrogative particle has dropped its preposition.

When Sulayman's letter reached her, not through the hand of a man but through a bird, she greatly esteemed Sulayman's kingdom and knew that one to whom birds are subjected, so that he sends them with a specific command to a specific person enclosed behind locked doors, is not unable to subdue the earth and its kings. So she informed them of the state of kings and inclined toward gifts and reconciliation, and she said: ﴿"Indeed, when kings enter a town"﴾ meaning: they overcome it, ﴿"they ruin it"﴾ meaning: they lay it waste by demolition, burning and cutting, and they humiliate the honored of its people by killing, plundering and capturing. Her saying here is a discrediting of their opinions regarding war, a warning for them, a protection of them, and an exaltation of Sulayman's kingdom. The apparent meaning is that ﴿"And thus do they act"﴾ is part of her speech, meaning: this is the unceasing custom of kings, of corruption and abasement. This was rooted in the house of kingship, so she saw and heard it. She mentioned it to reinforce what she had said about the state of kings. It is also said that it is part of Allah's speech, informing His Messenger (ﷺ) and his community, and confirming her report about kings when they overcome.

Since the custom of kings is to accept gifts, and since accepting them indicates satisfaction and affection, she said: ﴿"But I am sending them"﴾ meaning: to Sulayman and those with him, messengers with a ﴿"gift"﴾. The word "gift" came unspecified. They have mentioned various and conflicting views about what it was, and they have mentioned some of her stratagems and the state of Sulayman when the gift reached him and his conversation with her messengers, which only Allah knows. ﴿"Will wait to see"﴾ is coordinated with ﴿"sending"﴾. ﴿"What"﴾ (bima) is connected to ﴿"return"﴾ (yarji'u). Al-Hawfi held that the preposition (ba') is connected to "waiting to see" (nazira), and this is a gross error, and the "looking" here is also suspended. The clause is in the position of an object. This indicates that she did not trust that the gift would be accepted, but allowed for its rejection, and by this she wanted Sulayman's purpose to become clear to her. A "gift" (hadiyya) is a noun for what is given as a present, just as "bounty" (atiyya) is a noun for what is given. It is reported that she said to her people: If he is a worldly king, wealth will satisfy him, and we will deal with him accordingly; but if he is a prophet, wealth will not please him, and we should follow him in his religion. In the speech there is an omission, whose implied sense is: So she sent the gift; then when the messenger came to Sulayman, the messenger being the genus rather than the singular form. The pronoun in ﴿"return" (irji')﴾ and "the messenger" apply to the plural and singular, masculine and feminine alike. Abdullah read: ﴿"When they came"﴾ and read ﴿"return" (irji'u)﴾, making it refer to the word ﴿"the messengers"﴾.

﴿"Would you provide me with wealth?"﴾ is an interrogative of denial and disparagement, and in this there is an indication of his detachment from this world and that his heart was not attached to it, upon him be prayer and peace.

---

Then he mentioned God's blessing upon him, and that what God had given him of prophethood and vast dominion is better than what He had given you. "Rather, you are, in your gift that is presented to you, rejoicing, because you love this world." The word hadiyyah (gift) may be construed as annexed to the one who gives it or to the one to whom it is given, and here it is annexed to the recipient, which is the apparent reading. It is also permissible that it be annexed to the giver, meaning: "Rather, you are, in this gift of yours which you have sent, rejoicing with the joy of boasting over the kings, since you were able to send the like of it." It is also permissible that it be an expression of rejection, as if he said: "Rather, it is your right to take back your gift and rejoice in it."

The majority of the Seven Readers read ﴿أتُمِدُّونَنِي﴾ with two nuns, while some read it with the yā' (أتُمِدُّونَنِي with yā'). Hamzah read it by assimilating the nun of rafʿ (nūn al-rafʿ) into the nun of protection (nūn al-wiqāyah) and affirming the yā' of the speaker. Al-Musayyabi, on the authority of Nafi', read it with a single light nun.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: what is the difference between your saying, 'Will you aid me with wealth when I am richer than you?' and his saying it with the fā' (fa-)? I answer: If you say it with the wāw (wa-), you have made your addressee aware of my surplus over him in wealth, and yet he aids me with wealth. But if you say it with the fā', you have made him one from whom my condition is hidden, and I am informing him right now of what makes his aid unnecessary to me, as if I were saying to him: 'I reject what you have done, for I am independent of it.'" On this is revealed His saying: ﴿فَما آتانِيَ اللَّهُ﴾. If you ask: what is the aspect of the idrāb (the turning away/transition)? I answer: When he denied them the aid and gave a reason for his denial, he turned away from that to explaining the cause that moved them to it, which is that they do not know the cause of contentment or joy except that some portion of this world, which they know no other than, be given to them. End.

﴿ارْجِعْ إلَيْهِمْ﴾ is an address to the messenger who brought the gift, and he is al-Mundhir ibn ʿAmr, the leader of the delegation. The meaning: "Return to them with their gift." The reading of ʿAbdullah (Ibn Masʿud) was previously mentioned: ﴿ارْجِعُوا إلَيْهِمْ﴾ (ir-ji'u ilayhim, plural). Here ﴿ارْجِعُوا﴾ is intransitive, meaning: turn back and go away to them. It was also said that the address in "ir-ji' (return)" is to the hoopoe, carrying another letter.

Then Sulayman swore and said: ﴿فَلَنَأْتِيَنَّهم بِجُنُودٍ﴾ ("We shall surely come to them with armies"), threatening them, and there is an ellipsis in it, meaning: if they do not come to me submitting. This threat indicates that they were disbelievers, remaining upon disbelief at that time.

The pronoun in ﴿بِها﴾ ("with them") refers to the armies, which is a broken (collective) plural, so the pronoun may refer to it as it refers to the singular, as the Arabs say: "al-rijālu wa-aʿḍāduhā" (the men and their limbs). ʿAbdullah read ﴿بِهِمْ﴾ (with them). The meaning of ﴿لا قِبَلَ﴾ ("no power to resist") is "no strength," and the true meaning of qibal is confrontation and facing, i.e., you will not be able to confront them. The pronoun in ﴿مِنها﴾ ("from it") refers to Saba', which is the land of Bilqis and her people. ﴿أذِلَّةً﴾ ("humbled") is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl).

﴿وهم صاغِرُونَ﴾ ("while they are abased") is another circumstantial state. Dhull (humiliation) is the departure of the honour they were in, and ṣaghār (abasement) is their falling into captivity and servitude; it is not limited to their returning as commoners after having been kings. The coming of these two states is evidence for the permissibility of a single governing verb taking two states for one bearer of the state, which is a matter of scholarly disagreement. It may be said that the second here came as an emphasis of ﴿أذِلَّةً﴾, so that they are together as one state.

(p-75)﴿He said, "O chiefs, which of you will bring me her throne before they come to me in submission?"﴾ ﴿A powerful one (ʿifrīt) of the jinn said, "I will bring it to you before you rise from your place. Indeed, I am strong and trustworthy for it."﴾ ﴿One who had knowledge from the Book said, "I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you." And when he saw it set firmly in his presence, he said, "This is from the bounty of my Lord, to test me whether I will be grateful or ungrateful. And whoever is grateful, he is grateful only for his own self. And whoever is ungrateful, indeed my Lord is Free of need and Generous."﴾ ﴿He said, "Disguise her throne for her; we will see whether she is guided or is among those who are not guided."﴾ ﴿So when she came, it was said, "Is your throne like this?" She said, "It is as if it were it. And we were given knowledge before her, and we were Muslims (in submission)."﴾ ﴿And what she used to worship besides Allah barred her; indeed she was from a disbelieving people.﴾ ﴿It was said to her, "Enter the palace." And when she saw it, she thought it was a deep water, and she uncovered her shins. He said, "Indeed, it is a palace paved smooth with glass." She said, "My Lord, indeed I have wronged myself, and I have submitted with Solomon to Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾.

There is an omission in the speech, its estimated sense being: the messenger returned to her with the gift and informed her of what Solomon had sworn, so she prepared to set out to him, for she knew that he was a prophet and she had no power to fight a prophet. It is narrated that when she set out toward Solomon, she gave orders, so he (Solomon) placed her throne at the end of seven rooms, some within others, at the end of one of her palaces, and she locked the doors and appointed guards to protect it, and she set out toward Solomon with her elephants and followers.

ʿAbd Allah ibn Shaddad said: When she was a farsakh (about three miles) away from Solomon, he said, "Which of you will bring me her throne?" Ibn ʿAbbas said: Solomon was awe-inspiring; nothing was begun until he himself asked about it. One day he looked and saw a cloud of dust near him and said, "What is this?" They said, "Bilqis," so he said that (the words above).

They differed regarding Solomon's purpose in summoning her throne. Qatadah and Ibn Jurayj said: When the greatness and excellence of her throne was described to him, he wanted to take it before Islam would protect her and her people and prevent the seizure of their wealth, and Islam is on this religion. But this is distant, that such a thing would come from a prophet who was given a kingdom that was given to no one else. Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Zayd said: He summoned it to show her the power that is from Allah, and so that Solomon and Islam would prevail over her through this submission. Al-Zamakhshari pointed to an opinion, saying: "Perhaps it was revealed to him (peace be upon him) that her throne was secured, so he wanted to overcome her and show her, by this, some of the wonders that were produced by his hand, which were specific to him, along with her awareness of Allah's great power, and of what testifies to Solomon's prophethood and confirms it." End of quote. Al-Tabari said: He wanted to test the truthfulness of the hoopoe in his statement: "And she has a mighty throne" (Al-Naml: 23). But this is distant, because his truthfulness had already been shown in carrying the letter and what followed from its carrying, namely Bilqis's consultation with her people and her sending of the gift. It was said: He wanted it to be brought to him, then disguised and altered, then he would look to see whether she would recognize it or deny it, as a test of her intellect. The apparent order of these reports is according to the sequence in which they occurred in existence, and this is the view of the majority. From Ibn ʿAbbas it is reported that he said: "Which of you will bring me her throne?" when he began to examine the truthfulness of the hoopoe from its falsehood regarding his statement: "And she has a mighty throne" (Al-Naml: 23). In the ordering of the accounts there is then advancement and delay. And in His saying, "Which of you will bring me her throne?" there is evidence that it is permissible to seek help from some followers in the aims of kings, and evidence that some followers of the prophets may be given something that is not given to others, and evidence of the haste of the one from whom kings ask the fulfilment of a need, and the precedence of the devils in subjugation over humans, and their ability, by Allah's decree, to do what is far from human action.

Al-Jumhur read ʿIfrīt, and Abu Hayawa read it with a fatḥah on the ʿayn. Abu Rajaʾ, Abu al-Simmak, ʿĪsā, and it is narrated from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq read ʿIfriyah, with a kasrah on the ʿayn, a sukūn on the fāʾ, a kasrah on the rāʾ, followed by an open yāʾ, followed by the feminine tāʾ. Dhu al-Rummah said:

"As if it were a star in the wake of an ʿifriyah, hurled through the blackness of the night, shooting."

A group read ʿIfr, without yāʾ or tāʾ. It is said in the dialect of Ṭayyiʾ and Tamīm: ʿIfrāh, with an alif and the feminine tāʾ. There is also a sixth dialect: ʿUfāriyah, and a man may be described by it. Since it may also be applied to humans, it was specified by His saying "from the jinn." From Ibn ʿAbbas: his name was Ṣakhr. It is said: Kawrā. It is said: Dhakrān. And "I will bring it to you" (ātīka) may be a present-tense verb or an active participle. Qatadah, Mujahid, and Wahb said: "from your station" means from the seat of judgment, and he used to sit from dawn until noon every day. It is said: before you rise from your sitting and stand up.

"And indeed I am strong for it" means for bringing it, "strong" to carry it; "trustworthy" means I will not steal anything from it. Al-Hasan said: He was a disbeliever, but he was subjugated, and an ʿifrīt is only a disbeliever.

"He who had knowledge of the Book" — it is said he was from the angels, and he was Gabriel, as al-Nakhaʿi said. "The Book" is the Preserved Tablet, or the letter of Solomon to Bilqis. It is also said: an angel whom Allah strengthened Solomon with. It is also said: he was a man from humankind, named Āṣif ibn Barkhiyā, Solomon's scribe, who was a righteous and knowledgeable man, as the majority said. Or Asṭūām, or Hūd, or Malīkhā, as Qatadah said. Or Asṭūrus, or al-Khiḍr (peace be upon him), as Ibn Lahīʿah said. A group said: he was Ḍabbah ibn Udd, grandfather of the Banū Ḍabbah from the Arabs, and he was an excellent man who served Solomon, and was over a portion of his horses. These are conflicting opinions, and Allah has concealed his name, so his name should not be mentioned until a prophet reports it. Among the strangest opinions is that it was Solomon himself, as if he were saying to himself, "I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you," or that he addressed the ʿifrīt with it; al-Zamakhshari and others related this opinion, as if he regarded the ʿifrīt's statement as slow, so Solomon said this to him to belittle the ʿifrīt. "The Book" is the one sent down from Allah, or the Preserved Tablet, two views. As for the knowledge he was given, it is said: it is the Greatest Name of Allah, which is: "O Living, O Self-Subsisting." It is also said: "O Possessor of Majesty and Honour." It is also said in Hebrew: Ahyā Sharāhyā. Al-Hasan said: Allah, then al-Raḥmān.

The apparent meaning is that the return of the glance is literal, and that it is shorter in duration than the ʿifrīt's time. For this reason it is narrated that Solomon said: "I want something faster than that" when the ʿifrīt answered him. Since the one who looks is described as sending out his sight, as the poet said:

"And whenever you sent your gaze forth as a scout for your heart one day, the sights wearied you."

It was described as returning the glance, and the glance was described as returning. The meaning is that you send your glance, and before you return it, I have brought it to you, and it is before you. It is narrated that Āṣif said to Solomon (peace be upon him): "Extend your eyes until your glance reaches its end." So he extended his glance and looked toward Yemen. Āṣif called, and the throne vanished from its place in Maʾrib, then sprang forth beside Solomon's seat in Syria by the power of Allah, before he returned his glance. Ibn Jubayr and Qatadah said: before anyone on whom your glance falls, at the farthest point you can see, reaches you. Mujahid said: before you need to blink, that is, the duration in which you can extend your sight without blinking, and that is its return. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: These two views correspond to the view of those who said that the standing is from the seat of judgment, and those who said that the standing is from sitting; for the view that "return of the glance" is a blink, that is, before you close and open your eyes, since the second gives the shortest duration, and that is necessary. End of quote. It is also said: "your glance" means "what you are looking at," that is, before what you look at returns to you from the limit of your sight. This is the view of Ibn Jubayr and Qatadah mentioned earlier, since the one on whom your glance falls is what you are looking at. Al-Mawardi said: before your glance is withdrawn to you by death, so he informed him that he would come to him before his death. This is a distant interpretation; rather, the meaning is "I will bring it to you swiftly." It is also said: the return of the glance is metaphorical here, and it is of the type of figurative expression (majāz al-tamthīl), and what is intended is the shortness of the time for bringing it, as you say to your companion, "Do this in a moment," "in the return of a glance," or "in the blink of an eye," meaning speed: "I will bring it to you in a time faster than the time of the ʿifrīt."

"When he saw it set firmly in his presence": in the speech there is an omission, its estimated sense being: he called on Allah, and He brought it to him. "When he saw it," that is, Bilqis's throne. It is said: it descended upon Solomon from the air. It is said: it sprang from the earth. It is said: from beneath the throne of Solomon. "Set firmly" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), and "in his presence" is a complement dependent on it. When an adverbial phrase of place or time falls in the position of a state, the verb it depends on must be omitted. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: the verb governing the adverbial phrase appears in "set firmly," and this is what is always implied in every adverbial phrase that falls in the position of a state. Abu al-Baqāʾ said: "set firmly" means fixed, not shaking, and it is not the meaning of mere presence, for if it were so, it would not have been mentioned. End of quote. He took "set firmly" as an additional sense beyond absolute firmness, namely that it was not shaking, so that its meaning is different from the meaning of "in his presence." This is a good justification for mentioning the verb in the adverbial phrase used as a state. And it has been suggested that the verb be mentioned in what falls as a predicate of a prepositional phrase with a complete sense, in the poet's words:

"Glory is yours: if your Master is glorious, and if He is humbled, you are present in the midst of humiliation."

"He said, 'This is from the bounty of my Lord'": that is, this bringing of her throne and the attainment of what I wanted from it is from the bounty of my Lord upon me and His kindness. Then he gave the reason for that in his words, "to test me whether I will be grateful or ungrateful." Ibn ʿAbbas said: the meaning is: Shall I give thanks for the throne and its being brought, or shall I be ungrateful, when I see one who is below me in this world is more knowledgeable than I? End of quote. Solomon received the blessing and the bounty of Allah with thanks, for at that point it is a renewed blessing, and gratitude is a bond for blessings. "Shall I give thanks or shall I be ungrateful" is in the accusative position after "to test me," and it is suspended (taʿlīq), because it has the sense of a question, and the question has the sense of knowledge; the verb of testing is often suspended in this way, treating it as the verb of knowledge, even though it is not synonymous with it, since its real signified meaning is examination.

"And whoever is grateful, he is grateful only for his own self": that is, the reward of that gratitude returns to him, for he has preserved his soul from ingratitude for the blessing, and has done what is obligatory upon him of thanking Allah for His blessing upon him.

"And whoever is ungrateful": that is, to Allah's bounty and blessing upon him, "indeed my Lord is Free of need from his gratitude," the benefit of it does not return to Allah, for He is the Absolutely Free of need, the Generous by bestowing favours upon one who disbelieves His blessing. The apparent view is that His saying, "indeed my Lord is Free of need and Generous," is the response to the condition, and for this reason a fāʾ is implied in "Free of need," that is, free of need from his gratitude. It is permissible that the response is omitted, indicated by what precedes it of its counterpart, that is: "And whoever is ungrateful, then it is for himself," meaning that disbelief's punishment returns to him. It is also permissible that "mā" (whoever) is a relative pronoun, and the fāʾ entered into the predicate because it includes the sense of the condition.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 27, verses 38–44 (part 2 of 2):**

﴿He said, "Disguise her throne for her, so that we may see whether she will be guided or be among those who are not guided."﴾ It is related that the jinn sensed something from Sulayman, or suspected that he might marry Bilqis. They disliked this, and they slandered her to him, saying that she lacked intelligence and discernment, and that her leg was like the hoof of a beast. So he tested her intelligence and discernment by altering the throne, and tested her leg through the palace (al-sarh), so that she would uncover her shins before him.

As for the "disguising" (tankir) of her throne, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and al-Dahhak said: it was done by adding to it and subtracting from it. It was also said: by removing the gems and jewels that were on it. And it was said: by making its base its top and its front its back. Al-tankir means making it unrecognizable, changed from its form and appearance, just as a man disguises himself from people so that they do not recognize him.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿nanzur﴾ (we will see) in the jussive, as a response to the imperative (jawab al-amr, the answer that follows a command). Abu Haywa read it in the nominative, as a resumed sentence (isti'naf, a new clause), in which he informs of himself that he sees. The complement of ﴿ataHtadi﴾ (will she be guided) is omitted. The apparent meaning is: will she be guided to recognizing her throne, and its disguising will not be an obstacle to her recognizing it? Thereby her acute intelligence becomes evident, and it becomes clear that the condition of her throne was not hidden from him, even though they had sought to conceal it. Or: will she be guided to a correct answer when she is asked about it? Or: will she be guided to belief in the prophethood of Sulayman, peace be upon him, when she sees this miracle of the transporting of her throne from the place where she had left it, after she had locked the doors upon it and appointed guards for it?

﴿When she came﴾: there is an omission in the speech, meaning: so they disguised her throne and looked at what her answer would be when she was asked about it. ﴿When she came, it was said: "Is your throne like this?"﴾ That is, is the throne like this throne that you have seen, your throne that you left in your land? The construction was not "Is this your throne?" but came with the particle of comparison, so that this would not be a suggestion to her. When she saw it in a form she did not recognize, and some things of her throne were distinguishable in it, she did not affirm that it was it, nor did she categorically deny it. Rather she expressed it in the form of a comparison, saying: ﴿"As if it were it."﴾ This was from the excellence of her mind, since she did not affirm, in the probable case, either of the two permissible possibilities, that it was it or that it was not it, and she matched their comparison with her own comparison.

The apparent meaning is that His words, ﴿"And we were given knowledge before her, and we were Muslims"﴾, up to His words, ﴿"from a disbelieving people"﴾, are not from the speech of Bilqis, though they are connected to her speech. It was said: they are from the speech of Sulayman. It was said: they are from the speech of the people of Sulayman and his followers.

If it is from the words of Sulayman, it was said: "knowledge" here is particular, meaning: ﴿"we were given knowledge"﴾ of her Islam and her coming in obedience. ﴿"Before her"﴾, that is, before her coming. ﴿"And we were Muslims"﴾: monotheists, submissive.

Ibn Atiyyah said: there is an omission in the speech; its estimate is ﴿"as if it were it"﴾, and Sulayman said at that point: ﴿"And we were given knowledge before her"﴾, up to the end of the verse. He said this by way of enumerating the blessings of God Most High, and he said it according to what she knew and understood; he mentioned the blessing of God upon him and upon his forefathers. End of the summary.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿"And we were given knowledge"﴾ is from the speech of Sulayman and his council. (If you say:) to what did this speech and what is connected to it refer? (I say:) since the occasion in which she was asked about her throne, and she answered as she answered, was an occasion in which Sulayman and his council brought forth what is appropriate to their saying, "And we were given knowledge," such as saying, when she said "as if it were it": "She has been correct in her answer," so they matched the detailed account, while she was intelligent and sagacious. She had been granted Islam and knew the power of God and the soundness of prophethood through the signs that had preceded, at the time of the delegation of al-Mundhir. And by this wondrous matter of her throne they added to that their saying: (p-79) ﴿"And we were given knowledge, we ourselves, of God and His power and the soundness of the prophethood of Sulayman, what came from Him before her knowledge; and we have not ceased to be upon the religion of Islam."﴾ They thanked God for His favour upon them over her and for their preceding her in knowledge of God and Islam, and what had prevented her from advancing to Islam was the worship of the sun and her upbringing among the disbelievers.

It is permissible that it be from the speech of Bilqis, joined to her saying ﴿"as if it were it"﴾, and the meaning is: ﴿"And we were given knowledge of God and His power and the soundness of Sulayman's prophethood before this miracle"﴾, or before this condition, meaning what you have made clear of the signs at the time of the delegation of al-Mundhir, and we entered into Islam. Then God Most High said: ﴿"And he [i.e., what she worshipped] turned her away from what she had been, her going astray from the right path."﴾ It was said: ﴿"And He turned her away, or Sulayman did, from what she used to worship"﴾, with the omission of the preposition and the attachment of the verb. End of the quotation.

As for his saying, "It is permissible that it be from the speech of Bilqis," this is an opinion he has already advanced definitively, not merely as a permissible possibility. It was said: the meaning is "and we were given knowledge of the soundness of his prophethood through the signs that preceded, from the matter of the hoopoe and the messengers before this miracle, meaning bringing the throne." ﴿"And we were Muslims"﴾: obedient to your command and submissive to you.

The apparent meaning is that the agent of His words ﴿"and He turned her away"﴾ is His words ﴿"what she used to worship"﴾, and whether it is God or Sulayman. ﴿"What"﴾ is the object of ﴿"turned her away"﴾ with the preposition dropped; this was said by al-Tabari, and it is weak, permissible only in poetic necessity, such as the verse: "You pass by the abodes and do not turn aside," meaning: "away from the abodes." It is not among the places where the preposition is omitted. If the agent is "what she used to worship," then the object of turning away is Islam, the apparent meaning.

Al-Rummani said: the estimate is "awareness of the throne," because the believer is alert and the disbeliever is wicked.

The apparent meaning is that His words ﴿"and He turned her away"﴾ are conjoined to His words ﴿"and we were given"﴾ if it is from the speech of Sulayman, though it may admit the beginning of a report from God Most High to Muhammad, His prophet, and to his community. If ﴿"and we were given"﴾ is from the speech of Bilqis, then it is apparent that it is necessarily from the speech of God Most High and the speech of the one who said it is connected to His words, "Will you be guided, or will you be among those who are not guided?" The waw in ﴿"and He turned her away"﴾ is the waw of circumstance (waw al-hal), and the qad (indeed) is implied, which is disliked because of the long separation between them, and because inversion and reordering are not resorted to except in necessity.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿"innaHa"﴾ with a kasra on the hamza, while Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ibn Abi Ablah read it with a fatha. The fatha is either by estimating a preposition, meaning "because she," or it is in apposition to the agent, which is "what she used to worship."

Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi and others said: When Bilqis arrived, Sulayman commanded the jinn, and they made for him a palace (sarh), which is the courtyard's flat roof without a ceiling. They made it built like a cistern and filled it with water, and fish and frogs were placed in it, and in its middle a chair was set for Sulayman. When Bilqis reached it, she was told: "Enter upon the Prophet, peace be upon him." She saw the deep water and was frightened, but she had no choice but to obey the command, so she uncovered her shins. Sulayman saw her shins sound, free of what the jinn had said. When she reached this point, Sulayman said to her: "It is a palace smoothed with glass." At that point Bilqis submitted, yielded, embraced Islam and confessed against herself to wrongdoing.

In this narration there is an addition: that he placed his throne in the front of the palace and sat upon it, and the birds, the jinn and mankind gathered around it. Al-Zamakhshari said: he did this only to increase her awe of his affair, to confirm his prophethood for her, and to make her steadfast in the religion. End of the quotation.

The sarh is every high structure; from it comes "Build for me a tower (sarhan), that I may reach the means," and it derives from al-tasrih, which is the most explicit proclamation. Mujahid said: the sarh here is the pool. Ibn Isa said: the courtyard, and sarhat al-dar is its open yard. It was said: the sarh here is a palace of glass. In the speech there is an omission, meaning: so she entered it in obedience to the command.

Al-lujjah is abundant water. The uncovering of the shins is the custom of one who is wearing garments and wishes to wade through water to some destination. The purpose of the palace was only to dazzle, and the uncovering of the shin came about incidentally, unless what was related from the jinn is sound, that her shin was the shin of an animal with a hoof, in which case it is possible that verifying this was the intended purpose.

Ibn Kathir read ﴿"sa'aqiha"﴾ with a hamza, as recorded in the narration of al-Ikhriti, Wahb ibn Wadih, from him. Abu Ali said: it is weak, and likewise in the reading of Qunbul: "yukshafu 'an sa'q" (is uncovered of a shin). As for the hamzing of "al-su'uq" and "'ala su'uqihi," it is a well-known dialect (lughah) of hamzing a waw preceded by a damma. Abu Ali related that Abu Hayyah al-Numayri used to hamz every waw preceded by a damma, and he recited:

*"Dearest of those who kindle fires to me is Musa."*

The apparent meaning is that the agent is said to be Sulayman, and it is possible that the agent is the one who commanded her to enter the palace. Her wronging of herself was said to be by disbelief, and it was said: by her assumption that Sulayman intended to test her.

Ibn Atiyyah said: "ma'a" is an adverb built on a fatha; but when the 'ayn is made sukun, there is no dispute that it is a particle that came for a meaning. End of the quotation. The correct view is that it is an adverb, whether the 'ayn is vocalized with a fatha or made sukun. The sukun is not restricted to poetry, as some have claimed; rather it is a dialect of some Arabs. Its adverbial sense is figurative, and it is in fact a noun that indicates the meaning of companionship.

(p-75)﴿He said, "O chiefs, which of you will bring me her throne before they come to me in submission?"﴾ ﴿A powerful one (ʿifrīt) of the jinn said, "I will bring it to you before you rise from your place. Indeed, I am strong and trustworthy for it."﴾ ﴿One who had knowledge from the Book said, "I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you." And when he saw it set firmly in his presence, he said, "This is from the bounty of my Lord, to test me whether I will be grateful or ungrateful. And whoever is grateful, he is grateful only for his own self. And whoever is ungrateful, indeed my Lord is Free of need and Generous."﴾ ﴿He said, "Disguise her throne for her; we will see whether she is guided or is among those who are not guided."﴾ ﴿So when she came, it was said, "Is your throne like this?" She said, "It is as if it were it. And we were given knowledge before her, and we were Muslims (in submission)."﴾ ﴿And what she used to worship besides Allah barred her; indeed she was from a disbelieving people.﴾ ﴿It was said to her, "Enter the palace." And when she saw it, she thought it was a deep water, and she uncovered her shins. He said, "Indeed, it is a palace paved smooth with glass." She said, "My Lord, indeed I have wronged myself, and I have submitted with Solomon to Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾.

There is an omission in the speech, its estimated sense being: the messenger returned to her with the gift and informed her of what Solomon had sworn, so she prepared to set out to him, for she knew that he was a prophet and she had no power to fight a prophet. It is narrated that when she set out toward Solomon, she gave orders, so he (Solomon) placed her throne at the end of seven rooms, some within others, at the end of one of her palaces, and she locked the doors and appointed guards to protect it, and she set out toward Solomon with her elephants and followers.

ʿAbd Allah ibn Shaddad said: When she was a farsakh (about three miles) away from Solomon, he said, "Which of you will bring me her throne?" Ibn ʿAbbas said: Solomon was awe-inspiring; nothing was begun until he himself asked about it. One day he looked and saw a cloud of dust near him and said, "What is this?" They said, "Bilqis," so he said that (the words above).

They differed regarding Solomon's purpose in summoning her throne. Qatadah and Ibn Jurayj said: When the greatness and excellence of her throne was described to him, he wanted to take it before Islam would protect her and her people and prevent the seizure of their wealth, and Islam is on this religion. But this is distant, that such a thing would come from a prophet who was given a kingdom that was given to no one else. Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Zayd said: He summoned it to show her the power that is from Allah, and so that Solomon and Islam would prevail over her through this submission. Al-Zamakhshari pointed to an opinion, saying: "Perhaps it was revealed to him (peace be upon him) that her throne was secured, so he wanted to overcome her and show her, by this, some of the wonders that were produced by his hand, which were specific to him, along with her awareness of Allah's great power, and of what testifies to Solomon's prophethood and confirms it." End of quote. Al-Tabari said: He wanted to test the truthfulness of the hoopoe in his statement: "And she has a mighty throne" (Al-Naml: 23). But this is distant, because his truthfulness had already been shown in carrying the letter and what followed from its carrying, namely Bilqis's consultation with her people and her sending of the gift. It was said: He wanted it to be brought to him, then disguised and altered, then he would look to see whether she would recognize it or deny it, as a test of her intellect. The apparent order of these reports is according to the sequence in which they occurred in existence, and this is the view of the majority. From Ibn ʿAbbas it is reported that he said: "Which of you will bring me her throne?" when he began to examine the truthfulness of the hoopoe from its falsehood regarding his statement: "And she has a mighty throne" (Al-Naml: 23). In the ordering of the accounts there is then advancement and delay. And in His saying, "Which of you will bring me her throne?" there is evidence that it is permissible to seek help from some followers in the aims of kings, and evidence that some followers of the prophets may be given something that is not given to others, and evidence of the haste of the one from whom kings ask the fulfilment of a need, and the precedence of the devils in subjugation over humans, and their ability, by Allah's decree, to do what is far from human action.

Al-Jumhur read ʿIfrīt, and Abu Hayawa read it with a fatḥah on the ʿayn. Abu Rajaʾ, Abu al-Simmak, ʿĪsā, and it is narrated from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq read ʿIfriyah, with a kasrah on the ʿayn, a sukūn on the fāʾ, a kasrah on the rāʾ, followed by an open yāʾ, followed by the feminine tāʾ. Dhu al-Rummah said:

"As if it were a star in the wake of an ʿifriyah, hurled through the blackness of the night, shooting."

A group read ʿIfr, without yāʾ or tāʾ. It is said in the dialect of Ṭayyiʾ and Tamīm: ʿIfrāh, with an alif and the feminine tāʾ. There is also a sixth dialect: ʿUfāriyah, and a man may be described by it. Since it may also be applied to humans, it was specified by His saying "from the jinn." From Ibn ʿAbbas: his name was Ṣakhr. It is said: Kawrā. It is said: Dhakrān. And "I will bring it to you" (ātīka) may be a present-tense verb or an active participle. Qatadah, Mujahid, and Wahb said: "from your station" means from the seat of judgment, and he used to sit from dawn until noon every day. It is said: before you rise from your sitting and stand up.

"And indeed I am strong for it" means for bringing it, "strong" to carry it; "trustworthy" means I will not steal anything from it. Al-Hasan said: He was a disbeliever, but he was subjugated, and an ʿifrīt is only a disbeliever.

"He who had knowledge of the Book" — it is said he was from the angels, and he was Gabriel, as al-Nakhaʿi said. "The Book" is the Preserved Tablet, or the letter of Solomon to Bilqis. It is also said: an angel whom Allah strengthened Solomon with. It is also said: he was a man from humankind, named Āṣif ibn Barkhiyā, Solomon's scribe, who was a righteous and knowledgeable man, as the majority said. Or Asṭūām, or Hūd, or Malīkhā, as Qatadah said. Or Asṭūrus, or al-Khiḍr (peace be upon him), as Ibn Lahīʿah said. A group said: he was Ḍabbah ibn Udd, grandfather of the Banū Ḍabbah from the Arabs, and he was an excellent man who served Solomon, and was over a portion of his horses. These are conflicting opinions, and Allah has concealed his name, so his name should not be mentioned until a prophet reports it. Among the strangest opinions is that it was Solomon himself, as if he were saying to himself, "I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you," or that he addressed the ʿifrīt with it; al-Zamakhshari and others related this opinion, as if he regarded the ʿifrīt's statement as slow, so Solomon said this to him to belittle the ʿifrīt. "The Book" is the one sent down from Allah, or the Preserved Tablet, two views. As for the knowledge he was given, it is said: it is the Greatest Name of Allah, which is: "O Living, O Self-Subsisting." It is also said: "O Possessor of Majesty and Honour." It is also said in Hebrew: Ahyā Sharāhyā. Al-Hasan said: Allah, then al-Raḥmān.

The apparent meaning is that the return of the glance is literal, and that it is shorter in duration than the ʿifrīt's time. For this reason it is narrated that Solomon said: "I want something faster than that" when the ʿifrīt answered him. Since the one who looks is described as sending out his sight, as the poet said:

"And whenever you sent your gaze forth as a scout for your heart one day, the sights wearied you."

It was described as returning the glance, and the glance was described as returning. The meaning is that you send your glance, and before you return it, I have brought it to you, and it is before you. It is narrated that Āṣif said to Solomon (peace be upon him): "Extend your eyes until your glance reaches its end." So he extended his glance and looked toward Yemen. Āṣif called, and the throne vanished from its place in Maʾrib, then sprang forth beside Solomon's seat in Syria by the power of Allah, before he returned his glance. Ibn Jubayr and Qatadah said: before anyone on whom your glance falls, at the farthest point you can see, reaches you. Mujahid said: before you need to blink, that is, the duration in which you can extend your sight without blinking, and that is its return. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: These two views correspond to the view of those who said that the standing is from the seat of judgment, and those who said that the standing is from sitting; for the view that "return of the glance" is a blink, that is, before you close and open your eyes, since the second gives the shortest duration, and that is necessary. End of quote. It is also said: "your glance" means "what you are looking at," that is, before what you look at returns to you from the limit of your sight. This is the view of Ibn Jubayr and Qatadah mentioned earlier, since the one on whom your glance falls is what you are looking at. Al-Mawardi said: before your glance is withdrawn to you by death, so he informed him that he would come to him before his death. This is a distant interpretation; rather, the meaning is "I will bring it to you swiftly." It is also said: the return of the glance is metaphorical here, and it is of the type of figurative expression (majāz al-tamthīl), and what is intended is the shortness of the time for bringing it, as you say to your companion, "Do this in a moment," "in the return of a glance," or "in the blink of an eye," meaning speed: "I will bring it to you in a time faster than the time of the ʿifrīt."

"When he saw it set firmly in his presence": in the speech there is an omission, its estimated sense being: he called on Allah, and He brought it to him. "When he saw it," that is, Bilqis's throne. It is said: it descended upon Solomon from the air. It is said: it sprang from the earth. It is said: from beneath the throne of Solomon. "Set firmly" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), and "in his presence" is a complement dependent on it. When an adverbial phrase of place or time falls in the position of a state, the verb it depends on must be omitted. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: the verb governing the adverbial phrase appears in "set firmly," and this is what is always implied in every adverbial phrase that falls in the position of a state. Abu al-Baqāʾ said: "set firmly" means fixed, not shaking, and it is not the meaning of mere presence, for if it were so, it would not have been mentioned. End of quote. He took "set firmly" as an additional sense beyond absolute firmness, namely that it was not shaking, so that its meaning is different from the meaning of "in his presence." This is a good justification for mentioning the verb in the adverbial phrase used as a state. And it has been suggested that the verb be mentioned in what falls as a predicate of a prepositional phrase with a complete sense, in the poet's words:

"Glory is yours: if your Master is glorious, and if He is humbled, you are present in the midst of humiliation."

"He said, 'This is from the bounty of my Lord'": that is, this bringing of her throne and the attainment of what I wanted from it is from the bounty of my Lord upon me and His kindness. Then he gave the reason for that in his words, "to test me whether I will be grateful or ungrateful." Ibn ʿAbbas said: the meaning is: Shall I give thanks for the throne and its being brought, or shall I be ungrateful, when I see one who is below me in this world is more knowledgeable than I? End of quote. Solomon received the blessing and the bounty of Allah with thanks, for at that point it is a renewed blessing, and gratitude is a bond for blessings. "Shall I give thanks or shall I be ungrateful" is in the accusative position after "to test me," and it is suspended (taʿlīq), because it has the sense of a question, and the question has the sense of knowledge; the verb of testing is often suspended in this way, treating it as the verb of knowledge, even though it is not synonymous with it, since its real signified meaning is examination.

"And whoever is grateful, he is grateful only for his own self": that is, the reward of that gratitude returns to him, for he has preserved his soul from ingratitude for the blessing, and has done what is obligatory upon him of thanking Allah for His blessing upon him.

"And whoever is ungrateful": that is, to Allah's bounty and blessing upon him, "indeed my Lord is Free of need from his gratitude," the benefit of it does not return to Allah, for He is the Absolutely Free of need, the Generous by bestowing favours upon one who disbelieves His blessing. The apparent view is that His saying, "indeed my Lord is Free of need and Generous," is the response to the condition, and for this reason a fāʾ is implied in "Free of need," that is, free of need from his gratitude. It is permissible that the response is omitted, indicated by what precedes it of its counterpart, that is: "And whoever is ungrateful, then it is for himself," meaning that disbelief's punishment returns to him. It is also permissible that "mā" (whoever) is a relative pronoun, and the fāʾ entered into the predicate because it includes the sense of the condition.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 27, verses 38–44 (part 2 of 2):**

﴿He said, "Disguise her throne for her, so that we may see whether she will be guided or be among those who are not guided."﴾ It is related that the jinn sensed something from Sulayman, or suspected that he might marry Bilqis. They disliked this, and they slandered her to him, saying that she lacked intelligence and discernment, and that her leg was like the hoof of a beast. So he tested her intelligence and discernment by altering the throne, and tested her leg through the palace (al-sarh), so that she would uncover her shins before him.

As for the "disguising" (tankir) of her throne, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and al-Dahhak said: it was done by adding to it and subtracting from it. It was also said: by removing the gems and jewels that were on it. And it was said: by making its base its top and its front its back. Al-tankir means making it unrecognizable, changed from its form and appearance, just as a man disguises himself from people so that they do not recognize him.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿nanzur﴾ (we will see) in the jussive, as a response to the imperative (jawab al-amr, the answer that follows a command). Abu Haywa read it in the nominative, as a resumed sentence (isti'naf, a new clause), in which he informs of himself that he sees. The complement of ﴿ataHtadi﴾ (will she be guided) is omitted. The apparent meaning is: will she be guided to recognizing her throne, and its disguising will not be an obstacle to her recognizing it? Thereby her acute intelligence becomes evident, and it becomes clear that the condition of her throne was not hidden from him, even though they had sought to conceal it. Or: will she be guided to a correct answer when she is asked about it? Or: will she be guided to belief in the prophethood of Sulayman, peace be upon him, when she sees this miracle of the transporting of her throne from the place where she had left it, after she had locked the doors upon it and appointed guards for it?

﴿When she came﴾: there is an omission in the speech, meaning: so they disguised her throne and looked at what her answer would be when she was asked about it. ﴿When she came, it was said: "Is your throne like this?"﴾ That is, is the throne like this throne that you have seen, your throne that you left in your land? The construction was not "Is this your throne?" but came with the particle of comparison, so that this would not be a suggestion to her. When she saw it in a form she did not recognize, and some things of her throne were distinguishable in it, she did not affirm that it was it, nor did she categorically deny it. Rather she expressed it in the form of a comparison, saying: ﴿"As if it were it."﴾ This was from the excellence of her mind, since she did not affirm, in the probable case, either of the two permissible possibilities, that it was it or that it was not it, and she matched their comparison with her own comparison.

The apparent meaning is that His words, ﴿"And we were given knowledge before her, and we were Muslims"﴾, up to His words, ﴿"from a disbelieving people"﴾, are not from the speech of Bilqis, though they are connected to her speech. It was said: they are from the speech of Sulayman. It was said: they are from the speech of the people of Sulayman and his followers.

If it is from the words of Sulayman, it was said: "knowledge" here is particular, meaning: ﴿"we were given knowledge"﴾ of her Islam and her coming in obedience. ﴿"Before her"﴾, that is, before her coming. ﴿"And we were Muslims"﴾: monotheists, submissive.

Ibn Atiyyah said: there is an omission in the speech; its estimate is ﴿"as if it were it"﴾, and Sulayman said at that point: ﴿"And we were given knowledge before her"﴾, up to the end of the verse. He said this by way of enumerating the blessings of God Most High, and he said it according to what she knew and understood; he mentioned the blessing of God upon him and upon his forefathers. End of the summary.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿"And we were given knowledge"﴾ is from the speech of Sulayman and his council. (If you say:) to what did this speech and what is connected to it refer? (I say:) since the occasion in which she was asked about her throne, and she answered as she answered, was an occasion in which Sulayman and his council brought forth what is appropriate to their saying, "And we were given knowledge," such as saying, when she said "as if it were it": "She has been correct in her answer," so they matched the detailed account, while she was intelligent and sagacious. She had been granted Islam and knew the power of God and the soundness of prophethood through the signs that had preceded, at the time of the delegation of al-Mundhir. And by this wondrous matter of her throne they added to that their saying: (p-79) ﴿"And we were given knowledge, we ourselves, of God and His power and the soundness of the prophethood of Sulayman, what came from Him before her knowledge; and we have not ceased to be upon the religion of Islam."﴾ They thanked God for His favour upon them over her and for their preceding her in knowledge of God and Islam, and what had prevented her from advancing to Islam was the worship of the sun and her upbringing among the disbelievers.

It is permissible that it be from the speech of Bilqis, joined to her saying ﴿"as if it were it"﴾, and the meaning is: ﴿"And we were given knowledge of God and His power and the soundness of Sulayman's prophethood before this miracle"﴾, or before this condition, meaning what you have made clear of the signs at the time of the delegation of al-Mundhir, and we entered into Islam. Then God Most High said: ﴿"And he [i.e., what she worshipped] turned her away from what she had been, her going astray from the right path."﴾ It was said: ﴿"And He turned her away, or Sulayman did, from what she used to worship"﴾, with the omission of the preposition and the attachment of the verb. End of the quotation.

As for his saying, "It is permissible that it be from the speech of Bilqis," this is an opinion he has already advanced definitively, not merely as a permissible possibility. It was said: the meaning is "and we were given knowledge of the soundness of his prophethood through the signs that preceded, from the matter of the hoopoe and the messengers before this miracle, meaning bringing the throne." ﴿"And we were Muslims"﴾: obedient to your command and submissive to you.

The apparent meaning is that the agent of His words ﴿"and He turned her away"﴾ is His words ﴿"what she used to worship"﴾, and whether it is God or Sulayman. ﴿"What"﴾ is the object of ﴿"turned her away"﴾ with the preposition dropped; this was said by al-Tabari, and it is weak, permissible only in poetic necessity, such as the verse: "You pass by the abodes and do not turn aside," meaning: "away from the abodes." It is not among the places where the preposition is omitted. If the agent is "what she used to worship," then the object of turning away is Islam, the apparent meaning.

Al-Rummani said: the estimate is "awareness of the throne," because the believer is alert and the disbeliever is wicked.
