And whoever is grateful, he is grateful only for his own self. And whoever is ungrateful, indeed my Lord is Free of need and Generous."﴾ ﴿He said, "Disguise her throne for her; we will see whether she is guided or is among those who are not guided."﴾ ﴿So when she came, it was said, "Is your throne like this?" She said, "It is as if it were it. And we were given knowledge before her, and we were Muslims (in submission)."﴾ ﴿And what she used to worship besides Allah barred her; indeed she was from a disbelieving people.﴾ ﴿It was said to her, "Enter the palace." And when she saw it, she thought it was a deep water, and she uncovered her shins. He said, "Indeed, it is a palace paved smooth with glass." She said, "My Lord, indeed I have wronged myself, and I have submitted with Solomon to Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾.

There is an omission in the speech, its estimated sense being: the messenger returned to her with the gift and informed her of what Solomon had sworn, so she prepared to set out to him, for she knew that he was a prophet and she had no power to fight a prophet. It is narrated that when she set out toward Solomon, she gave orders, so he (Solomon) placed her throne at the end of seven rooms, some within others, at the end of one of her palaces, and she locked the doors and appointed guards to protect it, and she set out toward Solomon with her elephants and followers.

ʿAbd Allah ibn Shaddad said: When she was a farsakh (about three miles) away from Solomon, he said, "Which of you will bring me her throne?" Ibn ʿAbbas said: Solomon was awe-inspiring; nothing was begun until he himself asked about it. One day he looked and saw a cloud of dust near him and said, "What is this?" They said, "Bilqis," so he said that (the words above).

They differed regarding Solomon's purpose in summoning her throne. Qatadah and Ibn Jurayj said: When the greatness and excellence of her throne was described to him, he wanted to take it before Islam would protect her and her people and prevent the seizure of their wealth, and Islam is on this religion. But this is distant, that such a thing would come from a prophet who was given a kingdom that was given to no one else. Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Zayd said: He summoned it to show her the power that is from Allah, and so that Solomon and Islam would prevail over her through this submission. Al-Zamakhshari pointed to an opinion, saying: "Perhaps it was revealed to him (peace be upon him) that her throne was secured, so he wanted to overcome her and show her, by this, some of the wonders that were produced by his hand, which were specific to him, along with her awareness of Allah's great power, and of what testifies to Solomon's prophethood and confirms it." End of quote. Al-Tabari said: He wanted to test the truthfulness of the hoopoe in his statement: "And she has a mighty throne" (Al-Naml: 23). But this is distant, because his truthfulness had already been shown in carrying the letter and what followed from its carrying, namely Bilqis's consultation with her people and her sending of the gift. It was said: He wanted it to be brought to him, then disguised and altered, then he would look to see whether she would recognize it or deny it, as a test of her intellect. The apparent order of these reports is according to the sequence in which they occurred in existence, and this is the view of the majority. From Ibn ʿAbbas it is reported that he said: "Which of you will bring me her throne?" when he began to examine the truthfulness of the hoopoe from its falsehood regarding his statement: "And she has a mighty throne" (Al-Naml: 23). In the ordering of the accounts there is then advancement and delay. And in His saying, "Which of you will bring me her throne?" there is evidence that it is permissible to seek help from some followers in the aims of kings, and evidence that some followers of the prophets may be given something that is not given to others, and evidence of the haste of the one from whom kings ask the fulfilment of a need, and the precedence of the devils in subjugation over humans, and their ability, by Allah's decree, to do what is far from human action.

Al-Jumhur read ʿIfrīt, and Abu Hayawa read it with a fatḥah on the ʿayn. Abu Rajaʾ, Abu al-Simmak, ʿĪsā, and it is narrated from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq read ʿIfriyah, with a kasrah on the ʿayn, a sukūn on the fāʾ, a kasrah on the rāʾ, followed by an open yāʾ, followed by the feminine tāʾ. Dhu al-Rummah said:

"As if it were a star in the wake of an ʿifriyah, hurled through the blackness of the night, shooting."

A group read ʿIfr, without yāʾ or tāʾ. It is said in the dialect of Ṭayyiʾ and Tamīm: ʿIfrāh, with an alif and the feminine tāʾ. There is also a sixth dialect: ʿUfāriyah, and a man may be described by it. Since it may also be applied to humans, it was specified by His saying "from the jinn." From Ibn ʿAbbas: his name was Ṣakhr. It is said: Kawrā. It is said: Dhakrān. And "I will bring it to you" (ātīka) may be a present-tense verb or an active participle. Qatadah, Mujahid, and Wahb said: "from your station" means from the seat of judgment, and he used to sit from dawn until noon every day. It is said: before you rise from your sitting and stand up.

"And indeed I am strong for it" means for bringing it, "strong" to carry it; "trustworthy" means I will not steal anything from it. Al-Hasan said: He was a disbeliever, but he was subjugated, and an ʿifrīt is only a disbeliever.

"He who had knowledge of the Book" — it is said he was from the angels, and he was Gabriel, as al-Nakhaʿi said. "The Book" is the Preserved Tablet, or the letter of Solomon to Bilqis. It is also said: an angel whom Allah strengthened Solomon with. It is also said: he was a man from humankind, named Āṣif ibn Barkhiyā, Solomon's scribe, who was a righteous and knowledgeable man, as the majority said. Or Asṭūām, or Hūd, or Malīkhā, as Qatadah said. Or Asṭūrus, or al-Khiḍr (peace be upon him), as Ibn Lahīʿah said. A group said: he was Ḍabbah ibn Udd, grandfather of the Banū Ḍabbah from the Arabs, and he was an excellent man who served Solomon, and was over a portion of his horses. These are conflicting opinions, and Allah has concealed his name, so his name should not be mentioned until a prophet reports it. Among the strangest opinions is that it was Solomon himself, as if he were saying to himself, "I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you," or that he addressed the ʿifrīt with it; al-Zamakhshari and others related this opinion, as if he regarded the ʿifrīt's statement as slow, so Solomon said this to him to belittle the ʿifrīt. "The Book" is the one sent down from Allah, or the Preserved Tablet, two views. As for the knowledge he was given, it is said: it is the Greatest Name of Allah, which is: "O Living, O Self-Subsisting." It is also said: "O Possessor of Majesty and Honour." It is also said in Hebrew: Ahyā Sharāhyā. Al-Hasan said: Allah, then al-Raḥmān.

The apparent meaning is that the return of the glance is literal, and that it is shorter in duration than the ʿifrīt's time. For this reason it is narrated that Solomon said: "I want something faster than that" when the ʿifrīt answered him. Since the one who looks is described as sending out his sight, as the poet said:

"And whenever you sent your gaze forth as a scout for your heart one day, the sights wearied you."

It was described as returning the glance, and the glance was described as returning. The meaning is that you send your glance, and before you return it, I have brought it to you, and it is before you. It is narrated that Āṣif said to Solomon (peace be upon him): "Extend your eyes until your glance reaches its end." So he extended his glance and looked toward Yemen. Āṣif called, and the throne vanished from its place in Maʾrib, then sprang forth beside Solomon's seat in Syria by the power of Allah, before he returned his glance. Ibn Jubayr and Qatadah said: before anyone on whom your glance falls, at the farthest point you can see, reaches you. Mujahid said: before you need to blink, that is, the duration in which you can extend your sight without blinking, and that is its return. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: These two views correspond to the view of those who said that the standing is from the seat of judgment, and those who said that the standing is from sitting; for the view that "return of the glance" is a blink, that is, before you close and open your eyes, since the second gives the shortest duration, and that is necessary. End of quote. It is also said: "your glance" means "what you are looking at," that is, before what you look at returns to you from the limit of your sight. This is the view of Ibn Jubayr and Qatadah mentioned earlier, since the one on whom your glance falls is what you are looking at. Al-Mawardi said: before your glance is withdrawn to you by death, so he informed him that he would come to him before his death. This is a distant interpretation; rather, the meaning is "I will bring it to you swiftly." It is also said: the return of the glance is metaphorical here, and it is of the type of figurative expression (majāz al-tamthīl), and what is intended is the shortness of the time for bringing it, as you say to your companion, "Do this in a moment," "in the return of a glance," or "in the blink of an eye," meaning speed: "I will bring it to you in a time faster than the time of the ʿifrīt."

"When he saw it set firmly in his presence": in the speech there is an omission, its estimated sense being: he called on Allah, and He brought it to him. "When he saw it," that is, Bilqis's throne. It is said: it descended upon Solomon from the air. It is said: it sprang from the earth. It is said: from beneath the throne of Solomon. "Set firmly" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), and "in his presence" is a complement dependent on it. When an adverbial phrase of place or time falls in the position of a state, the verb it depends on must be omitted. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: the verb governing the adverbial phrase appears in "set firmly," and this is what is always implied in every adverbial phrase that falls in the position of a state. Abu al-Baqāʾ said: "set firmly" means fixed, not shaking, and it is not the meaning of mere presence, for if it were so, it would not have been mentioned. End of quote. He took "set firmly" as an additional sense beyond absolute firmness, namely that it was not shaking, so that its meaning is different from the meaning of "in his presence." This is a good justification for mentioning the verb in the adverbial phrase used as a state. And it has been suggested that the verb be mentioned in what falls as a predicate of a prepositional phrase with a complete sense, in the poet's words:

"Glory is yours: if your Master is glorious, and if He is humbled, you are present in the midst of humiliation."

"He said, 'This is from the bounty of my Lord'": that is, this bringing of her throne and the attainment of what I wanted from it is from the bounty of my Lord upon me and His kindness. Then he gave the reason for that in his words, "to test me whether I will be grateful or ungrateful." Ibn ʿAbbas said: the meaning is: Shall I give thanks for the throne and its being brought, or shall I be ungrateful, when I see one who is below me in this world is more knowledgeable than I? End of quote. Solomon received the blessing and the bounty of Allah with thanks, for at that point it is a renewed blessing, and gratitude is a bond for blessings. "Shall I give thanks or shall I be ungrateful" is in the accusative position after "to test me," and it is suspended (taʿlīq), because it has the sense of a question, and the question has the sense of knowledge; the verb of testing is often suspended in this way, treating it as the verb of knowledge, even though it is not synonymous with it, since its real signified meaning is examination.

"And whoever is grateful, he is grateful only for his own self": that is, the reward of that gratitude returns to him, for he has preserved his soul from ingratitude for the blessing, and has done what is obligatory upon him of thanking Allah for His blessing upon him.

"And whoever is ungrateful": that is, to Allah's bounty and blessing upon him, "indeed my Lord is Free of need from his gratitude," the benefit of it does not return to Allah, for He is the Absolutely Free of need, the Generous by bestowing favours upon one who disbelieves His blessing. The apparent view is that His saying, "indeed my Lord is Free of need and Generous," is the response to the condition, and for this reason a fāʾ is implied in "Free of need," that is, free of need from his gratitude. It is permissible that the response is omitted, indicated by what precedes it of its counterpart, that is: "And whoever is ungrateful, then it is for himself," meaning that disbelief's punishment returns to him. It is also permissible that "mā" (whoever) is a relative pronoun, and the fāʾ entered into the predicate because it includes the sense of the condition.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 27, verses 38–44 (part 2 of 2):**

﴿He said, "Disguise her throne for her, so that we may see whether she will be guided or be among those who are not guided."﴾ It is related that the jinn sensed something from Sulayman, or suspected that he might marry Bilqis. They disliked this, and they slandered her to him, saying that she lacked intelligence and discernment, and that her leg was like the hoof of a beast. So he tested her intelligence and discernment by altering the throne, and tested her leg through the palace (al-sarh), so that she would uncover her shins before him.

As for the "disguising" (tankir) of her throne, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and al-Dahhak said: it was done by adding to it and subtracting from it. It was also said: by removing the gems and jewels that were on it. And it was said: by making its base its top and its front its back. Al-tankir means making it unrecognizable, changed from its form and appearance, just as a man disguises himself from people so that they do not recognize him.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿nanzur﴾ (we will see) in the jussive, as a response to the imperative (jawab al-amr, the answer that follows a command). Abu Haywa read it in the nominative, as a resumed sentence (isti'naf, a new clause), in which he informs of himself that he sees. The complement of ﴿ataHtadi﴾ (will she be guided) is omitted. The apparent meaning is: will she be guided to recognizing her throne, and its disguising will not be an obstacle to her recognizing it? Thereby her acute intelligence becomes evident, and it becomes clear that the condition of her throne was not hidden from him, even though they had sought to conceal it. Or: will she be guided to a correct answer when she is asked about it? Or: will she be guided to belief in the prophethood of Sulayman, peace be upon him, when she sees this miracle of the transporting of her throne from the place where she had left it, after she had locked the doors upon it and appointed guards for it?

﴿When she came﴾: there is an omission in the speech, meaning: so they disguised her throne and looked at what her answer would be when she was asked about it. ﴿When she came, it was said: "Is your throne like this?"﴾ That is, is the throne like this throne that you have seen, your throne that you left in your land? The construction was not "Is this your throne?" but came with the particle of comparison, so that this would not be a suggestion to her. When she saw it in a form she did not recognize, and some things of her throne were distinguishable in it, she did not affirm that it was it, nor did she categorically deny it. Rather she expressed it in the form of a comparison, saying: ﴿"As if it were it."﴾ This was from the excellence of her mind, since she did not affirm, in the probable case, either of the two permissible possibilities, that it was it or that it was not it, and she matched their comparison with her own comparison.

The apparent meaning is that His words, ﴿"And we were given knowledge before her, and we were Muslims"﴾, up to His words, ﴿"from a disbelieving people"﴾, are not from the speech of Bilqis, though they are connected to her speech. It was said: they are from the speech of Sulayman. It was said: they are from the speech of the people of Sulayman and his followers.

If it is from the words of Sulayman, it was said: "knowledge" here is particular, meaning: ﴿"we were given knowledge"﴾ of her Islam and her coming in obedience. ﴿"Before her"﴾, that is, before her coming. ﴿"And we were Muslims"﴾: monotheists, submissive.

Ibn Atiyyah said: there is an omission in the speech; its estimate is ﴿"as if it were it"﴾, and Sulayman said at that point: ﴿"And we were given knowledge before her"﴾, up to the end of the verse. He said this by way of enumerating the blessings of God Most High, and he said it according to what she knew and understood; he mentioned the blessing of God upon him and upon his forefathers. End of the summary.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿"And we were given knowledge"﴾ is from the speech of Sulayman and his council. (If you say:) to what did this speech and what is connected to it refer? (I say:) since the occasion in which she was asked about her throne, and she answered as she answered, was an occasion in which Sulayman and his council brought forth what is appropriate to their saying, "And we were given knowledge," such as saying, when she said "as if it were it": "She has been correct in her answer," so they matched the detailed account, while she was intelligent and sagacious. She had been granted Islam and knew the power of God and the soundness of prophethood through the signs that had preceded, at the time of the delegation of al-Mundhir. And by this wondrous matter of her throne they added to that their saying: (p-79) ﴿"And we were given knowledge, we ourselves, of God and His power and the soundness of the prophethood of Sulayman, what came from Him before her knowledge; and we have not ceased to be upon the religion of Islam."﴾ They thanked God for His favour upon them over her and for their preceding her in knowledge of God and Islam, and what had prevented her from advancing to Islam was the worship of the sun and her upbringing among the disbelievers.

It is permissible that it be from the speech of Bilqis, joined to her saying ﴿"as if it were it"﴾, and the meaning is: ﴿"And we were given knowledge of God and His power and the soundness of Sulayman's prophethood before this miracle"﴾, or before this condition, meaning what you have made clear of the signs at the time of the delegation of al-Mundhir, and we entered into Islam. Then God Most High said: ﴿"And he [i.e., what she worshipped] turned her away from what she had been, her going astray from the right path."﴾ It was said: ﴿"And He turned her away, or Sulayman did, from what she used to worship"﴾, with the omission of the preposition and the attachment of the verb. End of the quotation.

As for his saying, "It is permissible that it be from the speech of Bilqis," this is an opinion he has already advanced definitively, not merely as a permissible possibility. It was said: the meaning is "and we were given knowledge of the soundness of his prophethood through the signs that preceded, from the matter of the hoopoe and the messengers before this miracle, meaning bringing the throne." ﴿"And we were Muslims"﴾: obedient to your command and submissive to you.

The apparent meaning is that the agent of His words ﴿"and He turned her away"﴾ is His words ﴿"what she used to worship"﴾, and whether it is God or Sulayman. ﴿"What"﴾ is the object of ﴿"turned her away"﴾ with the preposition dropped; this was said by al-Tabari, and it is weak, permissible only in poetic necessity, such as the verse: "You pass by the abodes and do not turn aside," meaning: "away from the abodes." It is not among the places where the preposition is omitted. If the agent is "what she used to worship," then the object of turning away is Islam, the apparent meaning.

Al-Rummani said: the estimate is "awareness of the throne," because the believer is alert and the disbeliever is wicked.

The apparent meaning is that His words ﴿"and He turned her away"﴾ are conjoined to His words ﴿"and we were given"﴾ if it is from the speech of Sulayman, though it may admit the beginning of a report from God Most High to Muhammad, His prophet, and to his community. If ﴿"and we were given"﴾ is from the speech of Bilqis, then it is apparent that it is necessarily from the speech of God Most High and the speech of the one who said it is connected to His words, "Will you be guided, or will you be among those who are not guided?" The waw in ﴿"and He turned her away"﴾ is the waw of circumstance (waw al-hal), and the qad (indeed) is implied, which is disliked because of the long separation between them, and because inversion and reordering are not resorted to except in necessity.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿"innaHa"﴾ with a kasra on the hamza, while Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ibn Abi Ablah read it with a fatha. The fatha is either by estimating a preposition, meaning "because she," or it is in apposition to the agent, which is "what she used to worship."

Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi and others said: When Bilqis arrived, Sulayman commanded the jinn, and they made for him a palace (sarh), which is the courtyard's flat roof without a ceiling. They made it built like a cistern and filled it with water, and fish and frogs were placed in it, and in its middle a chair was set for Sulayman. When Bilqis reached it, she was told: "Enter upon the Prophet, peace be upon him." She saw the deep water and was frightened, but she had no choice but to obey the command, so she uncovered her shins. Sulayman saw her shins sound, free of what the jinn had said. When she reached this point, Sulayman said to her: "It is a palace smoothed with glass." At that point Bilqis submitted, yielded, embraced Islam and confessed against herself to wrongdoing.

In this narration there is an addition: that he placed his throne in the front of the palace and sat upon it, and the birds, the jinn and mankind gathered around it. Al-Zamakhshari said: he did this only to increase her awe of his affair, to confirm his prophethood for her, and to make her steadfast in the religion. End of the quotation.

The sarh is every high structure; from it comes "Build for me a tower (sarhan), that I may reach the means," and it derives from al-tasrih, which is the most explicit proclamation. Mujahid said: the sarh here is the pool. Ibn Isa said: the courtyard, and sarhat al-dar is its open yard. It was said: the sarh here is a palace of glass. In the speech there is an omission, meaning: so she entered it in obedience to the command.

Al-lujjah is abundant water. The uncovering of the shins is the custom of one who is wearing garments and wishes to wade through water to some destination. The purpose of the palace was only to dazzle, and the uncovering of the shin came about incidentally, unless what was related from the jinn is sound, that her shin was the shin of an animal with a hoof, in which case it is possible that verifying this was the intended purpose.

Ibn Kathir read ﴿"sa'aqiha"﴾ with a hamza, as recorded in the narration of al-Ikhriti, Wahb ibn Wadih, from him. Abu Ali said: it is weak, and likewise in the reading of Qunbul: "yukshafu 'an sa'q" (is uncovered of a shin). As for the hamzing of "al-su'uq" and "'ala su'uqihi," it is a well-known dialect (lughah) of hamzing a waw preceded by a damma. Abu Ali related that Abu Hayyah al-Numayri used to hamz every waw preceded by a damma, and he recited:

*"Dearest of those who kindle fires to me is Musa."*

The apparent meaning is that the agent is said to be Sulayman, and it is possible that the agent is the one who commanded her to enter the palace. Her wronging of herself was said to be by disbelief, and it was said: by her assumption that Sulayman intended to test her.

Ibn Atiyyah said: "ma'a" is an adverb built on a fatha; but when the 'ayn is made sukun, there is no dispute that it is a particle that came for a meaning. End of the quotation. The correct view is that it is an adverb, whether the 'ayn is vocalized with a fatha or made sukun. The sukun is not restricted to poetry, as some have claimed; rather it is a dialect of some Arabs. Its adverbial sense is figurative, and it is in fact a noun that indicates the meaning of companionship.

(p-75)﴿He said, "O chiefs, which of you will bring me her throne before they come to me in submission?"﴾ ﴿A powerful one (ʿifrīt) of the jinn said, "I will bring it to you before you rise from your place. Indeed, I am strong and trustworthy for it."﴾ ﴿One who had knowledge from the Book said, "I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you." And when he saw it set firmly in his presence, he said, "This is from the bounty of my Lord, to test me whether I will be grateful or ungrateful. And whoever is grateful, he is grateful only for his own self. And whoever is ungrateful, indeed my Lord is Free of need and Generous."﴾ ﴿He said, "Disguise her throne for her; we will see whether she is guided or is among those who are not guided."﴾ ﴿So when she came, it was said, "Is your throne like this?" She said, "It is as if it were it. And we were given knowledge before her, and we were Muslims (in submission)."﴾ ﴿And what she used to worship besides Allah barred her; indeed she was from a disbelieving people.﴾ ﴿It was said to her, "Enter the palace." And when she saw it, she thought it was a deep water, and she uncovered her shins. He said, "Indeed, it is a palace paved smooth with glass." She said, "My Lord, indeed I have wronged myself, and I have submitted with Solomon to Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾.

There is an omission in the speech, its estimated sense being: the messenger returned to her with the gift and informed her of what Solomon had sworn, so she prepared to set out to him, for she knew that he was a prophet and she had no power to fight a prophet. It is narrated that when she set out toward Solomon, she gave orders, so he (Solomon) placed her throne at the end of seven rooms, some within others, at the end of one of her palaces, and she locked the doors and appointed guards to protect it, and she set out toward Solomon with her elephants and followers.

ʿAbd Allah ibn Shaddad said: When she was a farsakh (about three miles) away from Solomon, he said, "Which of you will bring me her throne?" Ibn ʿAbbas said: Solomon was awe-inspiring; nothing was begun until he himself asked about it. One day he looked and saw a cloud of dust near him and said, "What is this?" They said, "Bilqis," so he said that (the words above).

They differed regarding Solomon's purpose in summoning her throne. Qatadah and Ibn Jurayj said: When the greatness and excellence of her throne was described to him, he wanted to take it before Islam would protect her and her people and prevent the seizure of their wealth, and Islam is on this religion. But this is distant, that such a thing would come from a prophet who was given a kingdom that was given to no one else. Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Zayd said: He summoned it to show her the power that is from Allah, and so that Solomon and Islam would prevail over her through this submission. Al-Zamakhshari pointed to an opinion, saying: "Perhaps it was revealed to him (peace be upon him) that her throne was secured, so he wanted to overcome her and show her, by this, some of the wonders that were produced by his hand, which were specific to him, along with her awareness of Allah's great power, and of what testifies to Solomon's prophethood and confirms it." End of quote. Al-Tabari said: He wanted to test the truthfulness of the hoopoe in his statement: "And she has a mighty throne" (Al-Naml: 23). But this is distant, because his truthfulness had already been shown in carrying the letter and what followed from its carrying, namely Bilqis's consultation with her people and her sending of the gift. It was said: He wanted it to be brought to him, then disguised and altered, then he would look to see whether she would recognize it or deny it, as a test of her intellect. The apparent order of these reports is according to the sequence in which they occurred in existence, and this is the view of the majority. From Ibn ʿAbbas it is reported that he said: "Which of you will bring me her throne?" when he began to examine the truthfulness of the hoopoe from its falsehood regarding his statement: "And she has a mighty throne" (Al-Naml: 23). In the ordering of the accounts there is then advancement and delay. And in His saying, "Which of you will bring me her throne?" there is evidence that it is permissible to seek help from some followers in the aims of kings, and evidence that some followers of the prophets may be given something that is not given to others, and evidence of the haste of the one from whom kings ask the fulfilment of a need, and the precedence of the devils in subjugation over humans, and their ability, by Allah's decree, to do what is far from human action.

Al-Jumhur read ʿIfrīt, and Abu Hayawa read it with a fatḥah on the ʿayn. Abu Rajaʾ, Abu al-Simmak, ʿĪsā, and it is narrated from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq read ʿIfriyah, with a kasrah on the ʿayn, a sukūn on the fāʾ, a kasrah on the rāʾ, followed by an open yāʾ, followed by the feminine tāʾ. Dhu al-Rummah said:

"As if it were a star in the wake of an ʿifriyah, hurled through the blackness of the night, shooting."

A group read ʿIfr, without yāʾ or tāʾ. It is said in the dialect of Ṭayyiʾ and Tamīm: ʿIfrāh, with an alif and the feminine tāʾ. There is also a sixth dialect: ʿUfāriyah, and a man may be described by it. Since it may also be applied to humans, it was specified by His saying "from the jinn." From Ibn ʿAbbas: his name was Ṣakhr. It is said: Kawrā. It is said: Dhakrān. And "I will bring it to you" (ātīka) may be a present-tense verb or an active participle. Qatadah, Mujahid, and Wahb said: "from your station" means from the seat of judgment, and he used to sit from dawn until noon every day. It is said: before you rise from your sitting and stand up.

"And indeed I am strong for it" means for bringing it, "strong" to carry it; "trustworthy" means I will not steal anything from it. Al-Hasan said: He was a disbeliever, but he was subjugated, and an ʿifrīt is only a disbeliever.

"He who had knowledge of the Book" — it is said he was from the angels, and he was Gabriel, as al-Nakhaʿi said. "The Book" is the Preserved Tablet, or the letter of Solomon to Bilqis. It is also said: an angel whom Allah strengthened Solomon with. It is also said: he was a man from humankind, named Āṣif ibn Barkhiyā, Solomon's scribe, who was a righteous and knowledgeable man, as the majority said. Or Asṭūām, or Hūd, or Malīkhā, as Qatadah said. Or Asṭūrus, or al-Khiḍr (peace be upon him), as Ibn Lahīʿah said. A group said: he was Ḍabbah ibn Udd, grandfather of the Banū Ḍabbah from the Arabs, and he was an excellent man who served Solomon, and was over a portion of his horses. These are conflicting opinions, and Allah has concealed his name, so his name should not be mentioned until a prophet reports it. Among the strangest opinions is that it was Solomon himself, as if he were saying to himself, "I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you," or that he addressed the ʿifrīt with it; al-Zamakhshari and others related this opinion, as if he regarded the ʿifrīt's statement as slow, so Solomon said this to him to belittle the ʿifrīt. "The Book" is the one sent down from Allah, or the Preserved Tablet, two views. As for the knowledge he was given, it is said: it is the Greatest Name of Allah, which is: "O Living, O Self-Subsisting." It is also said: "O Possessor of Majesty and Honour." It is also said in Hebrew: Ahyā Sharāhyā. Al-Hasan said: Allah, then al-Raḥmān.

The apparent meaning is that the return of the glance is literal, and that it is shorter in duration than the ʿifrīt's time. For this reason it is narrated that Solomon said: "I want something faster than that" when the ʿifrīt answered him. Since the one who looks is described as sending out his sight, as the poet said:

"And whenever you sent your gaze forth as a scout for your heart one day, the sights wearied you."

It was described as returning the glance, and the glance was described as returning. The meaning is that you send your glance, and before you return it, I have brought it to you, and it is before you. It is narrated that Āṣif said to Solomon (peace be upon him): "Extend your eyes until your glance reaches its end." So he extended his glance and looked toward Yemen. Āṣif called, and the throne vanished from its place in Maʾrib, then sprang forth beside Solomon's seat in Syria by the power of Allah, before he returned his glance. Ibn Jubayr and Qatadah said: before anyone on whom your glance falls, at the farthest point you can see, reaches you. Mujahid said: before you need to blink, that is, the duration in which you can extend your sight without blinking, and that is its return. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: These two views correspond to the view of those who said that the standing is from the seat of judgment, and those who said that the standing is from sitting; for the view that "return of the glance" is a blink, that is, before you close and open your eyes, since the second gives the shortest duration, and that is necessary. End of quote. It is also said: "your glance" means "what you are looking at," that is, before what you look at returns to you from the limit of your sight. This is the view of Ibn Jubayr and Qatadah mentioned earlier, since the one on whom your glance falls is what you are looking at. Al-Mawardi said: before your glance is withdrawn to you by death, so he informed him that he would come to him before his death. This is a distant interpretation; rather, the meaning is "I will bring it to you swiftly." It is also said: the return of the glance is metaphorical here, and it is of the type of figurative expression (majāz al-tamthīl), and what is intended is the shortness of the time for bringing it, as you say to your companion, "Do this in a moment," "in the return of a glance," or "in the blink of an eye," meaning speed: "I will bring it to you in a time faster than the time of the ʿifrīt."

"When he saw it set firmly in his presence": in the speech there is an omission, its estimated sense being: he called on Allah, and He brought it to him. "When he saw it," that is, Bilqis's throne. It is said: it descended upon Solomon from the air. It is said: it sprang from the earth. It is said: from beneath the throne of Solomon. "Set firmly" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), and "in his presence" is a complement dependent on it. When an adverbial phrase of place or time falls in the position of a state, the verb it depends on must be omitted. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: the verb governing the adverbial phrase appears in "set firmly," and this is what is always implied in every adverbial phrase that falls in the position of a state. Abu al-Baqāʾ said: "set firmly" means fixed, not shaking, and it is not the meaning of mere presence, for if it were so, it would not have been mentioned. End of quote. He took "set firmly" as an additional sense beyond absolute firmness, namely that it was not shaking, so that its meaning is different from the meaning of "in his presence." This is a good justification for mentioning the verb in the adverbial phrase used as a state. And it has been suggested that the verb be mentioned in what falls as a predicate of a prepositional phrase with a complete sense, in the poet's words:

"Glory is yours: if your Master is glorious, and if He is humbled, you are present in the midst of humiliation."

"He said, 'This is from the bounty of my Lord'": that is, this bringing of her throne and the attainment of what I wanted from it is from the bounty of my Lord upon me and His kindness. Then he gave the reason for that in his words, "to test me whether I will be grateful or ungrateful." Ibn ʿAbbas said: the meaning is: Shall I give thanks for the throne and its being brought, or shall I be ungrateful, when I see one who is below me in this world is more knowledgeable than I? End of quote. Solomon received the blessing and the bounty of Allah with thanks, for at that point it is a renewed blessing, and gratitude is a bond for blessings. "Shall I give thanks or shall I be ungrateful" is in the accusative position after "to test me," and it is suspended (taʿlīq), because it has the sense of a question, and the question has the sense of knowledge; the verb of testing is often suspended in this way, treating it as the verb of knowledge, even though it is not synonymous with it, since its real signified meaning is examination.

"And whoever is grateful, he is grateful only for his own self": that is, the reward of that gratitude returns to him, for he has preserved his soul from ingratitude for the blessing, and has done what is obligatory upon him of thanking Allah for His blessing upon him.

"And whoever is ungrateful": that is, to Allah's bounty and blessing upon him, "indeed my Lord is Free of need from his gratitude," the benefit of it does not return to Allah, for He is the Absolutely Free of need, the Generous by bestowing favours upon one who disbelieves His blessing. The apparent view is that His saying, "indeed my Lord is Free of need and Generous," is the response to the condition, and for this reason a fāʾ is implied in "Free of need," that is, free of need from his gratitude. It is permissible that the response is omitted, indicated by what precedes it of its counterpart, that is: "And whoever is ungrateful, then it is for himself," meaning that disbelief's punishment returns to him. It is also permissible that "mā" (whoever) is a relative pronoun, and the fāʾ entered into the predicate because it includes the sense of the condition.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 27, verses 38–44 (part 2 of 2):**

﴿He said, "Disguise her throne for her, so that we may see whether she will be guided or be among those who are not guided."﴾ It is related that the jinn sensed something from Sulayman, or suspected that he might marry Bilqis. They disliked this, and they slandered her to him, saying that she lacked intelligence and discernment, and that her leg was like the hoof of a beast. So he tested her intelligence and discernment by altering the throne, and tested her leg through the palace (al-sarh), so that she would uncover her shins before him.

As for the "disguising" (tankir) of her throne, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and al-Dahhak said: it was done by adding to it and subtracting from it. It was also said: by removing the gems and jewels that were on it. And it was said: by making its base its top and its front its back. Al-tankir means making it unrecognizable, changed from its form and appearance, just as a man disguises himself from people so that they do not recognize him.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿nanzur﴾ (we will see) in the jussive, as a response to the imperative (jawab al-amr, the answer that follows a command). Abu Haywa read it in the nominative, as a resumed sentence (isti'naf, a new clause), in which he informs of himself that he sees. The complement of ﴿ataHtadi﴾ (will she be guided) is omitted. The apparent meaning is: will she be guided to recognizing her throne, and its disguising will not be an obstacle to her recognizing it? Thereby her acute intelligence becomes evident, and it becomes clear that the condition of her throne was not hidden from him, even though they had sought to conceal it. Or: will she be guided to a correct answer when she is asked about it? Or: will she be guided to belief in the prophethood of Sulayman, peace be upon him, when she sees this miracle of the transporting of her throne from the place where she had left it, after she had locked the doors upon it and appointed guards for it?

﴿When she came﴾: there is an omission in the speech, meaning: so they disguised her throne and looked at what her answer would be when she was asked about it. ﴿When she came, it was said: "Is your throne like this?"﴾ That is, is the throne like this throne that you have seen, your throne that you left in your land? The construction was not "Is this your throne?" but came with the particle of comparison, so that this would not be a suggestion to her. When she saw it in a form she did not recognize, and some things of her throne were distinguishable in it, she did not affirm that it was it, nor did she categorically deny it. Rather she expressed it in the form of a comparison, saying: ﴿"As if it were it."﴾ This was from the excellence of her mind, since she did not affirm, in the probable case, either of the two permissible possibilities, that it was it or that it was not it, and she matched their comparison with her own comparison.

The apparent meaning is that His words, ﴿"And we were given knowledge before her, and we were Muslims"﴾, up to His words, ﴿"from a disbelieving people"﴾, are not from the speech of Bilqis, though they are connected to her speech. It was said: they are from the speech of Sulayman. It was said: they are from the speech of the people of Sulayman and his followers.

If it is from the words of Sulayman, it was said: "knowledge" here is particular, meaning: ﴿"we were given knowledge"﴾ of her Islam and her coming in obedience. ﴿"Before her"﴾, that is, before her coming. ﴿"And we were Muslims"﴾: monotheists, submissive.

Ibn Atiyyah said: there is an omission in the speech; its estimate is ﴿"as if it were it"﴾, and Sulayman said at that point: ﴿"And we were given knowledge before her"﴾, up to the end of the verse. He said this by way of enumerating the blessings of God Most High, and he said it according to what she knew and understood; he mentioned the blessing of God upon him and upon his forefathers. End of the summary.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿"And we were given knowledge"﴾ is from the speech of Sulayman and his council. (If you say:) to what did this speech and what is connected to it refer? (I say:) since the occasion in which she was asked about her throne, and she answered as she answered, was an occasion in which Sulayman and his council brought forth what is appropriate to their saying, "And we were given knowledge," such as saying, when she said "as if it were it": "She has been correct in her answer," so they matched the detailed account, while she was intelligent and sagacious. She had been granted Islam and knew the power of God and the soundness of prophethood through the signs that had preceded, at the time of the delegation of al-Mundhir. And by this wondrous matter of her throne they added to that their saying: (p-79) ﴿"And we were given knowledge, we ourselves, of God and His power and the soundness of the prophethood of Sulayman, what came from Him before her knowledge; and we have not ceased to be upon the religion of Islam."﴾ They thanked God for His favour upon them over her and for their preceding her in knowledge of God and Islam, and what had prevented her from advancing to Islam was the worship of the sun and her upbringing among the disbelievers.

It is permissible that it be from the speech of Bilqis, joined to her saying ﴿"as if it were it"﴾, and the meaning is: ﴿"And we were given knowledge of God and His power and the soundness of Sulayman's prophethood before this miracle"﴾, or before this condition, meaning what you have made clear of the signs at the time of the delegation of al-Mundhir, and we entered into Islam. Then God Most High said: ﴿"And he [i.e., what she worshipped] turned her away from what she had been, her going astray from the right path."﴾ It was said: ﴿"And He turned her away, or Sulayman did, from what she used to worship"﴾, with the omission of the preposition and the attachment of the verb. End of the quotation.

As for his saying, "It is permissible that it be from the speech of Bilqis," this is an opinion he has already advanced definitively, not merely as a permissible possibility. It was said: the meaning is "and we were given knowledge of the soundness of his prophethood through the signs that preceded, from the matter of the hoopoe and the messengers before this miracle, meaning bringing the throne." ﴿"And we were Muslims"﴾: obedient to your command and submissive to you.

The apparent meaning is that the agent of His words ﴿"and He turned her away"﴾ is His words ﴿"what she used to worship"﴾, and whether it is God or Sulayman. ﴿"What"﴾ is the object of ﴿"turned her away"﴾ with the preposition dropped; this was said by al-Tabari, and it is weak, permissible only in poetic necessity, such as the verse: "You pass by the abodes and do not turn aside," meaning: "away from the abodes." It is not among the places where the preposition is omitted. If the agent is "what she used to worship," then the object of turning away is Islam, the apparent meaning.

Al-Rummani said: the estimate is "awareness of the throne," because the believer is alert and the disbeliever is wicked.

The apparent meaning is that His words ﴿"and He turned her away"﴾ are conjoined to His words ﴿"and we were given"﴾ if it is from the speech of Sulayman, though it may admit the beginning of a report from God Most High to Muhammad, His prophet, and to his community. If ﴿"and we were given"﴾ is from the speech of Bilqis, then it is apparent that it is necessarily from the speech of God Most High and the speech of the one who said it is connected to His words, "Will you be guided, or will you be among those who are not guided?" The waw in ﴿"and He turned her away"﴾ is the waw of circumstance (waw al-hal), and the qad (indeed) is implied, which is disliked because of the long separation between them, and because inversion and reordering are not resorted to except in necessity.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿"innaHa"﴾ with a kasra on the hamza, while Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ibn Abi Ablah read it with a fatha. The fatha is either by estimating a preposition, meaning "because she," or it is in apposition to the agent, which is "what she used to worship."

Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi and others said: When Bilqis arrived, Sulayman commanded the jinn, and they made for him a palace (sarh), which is the courtyard's flat roof without a ceiling. They made it built like a cistern and filled it with water, and fish and frogs were placed in it, and in its middle a chair was set for Sulayman. When Bilqis reached it, she was told: "Enter upon the Prophet, peace be upon him." She saw the deep water and was frightened, but she had no choice but to obey the command, so she uncovered her shins. Sulayman saw her shins sound, free of what the jinn had said. When she reached this point, Sulayman said to her: "It is a palace smoothed with glass." At that point Bilqis submitted, yielded, embraced Islam and confessed against herself to wrongdoing.

In this narration there is an addition: that he placed his throne in the front of the palace and sat upon it, and the birds, the jinn and mankind gathered around it. Al-Zamakhshari said: he did this only to increase her awe of his affair, to confirm his prophethood for her, and to make her steadfast in the religion. End of the quotation.

The sarh is every high structure; from it comes "Build for me a tower (sarhan), that I may reach the means," and it derives from al-tasrih, which is the most explicit proclamation. Mujahid said: the sarh here is the pool. Ibn Isa said: the courtyard, and sarhat al-dar is its open yard. It was said: the sarh here is a palace of glass. In the speech there is an omission, meaning: so she entered it in obedience to the command.

Al-lujjah is abundant water. The uncovering of the shins is the custom of one who is wearing garments and wishes to wade through water to some destination. The purpose of the palace was only to dazzle, and the uncovering of the shin came about incidentally, unless what was related from the jinn is sound, that her shin was the shin of an animal with a hoof, in which case it is possible that verifying this was the intended purpose.

Ibn Kathir read ﴿"sa'aqiha"﴾ with a hamza, as recorded in the narration of al-Ikhriti, Wahb ibn Wadih, from him. Abu Ali said: it is weak, and likewise in the reading of Qunbul: "yukshafu 'an sa'q" (is uncovered of a shin). As for the hamzing of "al-su'uq" and "'ala su'uqihi," it is a well-known dialect (lughah) of hamzing a waw preceded by a damma. Abu Ali related that Abu Hayyah al-Numayri used to hamz every waw preceded by a damma, and he recited:

*"Dearest of those who kindle fires to me is Musa."*

The apparent meaning is that the agent is said to be Sulayman, and it is possible that the agent is the one who commanded her to enter the palace. Her wronging of herself was said to be by disbelief, and it was said: by her assumption that Sulayman intended to test her.

Ibn Atiyyah said: "ma'a" is an adverb built on a fatha; but when the 'ayn is made sukun, there is no dispute that it is a particle that came for a meaning. End of the quotation. The correct view is that it is an adverb, whether the 'ayn is vocalized with a fatha or made sukun. The sukun is not restricted to poetry, as some have claimed; rather it is a dialect of some Arabs. Its adverbial sense is figurative, and it is in fact a noun that indicates the meaning of companionship.

(p. 81) Al-hadiqah (the garden) is an orchard, whether or not it has a wall around it. Al-hajiz is the barrier that separates two things. Al-fawj is a group. Al-jumud is the stillness of a thing and its lack of movement. Al-itqan is bringing a thing to its best state of perfection and soundness in its creation. It is derived from the Arabs' saying, "taqinu ardahum" (they made their land firm), when they let loose water mixed with clay into it, so that it became solid. Al-tiqn is the water that is poured into a pool, and it is what comes from the water's thickening. Kababtu al-rajul means I threw the man onto his face.

﴿And We had certainly sent to Thamud their brother Salih, [saying], "Worship Allah," but they became two factions disputing.﴾ ﴿He said, "O my people, why do you seek to hasten evil before good? Why do you not ask forgiveness of Allah, that you may receive mercy?"﴾ ﴿They said, "We consider you and those with you to be a bad omen." He said, "Your omen is with Allah; rather, you are a people being tested."﴾ ﴿And there were in the city nine men who spread corruption in the land and did not reform.﴾ ﴿They said, "Swear to one another by Allah that we will surely attack him and his family by night, and then we will say to his heir, 'We did not witness the destruction of his family, and indeed we are truthful.'"﴾ ﴿And they plotted a plot, and We plotted a plot, while they did not perceive.﴾ ﴿So see how was the outcome of their plot: that We destroyed them and their people, all of them.﴾ ﴿And those are their houses, fallen in ruin because they wronged. Indeed in that is a sign for a people who know.﴾ ﴿And We saved those who believed and used to fear Allah.﴾

(p. 82) Thamud is the "first 'Ad." Salih is their brother in lineage. When Allah mentioned the story of Musa, Dawud and Sulayman, who were from the Children of Israel, He mentioned the story of someone who was from the Arabs, to remind Quraysh and the Arabs by it, and to alert them that the prophets who came before them from among the Arabs used to call to the singling out of Allah, Exalted is He, in worship, so that they would know that they were in error by worshipping idols, and that the situation of the prophets, whether Arab or non-Arab, is calling to the worship of Allah.

The "an" in ﴿an uʿbudu﴾ (that worship) may be explanatory (mufassirah), because ﴿arsalna﴾ (We sent) includes the meaning of saying. It may also be a verbal-source particle (masdariyyah), meaning "bi-an uʿbudu" (with [the command] to worship), with the preposition removed. According to the first view, it has no place in grammatical analysis (iʿrab). According to the second, there is a disagreement about its place: is it in a position of accusative or of genitive?

The apparent reading is that the pronoun in ﴿fa-idha hum﴾ (then behold, they) refers back to Thamud, and that his people divided into two groups, a believing group and a disbelieving group. This has been explained in Surah al-A'raf in His saying: ﴿The eminent ones who were arrogant among his people said to those who were oppressed, to those among them who believed﴾ [al-A'raf: 75]. Al-Zamakhshari said: "By the two groups is meant Salih and his people, before any of them had believed." End of quotation. So he made the one group Salih and the other group his people.

"Idha" here is the sudden-occurrence "idha" (al-fujaʾiyyah), and He joined with the "fa" which indicates sequence, not delay. So the meaning is that they rushed to dispute immediately after Salih called them to the worship of Allah. The word ﴿yakhtasimun﴾ (they dispute) is in the plural according to meaning, because the two groups are plural. If the two groups are the believer and the disbeliever, then plurality is present in each group. What shows that the believing group is plural is His saying: ﴿Indeed, we disbelieve in that which you have believed﴾ [al-A'raf: 76], where He said "amantum" (you believed), which is a plural pronoun. If the believing group was Salih alone, then he had joined with his people, and the combined group is plural. ﴿Yakhtasimun﴾ was preferred over ﴿yakhtasimani﴾ (the two dispute), although the dual is permissible and eloquent in terms of form, because it is the end of a verse (maqta' fasl). The disputing among them is each group's claim that the truth is with them. Allah has mentioned their disputing in Surah al-A'raf.

Then Salih was gentle with his people and kind to them in address. He said, calling to them in a manner of tenderness toward them: ﴿Why do you seek to hasten evil?﴾, that is, to the occurrence of what would harm you, before the good state, which is the mercy of Allah. He had said to them in the story of the she-camel: ﴿And do not touch her with harm, lest there seize you a painful punishment﴾ [al-A'raf: 73]. They said to him: ﴿Bring us what you threaten us with, from the punishment of Allah﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 29]. It was also said: "Why do you hasten to the occurrence of sins from yourselves before obedience?" Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: what is the meaning of their hastening to evil before good? That happens only if both are expected, one before the other? I say: they used to say in their ignorance: 'The punishment that Salih promises us, if it happens according to his claim, then we will repent at that time and seek forgiveness, assuming that repentance is accepted at that time; and if it does not happen, then we are as we are.' So Salih, peace be upon him, addressed them according to their saying and belief." End of quotation.

Then he urged them toward what would repel evil from them, which is faith and seeking Allah's forgiveness for what preceded of disbelief. He tied that to the hope of mercy and did not state definitively that it would follow from their seeking forgiveness. In the exhortation there was an alert to their error in hastening punishment, and a declaration of their ignorance in their belief.

When he had been gentle with them in address, they became harsh toward him and said: ﴿We consider you and those with you to be a bad omen﴾, that is, we consider you and those who believed with you to be an omen of misfortune. This conjunction indicates that the two groups were believers and disbelievers, due to His saying ﴿and those with you﴾. They had experienced drought, and they made the cause of their drought the very person of Salih and those who believed with him. So He answered them with His saying: ﴿Your omen is with Allah﴾, that is, your portion in reality, of good or of evil, is with Allah and by His decree: if He wills, He provides for you, and if He wills, He withholds from you. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is possible that it means your deeds are written with Allah; from them has come down upon you what has come down as punishment for you and as a trial. And from this is His saying, 'Your omen is with you' [Yasin: 19], and 'every person We have fastened his omen to his neck' [al-Isra: 13]." It was read ﴿tatayyarna bika﴾ according to the original form. The meaning of "tatayyara bihi" is that he considered him an omen of misfortune, and "tatayyara minhu" (p. 83) means he recoiled from him. End of quotation.

Then he moved on to informing about their state, and said: ﴿Rather, you are a people being tested﴾, that is, you are being examined, or punished, or Satan tempts you by his whisperings to you of the omen-taking, or you are tested by his desires, that is, you are attached to them, as it is said: "So-and-so was smitten (futina) with so-and-so." The poet said:

"An ancient ailment among the children of Adam: one person's trial by another person."

These are the views that the wording *tuftanun* can bear. It is read *tuftanuna* with the second-person *ta'* (addressing *antum*, "you"), which is the common usage in the Arabic language. It may also be read *yuftanuna* with the third-person *ya'* (agreeing with the word *qawm*, "a people"), which is less common. The Arabs say: "You are a man who enjoins good," with either the *ta'* of address or the *ya'* of the third person.

"Al-madinah" (the city) is the gathering place and settlement of Thamud, and it is al-Hijr. The commentators (*mufassirun*, those who perform *tafsir*, i.e. exegesis) mentioned the names of the nine men, and there is disagreement about some of them. Their chief was Qudar ibn Salif. Their names cannot be fixed with certainty or precisely identified, so we have set aside mentioning them. They were the great men of the town, its wealthy people, and its wicked ones.

*Al-rahat* means from three to ten men, and *al-nafar* means from three to nine. The commentators agreed that the meaning is nine men. Al-Zamakhshari said: "The specification of *tis'ah* (nine) by *rahat* is permissible only because it carries the sense of a group, so it is as if it were said: nine persons (*anfus*)." End of quote. The other view, that the meaning is "nine men," is preferable, because if he attached it to *anfus*, he should have said *tis' anfus* with the feminine form, since the eloquent usage of *nafs* is feminine. Do you not see that they counted as an anomaly the poet's line:

"Thalathat anfusin wa thalath dhawd" ("three persons and three camels"),

where he used the *ta'* in *thalathah* (the feminine form with a masculine noun), whereas the eloquent form would have been *thalath anfus*. Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: "The more likely view is that what is intended is *tis'ah* as a collective, since the apparent meaning of *rahat* is a group and not a single individual. It is possible that they were tribes, and it is possible that they were included under the number because of the differences in their qualities and conditions, not because of the differences in their kinds." End of quote. It has been said: *rahat* is the name of a group, and it seems they were chiefs, each with a *rahat* of his own. Al-Kirmani said: "Its root is from *al-tarhit*, which is the magnifying of mouthfuls and the vigor of eating." End of quote.

*Rahat* is a collective noun (*ism jam'*). They agreed that its specification by *min* (from) is the eloquent usage, as in the Exalted saying: ﴿So take four of the birds﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 260]. They differed over whether a number may be attached to it as an annexation (*idafah*). Al-Akhfash held that this is not a regular practice, and whatever is reported of annexation to it is an exceptional usage. Sibawayh explicitly stated that one does not say *thalath ghanam* (three sheep). Others held that this is permissible and regular, though it is still rare. Some distinguished between a collective noun denoting a small number, such as *rahat*, *nafar* and *dhawd*, which may be annexed to a number, and one used for a large quantity, or one used for both, which may not be annexed to a number. This is the view of al-Mazini. We have lengthened the discussion of this issue in *Sharh al-Tashil* (the Commentary on *al-Tashil*).

*Yufsidun* (they corrupt) is a description (*sifah*) of "nine men." The meaning is that they corrupt with a great corruption that is not mixed with any reform, which is why He said: ﴿and they do not reform﴾. This is because one who commits corruption may sometimes also do reform at other times.

The majority recited *taqasamu* ("swear to one another"), and Ibn Abi Layla recited *tiqassamu*, without the *alif* and with a doubled *sin*. Both come from *al-qasam* (oath), *al-taqasum* and *al-taqsim*, like *al-tazahur* and *al-tazhir*.

The apparent meaning is that the word *taqasamu* is an imperative verb reported as speech, and this is the view of the majority: some of them urged others to swear to the night attack on Salih. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyyah permitted that *taqasamu* be a past verb in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), meaning "they said, swearing to one another." Al-Zamakhshari said: "*Taqasamu* may be an imperative and a declarative on the position of a circumstantial clause, with *qad* understood, meaning: they said, swearing to one another." End of quote. As for his phrase "and declarative," it is not correct, because "declarative" (*khabar*) is one of the two divisions of speech, since speech is divided into declarative and performative (*insha'*), and all its meanings, if you examine them, return to these two divisions.

He then said: "It has been recited *latubayyitannahu* with *ya'*, *ta'* and *nun*. With the *nun* and *ta'*, *taqasamu* may take both readings, meaning in *taqasamu billah*. The two readings are the imperative and the declarative in his view. With the *ya'*, it can only be a declarative." End of quote. The restriction by a circumstantial clause is only a matter of attributing the restriction, not of the attribution of the speech which is the predication (*isnad*). So when the term "declarative" is applied to it, that is on the assumption that if it were not a circumstantial clause it could be used as a declarative. Likewise their saying that the clause before it, which is a relative clause, is "declarative" is a figurative usage, and the meaning is that if it were not a relative clause it could be used as a declarative. This is a matter that is somewhat obscure, and it does not require supposing an implied element, since the occurrence of the past tense as a circumstantial clause without *qad* is very frequent, to the point that it should be used as a basis for analogy.

According to this parsing, it is possible that *billah* ("by God") is connected to *taqasamu*, which is the circumstantial clause, so it belongs to its complement and is not included within the speech. As for the reported speech, *latubayyitannahu* ("we will surely attack him") and what follows, it is possible that this and what follows is the reported speech.

The majority recited ﴿latubayyitannahu wa-ahlahu thumma lataqulanna﴾ ("we will surely attack him and his family, then we will surely say") with *nun* in both. Al-Hasan, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited with the *ta'* of the plural address. Mujahid, Ibn Wathhab, Talhah and al-A'mash recited with the *ya'* of the third person, with both verbs having a plural subject. Humayd ibn Qays recited with *ya'* of the third person in the first verb, with a plural subject, meaning *layubayyitunnahu* ("they will surely attack him," i.e., a group of us), and with *nun* in the second, meaning all of us say to his heir (*waliyyihi*). *Al-bayat* is the surprise attack upon the enemy. It is reported of Alexander (*al-Iskandar*) that when he was advised to use a night attack, he said: "It is not the custom of kings to steal victory." His *waliyy* is the seeker of vengeance for him if he is killed.

The majority recited *muhlaka*, with a *mim* vowel and a *fath* on the *lam*, from *ahlaka*. Hafs recited *mahlika*, with a *fath* on the *mim* and a *kasrah* on the *lam*. Abu Bakr recited with *fath* on both. As for the first reading, it may be a verbal noun, a time, or a place, meaning: we did not witness the destruction of his family, or the time of their destruction, or the place of their destruction. It follows from these two that if they did not witness the time or the place, they did not witness the destruction either. As for the second reading, analogy requires that it be for time and place, meaning: we did not witness the time of their destruction, nor its place. The third reading, by analogy, requires it to be a verbal noun, meaning: we did not witness his destruction. Al-Zamakhshari said: "They mentioned the three readings, and the verbal noun, time and place are possible." End of quote.

The apparent meaning in the statement is that a conjoined element is omitted, indicated by what precedes it, and the implied sense is: we did not witness the destruction of his family and his destruction. This is indicated by their saying ﴿latubayyitannahu wa-ahlahu﴾ and by what is reported, that they had resolved to kill him and kill his family. Omitting such a conjoined element is permissible in eloquent speech, as in His saying: ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [Al-Nahl: 81], meaning "and the cold." And the poet said:

"Fa-ma kana bayn al-khayr law ja'a salimam / Abu hujrin illa layali qala'il"
("Between me and the good, had he come safe, Abu Hujr was only a few nights away.")

meaning: between the good and between me.

Their saying ﴿and indeed we are truthful﴾ would then be a lie in the report. They led their people to believe that if they killed him and his family secretly, and no one noticed them, and they spoke that statement, they were truthful, while they were liars.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "(If you ask): How could they be truthful when they denied what they did, so that they brought the report contrary to what it reports? (I answer): It is as if they believed that when they attacked Salih and attacked his family, they combined the two attacks, then they said: ﴿we did not witness the destruction of his family﴾, so they mentioned one of them, and they were truthful, because they did both attacks together, not just one of them. In this there is decisive proof that lying (*al-kadhib*) is ugly among the unbelievers who do not know the Law (*al-shar'*) and its prohibitions, and it does not occur to their minds. Do you not see that they intended to kill the prophet of God, and did not consider it possible for themselves to be liars, until they made truthfulness in themselves a stratagem by which they fall short of lying?" End of quote.

It is astonishing that this man contrives these stratagems to make their statement ﴿and indeed we are truthful﴾ a statement of truth. Yet he knows that they denied Salih, and hamstrung the she-camel, which was among the greatest signs, and proceeded to kill a prophet and his family. Lying is not permissible for them, and yet he recites in the Book of God their lies against their prophets. God has stated this explicitly, and their lies against One to whom no secret is hidden: ﴿on the day when secrets are examined﴾ [Al-Tariq: 9]. And that is their saying: ﴿By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [Al-An'am: 23], and the saying of God, Exalted is He: ﴿Look how they lied against themselves﴾ [Al-An'am: 24]. What this man does is a distortion of the words of God, Exalted is He, in order to support his doctrine that lying is ugly among the unbelievers, and he devises this stratagem for them so that he makes them truthful in their report.

This man, although he was given the greatest share of the knowledge of the Qur'an, and combined the invention of meaning with eloquence of expression, nevertheless his book of *tafsir* contains criticizable matters. I was close to finishing writing these lines, having composed a poem on a person occupying himself with the Book of God, and I digressed into praising the book of al-Zamakhshari, mentioning some of its merits, then I drew attention to what it contains that must be avoided. I saw fit to include it here, so that whoever reads this book of mine may benefit and be alerted to the vices it contains. I said after mentioning what I praised him for:

"Wa-lakinnahu fihi majal li-naqid / wa-zallat su'in qad akhadhna al-makhaniqa"
("But in it there is room for a critic, and lapses of error that have seized the throats.")

"Fa-yuthbitu mawdu' al-ahadith jahilan / wa-yazu ila al-ma'sumi ma laysa la'iqa"
("He establishes fabricated hadiths in ignorance, and ascribes to the infallible what is not fitting.")

"Wa-yashtumu a'lam al-a'immati dallatan / wa-la siyyama in awlajuhu al-madayiqa"
("He reviles the great imams in error, especially if they are driven into straits.")

"Wa-yusbihu fi al-ma'na al-wajiz dalalatan / bi-takthiri alfaz tusamma al-shaqashiqa"
("He prolixes on the concise meaning in its indication, by multiplying words called *al-shaqashiq* (empty chatter).")

"Yuqawwilu fiha Allah ma laysa qa'ilan / wa-kana muhibban fi al-khitabati wamiqa"
("He puts into God's mouth what He did not say, and he was a lover of oratory, passionately fond of it.")

"Wa-yukhti'u fi tarkibihi li-kalamihi / fa-laysa li-ma qad rakkabuhu muwafiqa"
("He errs in composing his words, so that they do not agree with what they composed.")

"Wa-yansibu ibda' al-ma'ani li-nafsihi / li-yuwhima aghmaran wa-in kana saariqa"
("He ascribes the origination of meanings to himself, to deceive the ignorant, even though he is a thief.")

"Wa-yukhti'u fi fahm al-Qur'an li-annahu / yujawwizu i'rabam aba an yutabiqa"
("He errs in understanding the Qur'an, because he permits a parsing (*i'rab*) that refuses to agree.")

"Wa-kam bayna man yu'ta al-bayan salIqatan / wa-akhara 'anahu fa-ma huwa lahiqa"
("How great is the difference between one given eloquence by nature, and another who strained for it, and yet did not attain it.")

"Wa-yahtalu lil-alfaz hatta yudiruha / li-madhhabi su'in fihi asbaha mariqa"
("He contrives with words until he turns them to a wicked doctrine, through which he became an apostate.")

"Fa-ya khusrahu shaykhan takharraqa situ / maghariba takhriqi al-saba wa-mashariqa"
("Woe to him, an old man whose fame has spread to the west and east like the scattering of the east wind.")

"La-in lam tudarikahu min Allahi rahmatun / lasawfa yura lil-kafirina murafiqa"
("If he is not overtaken by a mercy from God, he will surely be seen as a companion of the unbelievers.")

Their scheming (*makrahum*) is what they concealed of plotting to kill Salih and his family. The scheming of God (*makr Allah*) is destroying them from where they do not perceive. It is likened to the scheming of a schemer by way of metaphor (*isti'arah*). Their scheming was pretending that they were travelling and hiding in a cave. It was said: or in a ravine (*shi'b*). Or it was their resolve to kill him and his family, and their oath that they had not been present at that. The scheming of God against them was the closing of a rock over the mouth of the cave and the ravine, and their destruction within it. Or it was the angels pelting them with stones, which they saw but did not see the one throwing them, when they drew their swords at night to kill him. These are two opinions. It was also said that God informed Salih of their scheme so that he left it, and that this is the scheming of God against them.

It is related that Salih, after the slaughter of the she-camel, informed them that the punishment would come after three days. These nine men agreed to kill Salih and his family at night, and said: "If he is lying in his threat, we will have inflicted upon him what he deserves; and if he is truthful, we will have hastened it before him and cooled our souls." They hid in a cave, and God destroyed them, as has been mentioned before, and destroyed their people as well, and each group was unaware of the destruction of the other.

Apparently "*kayfa*" is the predicate of *kana*, and "*'aqibatu*" is its noun. The clause is in the position of accusative after *unzur*, and it is suspended. The majority (*al-Jumhur*) read "*Inna*" with a kasra on the hamzah, as a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*). Al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq and the Kufans read it with a fatha, so "*anna*" is either a substitute for "*'aqibatu*", or a predicate for *kana*, and it would be in the position of a circumstantial accusative (*hal*), or the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: it, that is, the outcome, is their destruction. Or the estimate is: "because we...", and the preposition has been omitted. On both readings it is permissible for *kana* to be complete (*tammah*) with "*'aqibatu*" as its subject, or for it to be superfluous (*za'idah*) with "*'aqibatu*" as a subject whose predicate is "*kayfa*".

Ubayy read: "*an dammarnahum*", where *an* is the particle that governs the imperfect, and the permissible readings for *anna* apply to it, with the hamzah given a fatha. Abu al-Baqa' reported that some scholars permitted, in the reading of whoever gave the hamzah a fatha, that "*anna dammarnahum*" be a substitute for "*kayfa*". He said: others said it is not permitted, because a substitute for an interrogative requires repeating its particle, as in his saying: "How is Zayd, healthy or sick?"

When He, exalted is He, commanded them to consider what befell them of destruction in themselves, He explained that by pointing to their dwellings and how they were emptied of them, and the ruin and vacancy of the houses from their people, so that none of them remained of what the wrongdoers are punished with, since that indicates their complete eradication. In the Torah: "Son of Adam, do not wrong, lest your house be ruined." This is an indication of the destruction of the wrongdoer, since the ruin of his house follows his destruction. These are the houses about which the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to his companions, in the year of Tabuk: "Do not enter upon these punished people unless you are weeping," and so on in the hadith.

The majority read "*khawiyah*" in the accusative as a circumstantial accusative (*hal*). Al-Zamakhshari said: it is governed by what that demonstrative (*tilka*) indicates. Isa ibn Umar read "*khawiyatun*" in the nominative. Al-Zamakhshari said: as the predicate of an omitted subject. Ibn Atiyyah also said this, meaning: they are empty. He said: or as a predicate concerning *tilka*, and "*buyutuhum*" is a substitute, or as a second predicate. "*Khawiyah*" is a report, because of their wrongdoing, which is disbelief, and it derives from the emptiness of the belly. Ibn Abbas said: "*khawiyah*" means that its upper part has fallen onto its lower part.

"*Inna fi dhalika*": that is, in Our action toward Thamud, which is Our eradicating them by destruction and the emptying of their dwellings of them. Their houses were in Wadi al-Qura, between Medina and Syria.

"*Wa-anjayna alladhina amanu*": that is, through Salih, from the punishment that descended upon the disbelievers. Those who believed in him were four thousand. Salih departed with them to Hadramawt. Hadramawt was so named because when Salih, peace be upon him, entered it, he died there, and the believers built a city there called Hadurah. As for those who perished, a boil like a chickpea came out on their bodies; it turned red on the first day, yellow on the second, and black on the third. The slaughter of the she-camel was on Wednesday, and they perished on Sunday. Muqatil said: those boils burst, and Jibril, peace be upon him, shouted at them with one cry, and they were extinguished.

(p. 81) Al-hadiqah (the garden) is an orchard, whether or not it has a wall around it. Al-hajiz is the barrier that separates two things. Al-fawj is a group. Al-jumud is the stillness of a thing and its lack of movement. Al-itqan is bringing a thing to its best state of perfection and soundness in its creation. It is derived from the Arabs' saying, "taqinu ardahum" (they made their land firm), when they let loose water mixed with clay into it, so that it became solid. Al-tiqn is the water that is poured into a pool, and it is what comes from the water's thickening. Kababtu al-rajul means I threw the man onto his face.

﴿And We had certainly sent to Thamud their brother Salih, [saying], "Worship Allah," but they became two factions disputing.﴾ ﴿He said, "O my people, why do you seek to hasten evil before good? Why do you not ask forgiveness of Allah, that you may receive mercy?"﴾ ﴿They said, "We consider you and those with you to be a bad omen." He said, "Your omen is with Allah; rather, you are a people being tested."﴾ ﴿And there were in the city nine men who spread corruption in the land and did not reform.﴾ ﴿They said, "Swear to one another by Allah that we will surely attack him and his family by night, and then we will say to his heir, 'We did not witness the destruction of his family, and indeed we are truthful.'"﴾ ﴿And they plotted a plot, and We plotted a plot, while they did not perceive.﴾ ﴿So see how was the outcome of their plot: that We destroyed them and their people, all of them.﴾ ﴿And those are their houses, fallen in ruin because they wronged. Indeed in that is a sign for a people who know.﴾ ﴿And We saved those who believed and used to fear Allah.﴾

(p. 82) Thamud is the "first 'Ad." Salih is their brother in lineage. When Allah mentioned the story of Musa, Dawud and Sulayman, who were from the Children of Israel, He mentioned the story of someone who was from the Arabs, to remind Quraysh and the Arabs by it, and to alert them that the prophets who came before them from among the Arabs used to call to the singling out of Allah, Exalted is He, in worship, so that they would know that they were in error by worshipping idols, and that the situation of the prophets, whether Arab or non-Arab, is calling to the worship of Allah.

The "an" in ﴿an uʿbudu﴾ (that worship) may be explanatory (mufassirah), because ﴿arsalna﴾ (We sent) includes the meaning of saying. It may also be a verbal-source particle (masdariyyah), meaning "bi-an uʿbudu" (with [the command] to worship), with the preposition removed. According to the first view, it has no place in grammatical analysis (iʿrab). According to the second, there is a disagreement about its place: is it in a position of accusative or of genitive?

The apparent reading is that the pronoun in ﴿fa-idha hum﴾ (then behold, they) refers back to Thamud, and that his people divided into two groups, a believing group and a disbelieving group. This has been explained in Surah al-A'raf in His saying: ﴿The eminent ones who were arrogant among his people said to those who were oppressed, to those among them who believed﴾ [al-A'raf: 75]. Al-Zamakhshari said: "By the two groups is meant Salih and his people, before any of them had believed." End of quotation. So he made the one group Salih and the other group his people.

"Idha" here is the sudden-occurrence "idha" (al-fujaʾiyyah), and He joined with the "fa" which indicates sequence, not delay. So the meaning is that they rushed to dispute immediately after Salih called them to the worship of Allah. The word ﴿yakhtasimun﴾ (they dispute) is in the plural according to meaning, because the two groups are plural. If the two groups are the believer and the disbeliever, then plurality is present in each group. What shows that the believing group is plural is His saying: ﴿Indeed, we disbelieve in that which you have believed﴾ [al-A'raf: 76], where He said "amantum" (you believed), which is a plural pronoun.
