He tied that to the hope of mercy and did not state definitively that it would follow from their seeking forgiveness. In the exhortation there was an alert to their error in hastening punishment, and a declaration of their ignorance in their belief.

When he had been gentle with them in address, they became harsh toward him and said: ﴿We consider you and those with you to be a bad omen﴾, that is, we consider you and those who believed with you to be an omen of misfortune. This conjunction indicates that the two groups were believers and disbelievers, due to His saying ﴿and those with you﴾. They had experienced drought, and they made the cause of their drought the very person of Salih and those who believed with him. So He answered them with His saying: ﴿Your omen is with Allah﴾, that is, your portion in reality, of good or of evil, is with Allah and by His decree: if He wills, He provides for you, and if He wills, He withholds from you. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is possible that it means your deeds are written with Allah; from them has come down upon you what has come down as punishment for you and as a trial. And from this is His saying, 'Your omen is with you' [Yasin: 19], and 'every person We have fastened his omen to his neck' [al-Isra: 13]." It was read ﴿tatayyarna bika﴾ according to the original form. The meaning of "tatayyara bihi" is that he considered him an omen of misfortune, and "tatayyara minhu" (p. 83) means he recoiled from him. End of quotation.

Then he moved on to informing about their state, and said: ﴿Rather, you are a people being tested﴾, that is, you are being examined, or punished, or Satan tempts you by his whisperings to you of the omen-taking, or you are tested by his desires, that is, you are attached to them, as it is said: "So-and-so was smitten (futina) with so-and-so." The poet said:

"An ancient ailment among the children of Adam: one person's trial by another person."

These are the views that the wording *tuftanun* can bear. It is read *tuftanuna* with the second-person *ta'* (addressing *antum*, "you"), which is the common usage in the Arabic language. It may also be read *yuftanuna* with the third-person *ya'* (agreeing with the word *qawm*, "a people"), which is less common. The Arabs say: "You are a man who enjoins good," with either the *ta'* of address or the *ya'* of the third person.

"Al-madinah" (the city) is the gathering place and settlement of Thamud, and it is al-Hijr. The commentators (*mufassirun*, those who perform *tafsir*, i.e. exegesis) mentioned the names of the nine men, and there is disagreement about some of them. Their chief was Qudar ibn Salif. Their names cannot be fixed with certainty or precisely identified, so we have set aside mentioning them. They were the great men of the town, its wealthy people, and its wicked ones.

*Al-rahat* means from three to ten men, and *al-nafar* means from three to nine. The commentators agreed that the meaning is nine men. Al-Zamakhshari said: "The specification of *tis'ah* (nine) by *rahat* is permissible only because it carries the sense of a group, so it is as if it were said: nine persons (*anfus*)." End of quote. The other view, that the meaning is "nine men," is preferable, because if he attached it to *anfus*, he should have said *tis' anfus* with the feminine form, since the eloquent usage of *nafs* is feminine. Do you not see that they counted as an anomaly the poet's line:

"Thalathat anfusin wa thalath dhawd" ("three persons and three camels"),

where he used the *ta'* in *thalathah* (the feminine form with a masculine noun), whereas the eloquent form would have been *thalath anfus*. Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: "The more likely view is that what is intended is *tis'ah* as a collective, since the apparent meaning of *rahat* is a group and not a single individual. It is possible that they were tribes, and it is possible that they were included under the number because of the differences in their qualities and conditions, not because of the differences in their kinds." End of quote. It has been said: *rahat* is the name of a group, and it seems they were chiefs, each with a *rahat* of his own. Al-Kirmani said: "Its root is from *al-tarhit*, which is the magnifying of mouthfuls and the vigor of eating." End of quote.

*Rahat* is a collective noun (*ism jam'*). They agreed that its specification by *min* (from) is the eloquent usage, as in the Exalted saying: ﴿So take four of the birds﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 260]. They differed over whether a number may be attached to it as an annexation (*idafah*). Al-Akhfash held that this is not a regular practice, and whatever is reported of annexation to it is an exceptional usage. Sibawayh explicitly stated that one does not say *thalath ghanam* (three sheep). Others held that this is permissible and regular, though it is still rare. Some distinguished between a collective noun denoting a small number, such as *rahat*, *nafar* and *dhawd*, which may be annexed to a number, and one used for a large quantity, or one used for both, which may not be annexed to a number. This is the view of al-Mazini. We have lengthened the discussion of this issue in *Sharh al-Tashil* (the Commentary on *al-Tashil*).

*Yufsidun* (they corrupt) is a description (*sifah*) of "nine men." The meaning is that they corrupt with a great corruption that is not mixed with any reform, which is why He said: ﴿and they do not reform﴾. This is because one who commits corruption may sometimes also do reform at other times.

The majority recited *taqasamu* ("swear to one another"), and Ibn Abi Layla recited *tiqassamu*, without the *alif* and with a doubled *sin*. Both come from *al-qasam* (oath), *al-taqasum* and *al-taqsim*, like *al-tazahur* and *al-tazhir*.

The apparent meaning is that the word *taqasamu* is an imperative verb reported as speech, and this is the view of the majority: some of them urged others to swear to the night attack on Salih. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyyah permitted that *taqasamu* be a past verb in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), meaning "they said, swearing to one another." Al-Zamakhshari said: "*Taqasamu* may be an imperative and a declarative on the position of a circumstantial clause, with *qad* understood, meaning: they said, swearing to one another." End of quote. As for his phrase "and declarative," it is not correct, because "declarative" (*khabar*) is one of the two divisions of speech, since speech is divided into declarative and performative (*insha'*), and all its meanings, if you examine them, return to these two divisions.

He then said: "It has been recited *latubayyitannahu* with *ya'*, *ta'* and *nun*. With the *nun* and *ta'*, *taqasamu* may take both readings, meaning in *taqasamu billah*. The two readings are the imperative and the declarative in his view. With the *ya'*, it can only be a declarative." End of quote. The restriction by a circumstantial clause is only a matter of attributing the restriction, not of the attribution of the speech which is the predication (*isnad*). So when the term "declarative" is applied to it, that is on the assumption that if it were not a circumstantial clause it could be used as a declarative. Likewise their saying that the clause before it, which is a relative clause, is "declarative" is a figurative usage, and the meaning is that if it were not a relative clause it could be used as a declarative. This is a matter that is somewhat obscure, and it does not require supposing an implied element, since the occurrence of the past tense as a circumstantial clause without *qad* is very frequent, to the point that it should be used as a basis for analogy.

According to this parsing, it is possible that *billah* ("by God") is connected to *taqasamu*, which is the circumstantial clause, so it belongs to its complement and is not included within the speech. As for the reported speech, *latubayyitannahu* ("we will surely attack him") and what follows, it is possible that this and what follows is the reported speech.

The majority recited ﴿latubayyitannahu wa-ahlahu thumma lataqulanna﴾ ("we will surely attack him and his family, then we will surely say") with *nun* in both. Al-Hasan, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited with the *ta'* of the plural address. Mujahid, Ibn Wathhab, Talhah and al-A'mash recited with the *ya'* of the third person, with both verbs having a plural subject. Humayd ibn Qays recited with *ya'* of the third person in the first verb, with a plural subject, meaning *layubayyitunnahu* ("they will surely attack him," i.e., a group of us), and with *nun* in the second, meaning all of us say to his heir (*waliyyihi*). *Al-bayat* is the surprise attack upon the enemy. It is reported of Alexander (*al-Iskandar*) that when he was advised to use a night attack, he said: "It is not the custom of kings to steal victory." His *waliyy* is the seeker of vengeance for him if he is killed.

The majority recited *muhlaka*, with a *mim* vowel and a *fath* on the *lam*, from *ahlaka*. Hafs recited *mahlika*, with a *fath* on the *mim* and a *kasrah* on the *lam*. Abu Bakr recited with *fath* on both. As for the first reading, it may be a verbal noun, a time, or a place, meaning: we did not witness the destruction of his family, or the time of their destruction, or the place of their destruction. It follows from these two that if they did not witness the time or the place, they did not witness the destruction either. As for the second reading, analogy requires that it be for time and place, meaning: we did not witness the time of their destruction, nor its place. The third reading, by analogy, requires it to be a verbal noun, meaning: we did not witness his destruction. Al-Zamakhshari said: "They mentioned the three readings, and the verbal noun, time and place are possible." End of quote.

The apparent meaning in the statement is that a conjoined element is omitted, indicated by what precedes it, and the implied sense is: we did not witness the destruction of his family and his destruction. This is indicated by their saying ﴿latubayyitannahu wa-ahlahu﴾ and by what is reported, that they had resolved to kill him and kill his family. Omitting such a conjoined element is permissible in eloquent speech, as in His saying: ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [Al-Nahl: 81], meaning "and the cold." And the poet said:

"Fa-ma kana bayn al-khayr law ja'a salimam / Abu hujrin illa layali qala'il"
("Between me and the good, had he come safe, Abu Hujr was only a few nights away.")

meaning: between the good and between me.

Their saying ﴿and indeed we are truthful﴾ would then be a lie in the report. They led their people to believe that if they killed him and his family secretly, and no one noticed them, and they spoke that statement, they were truthful, while they were liars.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "(If you ask): How could they be truthful when they denied what they did, so that they brought the report contrary to what it reports? (I answer): It is as if they believed that when they attacked Salih and attacked his family, they combined the two attacks, then they said: ﴿we did not witness the destruction of his family﴾, so they mentioned one of them, and they were truthful, because they did both attacks together, not just one of them. In this there is decisive proof that lying (*al-kadhib*) is ugly among the unbelievers who do not know the Law (*al-shar'*) and its prohibitions, and it does not occur to their minds. Do you not see that they intended to kill the prophet of God, and did not consider it possible for themselves to be liars, until they made truthfulness in themselves a stratagem by which they fall short of lying?" End of quote.

It is astonishing that this man contrives these stratagems to make their statement ﴿and indeed we are truthful﴾ a statement of truth. Yet he knows that they denied Salih, and hamstrung the she-camel, which was among the greatest signs, and proceeded to kill a prophet and his family. Lying is not permissible for them, and yet he recites in the Book of God their lies against their prophets. God has stated this explicitly, and their lies against One to whom no secret is hidden: ﴿on the day when secrets are examined﴾ [Al-Tariq: 9]. And that is their saying: ﴿By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [Al-An'am: 23], and the saying of God, Exalted is He: ﴿Look how they lied against themselves﴾ [Al-An'am: 24]. What this man does is a distortion of the words of God, Exalted is He, in order to support his doctrine that lying is ugly among the unbelievers, and he devises this stratagem for them so that he makes them truthful in their report.

This man, although he was given the greatest share of the knowledge of the Qur'an, and combined the invention of meaning with eloquence of expression, nevertheless his book of *tafsir* contains criticizable matters. I was close to finishing writing these lines, having composed a poem on a person occupying himself with the Book of God, and I digressed into praising the book of al-Zamakhshari, mentioning some of its merits, then I drew attention to what it contains that must be avoided. I saw fit to include it here, so that whoever reads this book of mine may benefit and be alerted to the vices it contains. I said after mentioning what I praised him for:

"Wa-lakinnahu fihi majal li-naqid / wa-zallat su'in qad akhadhna al-makhaniqa"
("But in it there is room for a critic, and lapses of error that have seized the throats.")

"Fa-yuthbitu mawdu' al-ahadith jahilan / wa-yazu ila al-ma'sumi ma laysa la'iqa"
("He establishes fabricated hadiths in ignorance, and ascribes to the infallible what is not fitting.")

"Wa-yashtumu a'lam al-a'immati dallatan / wa-la siyyama in awlajuhu al-madayiqa"
("He reviles the great imams in error, especially if they are driven into straits.")

"Wa-yusbihu fi al-ma'na al-wajiz dalalatan / bi-takthiri alfaz tusamma al-shaqashiqa"
("He prolixes on the concise meaning in its indication, by multiplying words called *al-shaqashiq* (empty chatter).")

"Yuqawwilu fiha Allah ma laysa qa'ilan / wa-kana muhibban fi al-khitabati wamiqa"
("He puts into God's mouth what He did not say, and he was a lover of oratory, passionately fond of it.")

"Wa-yukhti'u fi tarkibihi li-kalamihi / fa-laysa li-ma qad rakkabuhu muwafiqa"
("He errs in composing his words, so that they do not agree with what they composed.")

"Wa-yansibu ibda' al-ma'ani li-nafsihi / li-yuwhima aghmaran wa-in kana saariqa"
("He ascribes the origination of meanings to himself, to deceive the ignorant, even though he is a thief.")

"Wa-yukhti'u fi fahm al-Qur'an li-annahu / yujawwizu i'rabam aba an yutabiqa"
("He errs in understanding the Qur'an, because he permits a parsing (*i'rab*) that refuses to agree.")

"Wa-kam bayna man yu'ta al-bayan salIqatan / wa-akhara 'anahu fa-ma huwa lahiqa"
("How great is the difference between one given eloquence by nature, and another who strained for it, and yet did not attain it.")

"Wa-yahtalu lil-alfaz hatta yudiruha / li-madhhabi su'in fihi asbaha mariqa"
("He contrives with words until he turns them to a wicked doctrine, through which he became an apostate.")

"Fa-ya khusrahu shaykhan takharraqa situ / maghariba takhriqi al-saba wa-mashariqa"
("Woe to him, an old man whose fame has spread to the west and east like the scattering of the east wind.")

"La-in lam tudarikahu min Allahi rahmatun / lasawfa yura lil-kafirina murafiqa"
("If he is not overtaken by a mercy from God, he will surely be seen as a companion of the unbelievers.")

Their scheming (*makrahum*) is what they concealed of plotting to kill Salih and his family. The scheming of God (*makr Allah*) is destroying them from where they do not perceive. It is likened to the scheming of a schemer by way of metaphor (*isti'arah*). Their scheming was pretending that they were travelling and hiding in a cave. It was said: or in a ravine (*shi'b*). Or it was their resolve to kill him and his family, and their oath that they had not been present at that. The scheming of God against them was the closing of a rock over the mouth of the cave and the ravine, and their destruction within it. Or it was the angels pelting them with stones, which they saw but did not see the one throwing them, when they drew their swords at night to kill him. These are two opinions. It was also said that God informed Salih of their scheme so that he left it, and that this is the scheming of God against them.

It is related that Salih, after the slaughter of the she-camel, informed them that the punishment would come after three days. These nine men agreed to kill Salih and his family at night, and said: "If he is lying in his threat, we will have inflicted upon him what he deserves; and if he is truthful, we will have hastened it before him and cooled our souls." They hid in a cave, and God destroyed them, as has been mentioned before, and destroyed their people as well, and each group was unaware of the destruction of the other.

Apparently "*kayfa*" is the predicate of *kana*, and "*'aqibatu*" is its noun. The clause is in the position of accusative after *unzur*, and it is suspended. The majority (*al-Jumhur*) read "*Inna*" with a kasra on the hamzah, as a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*). Al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq and the Kufans read it with a fatha, so "*anna*" is either a substitute for "*'aqibatu*", or a predicate for *kana*, and it would be in the position of a circumstantial accusative (*hal*), or the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: it, that is, the outcome, is their destruction. Or the estimate is: "because we...", and the preposition has been omitted. On both readings it is permissible for *kana* to be complete (*tammah*) with "*'aqibatu*" as its subject, or for it to be superfluous (*za'idah*) with "*'aqibatu*" as a subject whose predicate is "*kayfa*".

Ubayy read: "*an dammarnahum*", where *an* is the particle that governs the imperfect, and the permissible readings for *anna* apply to it, with the hamzah given a fatha. Abu al-Baqa' reported that some scholars permitted, in the reading of whoever gave the hamzah a fatha, that "*anna dammarnahum*" be a substitute for "*kayfa*". He said: others said it is not permitted, because a substitute for an interrogative requires repeating its particle, as in his saying: "How is Zayd, healthy or sick?"

When He, exalted is He, commanded them to consider what befell them of destruction in themselves, He explained that by pointing to their dwellings and how they were emptied of them, and the ruin and vacancy of the houses from their people, so that none of them remained of what the wrongdoers are punished with, since that indicates their complete eradication. In the Torah: "Son of Adam, do not wrong, lest your house be ruined." This is an indication of the destruction of the wrongdoer, since the ruin of his house follows his destruction. These are the houses about which the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to his companions, in the year of Tabuk: "Do not enter upon these punished people unless you are weeping," and so on in the hadith.

The majority read "*khawiyah*" in the accusative as a circumstantial accusative (*hal*). Al-Zamakhshari said: it is governed by what that demonstrative (*tilka*) indicates. Isa ibn Umar read "*khawiyatun*" in the nominative. Al-Zamakhshari said: as the predicate of an omitted subject. Ibn Atiyyah also said this, meaning: they are empty. He said: or as a predicate concerning *tilka*, and "*buyutuhum*" is a substitute, or as a second predicate. "*Khawiyah*" is a report, because of their wrongdoing, which is disbelief, and it derives from the emptiness of the belly. Ibn Abbas said: "*khawiyah*" means that its upper part has fallen onto its lower part.

"*Inna fi dhalika*": that is, in Our action toward Thamud, which is Our eradicating them by destruction and the emptying of their dwellings of them. Their houses were in Wadi al-Qura, between Medina and Syria.

"*Wa-anjayna alladhina amanu*": that is, through Salih, from the punishment that descended upon the disbelievers. Those who believed in him were four thousand. Salih departed with them to Hadramawt. Hadramawt was so named because when Salih, peace be upon him, entered it, he died there, and the believers built a city there called Hadurah. As for those who perished, a boil like a chickpea came out on their bodies; it turned red on the first day, yellow on the second, and black on the third. The slaughter of the she-camel was on Wednesday, and they perished on Sunday. Muqatil said: those boils burst, and Jibril, peace be upon him, shouted at them with one cry, and they were extinguished.

(p. 81) Al-hadiqah (the garden) is an orchard, whether or not it has a wall around it. Al-hajiz is the barrier that separates two things. Al-fawj is a group. Al-jumud is the stillness of a thing and its lack of movement. Al-itqan is bringing a thing to its best state of perfection and soundness in its creation. It is derived from the Arabs' saying, "taqinu ardahum" (they made their land firm), when they let loose water mixed with clay into it, so that it became solid. Al-tiqn is the water that is poured into a pool, and it is what comes from the water's thickening. Kababtu al-rajul means I threw the man onto his face.

﴿And We had certainly sent to Thamud their brother Salih, [saying], "Worship Allah," but they became two factions disputing.﴾ ﴿He said, "O my people, why do you seek to hasten evil before good? Why do you not ask forgiveness of Allah, that you may receive mercy?"﴾ ﴿They said, "We consider you and those with you to be a bad omen." He said, "Your omen is with Allah; rather, you are a people being tested."﴾ ﴿And there were in the city nine men who spread corruption in the land and did not reform.﴾ ﴿They said, "Swear to one another by Allah that we will surely attack him and his family by night, and then we will say to his heir, 'We did not witness the destruction of his family, and indeed we are truthful.'"﴾ ﴿And they plotted a plot, and We plotted a plot, while they did not perceive.﴾ ﴿So see how was the outcome of their plot: that We destroyed them and their people, all of them.﴾ ﴿And those are their houses, fallen in ruin because they wronged. Indeed in that is a sign for a people who know.﴾ ﴿And We saved those who believed and used to fear Allah.﴾

(p. 82) Thamud is the "first 'Ad." Salih is their brother in lineage. When Allah mentioned the story of Musa, Dawud and Sulayman, who were from the Children of Israel, He mentioned the story of someone who was from the Arabs, to remind Quraysh and the Arabs by it, and to alert them that the prophets who came before them from among the Arabs used to call to the singling out of Allah, Exalted is He, in worship, so that they would know that they were in error by worshipping idols, and that the situation of the prophets, whether Arab or non-Arab, is calling to the worship of Allah.

The "an" in ﴿an uʿbudu﴾ (that worship) may be explanatory (mufassirah), because ﴿arsalna﴾ (We sent) includes the meaning of saying. It may also be a verbal-source particle (masdariyyah), meaning "bi-an uʿbudu" (with [the command] to worship), with the preposition removed. According to the first view, it has no place in grammatical analysis (iʿrab). According to the second, there is a disagreement about its place: is it in a position of accusative or of genitive?

The apparent reading is that the pronoun in ﴿fa-idha hum﴾ (then behold, they) refers back to Thamud, and that his people divided into two groups, a believing group and a disbelieving group. This has been explained in Surah al-A'raf in His saying: ﴿The eminent ones who were arrogant among his people said to those who were oppressed, to those among them who believed﴾ [al-A'raf: 75]. Al-Zamakhshari said: "By the two groups is meant Salih and his people, before any of them had believed." End of quotation. So he made the one group Salih and the other group his people.

"Idha" here is the sudden-occurrence "idha" (al-fujaʾiyyah), and He joined with the "fa" which indicates sequence, not delay. So the meaning is that they rushed to dispute immediately after Salih called them to the worship of Allah. The word ﴿yakhtasimun﴾ (they dispute) is in the plural according to meaning, because the two groups are plural. If the two groups are the believer and the disbeliever, then plurality is present in each group. What shows that the believing group is plural is His saying: ﴿Indeed, we disbelieve in that which you have believed﴾ [al-A'raf: 76], where He said "amantum" (you believed), which is a plural pronoun. If the believing group was Salih alone, then he had joined with his people, and the combined group is plural. ﴿Yakhtasimun﴾ was preferred over ﴿yakhtasimani﴾ (the two dispute), although the dual is permissible and eloquent in terms of form, because it is the end of a verse (maqta' fasl). The disputing among them is each group's claim that the truth is with them. Allah has mentioned their disputing in Surah al-A'raf.

Then Salih was gentle with his people and kind to them in address. He said, calling to them in a manner of tenderness toward them: ﴿Why do you seek to hasten evil?﴾, that is, to the occurrence of what would harm you, before the good state, which is the mercy of Allah. He had said to them in the story of the she-camel: ﴿And do not touch her with harm, lest there seize you a painful punishment﴾ [al-A'raf: 73]. They said to him: ﴿Bring us what you threaten us with, from the punishment of Allah﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 29]. It was also said: "Why do you hasten to the occurrence of sins from yourselves before obedience?" Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: what is the meaning of their hastening to evil before good? That happens only if both are expected, one before the other? I say: they used to say in their ignorance: 'The punishment that Salih promises us, if it happens according to his claim, then we will repent at that time and seek forgiveness, assuming that repentance is accepted at that time; and if it does not happen, then we are as we are.' So Salih, peace be upon him, addressed them according to their saying and belief." End of quotation.

Then he urged them toward what would repel evil from them, which is faith and seeking Allah's forgiveness for what preceded of disbelief. He tied that to the hope of mercy and did not state definitively that it would follow from their seeking forgiveness. In the exhortation there was an alert to their error in hastening punishment, and a declaration of their ignorance in their belief.

When he had been gentle with them in address, they became harsh toward him and said: ﴿We consider you and those with you to be a bad omen﴾, that is, we consider you and those who believed with you to be an omen of misfortune. This conjunction indicates that the two groups were believers and disbelievers, due to His saying ﴿and those with you﴾. They had experienced drought, and they made the cause of their drought the very person of Salih and those who believed with him. So He answered them with His saying: ﴿Your omen is with Allah﴾, that is, your portion in reality, of good or of evil, is with Allah and by His decree: if He wills, He provides for you, and if He wills, He withholds from you. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is possible that it means your deeds are written with Allah; from them has come down upon you what has come down as punishment for you and as a trial. And from this is His saying, 'Your omen is with you' [Yasin: 19], and 'every person We have fastened his omen to his neck' [al-Isra: 13]." It was read ﴿tatayyarna bika﴾ according to the original form. The meaning of "tatayyara bihi" is that he considered him an omen of misfortune, and "tatayyara minhu" (p. 83) means he recoiled from him. End of quotation.

Then he moved on to informing about their state, and said: ﴿Rather, you are a people being tested﴾, that is, you are being examined, or punished, or Satan tempts you by his whisperings to you of the omen-taking, or you are tested by his desires, that is, you are attached to them, as it is said: "So-and-so was smitten (futina) with so-and-so." The poet said:

"An ancient ailment among the children of Adam: one person's trial by another person."

These are the views that the wording *tuftanun* can bear. It is read *tuftanuna* with the second-person *ta'* (addressing *antum*, "you"), which is the common usage in the Arabic language. It may also be read *yuftanuna* with the third-person *ya'* (agreeing with the word *qawm*, "a people"), which is less common. The Arabs say: "You are a man who enjoins good," with either the *ta'* of address or the *ya'* of the third person.

"Al-madinah" (the city) is the gathering place and settlement of Thamud, and it is al-Hijr. The commentators (*mufassirun*, those who perform *tafsir*, i.e. exegesis) mentioned the names of the nine men, and there is disagreement about some of them. Their chief was Qudar ibn Salif. Their names cannot be fixed with certainty or precisely identified, so we have set aside mentioning them. They were the great men of the town, its wealthy people, and its wicked ones.

*Al-rahat* means from three to ten men, and *al-nafar* means from three to nine. The commentators agreed that the meaning is nine men. Al-Zamakhshari said: "The specification of *tis'ah* (nine) by *rahat* is permissible only because it carries the sense of a group, so it is as if it were said: nine persons (*anfus*)." End of quote. The other view, that the meaning is "nine men," is preferable, because if he attached it to *anfus*, he should have said *tis' anfus* with the feminine form, since the eloquent usage of *nafs* is feminine. Do you not see that they counted as an anomaly the poet's line:

"Thalathat anfusin wa thalath dhawd" ("three persons and three camels"),

where he used the *ta'* in *thalathah* (the feminine form with a masculine noun), whereas the eloquent form would have been *thalath anfus*. Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: "The more likely view is that what is intended is *tis'ah* as a collective, since the apparent meaning of *rahat* is a group and not a single individual. It is possible that they were tribes, and it is possible that they were included under the number because of the differences in their qualities and conditions, not because of the differences in their kinds." End of quote. It has been said: *rahat* is the name of a group, and it seems they were chiefs, each with a *rahat* of his own. Al-Kirmani said: "Its root is from *al-tarhit*, which is the magnifying of mouthfuls and the vigor of eating." End of quote.

*Rahat* is a collective noun (*ism jam'*). They agreed that its specification by *min* (from) is the eloquent usage, as in the Exalted saying: ﴿So take four of the birds﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 260]. They differed over whether a number may be attached to it as an annexation (*idafah*). Al-Akhfash held that this is not a regular practice, and whatever is reported of annexation to it is an exceptional usage. Sibawayh explicitly stated that one does not say *thalath ghanam* (three sheep). Others held that this is permissible and regular, though it is still rare. Some distinguished between a collective noun denoting a small number, such as *rahat*, *nafar* and *dhawd*, which may be annexed to a number, and one used for a large quantity, or one used for both, which may not be annexed to a number. This is the view of al-Mazini. We have lengthened the discussion of this issue in *Sharh al-Tashil* (the Commentary on *al-Tashil*).

*Yufsidun* (they corrupt) is a description (*sifah*) of "nine men." The meaning is that they corrupt with a great corruption that is not mixed with any reform, which is why He said: ﴿and they do not reform﴾. This is because one who commits corruption may sometimes also do reform at other times.

The majority recited *taqasamu* ("swear to one another"), and Ibn Abi Layla recited *tiqassamu*, without the *alif* and with a doubled *sin*. Both come from *al-qasam* (oath), *al-taqasum* and *al-taqsim*, like *al-tazahur* and *al-tazhir*.

The apparent meaning is that the word *taqasamu* is an imperative verb reported as speech, and this is the view of the majority: some of them urged others to swear to the night attack on Salih. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyyah permitted that *taqasamu* be a past verb in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), meaning "they said, swearing to one another." Al-Zamakhshari said: "*Taqasamu* may be an imperative and a declarative on the position of a circumstantial clause, with *qad* understood, meaning: they said, swearing to one another." End of quote. As for his phrase "and declarative," it is not correct, because "declarative" (*khabar*) is one of the two divisions of speech, since speech is divided into declarative and performative (*insha'*), and all its meanings, if you examine them, return to these two divisions.

He then said: "It has been recited *latubayyitannahu* with *ya'*, *ta'* and *nun*. With the *nun* and *ta'*, *taqasamu* may take both readings, meaning in *taqasamu billah*. The two readings are the imperative and the declarative in his view. With the *ya'*, it can only be a declarative." End of quote. The restriction by a circumstantial clause is only a matter of attributing the restriction, not of the attribution of the speech which is the predication (*isnad*). So when the term "declarative" is applied to it, that is on the assumption that if it were not a circumstantial clause it could be used as a declarative. Likewise their saying that the clause before it, which is a relative clause, is "declarative" is a figurative usage, and the meaning is that if it were not a relative clause it could be used as a declarative. This is a matter that is somewhat obscure, and it does not require supposing an implied element, since the occurrence of the past tense as a circumstantial clause without *qad* is very frequent, to the point that it should be used as a basis for analogy.

According to this parsing, it is possible that *billah* ("by God") is connected to *taqasamu*, which is the circumstantial clause, so it belongs to its complement and is not included within the speech. As for the reported speech, *latubayyitannahu* ("we will surely attack him") and what follows, it is possible that this and what follows is the reported speech.

The majority recited ﴿latubayyitannahu wa-ahlahu thumma lataqulanna﴾ ("we will surely attack him and his family, then we will surely say") with *nun* in both. Al-Hasan, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited with the *ta'* of the plural address. Mujahid, Ibn Wathhab, Talhah and al-A'mash recited with the *ya'* of the third person, with both verbs having a plural subject. Humayd ibn Qays recited with *ya'* of the third person in the first verb, with a plural subject, meaning *layubayyitunnahu* ("they will surely attack him," i.e., a group of us), and with *nun* in the second, meaning all of us say to his heir (*waliyyihi*). *Al-bayat* is the surprise attack upon the enemy. It is reported of Alexander (*al-Iskandar*) that when he was advised to use a night attack, he said: "It is not the custom of kings to steal victory." His *waliyy* is the seeker of vengeance for him if he is killed.

The majority recited *muhlaka*, with a *mim* vowel and a *fath* on the *lam*, from *ahlaka*. Hafs recited *mahlika*, with a *fath* on the *mim* and a *kasrah* on the *lam*. Abu Bakr recited with *fath* on both. As for the first reading, it may be a verbal noun, a time, or a place, meaning: we did not witness the destruction of his family, or the time of their destruction, or the place of their destruction. It follows from these two that if they did not witness the time or the place, they did not witness the destruction either. As for the second reading, analogy requires that it be for time and place, meaning: we did not witness the time of their destruction, nor its place. The third reading, by analogy, requires it to be a verbal noun, meaning: we did not witness his destruction. Al-Zamakhshari said: "They mentioned the three readings, and the verbal noun, time and place are possible." End of quote.

The apparent meaning in the statement is that a conjoined element is omitted, indicated by what precedes it, and the implied sense is: we did not witness the destruction of his family and his destruction. This is indicated by their saying ﴿latubayyitannahu wa-ahlahu﴾ and by what is reported, that they had resolved to kill him and kill his family. Omitting such a conjoined element is permissible in eloquent speech, as in His saying: ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [Al-Nahl: 81], meaning "and the cold." And the poet said:

"Fa-ma kana bayn al-khayr law ja'a salimam / Abu hujrin illa layali qala'il"
("Between me and the good, had he come safe, Abu Hujr was only a few nights away.")

meaning: between the good and between me.

Their saying ﴿and indeed we are truthful﴾ would then be a lie in the report. They led their people to believe that if they killed him and his family secretly, and no one noticed them, and they spoke that statement, they were truthful, while they were liars.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "(If you ask): How could they be truthful when they denied what they did, so that they brought the report contrary to what it reports? (I answer): It is as if they believed that when they attacked Salih and attacked his family, they combined the two attacks, then they said: ﴿we did not witness the destruction of his family﴾, so they mentioned one of them, and they were truthful, because they did both attacks together, not just one of them. In this there is decisive proof that lying (*al-kadhib*) is ugly among the unbelievers who do not know the Law (*al-shar'*) and its prohibitions, and it does not occur to their minds. Do you not see that they intended to kill the prophet of God, and did not consider it possible for themselves to be liars, until they made truthfulness in themselves a stratagem by which they fall short of lying?" End of quote.

It is astonishing that this man contrives these stratagems to make their statement ﴿and indeed we are truthful﴾ a statement of truth. Yet he knows that they denied Salih, and hamstrung the she-camel, which was among the greatest signs, and proceeded to kill a prophet and his family. Lying is not permissible for them, and yet he recites in the Book of God their lies against their prophets. God has stated this explicitly, and their lies against One to whom no secret is hidden: ﴿on the day when secrets are examined﴾ [Al-Tariq: 9]. And that is their saying: ﴿By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [Al-An'am: 23], and the saying of God, Exalted is He: ﴿Look how they lied against themselves﴾ [Al-An'am: 24]. What this man does is a distortion of the words of God, Exalted is He, in order to support his doctrine that lying is ugly among the unbelievers, and he devises this stratagem for them so that he makes them truthful in their report.

This man, although he was given the greatest share of the knowledge of the Qur'an, and combined the invention of meaning with eloquence of expression, nevertheless his book of *tafsir* contains criticizable matters. I was close to finishing writing these lines, having composed a poem on a person occupying himself with the Book of God, and I digressed into praising the book of al-Zamakhshari, mentioning some of its merits, then I drew attention to what it contains that must be avoided. I saw fit to include it here, so that whoever reads this book of mine may benefit and be alerted to the vices it contains. I said after mentioning what I praised him for:

"Wa-lakinnahu fihi majal li-naqid / wa-zallat su'in qad akhadhna al-makhaniqa"
("But in it there is room for a critic, and lapses of error that have seized the throats.")

"Fa-yuthbitu mawdu' al-ahadith jahilan / wa-yazu ila al-ma'sumi ma laysa la'iqa"
("He establishes fabricated hadiths in ignorance, and ascribes to the infallible what is not fitting.")

"Wa-yashtumu a'lam al-a'immati dallatan / wa-la siyyama in awlajuhu al-madayiqa"
("He reviles the great imams in error, especially if they are driven into straits.")

"Wa-yusbihu fi al-ma'na al-wajiz dalalatan / bi-takthiri alfaz tusamma al-shaqashiqa"
("He prolixes on the concise meaning in its indication, by multiplying words called *al-shaqashiq* (empty chatter).")

"Yuqawwilu fiha Allah ma laysa qa'ilan / wa-kana muhibban fi al-khitabati wamiqa"
("He puts into God's mouth what He did not say, and he was a lover of oratory, passionately fond of it.")

"Wa-yukhti'u fi tarkibihi li-kalamihi / fa-laysa li-ma qad rakkabuhu muwafiqa"
("He errs in composing his words, so that they do not agree with what they composed.")

"Wa-yansibu ibda' al-ma'ani li-nafsihi / li-yuwhima aghmaran wa-in kana saariqa"
("He ascribes the origination of meanings to himself, to deceive the ignorant, even though he is a thief.")

"Wa-yukhti'u fi fahm al-Qur'an li-annahu / yujawwizu i'rabam aba an yutabiqa"
("He errs in understanding the Qur'an, because he permits a parsing (*i'rab*) that refuses to agree.")

"Wa-kam bayna man yu'ta al-bayan salIqatan / wa-akhara 'anahu fa-ma huwa lahiqa"
("How great is the difference between one given eloquence by nature, and another who strained for it, and yet did not attain it.")

"Wa-yahtalu lil-alfaz hatta yudiruha / li-madhhabi su'in fihi asbaha mariqa"
("He contrives with words until he turns them to a wicked doctrine, through which he became an apostate.")

"Fa-ya khusrahu shaykhan takharraqa situ / maghariba takhriqi al-saba wa-mashariqa"
("Woe to him, an old man whose fame has spread to the west and east like the scattering of the east wind.")

"La-in lam tudarikahu min Allahi rahmatun / lasawfa yura lil-kafirina murafiqa"
("If he is not overtaken by a mercy from God, he will surely be seen as a companion of the unbelievers.")

Their scheming (*makrahum*) is what they concealed of plotting to kill Salih and his family. The scheming of God (*makr Allah*) is destroying them from where they do not perceive. It is likened to the scheming of a schemer by way of metaphor (*isti'arah*). Their scheming was pretending that they were travelling and hiding in a cave. It was said: or in a ravine (*shi'b*). Or it was their resolve to kill him and his family, and their oath that they had not been present at that. The scheming of God against them was the closing of a rock over the mouth of the cave and the ravine, and their destruction within it. Or it was the angels pelting them with stones, which they saw but did not see the one throwing them, when they drew their swords at night to kill him. These are two opinions. It was also said that God informed Salih of their scheme so that he left it, and that this is the scheming of God against them.

It is related that Salih, after the slaughter of the she-camel, informed them that the punishment would come after three days. These nine men agreed to kill Salih and his family at night, and said: "If he is lying in his threat, we will have inflicted upon him what he deserves; and if he is truthful, we will have hastened it before him and cooled our souls." They hid in a cave, and God destroyed them, as has been mentioned before, and destroyed their people as well, and each group was unaware of the destruction of the other.

Apparently "*kayfa*" is the predicate of *kana*, and "*'aqibatu*" is its noun. The clause is in the position of accusative after *unzur*, and it is suspended. The majority (*al-Jumhur*) read "*Inna*" with a kasra on the hamzah, as a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*). Al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq and the Kufans read it with a fatha, so "*anna*" is either a substitute for "*'aqibatu*", or a predicate for *kana*, and it would be in the position of a circumstantial accusative (*hal*), or the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: it, that is, the outcome, is their destruction. Or the estimate is: "because we...", and the preposition has been omitted. On both readings it is permissible for *kana* to be complete (*tammah*) with "*'aqibatu*" as its subject, or for it to be superfluous (*za'idah*) with "*'aqibatu*" as a subject whose predicate is "*kayfa*".

Ubayy read: "*an dammarnahum*", where *an* is the particle that governs the imperfect, and the permissible readings for *anna* apply to it, with the hamzah given a fatha. Abu al-Baqa' reported that some scholars permitted, in the reading of whoever gave the hamzah a fatha, that "*anna dammarnahum*" be a substitute for "*kayfa*". He said: others said it is not permitted, because a substitute for an interrogative requires repeating its particle, as in his saying: "How is Zayd, healthy or sick?"

When He, exalted is He, commanded them to consider what befell them of destruction in themselves, He explained that by pointing to their dwellings and how they were emptied of them, and the ruin and vacancy of the houses from their people, so that none of them remained of what the wrongdoers are punished with, since that indicates their complete eradication. In the Torah: "Son of Adam, do not wrong, lest your house be ruined." This is an indication of the destruction of the wrongdoer, since the ruin of his house follows his destruction. These are the houses about which the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to his companions, in the year of Tabuk: "Do not enter upon these punished people unless you are weeping," and so on in the hadith.

The majority read "*khawiyah*" in the accusative as a circumstantial accusative (*hal*). Al-Zamakhshari said: it is governed by what that demonstrative (*tilka*) indicates. Isa ibn Umar read "*khawiyatun*" in the nominative. Al-Zamakhshari said: as the predicate of an omitted subject. Ibn Atiyyah also said this, meaning: they are empty. He said: or as a predicate concerning *tilka*, and "*buyutuhum*" is a substitute, or as a second predicate. "*Khawiyah*" is a report, because of their wrongdoing, which is disbelief, and it derives from the emptiness of the belly. Ibn Abbas said: "*khawiyah*" means that its upper part has fallen onto its lower part.

"*Inna fi dhalika*": that is, in Our action toward Thamud, which is Our eradicating them by destruction and the emptying of their dwellings of them. Their houses were in Wadi al-Qura, between Medina and Syria.

"*Wa-anjayna alladhina amanu*": that is, through Salih, from the punishment that descended upon the disbelievers. Those who believed in him were four thousand. Salih departed with them to Hadramawt. Hadramawt was so named because when Salih, peace be upon him, entered it, he died there, and the believers built a city there called Hadurah. As for those who perished, a boil like a chickpea came out on their bodies; it turned red on the first day, yellow on the second, and black on the third. The slaughter of the she-camel was on Wednesday, and they perished on Sunday. Muqatil said: those boils burst, and Jibril, peace be upon him, shouted at them with one cry, and they were extinguished.

(And Lut) is coordinated with (Salihan), meaning "and We sent Lut," or with (those who believed), meaning "and We saved Lut," or it is governed by an implied "remember" (udhkur), with (idh) as an appositive to it; these are the views. (Ata'tuna) is an interrogative of denunciation and rebuke. The act was first left vague in His words (al-fahisha) [the abomination], then specified in His words, "Indeed, you come to men lustfully instead of women." His words (wa antum tubsirun), "while you see," mean: you know the ugliness of this reprehensible deed that you have invented, and that it is among the greatest sins, and knowing the ugliness of a thing while committing it is greater in sin. Or it means: the traces of the sinners before you, or some of you look at others without concealing it or being ashamed to display it, out of shamelessness and indifference to the monstrous disobedience. These are three views. (Shahwatan) is in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi). (Tajhalun) has the second-person address predominating, as it does in (bal antum qawmun tuftanun). The meaning of (tajhalun) is: you do not know the consequence of what you are doing; or you act like foolish, reckless people; or you act like one who is ignorant that it is a great disobedience while knowing it. These are views. When he denounced them and attributed to them ignorance, and they had no argument for what they were committing of the abomination, they turned to contention and harm. The meaning of (yatatahharun) has already been mentioned in al-A'raf. The majority read (jawaba) in the accusative; al-Hasan and Ibn Abi Ishaq read it in the nominative. The majority read (qaddarnaha) with a doubled dal; Abu Bakr read it with a single dal. The rest of the verse has had its parallel explained in al-A'raf. (Sa'a) has the meaning of (bi'sa), and the object of the dispraise is omitted, meaning: their rain.

The act was first left vague in His words (al-fahisha) [the abomination], then specified in His words, "Indeed, you come to men lustfully instead of women." His words (wa antum tubsirun), "while you see," mean: you know the ugliness of this reprehensible deed that you have invented, and that it is among the greatest sins, and knowing the ugliness of a thing while committing it is greater in sin. Or it means: the traces of the sinners before you, or some of you look at others without concealing it or being ashamed to display it, out of shamelessness and indifference to the monstrous disobedience. These are three views. (Shahwatan) is in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi). (Tajhalun) has the second-person address predominating, as it does in (bal antum qawmun tuftanun). The meaning of (tajhalun) is: you do not know the consequence of what you are doing; or you act like foolish, reckless people; or you act like one who is ignorant that it is a great disobedience while knowing it. These are views. When he denounced them and attributed to them ignorance, and they had no argument for what they were committing of the abomination, they turned to contention and harm. The meaning of (yatatahharun) has already been mentioned in al-A'raf. The majority read (jawaba) in the accusative; al-Hasan and Ibn Abi Ishaq read it in the nominative. The majority read (qaddarnaha) with a doubled dal; Abu Bakr read it with a single dal. The rest of the verse has had its parallel explained in al-A'raf. (Sa'a) has the meaning of (bi'sa), and the object of the dispraise is omitted, meaning: their rain.

[p. 88] When he had finished relating the stories of this surah, He commanded His Messenger ﷺ to praise Him, exalted is He, and to greet with peace those He chose, and he began to differentiate the Necessary Existence (wajib al-wujud), God, exalted is He, from the idols and the religions that they associated with God and worshipped. He began this exposition to the Quraysh and others with the hamdala (the formula of praise, "al-hamdu lillah"), as though it were the opening of a sermon (khutba) for what he was about to present of proofs indicating the Oneness, the knowledge, and the power (of God). Muslims have followed this practice in the opening of their books, their sermons, and their admonitions, so they begin with praising God and blessing Muhammad, the Messenger of God ﷺ. Those who write epistles follow them in the openings of books of conquests, congratulations, and events of significance. It has been said: this passage is connected to what precedes it, and the Messenger, peace be upon him, was commanded to praise God for the destruction of the disbelieving nations, and to greet with peace the prophets and their followers who were saved.

It has been said: "qul" (say) is an address to Lot, peace be upon him, that he should praise God for the destruction of the disbelievers of his people, ﴿and greet with peace His servants whom He has chosen﴾. Ibn Atiyya attributed this view to al-Farra', and said: "This is a non-Arab (ajami) error from al-Farra'." Abu al-Simak recited, "qula al-hamdu lillah," and likewise "qula al-hamdu lillahi sayurikum" with a fatha on the lam. "His servants whom He has chosen" encompasses the prophets and their followers. Ibn Abbas said: the servants who are greeted with peace are the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ, whom He chose for His Prophet; and in singling them out for this there is a rebuke to the disbelieving contemporaries. Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: When God, exalted is He, mentioned the states of the prophets, and that whoever denied them was uprooted by punishment, and that this is removed from the nation of the Messenger, He commanded him to praise Him for the blessing He had singled him out with, and to greet with peace the prophets who endured the hardships of the message. End of quotation, and it has been condensed.

His saying: ﴿Is God better, or what they associate (with Him)?﴾ is an interrogation containing rebuke, reproach, and mockery of their state, and an alert to the point of difference between God, exalted is He, and the idols, since it is known to anyone with reason that there is no partnership in being better between God, exalted is He, and them. This type of comparative form (af'al al-tafdil) often comes where it is known and established that there is no partnership in it, and it is mentioned only as a means of binding the opponent and alerting him to the error of his practice. The apparent meaning is that this interrogation concerns the reality of the essences (khabariyyat al-dhawat). It has been said: it came according to the belief of the polytheists, since they believed their gods to be good in some respect. It has been said: there is an omission in the sentence in two places; the estimate is: "Is the Oneness of God better, or the worship of what they associate?" So "ma" in "am ma" means "alladhi" (that which). It has been said: "ma" is verbal-masdar (infinitive), and the omission is from the first: i.e., "Is the Oneness of God better, or your polytheism?" It has been said: "khayr" is not for comparison; it is like when you say, "Prayer is good," meaning good out of the various goods. It has been said: the estimate is "possessor of good." The apparent meaning is that "khayran" is an af'al al-tafdil, and that the interrogation in such a case comes to explain the corruption of what the opponent holds, to alert him to his error, and to bind him to admit that preference is restricted to one side and absent from the other. The majority read "tushrikun" with the taa of address; al-Hasan, [p. 89] Qatada, Asim, and Abu Amr read it with the yaa of absence. The "am" in "am ma" is connected (muttasila), because the meaning is: "Which of the two is better?" In "(am man khalaqa)" and what follows it, it is disjunctive (munfasila). When God mentioned "good," He, glorified is He, enumerated the goods and benefits which are the effects of His mercy and grace, as He enumerated them in other places of His Book, making them stand before them as witnesses to what He originated of created things, and that they find no alternative to admitting this to God, exalted is He.

The majority read "am man khalaqa" and in the four that follow it with a shadda on the mim, the mim of "am" being assimilated into the mim of "man." Al-A'mash read it with a light mim, making it the interrogative hamza, placed before "man," and "man" in both readings is a subject (mubtada') and its predicate. Ibn Atiyya said: its estimate is: "He disbelieves His blessing and doubts Him," and the like of this meaning. Al-Zamakhshari estimated it: "Is what they associate better?" so he estimated what was affirmed in the first interrogation. He began the interrogation with the name of the essence, then moved on to the attributes. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said in his book "Kitab al-Lawami'": "There must be a supposed corresponding clause (jumla mu'adila), and that which is supposed becomes like that which is spoken, for the indication of the context (fahwa) upon it. The estimate of that clause is: 'Is He who created the heavens like him who did not create?' and likewise its sisters, and he has made explicit in other than this place what was supposed in them, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is then He who creates like him who creates not?﴾ [al-Nahl: 17]." End of quotation. As for calling this estimate a "clause" (jumla): if he means by it a group of words, it is correct; but if he means the clause as defined in grammar, it is not so, rather it is a supposed item of the category of the singular (mufrad).

God, exalted is He, began by mentioning the creation of the settled place of the upper and lower worlds, and the sending down of what sustains the lower world, and He said: "for you" (lakum), i.e., for your sake, as a favour, and that all of that is for your sake. Then He said: ﴿so We caused to grow﴾, and this is a shift (iltifat) from the third person of absence to the first person of speech with the nun of majesty (nun al-'azama), indicating that He alone is singular in this, and that He did not cause those diverse gardens of varied kinds, colours, tastes, and scents to grow by one water except Him, exalted is He. This singling out is strengthened by His saying: ﴿It was not for you to cause their trees to grow﴾. Since the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the sending down of water from the sky, leave no doubt for the rational that this is not but from God, and since growth is something that a human may bring about by sowing, watering, and preparing, and it is permissible for the doer of a cause to be ascribed the act of the effect, He, exalted is He, made clear His singling out of that by way of shift and emphasized it by His saying: ﴿It was not for you to cause their trees to grow﴾. Do you not see that the one who brings about growth may not come in accordance with his intent? And even if he does, he is ignorant of its nature, its measure, and its manner, so how could he be its doer? "Bahja" means beauty, freshness, and loveliness, because the one who looks upon them is delighted (yabtahij), i.e., pleased and rejoices. The majority read "dhat" in the singular, "bahjatin" with the ha' sustained; the broken plural functions in the attribute as the singular does, as in His saying: ﴿spouses purified﴾ [al-Baqara: 25], and it is in the sense of a group. Ibn Abi Abla read "dhawat" in the plural, and "bahajatin" with the ha' vocalized with a fatha.

﴿It was not for you to cause their trees to grow﴾: it has already been stated that the negation of such an occurrence may be due to the impossibility of its happening in this way, or to the impossibility of its happening according to the Law (shar'an), or to the negation of preferability (nafy al-awwaliyya). The meaning here is that causing such a thing to grow is impossible for you, because it is the bringing forth of something from non-existence into existence, and this is not within the power of anyone but God, exalted is He. When He mentioned His favour upon them, He addressed them with that; then when He mentioned their blame, He shifted from address to absence and said: ﴿Rather, they are a people who ascribe equals (ya'dilun)﴾, either as a shift, or as an informing the Messenger ﷺ of their state, i.e., they deviate (ya'dilun) from the truth, or they make others equal to Him (ya'dilu bihi ghayrahu), i.e., they make for Him an equal and a likeness. It is read: "ilahan" with a fatha, in the sense of: "Do you call upon, or do you associate?" It is read: "a-ilahun" with the lightening of the two hamzas and softening of the second, with a separation between them by an alif. When God, exalted is He, mentioned that He originated the heavens and the earth, He mentioned something shared between the heaven and the earth, namely the sending down of water from the sky and the growth of gardens on the earth. Then He mentioned something specific to the earth, which is making it a "qarar" (a settled abode), i.e., a resting place for you, such that it is possible for you to dwell upon it and remain on it, and it is not turned by the celestial sphere (falak). It has been said: because it is insignificant compared to the sphere, like a dot in a millstone.

﴿And He placed rivers within it﴾, i.e., between its places, in its valleys and ravines, ﴿and He placed upon it firm mountains﴾, i.e., firm mountains, so that it does not tilt with you and sway. "Al-bahrani" are the sweet and the salty; "al-hajiz" is the separator, from His power, exalted is He; this is said by al-Dahhak. Mujahid said: the sea of the sky and the earth, and the barrier is of air. al-Hasan said: the sea of Persia and the Romans; al-Suddi said: the sea of Iraq and Syria, and the barrier is of earth. Ibn Atiyya said, preferring this view on the barrier: it is what God placed between them of barriers and obstructions of the earth, despite their thinness in some places and their subtlety, which, were it not for His power, the salt would swallow the sweet. Ibn Atiyya had already presented that the two seas are: the sweet in its entirety, and the salty bitter water in its entirety; and since each of them is great and independent, the operative element in His saying ﴿and He placed﴾ is repeated, so they are of the coordination (atf) of independent clauses, each of them being a favour, and they are not joined under one operative element, so that it would be coordination of singular words. Abu Abdullah al-Razi had, in mentioning these four favours, a discourse from the science of nature, according to his claim, and according to the philosophers (hukama'), which lies outside the ways of the Arabs, and it may be consulted in his book.

"Al-mudtarr" is a passive participle: the one whom illness, poverty, or some accident of the vicissitudes of time has compelled (ahwajahu) to take refuge in God and to humble himself before Him, so he calls upon Him to remove what has befallen him of that and to relieve him of it. Ibn Abbas said: it is the one who is exhausted (al-majhud). al-Suddi said: it is the one who has no strength or power. It has been said: it is the sinner when he seeks forgiveness, and His answering him is joined with His will, exalted is He; so not every compelled one who calls upon Him is answered by God in the removal of what afflicts him. Al-Zamakhshari said: the answering is contingent upon the object requested being a benefit, and for this reason supplication is not good unless it stipulates benefit in it. End of quotation, and this is according to the path of the Mu'tazila in considering what is beneficial (al-maslaha) from God, exalted is He.

﴿And removes the evil﴾: it is everything that is harmful, and it is general for every harm that moves out of the state of the one in distress, and it is specific to a more general one, which is what is harmful, whether what is removed is in the state of compulsion or in what is less than it. "Khulafa'" (successors): i.e., the earlier nations; or in commanding the good and forbidding the evil; or the successors of the Prophet ﷺ after him; or the successors of the disbelievers in their land, or in dominion and authority: these are sayings. al-Hasan in one narration read: "wanajʿaluk-um" with the nun of the speaker, as though it were a resumed statement of information and promise, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿He will surely make them successors in the earth﴾ [al-Nur: 55].

His saying: ﴿and makes you successors of the earth﴾ is a transition from the state of the one in compulsion to a rank different from the state of compulsion, which is the state of succession (khilafa); so these are two circumstantial adverbs (zarfan). How many have we seen in this world of those who reached a state of compulsion and then became a dominating king! The majority read "tadhakkarun" with the taa of address; al-Hasan, al-A'mash, and Abu Amr read it with the yaa of absence, and the dhal in both readings is doubled, because the taa is assimilated into it. Abu Haywa read "tatadhakkarun" with two taas. The darkness of the land is the darkness of the night, and this is the literal sense; and it extends figuratively to ignorance and to the obscurity of a matter, as one says: "the matter became dark to me." The poet said:

"The blindnesses of men have cleared away from youth"

That is, the ignorances of youth. Guidance on land comes through landmarks, and guidance at sea through the stars.

﴿Or who sends the winds as heralds of good news before His mercy?﴾ The explanation of a parallel to this clause has already passed. It is also read as *ʿammā tushrikūn* (عَمّا تُشْرِكُونَ) with the *tāʾ* of address, meaning "what you associate [with Him]."

﴿Or who originates creation﴾: The apparent meaning is that *al-khalq* (الخَلْقَ, "creation") refers to the created thing, and its *bady'* (بَدْءُ, "origination") is its bringing into being and its production. It appears that what is intended is whoever God will restore in the Hereafter from among mankind, the jinn, and the angels, not the whole of created things in general. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "What is meant is the children of Adam, in view of the mention of restoration, and restoration is the resurrection from the graves. It is possible that by *al-khalq* he means the verbal noun of *khalaqa* (creating), and that *yabdaʾu* and *yuʿīdu* (originates and restores) are used figuratively for perfecting and doing well, as you say: 'So-and-so originates and restores in such-and-such a matter' when he masters it." Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: how did He say to them, 'Or who originates creation and then restores it,' when they deny restoration? I answer: He has favored them by enabling them to know and to acknowledge, so there remains no excuse for them in denial." End of quotation.

Since bringing the children of Adam into being is a favor and a kindness toward them, and a favor is not complete except through provision, He said: ﴿Or who provides for you from the heaven﴾ by rain, ﴿and the earth﴾ by plants? ﴿Say: Bring your proof﴾, that is, produce your argument and your evidence for what you claim, in denying anything of what has been established above, ﴿if you are truthful﴾ in claiming that there is another god with God. So where is your proof for it? This refers back to all the interrogatives that preceded it, which were given in the form of affirmation (*taqrīr*), and it is fitting that each interrogative is concluded with what preceded it.

(p-91) When He mentioned the bringing into being of the higher and lower worlds, and the favor of sending down rain and causing gardens to grow, that required that none be worshipped except the Originator of the world and the Bestower of what sustains life. So He concluded with His saying: ﴿Nay, but they are a people who deviate﴾, that is, from His worship, or they set up others as equal to Him, from among what is created and originated. When He mentioned the making of the earth a resting place, the causing of rivers to flow, the setting of mountains firm, and that this was a reminder to reflect upon and think about that, He concluded with His saying: ﴿Nay, but most of them do not know﴾, since among them there are those who know and reflect on that. When He mentioned the answering of the distressed one's prayer, the removal of evil, and their being made successors on the earth, it was fitting that a person constantly recall this favor, so He concluded with His saying: "﴿Little do you remember﴾", indicating the continual forgetfulness that comes when one is in ease, and his distress ends and the evil is removed from him, as He said: ﴿He forgets what he used to call upon Him for before﴾ [Az-Zumar: 8]. When He mentioned guidance in darknesses and the sending of the winds as glad tidings, while their objects of worship neither guide nor send, and they associate them with God, He said, Exalted is He: ﴿Exalted is He above what they associate.﴾ Each of these clauses is followed by His saying: ﴿Is there a god with God?﴾, as an emphasis and affirmation that there is no god but Him, exalted is He.

It was said: The unbelievers asked about the time of the Hour, which the Messenger ﷺ had promised them, and they pressed him about it, so the verse was revealed: ﴿Say: None in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except God﴾, and so on. What comes immediately to mind is that *man* (مَن, "whoever") is the subject of *yaʿlamu* (يَعْلَمُ, "knows"), *al-ghayb* (الغَيْبَ, "the unseen") is the object, and *illā Allāh* (إلّا اللَّهُ, "except God") is a *istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ* (disjunctive exception, meaning an exception not included in the category of the preceding term), since He is not included in the meaning of the word *man*. It came in the nominative (*marfūʿ*) according to the dialect of Tamim. The verse indicates that He, exalted is He, is the one alone who has knowledge of the unseen.

From ʿĀʾisha, may God be pleased with her: "Whoever claims that Muhammad knows what will happen tomorrow has indeed committed a great slander against God, and God, exalted is He, says: ﴿Say: None in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except God﴾." It is not said that He is included in the meaning of *man*, so that *fī al-samāwāti wa-l-arḍi* (فِي السَّماواتِ والأرْضِ, "in the heavens and the earth") would be a real container for the created beings within them, and a figurative one with respect to Him, exalted is He, meaning that He is in them by His knowledge. This is because that would combine the real and the figurative, and most scholars deny it, and its denial is the correct view. Whoever permits it would hold that the exception may be a *istithnāʾ muttaṣil* (connected exception), and that it would be in the nominative as a *badal* (substitute) or a qualifier. The nominative is more eloquent than the accusative in an exception, because it is an exception from a preceding negation. The apparent meaning is the generality of the unseen. It was also said that what is meant is the unseen of the Hour.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: what motivates the choice of the Tamimi dialect over the Hijazi?" meaning in its being a disjunctive exception, since He is not included under *man*. "I did not choose the nominative according to the Tamimi dialect, nor did we choose the accusative according to the Hijazi dialect." He said: "I answer: a subtle rhetorical point called for this, in that He placed the excluded term in the manner of the saying: 'Except the antelopes,' after the saying: 'There is no companion in it,' so that the meaning returns to your saying: If God is among those in the heavens and the earth, then they know the unseen. He means that their knowledge of the unseen is as impossible as it is impossible for God to be among them. Just as the meaning of 'what is in the house, if the antelopes are a companion' is that there is a companion in it, based on the premise that it is empty of companions." End of quotation.

Al-Zamakhshari had earlier mentioned: "If you ask: why do I raise the name of God, when God, exalted is He, cannot be among those in the heavens and the earth? I answer: it came according to the dialect of the Banu Tamim, where they say: 'There is no one in the house except a donkey,' as if *aḥad* (أحد, "anyone") had not been mentioned, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"On the evening when lances do not avail in its place,
nor arrows, except the well-tempered Indian sword."

And his saying: "No one came to me except ʿAmr, and his brothers did not help him except his brothers." End of quotation. The summary of it is that he says: if it were in the accusative, it would be included under the term excepted from, and when it is in the nominative it is a substitute, and the substituted term is in the intention of being dropped, so the operator becomes as if it were left without an object, because the substitute is on the intention of repeating the operator. It is as if it were said: "Say: none knows the unseen except God." If *man* were parsed as the object and *al-ghayb* as its substitute, and *illā Allāh* as the subject, meaning: none knows the unseen of whoever is in the heavens and the earth except God, that is, the absent things that occur in the world, and they do not know of their occurrence, that is, their knowledge does not precede that, it would be a good interpretation, and God, exalted is He, would be the one specified by His prior knowledge of what happens in the world.

*Ayyāna* (أيّانَ, "when"): its discussion has already passed at the end of *al-Aʿrāf*. Here it is an interrogative noun meaning *matā* (متى, "when"), and it is governed by *yubʿathūn* (يَبْعَثُونَ, "they will be raised") and *yush'urūn* (يُشْعِرُونَ, "they perceive"), with the verb suspended (*muʿallaq*), and the clause containing the interrogative (p-92) is in the accusative position governed by it. As-Sulamī read *ʾiyyāna* with a kasra on the hamza, which is the dialect of his tribe, Banu Sulaym.

When He denied them knowledge of the unseen in general, He denied them this specific unseen, namely the time of the Hour and the resurrection, so it is negated twice: since it is included in the generality of the unseen, and it is also specifically stated.

**[Continuation of the commentary on 27:59–66, part 3 of 3]**

The majority of reciters read ﴿بَلِ ادّارَكَ﴾. Its original form is تَدارَكَ, and the تاء was assimilated into the دال and made quiescent, so a connecting hamzah (همزة الوصل, the hamzah used to begin a word that is pronounced only when it is not preceded by another word) was introduced.

Ubayy (Ubayy ibn Ka'b) read أمْ تَدارَكَ, keeping the original form and making أمْ replace بَلْ.

Sulayman ibn Yasar, the brother of Ata' (Ibn Yasar), read بَلِ ادَّرَكَ, moving the vowel of the hamzah onto the lam and doubling the دال. His reasoning was that the form's measure is افْتَعَلَ. He assimilated the دال, which is the first root letter (فاء الكلمة), into the تاء after changing the تاء into a دال, so the second consonant was changed to match the first. This is like the saying اثَّرَدَ, whose original form is اثْتَرَدَ, from الثَّرْد (crumbling bread into broth). The elided hamzah whose vowel was moved onto the lam is the interrogative hamzah (همزة الاستفهام). It was placed before the alif of connection (ألف الوصل), so the alif of connection was dropped. Then the hamzah itself was dropped and its vowel was placed on the lam of بَلْ.

Abu Raja', al-A'raj, Shaybah, Talhah and Tawbah al-Anbari read in the same way, except that they vowelled the lam of بَلْ with a kasrah. This is reported from Ibn Abbas, 'Asim and al-A'mash.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Abu Ja'far and the people of Makkah read بَلِ ادَّرَكَ on the measure افَّعَلَ, in the sense of تَفاعَلَ (the reciprocal form). This reading is also reported from Abu Bakr, from 'Asim.

Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) in one transmission, Ibn Abbas in another, Ibn Abi Jamrah and others on his authority, al-Hasan, Qatadah and Ibn Muhaysin read بَلْ آدْرَكَ, with a long vowel after the interrogative hamzah. The original form was أأدْرَكَ. They changed the second hamzah into an alif to lighten the pronunciation, disliking the combination of two hamzahs. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' rejected this transmission and its grammatical basis.

Abu Hatim said: "It is not permitted to use the interrogative after بَلْ, because بَلْ indicates affirmation, whereas the interrogative in this context is a denial, meaning: they did not [know]. Compare His saying, ﴿أشَهِدُوا خَلْقَهُمْ﴾ (Did they witness their creation? [al-Zukhruf 43:19]), meaning: they did not witness it. Therefore the two cannot occur together, because of the contradiction between affirmation and denial." End of quotation.

Some later scholars permitted the interrogative after بَلْ, and compared it to the speaker's saying: أخُبْزًا أكَلْتَ بَلْ أماءً شَرِبْتَ؟ (Did you eat bread, or did you drink water?), by dropping the first statement and taking up the second.

Mujahid read أمِ ادَّرَكَ, making أمْ replace بَلْ, with ادَّرَكَ on the measure افَّعَلَ.

Ibn Abbas also read بَلْ آدّارَكَ, with a hamzah placed before ادّارَكَ. This drops the connecting hamzah that was introduced, because of the assimilation and because the speech begins with a quiescent consonant.

Ibn Mas'ud also read بَلْ أأدَّرَكَ, with two hamzahs: the interrogative hamzah and the hamzah of أفَّعَلَ.

al-Hasan and al-A'raj also read بَلْ أدَّرَكَ, with one hamzah and the assimilation of the first root letter, which is the دال in the تاء of افْتَعَلَ, after the تاء had become a دال.

Warsh, in one transmission, read بَلِ ادَّرَكَ, dropping the hamzah of ادَّرَكَ and moving its vowel to the lam.

Ibn Abbas also read بَلى ادَّرَكَ, with بَلى, the particle of affirmation by which a negated interrogative is affirmed.

It was also read بَلْ آأدَّرَكَ, with an alif between the two hamzahs.

As for the reading of those who read it as an interrogative, Ibn Abbas said: "It is a rebuke, meaning: their knowledge did not reach [the Hereafter], as a denial against them." Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is an interrogative in the form of a denial that their knowledge has reached [the Hereafter]. The same applies to the reading أمِ ادَّرَكَ and أمْ تَدارَكَ, because أمْ here has the meaning of بَلْ together with the interrogative hamzah." End of quotation.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "It has the sense of mocking the disbelievers and rebuking them for something that is far from them, meaning: did they know the matter of the Hereafter, and did their knowledge reach it?"

As for the reading of those who read it as a statement, Ibn Abbas said: "The meaning is: بَلْ تَدارَكَ عِلْمُهم ما جَهِلُوهُ في الدُّنْيا (their knowledge caught up with what they had not known in this world), that is, they came to know it in the Hereafter, in the sense that their knowledge became complete in the Hereafter that everything they were promised is true. This is the true affirmation of knowledge for them, because they see with their own eyes in the Hereafter what they were promised unseen in this world. Its being in the past tense has the sense of the future, because reporting it is truthful, so it is as if it had already happened."

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "It may bear two meanings. The first: their knowledge reached its limit, as you say أدْرَكَ النَّباتُ (the plant reached maturity) and similar, meaning: their knowledge of the Hereafter reached its end and followed on until they would know its extent and believe, but they only have false suppositions. Or [it means] until they do not know its time. Here في is in the sense of بِ, attached to their knowledge, and knowledge may take بِ, as you say عِلْمِي بِزَيْدٍ كَذا (my knowledge of Zayd is such). This reading may be understood in the sense of a question and interrogation, and it comes as a denial because they did not perceive anything beneficial. The second: أدْرَكَ is in the sense of يُدْرِكُ (is reached), meaning their knowledge of the Hereafter will be attained on the Day of Resurrection, when they see the punishment and the realities they denied, whereas in this world they will not." This is the interpretation of Ibn Abbas, and al-Zajjaj inclined to it. The في keeps its original sense of location, attached to تَدارَكَ. End of quotation, with some summarising and addition.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "It has two aspects. The first: the causes of the firm establishment and completion of knowledge, that the Resurrection is certain with no doubt, have been available to them and they were enabled to know it, yet they are doubtful and ignorant. This is His saying, ﴿بَلْ هم في شَكٍّ مِنها بَلْ هم مِنها عَمُونَ﴾ (Nay, they are in doubt about it; nay, they are blind to it [27:66]). He means the polytheists among those in the heavens and the earth, because when they were among them He attributed the act to all of them, as one says بَنُو فُلانٍ فَعَلُوا كَذا (the sons of so-and-so did such-and-such), when only some of them did it.
