It is as if it were said: "Say: none knows the unseen except God." If *man* were parsed as the object and *al-ghayb* as its substitute, and *illā Allāh* as the subject, meaning: none knows the unseen of whoever is in the heavens and the earth except God, that is, the absent things that occur in the world, and they do not know of their occurrence, that is, their knowledge does not precede that, it would be a good interpretation, and God, exalted is He, would be the one specified by His prior knowledge of what happens in the world.

*Ayyāna* (أيّانَ, "when"): its discussion has already passed at the end of *al-Aʿrāf*. Here it is an interrogative noun meaning *matā* (متى, "when"), and it is governed by *yubʿathūn* (يَبْعَثُونَ, "they will be raised") and *yush'urūn* (يُشْعِرُونَ, "they perceive"), with the verb suspended (*muʿallaq*), and the clause containing the interrogative (p-92) is in the accusative position governed by it. As-Sulamī read *ʾiyyāna* with a kasra on the hamza, which is the dialect of his tribe, Banu Sulaym.

When He denied them knowledge of the unseen in general, He denied them this specific unseen, namely the time of the Hour and the resurrection, so it is negated twice: since it is included in the generality of the unseen, and it is also specifically stated.

**[Continuation of the commentary on 27:59–66, part 3 of 3]**

The majority of reciters read ﴿بَلِ ادّارَكَ﴾. Its original form is تَدارَكَ, and the تاء was assimilated into the دال and made quiescent, so a connecting hamzah (همزة الوصل, the hamzah used to begin a word that is pronounced only when it is not preceded by another word) was introduced.

Ubayy (Ubayy ibn Ka'b) read أمْ تَدارَكَ, keeping the original form and making أمْ replace بَلْ.

Sulayman ibn Yasar, the brother of Ata' (Ibn Yasar), read بَلِ ادَّرَكَ, moving the vowel of the hamzah onto the lam and doubling the دال. His reasoning was that the form's measure is افْتَعَلَ. He assimilated the دال, which is the first root letter (فاء الكلمة), into the تاء after changing the تاء into a دال, so the second consonant was changed to match the first. This is like the saying اثَّرَدَ, whose original form is اثْتَرَدَ, from الثَّرْد (crumbling bread into broth). The elided hamzah whose vowel was moved onto the lam is the interrogative hamzah (همزة الاستفهام). It was placed before the alif of connection (ألف الوصل), so the alif of connection was dropped. Then the hamzah itself was dropped and its vowel was placed on the lam of بَلْ.

Abu Raja', al-A'raj, Shaybah, Talhah and Tawbah al-Anbari read in the same way, except that they vowelled the lam of بَلْ with a kasrah. This is reported from Ibn Abbas, 'Asim and al-A'mash.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Abu Ja'far and the people of Makkah read بَلِ ادَّرَكَ on the measure افَّعَلَ, in the sense of تَفاعَلَ (the reciprocal form). This reading is also reported from Abu Bakr, from 'Asim.

Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) in one transmission, Ibn Abbas in another, Ibn Abi Jamrah and others on his authority, al-Hasan, Qatadah and Ibn Muhaysin read بَلْ آدْرَكَ, with a long vowel after the interrogative hamzah. The original form was أأدْرَكَ. They changed the second hamzah into an alif to lighten the pronunciation, disliking the combination of two hamzahs. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' rejected this transmission and its grammatical basis.

Abu Hatim said: "It is not permitted to use the interrogative after بَلْ, because بَلْ indicates affirmation, whereas the interrogative in this context is a denial, meaning: they did not [know]. Compare His saying, ﴿أشَهِدُوا خَلْقَهُمْ﴾ (Did they witness their creation? [al-Zukhruf 43:19]), meaning: they did not witness it. Therefore the two cannot occur together, because of the contradiction between affirmation and denial." End of quotation.

Some later scholars permitted the interrogative after بَلْ, and compared it to the speaker's saying: أخُبْزًا أكَلْتَ بَلْ أماءً شَرِبْتَ؟ (Did you eat bread, or did you drink water?), by dropping the first statement and taking up the second.

Mujahid read أمِ ادَّرَكَ, making أمْ replace بَلْ, with ادَّرَكَ on the measure افَّعَلَ.

Ibn Abbas also read بَلْ آدّارَكَ, with a hamzah placed before ادّارَكَ. This drops the connecting hamzah that was introduced, because of the assimilation and because the speech begins with a quiescent consonant.

Ibn Mas'ud also read بَلْ أأدَّرَكَ, with two hamzahs: the interrogative hamzah and the hamzah of أفَّعَلَ.

al-Hasan and al-A'raj also read بَلْ أدَّرَكَ, with one hamzah and the assimilation of the first root letter, which is the دال in the تاء of افْتَعَلَ, after the تاء had become a دال.

Warsh, in one transmission, read بَلِ ادَّرَكَ, dropping the hamzah of ادَّرَكَ and moving its vowel to the lam.

Ibn Abbas also read بَلى ادَّرَكَ, with بَلى, the particle of affirmation by which a negated interrogative is affirmed.

It was also read بَلْ آأدَّرَكَ, with an alif between the two hamzahs.

As for the reading of those who read it as an interrogative, Ibn Abbas said: "It is a rebuke, meaning: their knowledge did not reach [the Hereafter], as a denial against them." Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is an interrogative in the form of a denial that their knowledge has reached [the Hereafter]. The same applies to the reading أمِ ادَّرَكَ and أمْ تَدارَكَ, because أمْ here has the meaning of بَلْ together with the interrogative hamzah." End of quotation.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "It has the sense of mocking the disbelievers and rebuking them for something that is far from them, meaning: did they know the matter of the Hereafter, and did their knowledge reach it?"

As for the reading of those who read it as a statement, Ibn Abbas said: "The meaning is: بَلْ تَدارَكَ عِلْمُهم ما جَهِلُوهُ في الدُّنْيا (their knowledge caught up with what they had not known in this world), that is, they came to know it in the Hereafter, in the sense that their knowledge became complete in the Hereafter that everything they were promised is true. This is the true affirmation of knowledge for them, because they see with their own eyes in the Hereafter what they were promised unseen in this world. Its being in the past tense has the sense of the future, because reporting it is truthful, so it is as if it had already happened."

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "It may bear two meanings. The first: their knowledge reached its limit, as you say أدْرَكَ النَّباتُ (the plant reached maturity) and similar, meaning: their knowledge of the Hereafter reached its end and followed on until they would know its extent and believe, but they only have false suppositions. Or [it means] until they do not know its time. Here في is in the sense of بِ, attached to their knowledge, and knowledge may take بِ, as you say عِلْمِي بِزَيْدٍ كَذا (my knowledge of Zayd is such). This reading may be understood in the sense of a question and interrogation, and it comes as a denial because they did not perceive anything beneficial. The second: أدْرَكَ is in the sense of يُدْرِكُ (is reached), meaning their knowledge of the Hereafter will be attained on the Day of Resurrection, when they see the punishment and the realities they denied, whereas in this world they will not." This is the interpretation of Ibn Abbas, and al-Zajjaj inclined to it. The في keeps its original sense of location, attached to تَدارَكَ. End of quotation, with some summarising and addition.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "It has two aspects. The first: the causes of the firm establishment and completion of knowledge, that the Resurrection is certain with no doubt, have been available to them and they were enabled to know it, yet they are doubtful and ignorant. This is His saying, ﴿بَلْ هم في شَكٍّ مِنها بَلْ هم مِنها عَمُونَ﴾ (Nay, they are in doubt about it; nay, they are blind to it [27:66]). He means the polytheists among those in the heavens and the earth, because when they were among them He attributed the act to all of them, as one says بَنُو فُلانٍ فَعَلُوا كَذا (the sons of so-and-so did such-and-such), when only some of them did it. The second aspect: describing them with the firm establishment and completion of knowledge is mockery of them, as you say to the most ignorant of people ما أعْلَمَكَ (how learned you are!) in mockery. This is because they doubted and were blind to the means that lead to a knowledge that is in doubt, let alone that they would know the time of its occurrence, which has no means of being known. There is another aspect to ادَّرَكَ عِلْمُهم and ادّارَكَ: ادَّرَكَ may mean انْتَهى وفَنِيَ (come to an end and perish), from the saying ادَّرَكَتِ الثَّمَرَةُ (the fruit ripened and was finished), because that is its final limit, at which it is destroyed. al-Hasan interpreted it as اضْمَحَلَّ عِلْمُهم (their knowledge vanished), and تَدارَكَ, from تَدارَكَ بَنُو فُلانٍ (the sons of so-and-so followed one another into destruction)." End of quotation.

Al-Kirmani said: "Knowledge here means judgement and statement, that is, statements and judgements about the Hereafter followed on among them, and much discussion of it occurred among them. Some of them denied it, some doubted it, and some considered it far-fetched."

Al-Farra' said: "بَلِ ادَّرَكَ means it becomes in the sense of denial, and there are similar cases of this. That is, they did not know its occurrence and its existence, and this is indicated by ﴿بَلْ هم في شَكٍّ مِنها﴾. So في in the sentence takes the sense of بِ, meaning their knowledge did not reach the Hereafter." Al-Farra' said: "This interpretation is strengthened by the reading of those who read أدَّرَكَ with an interrogative." End of quotation.

As for the reading of those who read بَلى (yes) instead of بَلْ, as the particle of answer, Abu Hatim said: "If بَلى is an answer to a preceding statement, it may be used with an interrogative, as if some people had denied what preceded, the power [of God], and they were told: بَلى (yes indeed), affirming what they had denied. Then an interrogative was resumed after it and was set in parallel with His saying ﴿بَلْ هم في شَكٍّ مِنها﴾, in the sense of أمْ هم في شَكٍّ مِنها (or are they in doubt about it?), because the particles of conjunction may alternate. He stopped at the two sentences with His saying ﴿بَلْ هم مِنها عَمُونَ﴾." End of quotation. He means that the sense is: did their knowledge of the Hereafter reach [its completion], or did they doubt? So بَلْ here has the sense of أمْ, placed in parallel with the interrogative hamzah. This is very weak: that بَلْ should have the sense of أمْ and be set in parallel with the interrogative hamzah.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "(If you ask): then what of those who read بَلى ادَّرَكَ? (I answer): when بَلى came after His saying ﴿وما يَشْعُرُونَ﴾ (and they do not perceive [27:65]), its meaning was: بَلى يَشْعُرُونَ (yes, they perceive). Then perception was explained by His saying: ادَّرَكَ عِلْمُهم في الآخِرَةِ (their knowledge of the Hereafter has been attained), in the sense of mockery, whose meaning is the intensification of the denial of knowledge. It is as if He said: their perception of the time of the Hereafter is that they do not know its occurrence. This returns to the intensification of the denial of perception in the strongest possible way. As for those who read بَلى أدَّرَكَ with an interrogative, its meaning is: they perceive when they will be raised. Then He denied their knowledge of its occurrence, and when their knowledge of its occurrence is denied, they have no perception of the time of its occurrence, because knowledge of the time of an event follows knowledge of the event itself. (If you ask): what is the meaning of these three changes of direction (idrab)? (I answer): they are only a presentation of their conditions. He first described them as not perceiving the time of the resurrection, then as not knowing that the Resurrection is coming, then as floundering in doubt and uncertainty without removing it, though removal is possible. He made the Hereafter the origin and source of their blindness, and therefore he used مِن rather than عَنْ, because the consequence and the recompense are what made them like cattle that neither reflect nor see." End of quotation.

[p. 88] When he had finished relating the stories of this surah, He commanded His Messenger ﷺ to praise Him, exalted is He, and to greet with peace those He chose, and he began to differentiate the Necessary Existence (wajib al-wujud), God, exalted is He, from the idols and the religions that they associated with God and worshipped. He began this exposition to the Quraysh and others with the hamdala (the formula of praise, "al-hamdu lillah"), as though it were the opening of a sermon (khutba) for what he was about to present of proofs indicating the Oneness, the knowledge, and the power (of God). Muslims have followed this practice in the opening of their books, their sermons, and their admonitions, so they begin with praising God and blessing Muhammad, the Messenger of God ﷺ. Those who write epistles follow them in the openings of books of conquests, congratulations, and events of significance. It has been said: this passage is connected to what precedes it, and the Messenger, peace be upon him, was commanded to praise God for the destruction of the disbelieving nations, and to greet with peace the prophets and their followers who were saved.

It has been said: "qul" (say) is an address to Lot, peace be upon him, that he should praise God for the destruction of the disbelievers of his people, ﴿and greet with peace His servants whom He has chosen﴾. Ibn Atiyya attributed this view to al-Farra', and said: "This is a non-Arab (ajami) error from al-Farra'." Abu al-Simak recited, "qula al-hamdu lillah," and likewise "qula al-hamdu lillahi sayurikum" with a fatha on the lam. "His servants whom He has chosen" encompasses the prophets and their followers. Ibn Abbas said: the servants who are greeted with peace are the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ, whom He chose for His Prophet; and in singling them out for this there is a rebuke to the disbelieving contemporaries. Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: When God, exalted is He, mentioned the states of the prophets, and that whoever denied them was uprooted by punishment, and that this is removed from the nation of the Messenger, He commanded him to praise Him for the blessing He had singled him out with, and to greet with peace the prophets who endured the hardships of the message. End of quotation, and it has been condensed.

His saying: ﴿Is God better, or what they associate (with Him)?﴾ is an interrogation containing rebuke, reproach, and mockery of their state, and an alert to the point of difference between God, exalted is He, and the idols, since it is known to anyone with reason that there is no partnership in being better between God, exalted is He, and them. This type of comparative form (af'al al-tafdil) often comes where it is known and established that there is no partnership in it, and it is mentioned only as a means of binding the opponent and alerting him to the error of his practice. The apparent meaning is that this interrogation concerns the reality of the essences (khabariyyat al-dhawat). It has been said: it came according to the belief of the polytheists, since they believed their gods to be good in some respect. It has been said: there is an omission in the sentence in two places; the estimate is: "Is the Oneness of God better, or the worship of what they associate?" So "ma" in "am ma" means "alladhi" (that which). It has been said: "ma" is verbal-masdar (infinitive), and the omission is from the first: i.e., "Is the Oneness of God better, or your polytheism?" It has been said: "khayr" is not for comparison; it is like when you say, "Prayer is good," meaning good out of the various goods. It has been said: the estimate is "possessor of good." The apparent meaning is that "khayran" is an af'al al-tafdil, and that the interrogation in such a case comes to explain the corruption of what the opponent holds, to alert him to his error, and to bind him to admit that preference is restricted to one side and absent from the other. The majority read "tushrikun" with the taa of address; al-Hasan, [p. 89] Qatada, Asim, and Abu Amr read it with the yaa of absence. The "am" in "am ma" is connected (muttasila), because the meaning is: "Which of the two is better?" In "(am man khalaqa)" and what follows it, it is disjunctive (munfasila). When God mentioned "good," He, glorified is He, enumerated the goods and benefits which are the effects of His mercy and grace, as He enumerated them in other places of His Book, making them stand before them as witnesses to what He originated of created things, and that they find no alternative to admitting this to God, exalted is He.

The majority read "am man khalaqa" and in the four that follow it with a shadda on the mim, the mim of "am" being assimilated into the mim of "man." Al-A'mash read it with a light mim, making it the interrogative hamza, placed before "man," and "man" in both readings is a subject (mubtada') and its predicate. Ibn Atiyya said: its estimate is: "He disbelieves His blessing and doubts Him," and the like of this meaning. Al-Zamakhshari estimated it: "Is what they associate better?" so he estimated what was affirmed in the first interrogation. He began the interrogation with the name of the essence, then moved on to the attributes. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said in his book "Kitab al-Lawami'": "There must be a supposed corresponding clause (jumla mu'adila), and that which is supposed becomes like that which is spoken, for the indication of the context (fahwa) upon it. The estimate of that clause is: 'Is He who created the heavens like him who did not create?' and likewise its sisters, and he has made explicit in other than this place what was supposed in them, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is then He who creates like him who creates not?﴾ [al-Nahl: 17]." End of quotation. As for calling this estimate a "clause" (jumla): if he means by it a group of words, it is correct; but if he means the clause as defined in grammar, it is not so, rather it is a supposed item of the category of the singular (mufrad).

God, exalted is He, began by mentioning the creation of the settled place of the upper and lower worlds, and the sending down of what sustains the lower world, and He said: "for you" (lakum), i.e., for your sake, as a favour, and that all of that is for your sake. Then He said: ﴿so We caused to grow﴾, and this is a shift (iltifat) from the third person of absence to the first person of speech with the nun of majesty (nun al-'azama), indicating that He alone is singular in this, and that He did not cause those diverse gardens of varied kinds, colours, tastes, and scents to grow by one water except Him, exalted is He. This singling out is strengthened by His saying: ﴿It was not for you to cause their trees to grow﴾. Since the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the sending down of water from the sky, leave no doubt for the rational that this is not but from God, and since growth is something that a human may bring about by sowing, watering, and preparing, and it is permissible for the doer of a cause to be ascribed the act of the effect, He, exalted is He, made clear His singling out of that by way of shift and emphasized it by His saying: ﴿It was not for you to cause their trees to grow﴾. Do you not see that the one who brings about growth may not come in accordance with his intent? And even if he does, he is ignorant of its nature, its measure, and its manner, so how could he be its doer? "Bahja" means beauty, freshness, and loveliness, because the one who looks upon them is delighted (yabtahij), i.e., pleased and rejoices. The majority read "dhat" in the singular, "bahjatin" with the ha' sustained; the broken plural functions in the attribute as the singular does, as in His saying: ﴿spouses purified﴾ [al-Baqara: 25], and it is in the sense of a group. Ibn Abi Abla read "dhawat" in the plural, and "bahajatin" with the ha' vocalized with a fatha.

﴿It was not for you to cause their trees to grow﴾: it has already been stated that the negation of such an occurrence may be due to the impossibility of its happening in this way, or to the impossibility of its happening according to the Law (shar'an), or to the negation of preferability (nafy al-awwaliyya). The meaning here is that causing such a thing to grow is impossible for you, because it is the bringing forth of something from non-existence into existence, and this is not within the power of anyone but God, exalted is He. When He mentioned His favour upon them, He addressed them with that; then when He mentioned their blame, He shifted from address to absence and said: ﴿Rather, they are a people who ascribe equals (ya'dilun)﴾, either as a shift, or as an informing the Messenger ﷺ of their state, i.e., they deviate (ya'dilun) from the truth, or they make others equal to Him (ya'dilu bihi ghayrahu), i.e., they make for Him an equal and a likeness. It is read: "ilahan" with a fatha, in the sense of: "Do you call upon, or do you associate?" It is read: "a-ilahun" with the lightening of the two hamzas and softening of the second, with a separation between them by an alif. When God, exalted is He, mentioned that He originated the heavens and the earth, He mentioned something shared between the heaven and the earth, namely the sending down of water from the sky and the growth of gardens on the earth. Then He mentioned something specific to the earth, which is making it a "qarar" (a settled abode), i.e., a resting place for you, such that it is possible for you to dwell upon it and remain on it, and it is not turned by the celestial sphere (falak). It has been said: because it is insignificant compared to the sphere, like a dot in a millstone.

﴿And He placed rivers within it﴾, i.e., between its places, in its valleys and ravines, ﴿and He placed upon it firm mountains﴾, i.e., firm mountains, so that it does not tilt with you and sway. "Al-bahrani" are the sweet and the salty; "al-hajiz" is the separator, from His power, exalted is He; this is said by al-Dahhak. Mujahid said: the sea of the sky and the earth, and the barrier is of air. al-Hasan said: the sea of Persia and the Romans; al-Suddi said: the sea of Iraq and Syria, and the barrier is of earth. Ibn Atiyya said, preferring this view on the barrier: it is what God placed between them of barriers and obstructions of the earth, despite their thinness in some places and their subtlety, which, were it not for His power, the salt would swallow the sweet. Ibn Atiyya had already presented that the two seas are: the sweet in its entirety, and the salty bitter water in its entirety; and since each of them is great and independent, the operative element in His saying ﴿and He placed﴾ is repeated, so they are of the coordination (atf) of independent clauses, each of them being a favour, and they are not joined under one operative element, so that it would be coordination of singular words. Abu Abdullah al-Razi had, in mentioning these four favours, a discourse from the science of nature, according to his claim, and according to the philosophers (hukama'), which lies outside the ways of the Arabs, and it may be consulted in his book.

"Al-mudtarr" is a passive participle: the one whom illness, poverty, or some accident of the vicissitudes of time has compelled (ahwajahu) to take refuge in God and to humble himself before Him, so he calls upon Him to remove what has befallen him of that and to relieve him of it. Ibn Abbas said: it is the one who is exhausted (al-majhud). al-Suddi said: it is the one who has no strength or power. It has been said: it is the sinner when he seeks forgiveness, and His answering him is joined with His will, exalted is He; so not every compelled one who calls upon Him is answered by God in the removal of what afflicts him. Al-Zamakhshari said: the answering is contingent upon the object requested being a benefit, and for this reason supplication is not good unless it stipulates benefit in it. End of quotation, and this is according to the path of the Mu'tazila in considering what is beneficial (al-maslaha) from God, exalted is He.

﴿And removes the evil﴾: it is everything that is harmful, and it is general for every harm that moves out of the state of the one in distress, and it is specific to a more general one, which is what is harmful, whether what is removed is in the state of compulsion or in what is less than it. "Khulafa'" (successors): i.e., the earlier nations; or in commanding the good and forbidding the evil; or the successors of the Prophet ﷺ after him; or the successors of the disbelievers in their land, or in dominion and authority: these are sayings. al-Hasan in one narration read: "wanajʿaluk-um" with the nun of the speaker, as though it were a resumed statement of information and promise, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿He will surely make them successors in the earth﴾ [al-Nur: 55].

His saying: ﴿and makes you successors of the earth﴾ is a transition from the state of the one in compulsion to a rank different from the state of compulsion, which is the state of succession (khilafa); so these are two circumstantial adverbs (zarfan). How many have we seen in this world of those who reached a state of compulsion and then became a dominating king! The majority read "tadhakkarun" with the taa of address; al-Hasan, al-A'mash, and Abu Amr read it with the yaa of absence, and the dhal in both readings is doubled, because the taa is assimilated into it. Abu Haywa read "tatadhakkarun" with two taas. The darkness of the land is the darkness of the night, and this is the literal sense; and it extends figuratively to ignorance and to the obscurity of a matter, as one says: "the matter became dark to me." The poet said:

"The blindnesses of men have cleared away from youth"

That is, the ignorances of youth. Guidance on land comes through landmarks, and guidance at sea through the stars.

﴿Or who sends the winds as heralds of good news before His mercy?﴾ The explanation of a parallel to this clause has already passed. It is also read as *ʿammā tushrikūn* (عَمّا تُشْرِكُونَ) with the *tāʾ* of address, meaning "what you associate [with Him]."

﴿Or who originates creation﴾: The apparent meaning is that *al-khalq* (الخَلْقَ, "creation") refers to the created thing, and its *bady'* (بَدْءُ, "origination") is its bringing into being and its production. It appears that what is intended is whoever God will restore in the Hereafter from among mankind, the jinn, and the angels, not the whole of created things in general. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "What is meant is the children of Adam, in view of the mention of restoration, and restoration is the resurrection from the graves. It is possible that by *al-khalq* he means the verbal noun of *khalaqa* (creating), and that *yabdaʾu* and *yuʿīdu* (originates and restores) are used figuratively for perfecting and doing well, as you say: 'So-and-so originates and restores in such-and-such a matter' when he masters it." Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: how did He say to them, 'Or who originates creation and then restores it,' when they deny restoration? I answer: He has favored them by enabling them to know and to acknowledge, so there remains no excuse for them in denial." End of quotation.

Since bringing the children of Adam into being is a favor and a kindness toward them, and a favor is not complete except through provision, He said: ﴿Or who provides for you from the heaven﴾ by rain, ﴿and the earth﴾ by plants? ﴿Say: Bring your proof﴾, that is, produce your argument and your evidence for what you claim, in denying anything of what has been established above, ﴿if you are truthful﴾ in claiming that there is another god with God. So where is your proof for it? This refers back to all the interrogatives that preceded it, which were given in the form of affirmation (*taqrīr*), and it is fitting that each interrogative is concluded with what preceded it.

(p-91) When He mentioned the bringing into being of the higher and lower worlds, and the favor of sending down rain and causing gardens to grow, that required that none be worshipped except the Originator of the world and the Bestower of what sustains life. So He concluded with His saying: ﴿Nay, but they are a people who deviate﴾, that is, from His worship, or they set up others as equal to Him, from among what is created and originated. When He mentioned the making of the earth a resting place, the causing of rivers to flow, the setting of mountains firm, and that this was a reminder to reflect upon and think about that, He concluded with His saying: ﴿Nay, but most of them do not know﴾, since among them there are those who know and reflect on that. When He mentioned the answering of the distressed one's prayer, the removal of evil, and their being made successors on the earth, it was fitting that a person constantly recall this favor, so He concluded with His saying: "﴿Little do you remember﴾", indicating the continual forgetfulness that comes when one is in ease, and his distress ends and the evil is removed from him, as He said: ﴿He forgets what he used to call upon Him for before﴾ [Az-Zumar: 8]. When He mentioned guidance in darknesses and the sending of the winds as glad tidings, while their objects of worship neither guide nor send, and they associate them with God, He said, Exalted is He: ﴿Exalted is He above what they associate.﴾ Each of these clauses is followed by His saying: ﴿Is there a god with God?﴾, as an emphasis and affirmation that there is no god but Him, exalted is He.

It was said: The unbelievers asked about the time of the Hour, which the Messenger ﷺ had promised them, and they pressed him about it, so the verse was revealed: ﴿Say: None in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except God﴾, and so on. What comes immediately to mind is that *man* (مَن, "whoever") is the subject of *yaʿlamu* (يَعْلَمُ, "knows"), *al-ghayb* (الغَيْبَ, "the unseen") is the object, and *illā Allāh* (إلّا اللَّهُ, "except God") is a *istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ* (disjunctive exception, meaning an exception not included in the category of the preceding term), since He is not included in the meaning of the word *man*. It came in the nominative (*marfūʿ*) according to the dialect of Tamim. The verse indicates that He, exalted is He, is the one alone who has knowledge of the unseen.

From ʿĀʾisha, may God be pleased with her: "Whoever claims that Muhammad knows what will happen tomorrow has indeed committed a great slander against God, and God, exalted is He, says: ﴿Say: None in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except God﴾." It is not said that He is included in the meaning of *man*, so that *fī al-samāwāti wa-l-arḍi* (فِي السَّماواتِ والأرْضِ, "in the heavens and the earth") would be a real container for the created beings within them, and a figurative one with respect to Him, exalted is He, meaning that He is in them by His knowledge. This is because that would combine the real and the figurative, and most scholars deny it, and its denial is the correct view. Whoever permits it would hold that the exception may be a *istithnāʾ muttaṣil* (connected exception), and that it would be in the nominative as a *badal* (substitute) or a qualifier. The nominative is more eloquent than the accusative in an exception, because it is an exception from a preceding negation. The apparent meaning is the generality of the unseen. It was also said that what is meant is the unseen of the Hour.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: what motivates the choice of the Tamimi dialect over the Hijazi?" meaning in its being a disjunctive exception, since He is not included under *man*. "I did not choose the nominative according to the Tamimi dialect, nor did we choose the accusative according to the Hijazi dialect." He said: "I answer: a subtle rhetorical point called for this, in that He placed the excluded term in the manner of the saying: 'Except the antelopes,' after the saying: 'There is no companion in it,' so that the meaning returns to your saying: If God is among those in the heavens and the earth, then they know the unseen. He means that their knowledge of the unseen is as impossible as it is impossible for God to be among them. Just as the meaning of 'what is in the house, if the antelopes are a companion' is that there is a companion in it, based on the premise that it is empty of companions." End of quotation.

Al-Zamakhshari had earlier mentioned: "If you ask: why do I raise the name of God, when God, exalted is He, cannot be among those in the heavens and the earth? I answer: it came according to the dialect of the Banu Tamim, where they say: 'There is no one in the house except a donkey,' as if *aḥad* (أحد, "anyone") had not been mentioned, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"On the evening when lances do not avail in its place,
nor arrows, except the well-tempered Indian sword."

And his saying: "No one came to me except ʿAmr, and his brothers did not help him except his brothers." End of quotation. The summary of it is that he says: if it were in the accusative, it would be included under the term excepted from, and when it is in the nominative it is a substitute, and the substituted term is in the intention of being dropped, so the operator becomes as if it were left without an object, because the substitute is on the intention of repeating the operator. It is as if it were said: "Say: none knows the unseen except God." If *man* were parsed as the object and *al-ghayb* as its substitute, and *illā Allāh* as the subject, meaning: none knows the unseen of whoever is in the heavens and the earth except God, that is, the absent things that occur in the world, and they do not know of their occurrence, that is, their knowledge does not precede that, it would be a good interpretation, and God, exalted is He, would be the one specified by His prior knowledge of what happens in the world.

*Ayyāna* (أيّانَ, "when"): its discussion has already passed at the end of *al-Aʿrāf*. Here it is an interrogative noun meaning *matā* (متى, "when"), and it is governed by *yubʿathūn* (يَبْعَثُونَ, "they will be raised") and *yush'urūn* (يُشْعِرُونَ, "they perceive"), with the verb suspended (*muʿallaq*), and the clause containing the interrogative (p-92) is in the accusative position governed by it. As-Sulamī read *ʾiyyāna* with a kasra on the hamza, which is the dialect of his tribe, Banu Sulaym.

When He denied them knowledge of the unseen in general, He denied them this specific unseen, namely the time of the Hour and the resurrection, so it is negated twice: since it is included in the generality of the unseen, and it is also specifically stated.

**[Continuation of the commentary on 27:59–66, part 3 of 3]**

The majority of reciters read ﴿بَلِ ادّارَكَ﴾. Its original form is تَدارَكَ, and the تاء was assimilated into the دال and made quiescent, so a connecting hamzah (همزة الوصل, the hamzah used to begin a word that is pronounced only when it is not preceded by another word) was introduced.

Ubayy (Ubayy ibn Ka'b) read أمْ تَدارَكَ, keeping the original form and making أمْ replace بَلْ.

Sulayman ibn Yasar, the brother of Ata' (Ibn Yasar), read بَلِ ادَّرَكَ, moving the vowel of the hamzah onto the lam and doubling the دال. His reasoning was that the form's measure is افْتَعَلَ. He assimilated the دال, which is the first root letter (فاء الكلمة), into the تاء after changing the تاء into a دال, so the second consonant was changed to match the first. This is like the saying اثَّرَدَ, whose original form is اثْتَرَدَ, from الثَّرْد (crumbling bread into broth). The elided hamzah whose vowel was moved onto the lam is the interrogative hamzah (همزة الاستفهام). It was placed before the alif of connection (ألف الوصل), so the alif of connection was dropped. Then the hamzah itself was dropped and its vowel was placed on the lam of بَلْ.

Abu Raja', al-A'raj, Shaybah, Talhah and Tawbah al-Anbari read in the same way, except that they vowelled the lam of بَلْ with a kasrah. This is reported from Ibn Abbas, 'Asim and al-A'mash.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Abu Ja'far and the people of Makkah read بَلِ ادَّرَكَ on the measure افَّعَلَ, in the sense of تَفاعَلَ (the reciprocal form). This reading is also reported from Abu Bakr, from 'Asim.

Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) in one transmission, Ibn Abbas in another, Ibn Abi Jamrah and others on his authority, al-Hasan, Qatadah and Ibn Muhaysin read بَلْ آدْرَكَ, with a long vowel after the interrogative hamzah. The original form was أأدْرَكَ. They changed the second hamzah into an alif to lighten the pronunciation, disliking the combination of two hamzahs. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' rejected this transmission and its grammatical basis.

Abu Hatim said: "It is not permitted to use the interrogative after بَلْ, because بَلْ indicates affirmation, whereas the interrogative in this context is a denial, meaning: they did not [know]. Compare His saying, ﴿أشَهِدُوا خَلْقَهُمْ﴾ (Did they witness their creation? [al-Zukhruf 43:19]), meaning: they did not witness it. Therefore the two cannot occur together, because of the contradiction between affirmation and denial." End of quotation.

Some later scholars permitted the interrogative after بَلْ, and compared it to the speaker's saying: أخُبْزًا أكَلْتَ بَلْ أماءً شَرِبْتَ؟ (Did you eat bread, or did you drink water?), by dropping the first statement and taking up the second.

Mujahid read أمِ ادَّرَكَ, making أمْ replace بَلْ, with ادَّرَكَ on the measure افَّعَلَ.

Ibn Abbas also read بَلْ آدّارَكَ, with a hamzah placed before ادّارَكَ. This drops the connecting hamzah that was introduced, because of the assimilation and because the speech begins with a quiescent consonant.

Ibn Mas'ud also read بَلْ أأدَّرَكَ, with two hamzahs: the interrogative hamzah and the hamzah of أفَّعَلَ.

al-Hasan and al-A'raj also read بَلْ أدَّرَكَ, with one hamzah and the assimilation of the first root letter, which is the دال in the تاء of افْتَعَلَ, after the تاء had become a دال.

Warsh, in one transmission, read بَلِ ادَّرَكَ, dropping the hamzah of ادَّرَكَ and moving its vowel to the lam.

Ibn Abbas also read بَلى ادَّرَكَ, with بَلى, the particle of affirmation by which a negated interrogative is affirmed.

It was also read بَلْ آأدَّرَكَ, with an alif between the two hamzahs.

As for the reading of those who read it as an interrogative, Ibn Abbas said: "It is a rebuke, meaning: their knowledge did not reach [the Hereafter], as a denial against them." Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is an interrogative in the form of a denial that their knowledge has reached [the Hereafter]. The same applies to the reading أمِ ادَّرَكَ and أمْ تَدارَكَ, because أمْ here has the meaning of بَلْ together with the interrogative hamzah." End of quotation.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "It has the sense of mocking the disbelievers and rebuking them for something that is far from them, meaning: did they know the matter of the Hereafter, and did their knowledge reach it?"

As for the reading of those who read it as a statement, Ibn Abbas said: "The meaning is: بَلْ تَدارَكَ عِلْمُهم ما جَهِلُوهُ في الدُّنْيا (their knowledge caught up with what they had not known in this world), that is, they came to know it in the Hereafter, in the sense that their knowledge became complete in the Hereafter that everything they were promised is true. This is the true affirmation of knowledge for them, because they see with their own eyes in the Hereafter what they were promised unseen in this world. Its being in the past tense has the sense of the future, because reporting it is truthful, so it is as if it had already happened."

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "It may bear two meanings. The first: their knowledge reached its limit, as you say أدْرَكَ النَّباتُ (the plant reached maturity) and similar, meaning: their knowledge of the Hereafter reached its end and followed on until they would know its extent and believe, but they only have false suppositions. Or [it means] until they do not know its time. Here في is in the sense of بِ, attached to their knowledge, and knowledge may take بِ, as you say عِلْمِي بِزَيْدٍ كَذا (my knowledge of Zayd is such). This reading may be understood in the sense of a question and interrogation, and it comes as a denial because they did not perceive anything beneficial. The second: أدْرَكَ is in the sense of يُدْرِكُ (is reached), meaning their knowledge of the Hereafter will be attained on the Day of Resurrection, when they see the punishment and the realities they denied, whereas in this world they will not." This is the interpretation of Ibn Abbas, and al-Zajjaj inclined to it. The في keeps its original sense of location, attached to تَدارَكَ. End of quotation, with some summarising and addition.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "It has two aspects. The first: the causes of the firm establishment and completion of knowledge, that the Resurrection is certain with no doubt, have been available to them and they were enabled to know it, yet they are doubtful and ignorant. This is His saying, ﴿بَلْ هم في شَكٍّ مِنها بَلْ هم مِنها عَمُونَ﴾ (Nay, they are in doubt about it; nay, they are blind to it [27:66]). He means the polytheists among those in the heavens and the earth, because when they were among them He attributed the act to all of them, as one says بَنُو فُلانٍ فَعَلُوا كَذا (the sons of so-and-so did such-and-such), when only some of them did it. The second aspect: describing them with the firm establishment and completion of knowledge is mockery of them, as you say to the most ignorant of people ما أعْلَمَكَ (how learned you are!) in mockery. This is because they doubted and were blind to the means that lead to a knowledge that is in doubt, let alone that they would know the time of its occurrence, which has no means of being known. There is another aspect to ادَّرَكَ عِلْمُهم and ادّارَكَ: ادَّرَكَ may mean انْتَهى وفَنِيَ (come to an end and perish), from the saying ادَّرَكَتِ الثَّمَرَةُ (the fruit ripened and was finished), because that is its final limit, at which it is destroyed. al-Hasan interpreted it as اضْمَحَلَّ عِلْمُهم (their knowledge vanished), and تَدارَكَ, from تَدارَكَ بَنُو فُلانٍ (the sons of so-and-so followed one another into destruction)." End of quotation.

Al-Kirmani said: "Knowledge here means judgement and statement, that is, statements and judgements about the Hereafter followed on among them, and much discussion of it occurred among them. Some of them denied it, some doubted it, and some considered it far-fetched."

Al-Farra' said: "بَلِ ادَّرَكَ means it becomes in the sense of denial, and there are similar cases of this. That is, they did not know its occurrence and its existence, and this is indicated by ﴿بَلْ هم في شَكٍّ مِنها﴾. So في in the sentence takes the sense of بِ, meaning their knowledge did not reach the Hereafter." Al-Farra' said: "This interpretation is strengthened by the reading of those who read أدَّرَكَ with an interrogative." End of quotation.

As for the reading of those who read بَلى (yes) instead of بَلْ, as the particle of answer, Abu Hatim said: "If بَلى is an answer to a preceding statement, it may be used with an interrogative, as if some people had denied what preceded, the power [of God], and they were told: بَلى (yes indeed), affirming what they had denied. Then an interrogative was resumed after it and was set in parallel with His saying ﴿بَلْ هم في شَكٍّ مِنها﴾, in the sense of أمْ هم في شَكٍّ مِنها (or are they in doubt about it?), because the particles of conjunction may alternate. He stopped at the two sentences with His saying ﴿بَلْ هم مِنها عَمُونَ﴾." End of quotation. He means that the sense is: did their knowledge of the Hereafter reach [its completion], or did they doubt? So بَلْ here has the sense of أمْ, placed in parallel with the interrogative hamzah. This is very weak: that بَلْ should have the sense of أمْ and be set in parallel with the interrogative hamzah.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "(If you ask): then what of those who read بَلى ادَّرَكَ? (I answer): when بَلى came after His saying ﴿وما يَشْعُرُونَ﴾ (and they do not perceive [27:65]), its meaning was: بَلى يَشْعُرُونَ (yes, they perceive). Then perception was explained by His saying: ادَّرَكَ عِلْمُهم في الآخِرَةِ (their knowledge of the Hereafter has been attained), in the sense of mockery, whose meaning is the intensification of the denial of knowledge. It is as if He said: their perception of the time of the Hereafter is that they do not know its occurrence. This returns to the intensification of the denial of perception in the strongest possible way. As for those who read بَلى أدَّرَكَ with an interrogative, its meaning is: they perceive when they will be raised. Then He denied their knowledge of its occurrence, and when their knowledge of its occurrence is denied, they have no perception of the time of its occurrence, because knowledge of the time of an event follows knowledge of the event itself. (If you ask): what is the meaning of these three changes of direction (idrab)? (I answer): they are only a presentation of their conditions. He first described them as not perceiving the time of the resurrection, then as not knowing that the Resurrection is coming, then as floundering in doubt and uncertainty without removing it, though removal is possible. He made the Hereafter the origin and source of their blindness, and therefore he used مِن rather than عَنْ, because the consequence and the recompense are what made them like cattle that neither reflect nor see." End of quotation.

[p. 88] When he had finished relating the stories of this surah, He commanded His Messenger ﷺ to praise Him, exalted is He, and to greet with peace those He chose, and he began to differentiate the Necessary Existence (wajib al-wujud), God, exalted is He, from the idols and the religions that they associated with God and worshipped. He began this exposition to the Quraysh and others with the hamdala (the formula of praise, "al-hamdu lillah"), as though it were the opening of a sermon (khutba) for what he was about to present of proofs indicating the Oneness, the knowledge, and the power (of God). Muslims have followed this practice in the opening of their books, their sermons, and their admonitions, so they begin with praising God and blessing Muhammad, the Messenger of God ﷺ. Those who write epistles follow them in the openings of books of conquests, congratulations, and events of significance. It has been said: this passage is connected to what precedes it, and the Messenger, peace be upon him, was commanded to praise God for the destruction of the disbelieving nations, and to greet with peace the prophets and their followers who were saved.

It has been said: "qul" (say) is an address to Lot, peace be upon him, that he should praise God for the destruction of the disbelievers of his people, ﴿and greet with peace His servants whom He has chosen﴾. Ibn Atiyya attributed this view to al-Farra', and said: "This is a non-Arab (ajami) error from al-Farra'." Abu al-Simak recited, "qula al-hamdu lillah," and likewise "qula al-hamdu lillahi sayurikum" with a fatha on the lam. "His servants whom He has chosen" encompasses the prophets and their followers. Ibn Abbas said: the servants who are greeted with peace are the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ, whom He chose for His Prophet; and in singling them out for this there is a rebuke to the disbelieving contemporaries. Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: When God, exalted is He, mentioned the states of the prophets, and that whoever denied them was uprooted by punishment, and that this is removed from the nation of the Messenger, He commanded him to praise Him for the blessing He had singled him out with, and to greet with peace the prophets who endured the hardships of the message. End of quotation, and it has been condensed.

His saying: ﴿Is God better, or what they associate (with Him)?﴾ is an interrogation containing rebuke, reproach, and mockery of their state, and an alert to the point of difference between God, exalted is He, and the idols, since it is known to anyone with reason that there is no partnership in being better between God, exalted is He, and them. This type of comparative form (af'al al-tafdil) often comes where it is known and established that there is no partnership in it, and it is mentioned only as a means of binding the opponent and alerting him to the error of his practice. The apparent meaning is that this interrogation concerns the reality of the essences (khabariyyat al-dhawat). It has been said: it came according to the belief of the polytheists, since they believed their gods to be good in some respect. It has been said: there is an omission in the sentence in two places; the estimate is: "Is the Oneness of God better, or the worship of what they associate?" So "ma" in "am ma" means "alladhi" (that which). It has been said: "ma" is verbal-masdar (infinitive), and the omission is from the first: i.e., "Is the Oneness of God better, or your polytheism?" It has been said: "khayr" is not for comparison; it is like when you say, "Prayer is good," meaning good out of the various goods. It has been said: the estimate is "possessor of good." The apparent meaning is that "khayran" is an af'al al-tafdil, and that the interrogation in such a case comes to explain the corruption of what the opponent holds, to alert him to his error, and to bind him to admit that preference is restricted to one side and absent from the other. The majority read "tushrikun" with the taa of address; al-Hasan, [p. 89] Qatada, Asim, and Abu Amr read it with the yaa of absence. The "am" in "am ma" is connected (muttasila), because the meaning is: "Which of the two is better?" In "(am man khalaqa)" and what follows it, it is disjunctive (munfasila). When God mentioned "good," He, glorified is He, enumerated the goods and benefits which are the effects of His mercy and grace, as He enumerated them in other places of His Book, making them stand before them as witnesses to what He originated of created things, and that they find no alternative to admitting this to God, exalted is He.

The majority read "am man khalaqa" and in the four that follow it with a shadda on the mim, the mim of "am" being assimilated into the mim of "man." Al-A'mash read it with a light mim, making it the interrogative hamza, placed before "man," and "man" in both readings is a subject (mubtada') and its predicate. Ibn Atiyya said: its estimate is: "He disbelieves His blessing and doubts Him," and the like of this meaning. Al-Zamakhshari estimated it: "Is what they associate better?" so he estimated what was affirmed in the first interrogation. He began the interrogation with the name of the essence, then moved on to the attributes. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said in his book "Kitab al-Lawami'": "There must be a supposed corresponding clause (jumla mu'adila), and that which is supposed becomes like that which is spoken, for the indication of the context (fahwa) upon it. The estimate of that clause is: 'Is He who created the heavens like him who did not create?' and likewise its sisters, and he has made explicit in other than this place what was supposed in them, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is then He who creates like him who creates not?﴾ [al-Nahl: 17]." End of quotation. As for calling this estimate a "clause" (jumla): if he means by it a group of words, it is correct; but if he means the clause as defined in grammar, it is not so, rather it is a supposed item of the category of the singular (mufrad).

God, exalted is He, began by mentioning the creation of the settled place of the upper and lower worlds, and the sending down of what sustains the lower world, and He said: "for you" (lakum), i.e., for your sake, as a favour, and that all of that is for your sake. Then He said: ﴿so We caused to grow﴾, and this is a shift (iltifat) from the third person of absence to the first person of speech with the nun of majesty (nun al-'azama), indicating that He alone is singular in this, and that He did not cause those diverse gardens of varied kinds, colours, tastes, and scents to grow by one water except Him, exalted is He. This singling out is strengthened by His saying: ﴿It was not for you to cause their trees to grow﴾. Since the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the sending down of water from the sky, leave no doubt for the rational that this is not but from God, and since growth is something that a human may bring about by sowing, watering, and preparing, and it is permissible for the doer of a cause to be ascribed the act of the effect, He, exalted is He, made clear His singling out of that by way of shift and emphasized it by His saying: ﴿It was not for you to cause their trees to grow﴾. Do you not see that the one who brings about growth may not come in accordance with his intent? And even if he does, he is ignorant of its nature, its measure, and its manner, so how could he be its doer? "Bahja" means beauty, freshness, and loveliness, because the one who looks upon them is delighted (yabtahij), i.e., pleased and rejoices. The majority read "dhat" in the singular, "bahjatin" with the ha' sustained; the broken plural functions in the attribute as the singular does, as in His saying: ﴿spouses purified﴾ [al-Baqara: 25], and it is in the sense of a group. Ibn Abi Abla read "dhawat" in the plural, and "bahajatin" with the ha' vocalized with a fatha.

﴿It was not for you to cause their trees to grow﴾: it has already been stated that the negation of such an occurrence may be due to the impossibility of its happening in this way, or to the impossibility of its happening according to the Law (shar'an), or to the negation of preferability (nafy al-awwaliyya). The meaning here is that causing such a thing to grow is impossible for you, because it is the bringing forth of something from non-existence into existence, and this is not within the power of anyone but God, exalted is He. When He mentioned His favour upon them, He addressed them with that; then when He mentioned their blame, He shifted from address to absence and said: ﴿Rather, they are a people who ascribe equals (ya'dilun)﴾, either as a shift, or as an informing the Messenger ﷺ of their state, i.e., they deviate (ya'dilun) from the truth, or they make others equal to Him (ya'dilu bihi ghayrahu), i.e., they make for Him an equal and a likeness. It is read: "ilahan" with a fatha, in the sense of: "Do you call upon, or do you associate?" It is read: "a-ilahun" with the lightening of the two hamzas and softening of the second, with a separation between them by an alif. When God, exalted is He, mentioned that He originated the heavens and the earth, He mentioned something shared between the heaven and the earth, namely the sending down of water from the sky and the growth of gardens on the earth. Then He mentioned something specific to the earth, which is making it a "qarar" (a settled abode), i.e., a resting place for you, such that it is possible for you to dwell upon it and remain on it, and it is not turned by the celestial sphere (falak). It has been said: because it is insignificant compared to the sphere, like a dot in a millstone.

﴿And He placed rivers within it﴾, i.e., between its places, in its valleys and ravines, ﴿and He placed upon it firm mountains﴾, i.e., firm mountains, so that it does not tilt with you and sway. "Al-bahrani" are the sweet and the salty; "al-hajiz" is the separator, from His power, exalted is He; this is said by al-Dahhak. Mujahid said: the sea of the sky and the earth, and the barrier is of air. al-Hasan said: the sea of Persia and the Romans; al-Suddi said: the sea of Iraq and Syria, and the barrier is of earth. Ibn Atiyya said, preferring this view on the barrier: it is what God placed between them of barriers and obstructions of the earth, despite their thinness in some places and their subtlety, which, were it not for His power, the salt would swallow the sweet. Ibn Atiyya had already presented that the two seas are: the sweet in its entirety, and the salty bitter water in its entirety; and since each of them is great and independent, the operative element in His saying ﴿and He placed﴾ is repeated, so they are of the coordination (atf) of independent clauses, each of them being a favour, and they are not joined under one operative element, so that it would be coordination of singular words. Abu Abdullah al-Razi had, in mentioning these four favours, a discourse from the science of nature, according to his claim, and according to the philosophers (hukama'), which lies outside the ways of the Arabs, and it may be consulted in his book.

"Al-mudtarr" is a passive participle: the one whom illness, poverty, or some accident of the vicissitudes of time has compelled (ahwajahu) to take refuge in God and to humble himself before Him, so he calls upon Him to remove what has befallen him of that and to relieve him of it. Ibn Abbas said: it is the one who is exhausted (al-majhud). al-Suddi said: it is the one who has no strength or power. It has been said: it is the sinner when he seeks forgiveness, and His answering him is joined with His will, exalted is He; so not every compelled one who calls upon Him is answered by God in the removal of what afflicts him. Al-Zamakhshari said: the answering is contingent upon the object requested being a benefit, and for this reason supplication is not good unless it stipulates benefit in it. End of quotation, and this is according to the path of the Mu'tazila in considering what is beneficial (al-maslaha) from God, exalted is He.

﴿And removes the evil﴾: it is everything that is harmful, and it is general for every harm that moves out of the state of the one in distress, and it is specific to a more general one, which is what is harmful, whether what is removed is in the state of compulsion or in what is less than it. "Khulafa'" (successors): i.e., the earlier nations; or in commanding the good and forbidding the evil; or the successors of the Prophet ﷺ after him; or the successors of the disbelievers in their land, or in dominion and authority: these are sayings. al-Hasan in one narration read: "wanajʿaluk-um" with the nun of the speaker, as though it were a resumed statement of information and promise, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿He will surely make them successors in the earth﴾ [al-Nur: 55].

His saying: ﴿and makes you successors of the earth﴾ is a transition from the state of the one in compulsion to a rank different from the state of compulsion, which is the state of succession (khilafa); so these are two circumstantial adverbs (zarfan). How many have we seen in this world of those who reached a state of compulsion and then became a dominating king! The majority read "tadhakkarun" with the taa of address; al-Hasan, al-A'mash, and Abu Amr read it with the yaa of absence, and the dhal in both readings is doubled, because the taa is assimilated into it. Abu Haywa read "tatadhakkarun" with two taas. The darkness of the land is the darkness of the night, and this is the literal sense; and it extends figuratively to ignorance and to the obscurity of a matter, as one says: "the matter became dark to me." The poet said:

"The blindnesses of men have cleared away from youth"

That is, the ignorances of youth. Guidance on land comes through landmarks, and guidance at sea through the stars.

﴿Or who sends the winds as heralds of good news before His mercy?﴾ The explanation of a parallel to this clause has already passed. It is also read as *ʿammā tushrikūn* (عَمّا تُشْرِكُونَ) with the *tāʾ* of address, meaning "what you associate [with Him]."

﴿Or who originates creation﴾: The apparent meaning is that *al-khalq* (الخَلْقَ, "creation") refers to the created thing, and its *bady'* (بَدْءُ, "origination") is its bringing into being and its production. It appears that what is intended is whoever God will restore in the Hereafter from among mankind, the jinn, and the angels, not the whole of created things in general. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "What is meant is the children of Adam, in view of the mention of restoration, and restoration is the resurrection from the graves. It is possible that by *al-khalq* he means the verbal noun of *khalaqa* (creating), and that *yabdaʾu* and *yuʿīdu* (originates and restores) are used figuratively for perfecting and doing well, as you say: 'So-and-so originates and restores in such-and-such a matter' when he masters it." Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: how did He say to them, 'Or who originates creation and then restores it,' when they deny restoration? I answer: He has favored them by enabling them to know and to acknowledge, so there remains no excuse for them in denial." End of quotation.

Since bringing the children of Adam into being is a favor and a kindness toward them, and a favor is not complete except through provision, He said: ﴿Or who provides for you from the heaven﴾ by rain, ﴿and the earth﴾ by plants? ﴿Say: Bring your proof﴾, that is, produce your argument and your evidence for what you claim, in denying anything of what has been established above, ﴿if you are truthful﴾ in claiming that there is another god with God. So where is your proof for it? This refers back to all the interrogatives that preceded it, which were given in the form of affirmation (*taqrīr*), and it is fitting that each interrogative is concluded with what preceded it.

(p-91) When He mentioned the bringing into being of the higher and lower worlds, and the favor of sending down rain and causing gardens to grow, that required that none be worshipped except the Originator of the world and the Bestower of what sustains life. So He concluded with His saying: ﴿Nay, but they are a people who deviate﴾, that is, from His worship, or they set up others as equal to Him, from among what is created and originated. When He mentioned the making of the earth a resting place, the causing of rivers to flow, the setting of mountains firm, and that this was a reminder to reflect upon and think about that, He concluded with His saying: ﴿Nay, but most of them do not know﴾, since among them there are those who know and reflect on that. When He mentioned the answering of the distressed one's prayer, the removal of evil, and their being made successors on the earth, it was fitting that a person constantly recall this favor, so He concluded with His saying: "﴿Little do you remember﴾", indicating the continual forgetfulness that comes when one is in ease, and his distress ends and the evil is removed from him, as He said: ﴿He forgets what he used to call upon Him for before﴾ [Az-Zumar: 8]. When He mentioned guidance in darknesses and the sending of the winds as glad tidings, while their objects of worship neither guide nor send, and they associate them with God, He said, Exalted is He: ﴿Exalted is He above what they associate.﴾ Each of these clauses is followed by His saying: ﴿Is there a god with God?﴾, as an emphasis and affirmation that there is no god but Him, exalted is He.

It was said: The unbelievers asked about the time of the Hour, which the Messenger ﷺ had promised them, and they pressed him about it, so the verse was revealed: ﴿Say: None in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except God﴾, and so on. What comes immediately to mind is that *man* (مَن, "whoever") is the subject of *yaʿlamu* (يَعْلَمُ, "knows"), *al-ghayb* (الغَيْبَ, "the unseen") is the object, and *illā Allāh* (إلّا اللَّهُ, "except God") is a *istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ* (disjunctive exception, meaning an exception not included in the category of the preceding term), since He is not included in the meaning of the word *man*. It came in the nominative (*marfūʿ*) according to the dialect of Tamim. The verse indicates that He, exalted is He, is the one alone who has knowledge of the unseen.

From ʿĀʾisha, may God be pleased with her: "Whoever claims that Muhammad knows what will happen tomorrow has indeed committed a great slander against God, and God, exalted is He, says: ﴿Say: None in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except God﴾." It is not said that He is included in the meaning of *man*, so that *fī al-samāwāti wa-l-arḍi* (فِي السَّماواتِ والأرْضِ, "in the heavens and the earth") would be a real container for the created beings within them, and a figurative one with respect to Him, exalted is He, meaning that He is in them by His knowledge. This is because that would combine the real and the figurative, and most scholars deny it, and its denial is the correct view. Whoever permits it would hold that the exception may be a *istithnāʾ muttaṣil* (connected exception), and that it would be in the nominative as a *badal* (substitute) or a qualifier. The nominative is more eloquent than the accusative in an exception, because it is an exception from a preceding negation. The apparent meaning is the generality of the unseen. It was also said that what is meant is the unseen of the Hour.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: what motivates the choice of the Tamimi dialect over the Hijazi?" meaning in its being a disjunctive exception, since He is not included under *man*. "I did not choose the nominative according to the Tamimi dialect, nor did we choose the accusative according to the Hijazi dialect." He said: "I answer: a subtle rhetorical point called for this, in that He placed the excluded term in the manner of the saying: 'Except the antelopes,' after the saying: 'There is no companion in it,' so that the meaning returns to your saying: If God is among those in the heavens and the earth, then they know the unseen. He means that their knowledge of the unseen is as impossible as it is impossible for God to be among them. Just as the meaning of 'what is in the house, if the antelopes are a companion' is that there is a companion in it, based on the premise that it is empty of companions." End of quotation.

Al-Zamakhshari had earlier mentioned: "If you ask: why do I raise the name of God, when God, exalted is He, cannot be among those in the heavens and the earth? I answer: it came according to the dialect of the Banu Tamim, where they say: 'There is no one in the house except a donkey,' as if *aḥad* (أحد, "anyone") had not been mentioned, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"On the evening when lances do not avail in its place,
nor arrows, except the well-tempered Indian sword."

And his saying: "No one came to me except ʿAmr, and his brothers did not help him except his brothers." End of quotation. The summary of it is that he says: if it were in the accusative, it would be included under the term excepted from, and when it is in the nominative it is a substitute, and the substituted term is in the intention of being dropped, so the operator becomes as if it were left without an object, because the substitute is on the intention of repeating the operator. It is as if it were said: "Say: none knows the unseen except God." If *man* were parsed as the object and *al-ghayb* as its substitute, and *illā Allāh* as the subject, meaning: none knows the unseen of whoever is in the heavens and the earth except God, that is, the absent things that occur in the world, and they do not know of their occurrence, that is, their knowledge does not precede that, it would be a good interpretation, and God, exalted is He, would be the one specified by His prior knowledge of what happens in the world.

*Ayyāna* (أيّانَ, "when"): its discussion has already passed at the end of *al-Aʿrāf*. Here it is an interrogative noun meaning *matā* (متى, "when"), and it is governed by *yubʿathūn* (يَبْعَثُونَ, "they will be raised") and *yush'urūn* (يُشْعِرُونَ, "they perceive"), with the verb suspended (*muʿallaq*), and the clause containing the interrogative (p-92) is in the accusative position governed by it. As-Sulamī read *ʾiyyāna* with a kasra on the hamza, which is the dialect of his tribe, Banu Sulaym.

When He denied them knowledge of the unseen in general, He denied them this specific unseen, namely the time of the Hour and the resurrection, so it is negated twice: since it is included in the generality of the unseen, and it is also specifically stated.

**[Continuation of the commentary on 27:59–66, part 3 of 3]**

The majority of reciters read ﴿بَلِ ادّارَكَ﴾. Its original form is تَدارَكَ, and the تاء was assimilated into the دال and made quiescent, so a connecting hamzah (همزة الوصل, the hamzah used to begin a word that is pronounced only when it is not preceded by another word) was introduced.

Ubayy (Ubayy ibn Ka'b) read أمْ تَدارَكَ, keeping the original form and making أمْ replace بَلْ.

Sulayman ibn Yasar, the brother of Ata' (Ibn Yasar), read بَلِ ادَّرَكَ, moving the vowel of the hamzah onto the lam and doubling the دال. His reasoning was that the form's measure is افْتَعَلَ. He assimilated the دال, which is the first root letter (فاء الكلمة), into the تاء after changing the تاء into a دال, so the second consonant was changed to match the first. This is like the saying اثَّرَدَ, whose original form is اثْتَرَدَ, from الثَّرْد (crumbling bread into broth). The elided hamzah whose vowel was moved onto the lam is the interrogative hamzah (همزة الاستفهام). It was placed before the alif of connection (ألف الوصل), so the alif of connection was dropped. Then the hamzah itself was dropped and its vowel was placed on the lam of بَلْ.

Abu Raja', al-A'raj, Shaybah, Talhah and Tawbah al-Anbari read in the same way, except that they vowelled the lam of بَلْ with a kasrah. This is reported from Ibn Abbas, 'Asim and al-A'mash.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Abu Ja'far and the people of Makkah read بَلِ ادَّرَكَ on the measure افَّعَلَ, in the sense of تَفاعَلَ (the reciprocal form). This reading is also reported from Abu Bakr, from 'Asim.

Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) in one transmission, Ibn Abbas in another, Ibn Abi Jamrah and others on his authority, al-Hasan, Qatadah and Ibn Muhaysin read بَلْ آدْرَكَ, with a long vowel after the interrogative hamzah. The original form was أأدْرَكَ. They changed the second hamzah into an alif to lighten the pronunciation, disliking the combination of two hamzahs. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' rejected this transmission and its grammatical basis.

Abu Hatim said: "It is not permitted to use the interrogative after بَلْ, because بَلْ indicates affirmation, whereas the interrogative in this context is a denial, meaning: they did not [know]. Compare His saying, ﴿أشَهِدُوا خَلْقَهُمْ﴾ (Did they witness their creation? [al-Zukhruf 43:19]), meaning: they did not witness it. Therefore the two cannot occur together, because of the contradiction between affirmation and denial." End of quotation.

Some later scholars permitted the interrogative after بَلْ, and compared it to the speaker's saying: أخُبْزًا أكَلْتَ بَلْ أماءً شَرِبْتَ؟ (Did you eat bread, or did you drink water?), by dropping the first statement and taking up the second.

Mujahid read أمِ ادَّرَكَ, making أمْ replace بَلْ, with ادَّرَكَ on the measure افَّعَلَ.

Ibn Abbas also read بَلْ آدّارَكَ, with a hamzah placed before ادّارَكَ. This drops the connecting hamzah that was introduced, because of the assimilation and because the speech begins with a quiescent consonant.

Ibn Mas'ud also read بَلْ أأدَّرَكَ, with two hamzahs: the interrogative hamzah and the hamzah of أفَّعَلَ.

al-Hasan and al-A'raj also read بَلْ أدَّرَكَ, with one hamzah and the assimilation of the first root letter, which is the دال in the تاء of افْتَعَلَ, after the تاء had become a دال.

Warsh, in one transmission, read بَلِ ادَّرَكَ, dropping the hamzah of ادَّرَكَ and moving its vowel to the lam.

Ibn Abbas also read بَلى ادَّرَكَ, with بَلى, the particle of affirmation by which a negated interrogative is affirmed.

It was also read بَلْ آأدَّرَكَ, with an alif between the two hamzahs.

As for the reading of those who read it as an interrogative, Ibn Abbas said: "It is a rebuke, meaning: their knowledge did not reach [the Hereafter], as a denial against them." Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is an interrogative in the form of a denial that their knowledge has reached [the Hereafter]. The same applies to the reading أمِ ادَّرَكَ and أمْ تَدارَكَ, because أمْ here has the meaning of بَلْ together with the interrogative hamzah." End of quotation.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "It has the sense of mocking the disbelievers and rebuking them for something that is far from them, meaning: did they know the matter of the Hereafter, and did their knowledge reach it?"

As for the reading of those who read it as a statement, Ibn Abbas said: "The meaning is: بَلْ تَدارَكَ عِلْمُهم ما جَهِلُوهُ في الدُّنْيا (their knowledge caught up with what they had not known in this world), that is, they came to know it in the Hereafter, in the sense that their knowledge became complete in the Hereafter that everything they were promised is true. This is the true affirmation of knowledge for them, because they see with their own eyes in the Hereafter what they were promised unseen in this world. Its being in the past tense has the sense of the future, because reporting it is truthful, so it is as if it had already happened."

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "It may bear two meanings. The first: their knowledge reached its limit, as you say أدْرَكَ النَّباتُ (the plant reached maturity) and similar, meaning: their knowledge of the Hereafter reached its end and followed on until they would know its extent and believe, but they only have false suppositions. Or [it means] until they do not know its time. Here في is in the sense of بِ, attached to their knowledge, and knowledge may take بِ, as you say عِلْمِي بِزَيْدٍ كَذا (my knowledge of Zayd is such). This reading may be understood in the sense of a question and interrogation, and it comes as a denial because they did not perceive anything beneficial. The second: أدْرَكَ is in the sense of يُدْرِكُ (is reached), meaning their knowledge of the Hereafter will be attained on the Day of Resurrection, when they see the punishment and the realities they denied, whereas in this world they will not." This is the interpretation of Ibn Abbas, and al-Zajjaj inclined to it. The في keeps its original sense of location, attached to تَدارَكَ. End of quotation, with some summarising and addition.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "It has two aspects. The first: the causes of the firm establishment and completion of knowledge, that the Resurrection is certain with no doubt, have been available to them and they were enabled to know it, yet they are doubtful and ignorant. This is His saying, ﴿بَلْ هم في شَكٍّ مِنها بَلْ هم مِنها عَمُونَ﴾ (Nay, they are in doubt about it; nay, they are blind to it [27:66]). He means the polytheists among those in the heavens and the earth, because when they were among them He attributed the act to all of them, as one says بَنُو فُلانٍ فَعَلُوا كَذا (the sons of so-and-so did such-and-such), when only some of them did it. The second aspect: describing them with the firm establishment and completion of knowledge is mockery of them, as you say to the most ignorant of people ما أعْلَمَكَ (how learned you are!) in mockery. This is because they doubted and were blind to the means that lead to a knowledge that is in doubt, let alone that they would know the time of its occurrence, which has no means of being known. There is another aspect to ادَّرَكَ عِلْمُهم and ادّارَكَ: ادَّرَكَ may mean انْتَهى وفَنِيَ (come to an end and perish), from the saying ادَّرَكَتِ الثَّمَرَةُ (the fruit ripened and was finished), because that is its final limit, at which it is destroyed. al-Hasan interpreted it as اضْمَحَلَّ عِلْمُهم (their knowledge vanished), and تَدارَكَ, from تَدارَكَ بَنُو فُلانٍ (the sons of so-and-so followed one another into destruction)." End of quotation.

Al-Kirmani said: "Knowledge here means judgement and statement, that is, statements and judgements about the Hereafter followed on among them, and much discussion of it occurred among them. Some of them denied it, some doubted it, and some considered it far-fetched."

Al-Farra' said: "بَلِ ادَّرَكَ means it becomes in the sense of denial, and there are similar cases of this. That is, they did not know its occurrence and its existence, and this is indicated by ﴿بَلْ هم في شَكٍّ مِنها﴾. So في in the sentence takes the sense of بِ, meaning their knowledge did not reach the Hereafter." Al-Farra' said: "This interpretation is strengthened by the reading of those who read أدَّرَكَ with an interrogative." End of quotation.

As for the reading of those who read بَلى (yes) instead of بَلْ, as the particle of answer, Abu Hatim said: "If بَلى is an answer to a preceding statement, it may be used with an interrogative, as if some people had denied what preceded, the power [of God], and they were told: بَلى (yes indeed), affirming what they had denied. Then an interrogative was resumed after it and was set in parallel with His saying ﴿بَلْ هم في شَكٍّ مِنها﴾, in the sense of أمْ هم في شَكٍّ مِنها (or are they in doubt about it?), because the particles of conjunction may alternate. He stopped at the two sentences with His saying ﴿بَلْ هم مِنها عَمُونَ﴾." End of quotation. He means that the sense is: did their knowledge of the Hereafter reach [its completion], or did they doubt? So بَلْ here has the sense of أمْ, placed in parallel with the interrogative hamzah. This is very weak: that بَلْ should have the sense of أمْ and be set in parallel with the interrogative hamzah.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "(If you ask): then what of those who read بَلى ادَّرَكَ? (I answer): when بَلى came after His saying ﴿وما يَشْعُرُونَ﴾ (and they do not perceive [27:65]), its meaning was: بَلى يَشْعُرُونَ (yes, they perceive). Then perception was explained by His saying: ادَّرَكَ عِلْمُهم في الآخِرَةِ (their knowledge of the Hereafter has been attained), in the sense of mockery, whose meaning is the intensification of the denial of knowledge. It is as if He said: their perception of the time of the Hereafter is that they do not know its occurrence. This returns to the intensification of the denial of perception in the strongest possible way. As for those who read بَلى أدَّرَكَ with an interrogative, its meaning is: they perceive when they will be raised. Then He denied their knowledge of its occurrence, and when their knowledge of its occurrence is denied, they have no perception of the time of its occurrence, because knowledge of the time of an event follows knowledge of the event itself. (If you ask): what is the meaning of these three changes of direction (idrab)? (I answer): they are only a presentation of their conditions. He first described them as not perceiving the time of the resurrection, then as not knowing that the Resurrection is coming, then as floundering in doubt and uncertainty without removing it, though removal is possible. He made the Hereafter the origin and source of their blindness, and therefore he used مِن rather than عَنْ, because the consequence and the recompense are what made them like cattle that neither reflect nor see." End of quotation.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 27, verses 67–82 (part 1 of 2):**

(p. 94) ﴿The disbelievers say: "When we have become dust, and our fathers too, shall we really be brought forth?"﴾ ﴿"We and our fathers were certainly promised this before.
