Indeed, you are upon the clear truth.﴾ ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear, nor can you make the deaf hear the call when they turn away, retreating.﴾ ﴿Nor can you guide the blind out of their error. You will not make hear except those who believe in Our verses, so they are Muslims [submitting].﴾ ﴿And when the word befalls them, We will bring forth for them a creature from the earth which will speak to them, [saying] that people were not certain of Our signs.﴾

When the Most High had mentioned that He alone has knowledge of the unseen, and that among it is the time of the Hour, and that they have no awareness of its time, and that the disbelievers are in doubt about it and blind to it, it was fitting to mention their statements in denying it, and that what they were promised of it is not true; rather, it is only what the ancients wrote down, without any report of it being a reality.

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read ﴿أئِذا، أئِنّا﴾ [a'idhā, a'innā] with the two interrogatives combined, the second being changed to a yā' (ya). Abu 'Amr separated the two with an alif. 'Asim and Hamzah read both with two hamzas. Nafi' read ﴿إذا﴾ with a kasrah-marked hamzah, and ﴿آينّا﴾ with the interrogative hamzah, the second changed to a yā', with a madd between them. The rest read ﴿آئِذا﴾ with a prolonged interrogative, and ﴿إنّنا﴾ with two nūns without an interrogative. The governing element (al-'amil) of ﴿إذا﴾ is omitted, indicated by the meaning of the second clause; its estimated form is "will come out." It is impossible for ﴿لَمُخْرَجُونَ﴾ to govern it, because each of ''inna'' and the lam of initiation (lam al-ibtida') and the interrogative prevents what follows them from governing what precedes them, except the lam that falls in the predicate of ''inna'', for the complement of the predicate may precede it and the predicate, as established in the science of grammar (ʿilm al-naḥw).

﴿وآباؤنا﴾ [and our fathers] is coordinated with the subject of ''kāna'' (kāna's noun), and that separation by the predicate of ''kāna'' is permissible. The bringing forth here is from the graves, alive, with their spirits returned to their bodies. Combining the interrogative in ''idhā'' and in ''innā'' is a denial upon a denial, and an emphasis on the impossibility of that occurring. The pronoun in ''a'innā'' refers to them and to their fathers, because their becoming dust is inclusive of all of them. Then they mentioned that they had been promised this, they and their fathers, but none of this promised thing had come to pass; then they affirmed and restricted that it was among the fabrications of those who came before. Here the object of the promise, which is ''hādhā'' [this], is placed first, while in another verse it is placed later, according to the context in which the speech was delivered. Where the report about them concerning the denial of resurrection and the Hereafter was emphasized, they gave it priority by placing it first out of concern; and where that was not the case, they aimed at denying the bringing into existence of the one who is resurrected, so they placed that first and delayed the object of the promise.

Then He commanded His Prophet to tell them to travel through the earth. The discussion of this verse has preceded in the beginning of al-An'am. By "the criminals" he meant the disbelievers. Then He consoled His Prophet, saying: ﴿Do not grieve over them﴾, meaning, regarding their not having submitted or yielded to what you have brought. ﴿And do not be in distress﴾, meaning, in a hardship and a matter that is difficult for you, ﴿because of what they plot﴾, for their plotting returns upon them, not upon you, and Allah protects you from them. The reading ''ḍīq'' (ضِيقٍ) has been mentioned, with a kasrah and a fatḥah on the ḍād, and both are verbal nouns (maṣdar). Abu 'Ali (al-Farisi) disliked that the one with the fatḥah on the ḍād should be the original ''ḍayyiq'', with the yā' doubled, then lightened, like ''layn'' from ''layyin'', because that requires deleting the modified noun and setting the adjective in its place, and it is not among the adjectives that stand in for the modified noun in a regular manner. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that, saying: "It may also be intended as: in a narrow matter of their plotting."

When the Quraysh hastened [to ask] about the matter of the Hour, or about the punishment promised to them, and asked about the time of what was promised, mockingly, it was said to him: ﴿Say: "Perhaps some of it has drawn close to you."﴾ That is, it has followed you soon, and some of what you hastened for has become like a rider that follows you. This was the punishment of the Day of Badr. It was also said: the punishment of the grave. The majority read ''radifa'' (رَدِفَ) with a kasrah on the dāl. Ibn Hurmuz read it with a fatḥah, and both are dialects. Its original form is transitive, in the sense of "followed" and "overtook," so it may be understood as implying the intransitive meaning, and therefore Ibn 'Abbas and others interpreted it as ''azifa'' and ''qariba'' (drew near and approached), since what comes after a thing is near to it, within its meaning, or with an extension. The lam in its object serves to emphasize the arrival of the verb to it, as the ba' was added in ﴿and do not cast yourselves by your own hands [into destruction]﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:195], as al-Zamakhshari said. It has also been construed with ''min'' by way of implicit meaning (taḍmīn) for what is transitive with it. The poet said:

*"So when we followed closely upon ʿUmayr and his companions, they turned back swiftly, while death was driving them on."*

meaning, they approached ʿUmayr. It was also said: ''radifahu'' and ''radifa lahu'' are two dialects. It was also said: the verb is construed according to the verbal noun, meaning "the following for you." And ''baʿḍ'' [some] is according to the estimate of "the following of some of what you hasten for," and this involves a strain from which the Qur'an is to be exempted. It was also said: the lam in ''lakum'' is attached to the object for which (the causal), and the direct object is omitted, its estimate being: "He caused the creation to follow for your sake," and this is weak. It was also said: the subject of ''radifa'' is a pronoun referring to the promise, then He said: ''lakum baʿḍu mā tastaʿjilūn'' [some of what you hasten for is for you], as a subject and predicate. This involves a disjointing of the speech and a departure from the apparent sense without any need that calls for it.

﴿Indeed, your Lord is full of bounty﴾, meaning, bounties upon them by delaying their punishment for their sins and their disbelief. The object of ''yashkurūn'' [they give thanks] is omitted, meaning: they do not thank Him for His blessings upon them; or ''lā yashkurūn'' means "they do not know the right of the blessing," and the absence of their knowledge of the blessing is expressed by the absence of what follows from knowing it, which is gratitude.

Then the Most High informed of the breadth of His knowledge, beginning with what concerns humankind, then generalizing to every hidden thing. He expressed it by ''ṣudūr'' [breasts/chests], which is the locus of the hearts, in which thought and reasoning reside, as He said: ﴿But it is the hearts within the breasts that go blind﴾ [al-Hajj 22:46], regarding the state within them, namely the hearts. He attributed the disclosure to their persons, because disclosure is among the actions of the limbs. Since what is concealed in the breast is what prompts what appears on the limbs, and the cause of its manifestation is that concealing precedes informing. The majority read ﴿ما تُكِنُّ﴾ [what they conceal], from ''akanna al-shay'' [he hid the thing]. Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd, and Ibn al-Sumayfa' read it with a fatḥah on the tā' and a ḍammah on the kāf, from ''kanna al-shay'' [he covered the thing]. The meaning: what they hide and what they disclose of enmity toward the Messenger and their schemes.

The apparent generality of His saying ''min ghā'ibah'' [any hidden thing] is: there is no thing in the utmost state of concealment and obscurity but that it is in a Book with Allah and in the hidden store of His knowledge. It was also said: what was hidden from them of the punishment of heaven and earth. It was also said: it is the Day of Resurrection and its terrors; this was reported by al-Hasan. The "Book" is the Preserved Tablet (al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ). It was also said: the deeds of the servants have been recorded in order that they be recompensed for them. The author of al-Ghunyan (Ṣāḥib al-Ghunyān) said: meaning, an incident that is hidden, or a calamity that befalls. Ibn 'Abbas said: meaning, there is no secret thing in the heavens and the earth, nor an open one, so he sufficed with mentioning the secret instead of its opposite. Al-Zamakhshari said: that which is hidden and concealed is called ''ghā'ibah'' [hidden] and ''khāfiyah'' [concealed], and the tā' in both is like its role in ''ʿāqibah'' [outcome] and ''ʿāfiyah'' [well-being], and their parallels are ''naṭīḥah'' [the gored animal], ''dhabīḥah'' [the slaughtered animal], and ''ramiyyah'' [the shot animal], in that they are nouns and not adjectives. It is permissible that these two be adjectives, and the tā' in them is for intensification, like the ''riwāyah'' [transmission] in their saying: "Woe to the poet for the evil of his transmission," as if he said: "there is no thing of extreme hiddenness and obscurity but that Allah knows it, encompasses it, and has recorded it in the Clear Tablet, which is manifest to whoever among the angels looks into it." End of quote.

When the Most High mentioned the origin and the return, He mentioned what pertains to prophethood, and the major basis for establishing the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ is the Qur'an. Among its miraculous qualities is its report of the narratives it contains, which agree with what is in the Torah and the Gospel, together with the knowledge that he was unlettered, who had not mixed with scholars nor occupied himself with teaching. The Children of Israel are the Jews and the Christians. It relates to them most of what they differed about, in its proper form, and clarifies it for them; had they been fair, they would have submitted. Among what they differed about is the matter of the Messiah: they formed factions concerning it; some said he is Allah, some said he is the son of Allah, some said he is the third of three, and some said he is a prophet like the other prophets. They held councils for this and diverged in their creeds, and they disputed about matters until some of them cursed others.

The apparent sense is the generality of the believers, and it was also said: it refers to those among the Children of Israel who believed. As for ''al-qaḍāʾ'' [judgment] and ''al-ḥukm'' [ruling]: although it becomes apparent that they are synonyms, it was said that what is meant here is justice, meaning, by His justice, because He judges only with justice. It was also said: what is meant by His wisdom (ḥikmah) is judgment. It was said: this is indicated by the reading of one who read ''biḥikamihi'' with a kasrah on the ḥā' and a fatḥah on the kāf, the plural of ''ḥikmah'', and that is the reading of Junāḥ ibn Jaysh. Since judgment requires the execution of what is judged and knowledge of what is ruled upon, these two attributes came after it, namely: the Mighty, that is, the Dominant, the Powerful, and the All-Knowing. Then the Most High commanded him to rely upon Him, and informed him that he is upon the clear truth that has no doubt in it. This is like a reasoning for trusting in Him, and in it is evidence that whoever is upon the truth is entitled to trust in Allah, for He will support him and not forsake him.

Since the Qur'an and what Allah related in it is hardly beneficial to them, the Most High informed about them that they are dead of heart, or they were likened to the dead, even though they were living with sound sight; for when it is recited to them their ears do not retain it, so their state, due to the lack of benefit from hearing, was like the state of the dead. The majority read ﴿ولا تَسْمَعُ الصُّمُّ﴾ [nor can the deaf hear] here and in al-Rūm with a ḍammah on the tā' and a kasrah on the mīm, with ''al-ṣummu'' in the nominative. Since the dead cannot hear, no complement was mentioned for him, but rather the causing to hear was negated, meaning: no causing of hearing from you can ever reach them, due to their lack of receptivity. As for the deaf person, he may at times be in a state in which he can be made to hear and can hear, so the complement of the verb, which is the call, was mentioned. The word ''idhā'' [when] governs ''tasmaʿu'' [you hear], and the negation of causing to hear or of hearing was restricted by this temporal clause and what follows it, for emphasis regarding the state of the deaf person; because when he turns away from the caller, retreating, he is further from perceiving his voice.

He likened them first to the dead, then to the deaf in a certain state, then to the blind, saying: ﴿Nor can you guide the blind﴾ [out of their error], since they lose the way, and no one can remove that from them and turn them into guided, seeing people except Allah, the Most High. The majority read ''bihādī al-ʿum'' [guide the blind] as an active participle with its object in the genitive; Yaḥyā ibn al-Ḥārith and Abū Ḥaywah read ''bihādin'' with tanwīn, and ''al-ʿumya'' [the blind] in the accusative; al-A'mash, Ṭalḥah, Ibn Wathhāb, Ibn Ya'mur, and Ḥamzah read ''tahdī'' [you guide], the present tense of ''hadā'', with ''al-ʿumya'' in the accusative; Ibn Mas'ūd read ''wa-mā anta tahtadī'', with ''an'' added after ''mā'', and ''yahtadī'' is the present of ''ihtadā'', and ''al-ʿumyu'' in the nominative. The meaning: it is not within your capacity to introduce guidance into the heart of one who is blind to the truth and has not looked at it with the eye of his heart.

﴿You will not make hear except those who believe in Our verses﴾, and they are those whom Allah knows will affirm His signs.

﴿So they are Muslims﴾, submitting to the truth. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Muslims" means sincere, from His saying: ﴿Yes, whoever submits his face to Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:112], meaning He made it wholly and purely for Allah. End of quote.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 27, verses 67–82 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And when the word comes due against them﴾, i.e., when the promise of their punishment, which the eternal decree from Allah contains, is fulfilled, as in His saying: ﴿the word of punishment has come due against the disbelievers﴾ [al-Zumar: 71]. The meaning is: when Allah wills to carry out upon the disbelievers the punishment that His prior knowledge concerning them determined, He will bring forth for them a beast (dabbah) that emerges from the earth. "Waqa'a" (came due, took place) is an expression for being established and necessary. As for "al-qawl" (the word), it is either by eliding a modifier, meaning "the content of the word," or the word "qawl" is used for "maqul" (what is said), since what is said is conveyed through speech, namely what they were promised of the Hour and the punishment. Ibn Mas'ud said: ﴿the word comes due against them﴾ happens through the death of the scholars, the departure of knowledge, and the lifting of the Qur'an. End. It is narrated that its emergence will be when goodness ceases, when no one is commanded to do right, when no one is forbidden from wrong, and when no one repentant or penitent remains. In a hadith: "That the beast and the rising of the sun from the west are among the first of the signs" (al-ashrat, the major portents), but it does not specify which is first. Likewise the Dajjal (the Antichrist). The apparent sense of the hadiths is that the rising of the sun is the last of them, and the apparent sense is that the beast that emerges is one. It is also narrated that in every land a beast will emerge of the kind whose species is established on the earth, and that it is not one, so that His saying "dabbah" (a beast) is a generic noun (ism jins, a noun denoting a whole category). They differed concerning its nature, its form, the place of its emergence, the number of its emergences, the extent of what emerges from it, what it does to people, and what it emerges with, in a confused disagreement, some of it contradicting other parts and some of it refuting others; so we have set aside mention of it, because transmitting it is blackening paper with what is not authentic and wasting the time of its transmission.

The apparent reading of His saying ﴿tukallimuhum﴾ (speaks to them) is with the doubled letter (tashdid), which is the reading of the majority, from "kalam" (speech). This is supported by Ubayy's reading: tunabbi'uhum (informs them), and in some readings: tuhaddithuhum (tells them), which is the reading of Yahya ibn Sallam. Abdullah's reading is: "bi-anna al-nas" (that the people). Al-Suddi said: it speaks to them about the falsehood of all religions except Islam. It is said: it addresses them, saying to the believer: "This is a believer," and to the disbeliever: "This is a disbeliever." It is also said that the meaning of "tukallimuhum" is: it wounds them, from "kalm" (wound), and the doubling is for intensity. This is supported by the reading of Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, Abu Zur'a, al-Jahdari, Abu Haywa, and Ibn Abi Abla: "tuklimuhum," with a fatha on the ta', a sukun on the kaf, and a light lam. Also the reading of one who read "tajrahuhum" (wounds them) in place of "tukallimuhum." Abu al-Hawra asked Ibn Abbas: "Does it say tukallimu or tuklimu?" He said: "It does all of that: it speaks to the believer and wounds the disbeliever." End. It is narrated that it brands the disbeliever on his forehead and darkens him, and wipes over the face of the believer so that it whitens him.

The Kufans and Zayd ibn Ali read "anna al-nas" with a fatha on the hamza, and Ibn Mas'ud read "bi-anna" (and this has been mentioned). The rest of the seven readers read "inna," with a kasra on the hamza. The kasra allows that it is part of Allah's speech, which is the apparent sense given His saying "bi-ayatina" (by Our signs), and it allows that it is part of the speech of the beast. This is narrated from Ibn Abbas. The kasra of "inna" here is according to the saying (al-qawl), either by supposing an implied "qal" (said), or by treating "tukallimuhum" as if it were "taqulu lahum" (says to them). His saying ﴿bi-ayatina﴾ (by Our signs) is either by eliding a modifier, or because they are particular to Allah, as when some intimates of a king say: "our horses and our lands." On the reading with the fatha, the estimate is "bi-anna" like the reading of Abdullah. The apparent sense is that it is connected to "tukallimuhum," meaning: it addresses them with this speech. It is permissible that the ba' (bi), whether pronounced or implied, is causal, meaning: it addresses them or wounds them because of their failure to have certainty in Our signs.

They held councils for this and diverged in their creeds, and they disputed about matters until some of them cursed others.

The apparent sense is the generality of the believers, and it was also said: it refers to those among the Children of Israel who believed. As for ''al-qaḍāʾ'' [judgment] and ''al-ḥukm'' [ruling]: although it becomes apparent that they are synonyms, it was said that what is meant here is justice, meaning, by His justice, because He judges only with justice. It was also said: what is meant by His wisdom (ḥikmah) is judgment. It was said: this is indicated by the reading of one who read ''biḥikamihi'' with a kasrah on the ḥā' and a fatḥah on the kāf, the plural of ''ḥikmah'', and that is the reading of Junāḥ ibn Jaysh. Since judgment requires the execution of what is judged and knowledge of what is ruled upon, these two attributes came after it, namely: the Mighty, that is, the Dominant, the Powerful, and the All-Knowing. This is like a reasoning for trusting in Him, and in it is evidence that whoever is upon the truth is entitled to trust in Allah, for He will support him and not forsake him.

Since the Qur'an and what Allah related in it is hardly beneficial to them, the Most High informed about them that they are dead of heart, or they were likened to the dead, even though they were living with sound sight; for when it is recited to them their ears do not retain it, so their state, due to the lack of benefit from hearing, was like the state of the dead. The majority read ﴿ولا تَسْمَعُ الصُّمُّ﴾ [nor can the deaf hear] here and in al-Rūm with a ḍammah on the tā' and a kasrah on the mīm, with ''al-ṣummu'' in the nominative. As for the deaf person, he may at times be in a state in which he can be made to hear and can hear, so the complement of the verb, which is the call, was mentioned. The word ''idhā'' [when] governs ''tasmaʿu'' [you hear], and the negation of causing to hear or of hearing was restricted by this temporal clause and what follows it, for emphasis regarding the state of the deaf person; because when he turns away from the caller, retreating, he is further from perceiving his voice.

He likened them first to the dead, then to the deaf in a certain state, then to the blind, saying: ﴿Nor can you guide the blind﴾ [out of their error], since they lose the way, and no one can remove that from them and turn them into guided, seeing people except Allah, the Most High. ﴿You will not make hear except those who believe in Our verses﴾, and they are those whom Allah knows will affirm His signs.

﴿So they are Muslims﴾, submitting to the truth. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Muslims" means sincere, from His saying: ﴿Yes, whoever submits his face to Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:112], meaning He made it wholly and purely for Allah. End of quote.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 27, verses 67–82 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And when the word comes due against them﴾, i.e., when the promise of their punishment, which the eternal decree from Allah contains, is fulfilled, as in His saying: ﴿the word of punishment has come due against the disbelievers﴾ [al-Zumar: 71]. The meaning is: when Allah wills to carry out upon the disbelievers the punishment that His prior knowledge concerning them determined, He will bring forth for them a beast (dabbah) that emerges from the earth. "Waqa'a" (came due, took place) is an expression for being established and necessary. As for "al-qawl" (the word), it is either by eliding a modifier, meaning "the content of the word," or the word "qawl" is used for "maqul" (what is said), since what is said is conveyed through speech, namely what they were promised of the Hour and the punishment. Ibn Mas'ud said: ﴿the word comes due against them﴾ happens through the death of the scholars, the departure of knowledge, and the lifting of the Qur'an. End. It is narrated that its emergence will be when goodness ceases, when no one is commanded to do right, when no one is forbidden from wrong, and when no one repentant or penitent remains. In a hadith: "That the beast and the rising of the sun from the west are among the first of the signs" (al-ashrat, the major portents), but it does not specify which is first. Likewise the Dajjal (the Antichrist). The apparent sense of the hadiths is that the rising of the sun is the last of them, and the apparent sense is that the beast that emerges is one. It is also narrated that in every land a beast will emerge of the kind whose species is established on the earth, and that it is not one, so that His saying "dabbah" (a beast) is a generic noun (ism jins, a noun denoting a whole category). They differed concerning its nature, its form, the place of its emergence, the number of its emergences, the extent of what emerges from it, what it does to people, and what it emerges with, in a confused disagreement, some of it contradicting other parts and some of it refuting others; so we have set aside mention of it, because transmitting it is blackening paper with what is not authentic and wasting the time of its transmission.

The apparent reading of His saying ﴿tukallimuhum﴾ (speaks to them) is with the doubled letter (tashdid), which is the reading of the majority, from "kalam" (speech). This is supported by Ubayy's reading: tunabbi'uhum (informs them), and in some readings: tuhaddithuhum (tells them), which is the reading of Yahya ibn Sallam. Abdullah's reading is: "bi-anna al-nas" (that the people). Al-Suddi said: it speaks to them about the falsehood of all religions except Islam. It is said: it addresses them, saying to the believer: "This is a believer," and to the disbeliever: "This is a disbeliever." It is also said that the meaning of "tukallimuhum" is: it wounds them, from "kalm" (wound), and the doubling is for intensity. This is supported by the reading of Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, Abu Zur'a, al-Jahdari, Abu Haywa, and Ibn Abi Abla: "tuklimuhum," with a fatha on the ta', a sukun on the kaf, and a light lam. Also the reading of one who read "tajrahuhum" (wounds them) in place of "tukallimuhum." Abu al-Hawra asked Ibn Abbas: "Does it say tukallimu or tuklimu?" He said: "It does all of that: it speaks to the believer and wounds the disbeliever." End. It is narrated that it brands the disbeliever on his forehead and darkens him, and wipes over the face of the believer so that it whitens him.

The Kufans and Zayd ibn Ali read "anna al-nas" with a fatha on the hamza, and Ibn Mas'ud read "bi-anna" (and this has been mentioned). The rest of the seven readers read "inna," with a kasra on the hamza. The kasra allows that it is part of Allah's speech, which is the apparent sense given His saying "bi-ayatina" (by Our signs), and it allows that it is part of the speech of the beast. This is narrated from Ibn Abbas. The kasra of "inna" here is according to the saying (al-qawl), either by supposing an implied "qal" (said), or by treating "tukallimuhum" as if it were "taqulu lahum" (says to them). His saying ﴿bi-ayatina﴾ (by Our signs) is either by eliding a modifier, or because they are particular to Allah, as when some intimates of a king say: "our horses and our lands." On the reading with the fatha, the estimate is "bi-anna" like the reading of Abdullah. The apparent sense is that it is connected to "tukallimuhum," meaning: it addresses them with this speech. It is permissible that the ba' (bi), whether pronounced or implied, is causal, meaning: it addresses them or wounds them because of their failure to have certainty in Our signs.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 27, verses 67–82 (part 1 of 2):**

(p. 94) ﴿The disbelievers say: "When we have become dust, and our fathers too, shall we really be brought forth?"﴾ ﴿"We and our fathers were certainly promised this before. This is nothing but the fables of the ancients."﴾ ﴿Say: "Travel through the earth and see what was the end of the criminals."﴾ ﴿Do not grieve over them, and do not be distressed by what they plot.﴾ ﴿They say: "When will this promise be, if you are truthful?"﴾ ﴿Say: "Perhaps some of what you are hastening for has drawn close to you."﴾ ﴿Indeed your Lord is full of bounty toward people, but most of them do not give thanks.﴾ ﴿Indeed your Lord knows what their breasts conceal and what they disclose.﴾ ﴿And there is no hidden thing in the heaven or the earth but that it is in a clear Book.﴾ ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an relates to the Children of Israel most of that over which they differ.﴾ ﴿And indeed it is a guidance and a mercy for the believers.﴾ ﴿Indeed your Lord will judge between them by His judgment, and He is the Mighty, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿So rely upon Allah. Indeed, you are upon the clear truth.﴾ ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear, nor can you make the deaf hear the call when they turn away, retreating.﴾ ﴿Nor can you guide the blind out of their error. You will not make hear except those who believe in Our verses, so they are Muslims [submitting].﴾ ﴿And when the word befalls them, We will bring forth for them a creature from the earth which will speak to them, [saying] that people were not certain of Our signs.﴾

When the Most High had mentioned that He alone has knowledge of the unseen, and that among it is the time of the Hour, and that they have no awareness of its time, and that the disbelievers are in doubt about it and blind to it, it was fitting to mention their statements in denying it, and that what they were promised of it is not true; rather, it is only what the ancients wrote down, without any report of it being a reality.

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read ﴿أئِذا، أئِنّا﴾ [a'idhā, a'innā] with the two interrogatives combined, the second being changed to a yā' (ya). Abu 'Amr separated the two with an alif. 'Asim and Hamzah read both with two hamzas. Nafi' read ﴿إذا﴾ with a kasrah-marked hamzah, and ﴿آينّا﴾ with the interrogative hamzah, the second changed to a yā', with a madd between them. The rest read ﴿آئِذا﴾ with a prolonged interrogative, and ﴿إنّنا﴾ with two nūns without an interrogative. The governing element (al-'amil) of ﴿إذا﴾ is omitted, indicated by the meaning of the second clause; its estimated form is "will come out." It is impossible for ﴿لَمُخْرَجُونَ﴾ to govern it, because each of ''inna'' and the lam of initiation (lam al-ibtida') and the interrogative prevents what follows them from governing what precedes them, except the lam that falls in the predicate of ''inna'', for the complement of the predicate may precede it and the predicate, as established in the science of grammar (ʿilm al-naḥw).

﴿وآباؤنا﴾ [and our fathers] is coordinated with the subject of ''kāna'' (kāna's noun), and that separation by the predicate of ''kāna'' is permissible. The bringing forth here is from the graves, alive, with their spirits returned to their bodies. Combining the interrogative in ''idhā'' and in ''innā'' is a denial upon a denial, and an emphasis on the impossibility of that occurring. The pronoun in ''a'innā'' refers to them and to their fathers, because their becoming dust is inclusive of all of them. Then they mentioned that they had been promised this, they and their fathers, but none of this promised thing had come to pass; then they affirmed and restricted that it was among the fabrications of those who came before. Here the object of the promise, which is ''hādhā'' [this], is placed first, while in another verse it is placed later, according to the context in which the speech was delivered. Where the report about them concerning the denial of resurrection and the Hereafter was emphasized, they gave it priority by placing it first out of concern; and where that was not the case, they aimed at denying the bringing into existence of the one who is resurrected, so they placed that first and delayed the object of the promise.

Then He commanded His Prophet to tell them to travel through the earth. The discussion of this verse has preceded in the beginning of al-An'am. By "the criminals" he meant the disbelievers. Then He consoled His Prophet, saying: ﴿Do not grieve over them﴾, meaning, regarding their not having submitted or yielded to what you have brought. ﴿And do not be in distress﴾, meaning, in a hardship and a matter that is difficult for you, ﴿because of what they plot﴾, for their plotting returns upon them, not upon you, and Allah protects you from them. The reading ''ḍīq'' (ضِيقٍ) has been mentioned, with a kasrah and a fatḥah on the ḍād, and both are verbal nouns (maṣdar). Abu 'Ali (al-Farisi) disliked that the one with the fatḥah on the ḍād should be the original ''ḍayyiq'', with the yā' doubled, then lightened, like ''layn'' from ''layyin'', because that requires deleting the modified noun and setting the adjective in its place, and it is not among the adjectives that stand in for the modified noun in a regular manner. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that, saying: "It may also be intended as: in a narrow matter of their plotting."

When the Quraysh hastened [to ask] about the matter of the Hour, or about the punishment promised to them, and asked about the time of what was promised, mockingly, it was said to him: ﴿Say: "Perhaps some of it has drawn close to you."﴾ That is, it has followed you soon, and some of what you hastened for has become like a rider that follows you. This was the punishment of the Day of Badr. It was also said: the punishment of the grave. The majority read ''radifa'' (رَدِفَ) with a kasrah on the dāl. Ibn Hurmuz read it with a fatḥah, and both are dialects. Its original form is transitive, in the sense of "followed" and "overtook," so it may be understood as implying the intransitive meaning, and therefore Ibn 'Abbas and others interpreted it as ''azifa'' and ''qariba'' (drew near and approached), since what comes after a thing is near to it, within its meaning, or with an extension. The lam in its object serves to emphasize the arrival of the verb to it, as the ba' was added in ﴿and do not cast yourselves by your own hands [into destruction]﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:195], as al-Zamakhshari said. It has also been construed with ''min'' by way of implicit meaning (taḍmīn) for what is transitive with it. The poet said:

*"So when we followed closely upon ʿUmayr and his companions, they turned back swiftly, while death was driving them on."*

meaning, they approached ʿUmayr. It was also said: ''radifahu'' and ''radifa lahu'' are two dialects. It was also said: the verb is construed according to the verbal noun, meaning "the following for you." And ''baʿḍ'' [some] is according to the estimate of "the following of some of what you hasten for," and this involves a strain from which the Qur'an is to be exempted. It was also said: the lam in ''lakum'' is attached to the object for which (the causal), and the direct object is omitted, its estimate being: "He caused the creation to follow for your sake," and this is weak. It is also narrated that in every land a beast will emerge of the kind whose species is established on the earth, and that it is not one, so that His saying "dabbah" (a beast) is a generic noun (ism jins, a noun denoting a whole category). They differed concerning its nature, its form, the place of its emergence, the number of its emergences, the extent of what emerges from it, what it does to people, and what it emerges with, in a confused disagreement, some of it contradicting other parts and some of it refuting others; so we have set aside mention of it, because transmitting it is blackening paper with what is not authentic and wasting the time of its transmission.

The apparent reading of His saying ﴿tukallimuhum﴾ (speaks to them) is with the doubled letter (tashdid), which is the reading of the majority, from "kalam" (speech). This is supported by Ubayy's reading: tunabbi'uhum (informs them), and in some readings: tuhaddithuhum (tells them), which is the reading of Yahya ibn Sallam. **Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 27, verses 67–82 (part 1 of 2):**

(p. 94) ﴿The disbelievers say: "When we have become dust, and our fathers too, shall we really be brought forth?"﴾ ﴿"We and our fathers were certainly promised this before. This is nothing but the fables of the ancients."﴾ ﴿Say: "Travel through the earth and see what was the end of the criminals."﴾ ﴿Do not grieve over them, and do not be distressed by what they plot.﴾ ﴿They say: "When will this promise be, if you are truthful?"﴾ ﴿Say: "Perhaps some of what you are hastening for has drawn close to you."﴾ ﴿Indeed your Lord is full of bounty toward people, but most of them do not give thanks.﴾ ﴿Indeed your Lord knows what their breasts conceal and what they disclose.﴾ ﴿And there is no hidden thing in the heaven or the earth but that it is in a clear Book.﴾ ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an relates to the Children of Israel most of that over which they differ.﴾ ﴿And indeed it is a guidance and a mercy for the believers.﴾ ﴿Indeed your Lord will judge between them by His judgment, and He is the Mighty, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿So rely upon Allah. Indeed, you are upon the clear truth.﴾ ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear, nor can you make the deaf hear the call when they turn away, retreating.﴾ ﴿Nor can you guide the blind out of their error. You will not make hear except those who believe in Our verses, so they are Muslims [submitting].﴾ ﴿And when the word befalls them, We will bring forth for them a creature from the earth which will speak to them, [saying] that people were not certain of Our signs.﴾

When the Most High had mentioned that He alone has knowledge of the unseen, and that among it is the time of the Hour, and that they have no awareness of its time, and that the disbelievers are in doubt about it and blind to it, it was fitting to mention their statements in denying it, and that what they were promised of it is not true; rather, it is only what the ancients wrote down, without any report of it being a reality.

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read ﴿أئِذا، أئِنّا﴾ [a'idhā, a'innā] with the two interrogatives combined, the second being changed to a yā' (ya). Abu 'Amr separated the two with an alif. 'Asim and Hamzah read both with two hamzas. Nafi' read ﴿إذا﴾ with a kasrah-marked hamzah, and ﴿آينّا﴾ with the interrogative hamzah, the second changed to a yā', with a madd between them. The rest read ﴿آئِذا﴾ with a prolonged interrogative, and ﴿إنّنا﴾ with two nūns without an interrogative. The governing element (al-'amil) of ﴿إذا﴾ is omitted, indicated by the meaning of the second clause; its estimated form is "will come out." It is impossible for ﴿لَمُخْرَجُونَ﴾ to govern it, because each of ''inna'' and the lam of initiation (lam al-ibtida') and the interrogative prevents what follows them from governing what precedes them, except the lam that falls in the predicate of ''inna'', for the complement of the predicate may precede it and the predicate, as established in the science of grammar (ʿilm al-naḥw).

﴿وآباؤنا﴾ [and our fathers] is coordinated with the subject of ''kāna'' (kāna's noun), and that separation by the predicate of ''kāna'' is permissible. The bringing forth here is from the graves, alive, with their spirits returned to their bodies. Combining the interrogative in ''idhā'' and in ''innā'' is a denial upon a denial, and an emphasis on the impossibility of that occurring. The pronoun in ''a'innā'' refers to them and to their fathers, because their becoming dust is inclusive of all of them. Then they mentioned that they had been promised this, they and their fathers, but none of this promised thing had come to pass; then they affirmed and restricted that it was among the fabrications of those who came before. Here the object of the promise, which is ''hādhā'' [this], is placed first, while in another verse it is placed later, according to the context in which the speech was delivered. Where the report about them concerning the denial of resurrection and the Hereafter was emphasized, they gave it priority by placing it first out of concern; and where that was not the case, they aimed at denying the bringing into existence of the one who is resurrected, so they placed that first and delayed the object of the promise.

Then He commanded His Prophet to tell them to travel through the earth. The discussion of this verse has preceded in the beginning of al-An'am. By "the criminals" he meant the disbelievers. Then He consoled His Prophet, saying: ﴿Do not grieve over them﴾, meaning, regarding their not having submitted or yielded to what you have brought. ﴿And do not be in distress﴾, meaning, in a hardship and a matter that is difficult for you, ﴿because of what they plot﴾, for their plotting returns upon them, not upon you, and Allah protects you from them. The reading ''ḍīq'' (ضِيقٍ) has been mentioned, with a kasrah and a fatḥah on the ḍād, and both are verbal nouns (maṣdar). Abu 'Ali (al-Farisi) disliked that the one with the fatḥah on the ḍād should be the original ''ḍayyiq'', with the yā' doubled, then lightened, like ''layn'' from ''layyin'', because that requires deleting the modified noun and setting the adjective in its place, and it is not among the adjectives that stand in for the modified noun in a regular manner. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that, saying: "It may also be intended as: in a narrow matter of their plotting."

When the Quraysh hastened [to ask] about the matter of the Hour, or about the punishment promised to them, and asked about the time of what was promised, mockingly, it was said to him: ﴿Say: "Perhaps some of it has drawn close to you."﴾ That is, it has followed you soon, and some of what you hastened for has become like a rider that follows you. This was the punishment of the Day of Badr. It was also said: the punishment of the grave. The majority read ''radifa'' (رَدِفَ) with a kasrah on the dāl. Ibn Hurmuz read it with a fatḥah, and both are dialects. Its original form is transitive, in the sense of "followed" and "overtook," so it may be understood as implying the intransitive meaning, and therefore Ibn 'Abbas and others interpreted it as ''azifa'' and ''qariba'' (drew near and approached), since what comes after a thing is near to it, within its meaning, or with an extension. The lam in its object serves to emphasize the arrival of the verb to it, as the ba' was added in ﴿and do not cast yourselves by your own hands [into destruction]﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:195], as al-Zamakhshari said. It has also been construed with ''min'' by way of implicit meaning (taḍmīn) for what is transitive with it. The poet said:

*"So when we followed closely upon ʿUmayr and his companions, they turned back swiftly, while death was driving them on."*

meaning, they approached ʿUmayr. It was also said: ''radifahu'' and ''radifa lahu'' are two dialects. It was also said: the verb is construed according to the verbal noun, meaning "the following for you." And ''baʿḍ'' [some] is according to the estimate of "the following of some of what you hasten for," and this involves a strain from which the Qur'an is to be exempted. It was also said: the lam in ''lakum'' is attached to the object for which (the causal), and the direct object is omitted, its estimate being: "He caused the creation to follow for your sake," and this is weak. It was also said: the subject of ''radifa'' is a pronoun referring to the promise, then He said: ''lakum baʿḍu mā tastaʿjilūn'' [some of what you hasten for is for you], as a subject and predicate. This involves a disjointing of the speech and a departure from the apparent sense without any need that calls for it.

﴿Indeed, your Lord is full of bounty﴾, meaning, bounties upon them by delaying their punishment for their sins and their disbelief. The object of ''yashkurūn'' [they give thanks] is omitted, meaning: they do not thank Him for His blessings upon them; or ''lā yashkurūn'' means "they do not know the right of the blessing," and the absence of their knowledge of the blessing is expressed by the absence of what follows from knowing it, which is gratitude.

Then the Most High informed of the breadth of His knowledge, beginning with what concerns humankind, then generalizing to every hidden thing. He expressed it by ''ṣudūr'' [breasts/chests], which is the locus of the hearts, in which thought and reasoning reside, as He said: ﴿But it is the hearts within the breasts that go blind﴾ [al-Hajj 22:46], regarding the state within them, namely the hearts. He attributed the disclosure to their persons, because disclosure is among the actions of the limbs. Since what is concealed in the breast is what prompts what appears on the limbs, and the cause of its manifestation is that concealing precedes informing. The majority read ﴿ما تُكِنُّ﴾ [what they conceal], from ''akanna al-shay'' [he hid the thing]. Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd, and Ibn al-Sumayfa' read it with a fatḥah on the tā' and a ḍammah on the kāf, from ''kanna al-shay'' [he covered the thing]. The meaning: what they hide and what they disclose of enmity toward the Messenger and their schemes.

The apparent generality of His saying ''min ghā'ibah'' [any hidden thing] is: there is no thing in the utmost state of concealment and obscurity but that it is in a Book with Allah and in the hidden store of His knowledge. It was also said: what was hidden from them of the punishment of heaven and earth. It was also said: it is the Day of Resurrection and its terrors; this was reported by al-Hasan. The "Book" is the Preserved Tablet (al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ). It was also said: the deeds of the servants have been recorded in order that they be recompensed for them. The author of al-Ghunyan (Ṣāḥib al-Ghunyān) said: meaning, an incident that is hidden, or a calamity that befalls. Ibn 'Abbas said: meaning, there is no secret thing in the heavens and the earth, nor an open one, so he sufficed with mentioning the secret instead of its opposite. Al-Zamakhshari said: that which is hidden and concealed is called ''ghā'ibah'' [hidden] and ''khāfiyah'' [concealed], and the tā' in both is like its role in ''ʿāqibah'' [outcome] and ''ʿāfiyah'' [well-being], and their parallels are ''naṭīḥah'' [the gored animal], ''dhabīḥah'' [the slaughtered animal], and ''ramiyyah'' [the shot animal], in that they are nouns and not adjectives. It is permissible that these two be adjectives, and the tā' in them is for intensification, like the ''riwāyah'' [transmission] in their saying: "Woe to the poet for the evil of his transmission," as if he said: "there is no thing of extreme hiddenness and obscurity but that Allah knows it, encompasses it, and has recorded it in the Clear Tablet, which is manifest to whoever among the angels looks into it." End of quote.

When the Most High mentioned the origin and the return, He mentioned what pertains to prophethood, and the major basis for establishing the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ is the Qur'an. Among its miraculous qualities is its report of the narratives it contains, which agree with what is in the Torah and the Gospel, together with the knowledge that he was unlettered, who had not mixed with scholars nor occupied himself with teaching. The Children of Israel are the Jews and the Christians. It relates to them most of what they differed about, in its proper form, and clarifies it for them; had they been fair, they would have submitted. Among what they differed about is the matter of the Messiah: they formed factions concerning it; some said he is Allah, some said he is the son of Allah, some said he is the third of three, and some said he is a prophet like the other prophets. They held councils for this and diverged in their creeds, and they disputed about matters until some of them cursed others.

The apparent sense is the generality of the believers, and it was also said: it refers to those among the Children of Israel who believed. As for ''al-qaḍāʾ'' [judgment] and ''al-ḥukm'' [ruling]: although it becomes apparent that they are synonyms, it was said that what is meant here is justice, meaning, by His justice, because He judges only with justice. It was also said: what is meant by His wisdom (ḥikmah) is judgment. It was said: this is indicated by the reading of one who read ''biḥikamihi'' with a kasrah on the ḥā' and a fatḥah on the kāf, the plural of ''ḥikmah'', and that is the reading of Junāḥ ibn Jaysh. Since judgment requires the execution of what is judged and knowledge of what is ruled upon, these two attributes came after it, namely: the Mighty, that is, the Dominant, the Powerful, and the All-Knowing. Then the Most High commanded him to rely upon Him, and informed him that he is upon the clear truth that has no doubt in it. This is like a reasoning for trusting in Him, and in it is evidence that whoever is upon the truth is entitled to trust in Allah, for He will support him and not forsake him.

Since the Qur'an and what Allah related in it is hardly beneficial to them, the Most High informed about them that they are dead of heart, or they were likened to the dead, even though they were living with sound sight; for when it is recited to them their ears do not retain it, so their state, due to the lack of benefit from hearing, was like the state of the dead. The majority read ﴿ولا تَسْمَعُ الصُّمُّ﴾ [nor can the deaf hear] here and in al-Rūm with a ḍammah on the tā' and a kasrah on the mīm, with ''al-ṣummu'' in the nominative. Since the dead cannot hear, no complement was mentioned for him, but rather the causing to hear was negated, meaning: no causing of hearing from you can ever reach them, due to their lack of receptivity. As for the deaf person, he may at times be in a state in which he can be made to hear and can hear, so the complement of the verb, which is the call, was mentioned. The word ''idhā'' [when] governs ''tasmaʿu'' [you hear], and the negation of causing to hear or of hearing was restricted by this temporal clause and what follows it, for emphasis regarding the state of the deaf person; because when he turns away from the caller, retreating, he is further from perceiving his voice.

He likened them first to the dead, then to the deaf in a certain state, then to the blind, saying: ﴿Nor can you guide the blind﴾ [out of their error], since they lose the way, and no one can remove that from them and turn them into guided, seeing people except Allah, the Most High. The majority read ''bihādī al-ʿum'' [guide the blind] as an active participle with its object in the genitive; Yaḥyā ibn al-Ḥārith and Abū Ḥaywah read ''bihādin'' with tanwīn, and ''al-ʿumya'' [the blind] in the accusative; al-A'mash, Ṭalḥah, Ibn Wathhāb, Ibn Ya'mur, and Ḥamzah read ''tahdī'' [you guide], the present tense of ''hadā'', with ''al-ʿumya'' in the accusative; Ibn Mas'ūd read ''wa-mā anta tahtadī'', with ''an'' added after ''mā'', and ''yahtadī'' is the present of ''ihtadā'', and ''al-ʿumyu'' in the nominative. The meaning: it is not within your capacity to introduce guidance into the heart of one who is blind to the truth and has not looked at it with the eye of his heart.

﴿You will not make hear except those who believe in Our verses﴾, and they are those whom Allah knows will affirm His signs.

﴿So they are Muslims﴾, submitting to the truth. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Muslims" means sincere, from His saying: ﴿Yes, whoever submits his face to Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:112], meaning He made it wholly and purely for Allah. End of quote.

Abu 'Ali (al-Farisi) disliked that the one with the fatḥah on the ḍād should be the original ''ḍayyiq'', with the yā' doubled, then lightened, like ''layn'' from ''layyin'', because that requires deleting the modified noun and setting the adjective in its place, and it is not among the adjectives that stand in for the modified noun in a regular manner. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that, saying: "It may also be intended as: in a narrow matter of their plotting."

When the Quraysh hastened [to ask] about the matter of the Hour, or about the punishment promised to them, and asked about the time of what was promised, mockingly, it was said to him: ﴿Say: "Perhaps some of it has drawn close to you."﴾ That is, it has followed you soon, and some of what you hastened for has become like a rider that follows you. This was the punishment of the Day of Badr. It was also said: the punishment of the grave. The majority read ''radifa'' (رَدِفَ) with a kasrah on the dāl. Ibn Hurmuz read it with a fatḥah, and both are dialects. Its original form is transitive, in the sense of "followed" and "overtook," so it may be understood as implying the intransitive meaning, and therefore Ibn 'Abbas and others interpreted it as ''azifa'' and ''qariba'' (drew near and approached), since what comes after a thing is near to it, within its meaning, or with an extension. The lam in its object serves to emphasize the arrival of the verb to it, as the ba' was added in ﴿and do not cast yourselves by your own hands [into destruction]﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:195], as al-Zamakhshari said. It has also been construed with ''min'' by way of implicit meaning (taḍmīn) for what is transitive with it. The poet said:

*"So when we followed closely upon ʿUmayr and his companions, they turned back swiftly, while death was driving them on."*

meaning, they approached ʿUmayr. It was also said: ''radifahu'' and ''radifa lahu'' are two dialects. It was also said: the verb is construed according to the verbal noun, meaning "the following for you." And ''baʿḍ'' [some] is according to the estimate of "the following of some of what you hasten for," and this involves a strain from which the Qur'an is to be exempted. It was also said: the lam in ''lakum'' is attached to the object for which (the causal), and the direct object is omitted, its estimate being: "He caused the creation to follow for your sake," and this is weak. It was also said: the subject of ''radifa'' is a pronoun referring to the promise, then He said: ''lakum baʿḍu mā tastaʿjilūn'' [some of what you hasten for is for you], as a subject and predicate. This involves a disjointing of the speech and a departure from the apparent sense without any need that calls for it.

﴿Indeed, your Lord is full of bounty﴾, meaning, bounties upon them by delaying their punishment for their sins and their disbelief. The object of ''yashkurūn'' [they give thanks] is omitted, meaning: they do not thank Him for His blessings upon them; or ''lā yashkurūn'' means "they do not know the right of the blessing," and the absence of their knowledge of the blessing is expressed by the absence of what follows from knowing it, which is gratitude.

Then the Most High informed of the breadth of His knowledge, beginning with what concerns humankind, then generalizing to every hidden thing. He expressed it by ''ṣudūr'' [breasts/chests], which is the locus of the hearts, in which thought and reasoning reside, as He said: ﴿But it is the hearts within the breasts that go blind﴾ [al-Hajj 22:46], regarding the state within them, namely the hearts. He attributed the disclosure to their persons, because disclosure is among the actions of the limbs. Since what is concealed in the breast is what prompts what appears on the limbs, and the cause of its manifestation is that concealing precedes informing. The majority read ﴿ما تُكِنُّ﴾ [what they conceal], from ''akanna al-shay'' [he hid the thing]. Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd, and Ibn al-Sumayfa' read it with a fatḥah on the tā' and a ḍammah on the kāf, from ''kanna al-shay'' [he covered the thing]. The meaning: what they hide and what they disclose of enmity toward the Messenger and their schemes.

The apparent generality of His saying ''min ghā'ibah'' [any hidden thing] is: there is no thing in the utmost state of concealment and obscurity but that it is in a Book with Allah and in the hidden store of His knowledge. It was also said: what was hidden from them of the punishment of heaven and earth. It was also said: it is the Day of Resurrection and its terrors; this was reported by al-Hasan. The "Book" is the Preserved Tablet (al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ). It was also said: the deeds of the servants have been recorded in order that they be recompensed for them. The author of al-Ghunyan (Ṣāḥib al-Ghunyān) said: meaning, an incident that is hidden, or a calamity that befalls. Ibn 'Abbas said: meaning, there is no secret thing in the heavens and the earth, nor an open one, so he sufficed with mentioning the secret instead of its opposite. Al-Zamakhshari said: that which is hidden and concealed is called ''ghā'ibah'' [hidden] and ''khāfiyah'' [concealed], and the tā' in both is like its role in ''ʿāqibah'' [outcome] and ''ʿāfiyah'' [well-being], and their parallels are ''naṭīḥah'' [the gored animal], ''dhabīḥah'' [the slaughtered animal], and ''ramiyyah'' [the shot animal], in that they are nouns and not adjectives. It is permissible that these two be adjectives, and the tā' in them is for intensification, like the ''riwāyah'' [transmission] in their saying: "Woe to the poet for the evil of his transmission," as if he said: "there is no thing of extreme hiddenness and obscurity but that Allah knows it, encompasses it, and has recorded it in the Clear Tablet, which is manifest to whoever among the angels looks into it." End of quote.

It was also said: what is meant by His wisdom (ḥikmah) is judgment. Since the dead cannot hear, no complement was mentioned for him, but rather the causing to hear was negated, meaning: no causing of hearing from you can ever reach them, due to their lack of receptivity. As for the deaf person, he may at times be in a state in which he can be made to hear and can hear, so the complement of the verb, which is the call, was mentioned. The word ''idhā'' [when] governs ''tasmaʿu'' [you hear], and the negation of causing to hear or of hearing was restricted by this temporal clause and what follows it, for emphasis regarding the state of the deaf person; because when he turns away from the caller, retreating, he is further from perceiving his voice.

He likened them first to the dead, then to the deaf in a certain state, then to the blind, saying: ﴿Nor can you guide the blind﴾ [out of their error], since they lose the way, and no one can remove that from them and turn them into guided, seeing people except Allah, the Most High. The majority read ''bihādī al-ʿum'' [guide the blind] as an active participle with its object in the genitive; Yaḥyā ibn al-Ḥārith and Abū Ḥaywah read ''bihādin'' with tanwīn, and ''al-ʿumya'' [the blind] in the accusative; al-A'mash, Ṭalḥah, Ibn Wathhāb, Ibn Ya'mur, and Ḥamzah read ''tahdī'' [you guide], the present tense of ''hadā'', with ''al-ʿumya'' in the accusative; Ibn Mas'ūd read ''wa-mā anta tahtadī'', with ''an'' added after ''mā'', and ''yahtadī'' is the present of ''ihtadā'', and ''al-ʿumyu'' in the nominative. The meaning: it is not within your capacity to introduce guidance into the heart of one who is blind to the truth and has not looked at it with the eye of his heart.

﴿You will not make hear except those who believe in Our verses﴾, and they are those whom Allah knows will affirm His signs.

﴿So they are Muslims﴾, submitting to the truth. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Muslims" means sincere, from His saying: ﴿Yes, whoever submits his face to Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:112], meaning He made it wholly and purely for Allah. End of quote.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 27, verses 67–82 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And when the word comes due against them﴾, i.e., when the promise of their punishment, which the eternal decree from Allah contains, is fulfilled, as in His saying: ﴿the word of punishment has come due against the disbelievers﴾ [al-Zumar: 71]. The meaning is: when Allah wills to carry out upon the disbelievers the punishment that His prior knowledge concerning them determined, He will bring forth for them a beast (dabbah) that emerges from the earth. "Waqa'a" (came due, took place) is an expression for being established and necessary. As for "al-qawl" (the word), it is either by eliding a modifier, meaning "the content of the word," or the word "qawl" is used for "maqul" (what is said), since what is said is conveyed through speech, namely what they were promised of the Hour and the punishment. Ibn Mas'ud said: ﴿the word comes due against them﴾ happens through the death of the scholars, the departure of knowledge, and the lifting of the Qur'an. End. It is narrated that its emergence will be when goodness ceases, when no one is commanded to do right, when no one is forbidden from wrong, and when no one repentant or penitent remains. In a hadith: "That the beast and the rising of the sun from the west are among the first of the signs" (al-ashrat, the major portents), but it does not specify which is first. Likewise the Dajjal (the Antichrist). The apparent sense of the hadiths is that the rising of the sun is the last of them, and the apparent sense is that the beast that emerges is one. It is also narrated that in every land a beast will emerge of the kind whose species is established on the earth, and that it is not one, so that His saying "dabbah" (a beast) is a generic noun (ism jins, a noun denoting a whole category). They differed concerning its nature, its form, the place of its emergence, the number of its emergences, the extent of what emerges from it, what it does to people, and what it emerges with, in a confused disagreement, some of it contradicting other parts and some of it refuting others; so we have set aside mention of it, because transmitting it is blackening paper with what is not authentic and wasting the time of its transmission.

The apparent reading of His saying ﴿tukallimuhum﴾ (speaks to them) is with the doubled letter (tashdid), which is the reading of the majority, from "kalam" (speech). This is supported by Ubayy's reading: tunabbi'uhum (informs them), and in some readings: tuhaddithuhum (tells them), which is the reading of Yahya ibn Sallam. Abdullah's reading is: "bi-anna al-nas" (that the people). Al-Suddi said: it speaks to them about the falsehood of all religions except Islam. It is said: it addresses them, saying to the believer: "This is a believer," and to the disbeliever: "This is a disbeliever." It is also said that the meaning of "tukallimuhum" is: it wounds them, from "kalm" (wound), and the doubling is for intensity. This is supported by the reading of Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, Abu Zur'a, al-Jahdari, Abu Haywa, and Ibn Abi Abla: "tuklimuhum," with a fatha on the ta', a sukun on the kaf, and a light lam. Also the reading of one who read "tajrahuhum" (wounds them) in place of "tukallimuhum." Abu al-Hawra asked Ibn Abbas: "Does it say tukallimu or tuklimu?" He said: "It does all of that: it speaks to the believer and wounds the disbeliever." End. It is narrated that it brands the disbeliever on his forehead and darkens him, and wipes over the face of the believer so that it whitens him.

The Kufans and Zayd ibn Ali read "anna al-nas" with a fatha on the hamza, and Ibn Mas'ud read "bi-anna" (and this has been mentioned). The rest of the seven readers read "inna," with a kasra on the hamza. The kasra allows that it is part of Allah's speech, which is the apparent sense given His saying "bi-ayatina" (by Our signs), and it allows that it is part of the speech of the beast. This is narrated from Ibn Abbas. The kasra of "inna" here is according to the saying (al-qawl), either by supposing an implied "qal" (said), or by treating "tukallimuhum" as if it were "taqulu lahum" (says to them). His saying ﴿bi-ayatina﴾ (by Our signs) is either by eliding a modifier, or because they are particular to Allah, as when some intimates of a king say: "our horses and our lands." On the reading with the fatha, the estimate is "bi-anna" like the reading of Abdullah. The apparent sense is that it is connected to "tukallimuhum," meaning: it addresses them with this speech. It is permissible that the ba' (bi), whether pronounced or implied, is causal, meaning: it addresses them or wounds them because of their failure to have certainty in Our signs.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 27, verses 67–82 (part 1 of 2):**

(p. 94) ﴿The disbelievers say: "When we have become dust, and our fathers too, shall we really be brought forth?"﴾ ﴿"We and our fathers were certainly promised this before. This is nothing but the fables of the ancients."﴾ ﴿Say: "Travel through the earth and see what was the end of the criminals."﴾ ﴿Do not grieve over them, and do not be distressed by what they plot.﴾ ﴿They say: "When will this promise be, if you are truthful?"﴾ ﴿Say: "Perhaps some of what you are hastening for has drawn close to you."﴾ ﴿Indeed your Lord is full of bounty toward people, but most of them do not give thanks.﴾ ﴿Indeed your Lord knows what their breasts conceal and what they disclose.﴾ ﴿And there is no hidden thing in the heaven or the earth but that it is in a clear Book.﴾ ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an relates to the Children of Israel most of that over which they differ.﴾ ﴿And indeed it is a guidance and a mercy for the believers.﴾ ﴿Indeed your Lord will judge between them by His judgment, and He is the Mighty, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿So rely upon Allah. Indeed, you are upon the clear truth.﴾ ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear, nor can you make the deaf hear the call when they turn away, retreating.﴾ ﴿Nor can you guide the blind out of their error. You will not make hear except those who believe in Our verses, so they are Muslims [submitting].﴾ ﴿And when the word befalls them, We will bring forth for them a creature from the earth which will speak to them, [saying] that people were not certain of Our signs.﴾

'Asim and Hamzah read both with two hamzas. Nafi' read ﴿إذا﴾ with a kasrah-marked hamzah, and ﴿آينّا﴾ with the interrogative hamzah, the second changed to a yā', with a madd between them. The majority read ﴿ولا تَسْمَعُ الصُّمُّ﴾ [nor can the deaf hear] here and in al-Rūm with a ḍammah on the tā' and a kasrah on the mīm, with ''al-ṣummu'' in the nominative. Since the dead cannot hear, no complement was mentioned for him, but rather the causing to hear was negated, meaning: no causing of hearing from you can ever reach them, due to their lack of receptivity. As for the deaf person, he may at times be in a state in which he can be made to hear and can hear, so the complement of the verb, which is the call, was mentioned. The word ''idhā'' [when] governs ''tasmaʿu'' [you hear], and the negation of causing to hear or of hearing was restricted by this temporal clause and what follows it, for emphasis regarding the state of the deaf person; because when he turns away from the caller, retreating, he is further from perceiving his voice.

He likened them first to the dead, then to the deaf in a certain state, then to the blind, saying: ﴿Nor can you guide the blind﴾ [out of their error], since they lose the way, and no one can remove that from them and turn them into guided, seeing people except Allah, the Most High. The majority read ''bihādī al-ʿum'' [guide the blind] as an active participle with its object in the genitive; Yaḥyā ibn al-Ḥārith and Abū Ḥaywah read ''bihādin'' with tanwīn, and ''al-ʿumya'' [the blind] in the accusative; al-A'mash, Ṭalḥah, Ibn Wathhāb, Ibn Ya'mur, and Ḥamzah read ''tahdī'' [you guide], the present tense of ''hadā'', with ''al-ʿumya'' in the accusative; Ibn Mas'ūd read ''wa-mā anta tahtadī'', with ''an'' added after ''mā'', and ''yahtadī'' is the present of ''ihtadā'', and ''al-ʿumyu'' in the nominative. The meaning: it is not within your capacity to introduce guidance into the heart of one who is blind to the truth and has not looked at it with the eye of his heart.

﴿You will not make hear except those who believe in Our verses﴾, and they are those whom Allah knows will affirm His signs.

﴿So they are Muslims﴾, submitting to the truth. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Muslims" means sincere, from His saying: ﴿Yes, whoever submits his face to Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:112], meaning He made it wholly and purely for Allah. End of quote.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 27, verses 67–82 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And when the word comes due against them﴾, i.e., when the promise of their punishment, which the eternal decree from Allah contains, is fulfilled, as in His saying: ﴿the word of punishment has come due against the disbelievers﴾ [al-Zumar: 71]. The meaning is: when Allah wills to carry out upon the disbelievers the punishment that His prior knowledge concerning them determined, He will bring forth for them a beast (dabbah) that emerges from the earth. "Waqa'a" (came due, took place) is an expression for being established and necessary. As for "al-qawl" (the word), it is either by eliding a modifier, meaning "the content of the word," or the word "qawl" is used for "maqul" (what is said), since what is said is conveyed through speech, namely what they were promised of the Hour and the punishment. Ibn Mas'ud said: ﴿the word comes due against them﴾ happens through the death of the scholars, the departure of knowledge, and the lifting of the Qur'an. End. It is narrated that its emergence will be when goodness ceases, when no one is commanded to do right, when no one is forbidden from wrong, and when no one repentant or penitent remains. In a hadith: "That the beast and the rising of the sun from the west are among the first of the signs" (al-ashrat, the major portents), but it does not specify which is first. Likewise the Dajjal (the Antichrist). The apparent sense of the hadiths is that the rising of the sun is the last of them, and the apparent sense is that the beast that emerges is one. It is also narrated that in every land a beast will emerge of the kind whose species is established on the earth, and that it is not one, so that His saying "dabbah" (a beast) is a generic noun (ism jins, a noun denoting a whole category). They differed concerning its nature, its form, the place of its emergence, the number of its emergences, the extent of what emerges from it, what it does to people, and what it emerges with, in a confused disagreement, some of it contradicting other parts and some of it refuting others; so we have set aside mention of it, because transmitting it is blackening paper with what is not authentic and wasting the time of its transmission.

The apparent reading of His saying ﴿tukallimuhum﴾ (speaks to them) is with the doubled letter (tashdid), which is the reading of the majority, from "kalam" (speech). This is supported by Ubayy's reading: tunabbi'uhum (informs them), and in some readings: tuhaddithuhum (tells them), which is the reading of Yahya ibn Sallam. Abdullah's reading is: "bi-anna al-nas" (that the people). Al-Suddi said: it speaks to them about the falsehood of all religions except Islam. It is said: it addresses them, saying to the believer: "This is a believer," and to the disbeliever: "This is a disbeliever." It is also said that the meaning of "tukallimuhum" is: it wounds them, from "kalm" (wound), and the doubling is for intensity. This is supported by the reading of Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, Abu Zur'a, al-Jahdari, Abu Haywa, and Ibn Abi Abla: "tuklimuhum," with a fatha on the ta', a sukun on the kaf, and a light lam. Also the reading of one who read "tajrahuhum" (wounds them) in place of "tukallimuhum." Abu al-Hawra asked Ibn Abbas: "Does it say tukallimu or tuklimu?" He said: "It does all of that: it speaks to the believer and wounds the disbeliever." End. It is narrated that it brands the disbeliever on his forehead and darkens him, and wipes over the face of the believer so that it whitens him.

The Kufans and Zayd ibn Ali read "anna al-nas" with a fatha on the hamza, and Ibn Mas'ud read "bi-anna" (and this has been mentioned). The rest of the seven readers read "inna," with a kasra on the hamza. The kasra allows that it is part of Allah's speech, which is the apparent sense given His saying "bi-ayatina" (by Our signs), and it allows that it is part of the speech of the beast. On the reading with the fatha, the estimate is "bi-anna" like the reading of Abdullah. The apparent sense is that it is connected to "tukallimuhum," meaning: it addresses them with this speech.
