**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 27, verses 67–82 (part 1 of 2):**

(p. 94) ﴿The disbelievers say: "When we have become dust, and our fathers too, shall we really be brought forth?"﴾ ﴿"We and our fathers were certainly promised this before. This is nothing but the fables of the ancients."﴾ ﴿Say: "Travel through the earth and see what was the end of the criminals."﴾ ﴿Do not grieve over them, and do not be distressed by what they plot.﴾ ﴿They say: "When will this promise be, if you are truthful?"﴾ ﴿Say: "Perhaps some of what you are hastening for has drawn close to you."﴾ ﴿Indeed your Lord is full of bounty toward people, but most of them do not give thanks.﴾ ﴿Indeed your Lord knows what their breasts conceal and what they disclose.﴾ ﴿And there is no hidden thing in the heaven or the earth but that it is in a clear Book.﴾ ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an relates to the Children of Israel most of that over which they differ.﴾ ﴿And indeed it is a guidance and a mercy for the believers.﴾ ﴿Indeed your Lord will judge between them by His judgment, and He is the Mighty, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿So rely upon Allah. Indeed, you are upon the clear truth.﴾ ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear, nor can you make the deaf hear the call when they turn away, retreating.﴾ ﴿Nor can you guide the blind out of their error. You will not make hear except those who believe in Our verses, so they are Muslims [submitting].﴾ ﴿And when the word befalls them, We will bring forth for them a creature from the earth which will speak to them, [saying] that people were not certain of Our signs.﴾

When the Most High had mentioned that He alone has knowledge of the unseen, and that among it is the time of the Hour, and that they have no awareness of its time, and that the disbelievers are in doubt about it and blind to it, it was fitting to mention their statements in denying it, and that what they were promised of it is not true; rather, it is only what the ancients wrote down, without any report of it being a reality.

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read ﴿أئِذا، أئِنّا﴾ [a'idhā, a'innā] with the two interrogatives combined, the second being changed to a yā' (ya). Abu 'Amr separated the two with an alif. 'Asim and Hamzah read both with two hamzas. Nafi' read ﴿إذا﴾ with a kasrah-marked hamzah, and ﴿آينّا﴾ with the interrogative hamzah, the second changed to a yā', with a madd between them. The rest read ﴿آئِذا﴾ with a prolonged interrogative, and ﴿إنّنا﴾ with two nūns without an interrogative. The governing element (al-'amil) of ﴿إذا﴾ is omitted, indicated by the meaning of the second clause; its estimated form is "will come out." It is impossible for ﴿لَمُخْرَجُونَ﴾ to govern it, because each of ''inna'' and the lam of initiation (lam al-ibtida') and the interrogative prevents what follows them from governing what precedes them, except the lam that falls in the predicate of ''inna'', for the complement of the predicate may precede it and the predicate, as established in the science of grammar (ʿilm al-naḥw).

﴿وآباؤنا﴾ [and our fathers] is coordinated with the subject of ''kāna'' (kāna's noun), and that separation by the predicate of ''kāna'' is permissible. The bringing forth here is from the graves, alive, with their spirits returned to their bodies. Combining the interrogative in ''idhā'' and in ''innā'' is a denial upon a denial, and an emphasis on the impossibility of that occurring. The pronoun in ''a'innā'' refers to them and to their fathers, because their becoming dust is inclusive of all of them. Then they mentioned that they had been promised this, they and their fathers, but none of this promised thing had come to pass; then they affirmed and restricted that it was among the fabrications of those who came before. Here the object of the promise, which is ''hādhā'' [this], is placed first, while in another verse it is placed later, according to the context in which the speech was delivered. Where the report about them concerning the denial of resurrection and the Hereafter was emphasized, they gave it priority by placing it first out of concern; and where that was not the case, they aimed at denying the bringing into existence of the one who is resurrected, so they placed that first and delayed the object of the promise.

Then He commanded His Prophet to tell them to travel through the earth. The discussion of this verse has preceded in the beginning of al-An'am. By "the criminals" he meant the disbelievers. Then He consoled His Prophet, saying: ﴿Do not grieve over them﴾, meaning, regarding their not having submitted or yielded to what you have brought. ﴿And do not be in distress﴾, meaning, in a hardship and a matter that is difficult for you, ﴿because of what they plot﴾, for their plotting returns upon them, not upon you, and Allah protects you from them. The reading ''ḍīq'' (ضِيقٍ) has been mentioned, with a kasrah and a fatḥah on the ḍād, and both are verbal nouns (maṣdar). Abu 'Ali (al-Farisi) disliked that the one with the fatḥah on the ḍād should be the original ''ḍayyiq'', with the yā' doubled, then lightened, like ''layn'' from ''layyin'', because that requires deleting the modified noun and setting the adjective in its place, and it is not among the adjectives that stand in for the modified noun in a regular manner. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that, saying: "It may also be intended as: in a narrow matter of their plotting."

When the Quraysh hastened [to ask] about the matter of the Hour, or about the punishment promised to them, and asked about the time of what was promised, mockingly, it was said to him: ﴿Say: "Perhaps some of it has drawn close to you."﴾ That is, it has followed you soon, and some of what you hastened for has become like a rider that follows you. This was the punishment of the Day of Badr. It was also said: the punishment of the grave. The majority read ''radifa'' (رَدِفَ) with a kasrah on the dāl. Ibn Hurmuz read it with a fatḥah, and both are dialects. Its original form is transitive, in the sense of "followed" and "overtook," so it may be understood as implying the intransitive meaning, and therefore Ibn 'Abbas and others interpreted it as ''azifa'' and ''qariba'' (drew near and approached), since what comes after a thing is near to it, within its meaning, or with an extension. The lam in its object serves to emphasize the arrival of the verb to it, as the ba' was added in ﴿and do not cast yourselves by your own hands [into destruction]﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:195], as al-Zamakhshari said. It has also been construed with ''min'' by way of implicit meaning (taḍmīn) for what is transitive with it. The poet said:

*"So when we followed closely upon ʿUmayr and his companions, they turned back swiftly, while death was driving them on."*

meaning, they approached ʿUmayr. It was also said: ''radifahu'' and ''radifa lahu'' are two dialects. It was also said: the verb is construed according to the verbal noun, meaning "the following for you." And ''baʿḍ'' [some] is according to the estimate of "the following of some of what you hasten for," and this involves a strain from which the Qur'an is to be exempted. It was also said: the lam in ''lakum'' is attached to the object for which (the causal), and the direct object is omitted, its estimate being: "He caused the creation to follow for your sake," and this is weak. It was also said: the subject of ''radifa'' is a pronoun referring to the promise, then He said: ''lakum baʿḍu mā tastaʿjilūn'' [some of what you hasten for is for you], as a subject and predicate. This involves a disjointing of the speech and a departure from the apparent sense without any need that calls for it.

﴿Indeed, your Lord is full of bounty﴾, meaning, bounties upon them by delaying their punishment for their sins and their disbelief. The object of ''yashkurūn'' [they give thanks] is omitted, meaning: they do not thank Him for His blessings upon them; or ''lā yashkurūn'' means "they do not know the right of the blessing," and the absence of their knowledge of the blessing is expressed by the absence of what follows from knowing it, which is gratitude.

Then the Most High informed of the breadth of His knowledge, beginning with what concerns humankind, then generalizing to every hidden thing. He expressed it by ''ṣudūr'' [breasts/chests], which is the locus of the hearts, in which thought and reasoning reside, as He said: ﴿But it is the hearts within the breasts that go blind﴾ [al-Hajj 22:46], regarding the state within them, namely the hearts. He attributed the disclosure to their persons, because disclosure is among the actions of the limbs. Since what is concealed in the breast is what prompts what appears on the limbs, and the cause of its manifestation is that concealing precedes informing. The majority read ﴿ما تُكِنُّ﴾ [what they conceal], from ''akanna al-shay'' [he hid the thing]. Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd, and Ibn al-Sumayfa' read it with a fatḥah on the tā' and a ḍammah on the kāf, from ''kanna al-shay'' [he covered the thing]. The meaning: what they hide and what they disclose of enmity toward the Messenger and their schemes.

The apparent generality of His saying ''min ghā'ibah'' [any hidden thing] is: there is no thing in the utmost state of concealment and obscurity but that it is in a Book with Allah and in the hidden store of His knowledge. It was also said: what was hidden from them of the punishment of heaven and earth. It was also said: it is the Day of Resurrection and its terrors; this was reported by al-Hasan. The "Book" is the Preserved Tablet (al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ). It was also said: the deeds of the servants have been recorded in order that they be recompensed for them. The author of al-Ghunyan (Ṣāḥib al-Ghunyān) said: meaning, an incident that is hidden, or a calamity that befalls. Ibn 'Abbas said: meaning, there is no secret thing in the heavens and the earth, nor an open one, so he sufficed with mentioning the secret instead of its opposite. Al-Zamakhshari said: that which is hidden and concealed is called ''ghā'ibah'' [hidden] and ''khāfiyah'' [concealed], and the tā' in both is like its role in ''ʿāqibah'' [outcome] and ''ʿāfiyah'' [well-being], and their parallels are ''naṭīḥah'' [the gored animal], ''dhabīḥah'' [the slaughtered animal], and ''ramiyyah'' [the shot animal], in that they are nouns and not adjectives. It is permissible that these two be adjectives, and the tā' in them is for intensification, like the ''riwāyah'' [transmission] in their saying: "Woe to the poet for the evil of his transmission," as if he said: "there is no thing of extreme hiddenness and obscurity but that Allah knows it, encompasses it, and has recorded it in the Clear Tablet, which is manifest to whoever among the angels looks into it." End of quote.

When the Most High mentioned the origin and the return, He mentioned what pertains to prophethood, and the major basis for establishing the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ is the Qur'an. Among its miraculous qualities is its report of the narratives it contains, which agree with what is in the Torah and the Gospel, together with the knowledge that he was unlettered, who had not mixed with scholars nor occupied himself with teaching. The Children of Israel are the Jews and the Christians. It relates to them most of what they differed about, in its proper form, and clarifies it for them; had they been fair, they would have submitted. Among what they differed about is the matter of the Messiah: they formed factions concerning it; some said he is Allah, some said he is the son of Allah, some said he is the third of three, and some said he is a prophet like the other prophets. They held councils for this and diverged in their creeds, and they disputed about matters until some of them cursed others.

The apparent sense is the generality of the believers, and it was also said: it refers to those among the Children of Israel who believed. As for ''al-qaḍāʾ'' [judgment] and ''al-ḥukm'' [ruling]: although it becomes apparent that they are synonyms, it was said that what is meant here is justice, meaning, by His justice, because He judges only with justice. It was also said: what is meant by His wisdom (ḥikmah) is judgment. It was said: this is indicated by the reading of one who read ''biḥikamihi'' with a kasrah on the ḥā' and a fatḥah on the kāf, the plural of ''ḥikmah'', and that is the reading of Junāḥ ibn Jaysh. Since judgment requires the execution of what is judged and knowledge of what is ruled upon, these two attributes came after it, namely: the Mighty, that is, the Dominant, the Powerful, and the All-Knowing. **Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 27, verses 67–82 (part 1 of 2):**

(p. 94) ﴿The disbelievers say: "When we have become dust, and our fathers too, shall we really be brought forth?"﴾ ﴿"We and our fathers were certainly promised this before. This is nothing but the fables of the ancients."﴾ ﴿Say: "Travel through the earth and see what was the end of the criminals."﴾ ﴿Do not grieve over them, and do not be distressed by what they plot.﴾ ﴿They say: "When will this promise be, if you are truthful?"﴾ ﴿Say: "Perhaps some of what you are hastening for has drawn close to you."﴾ ﴿Indeed your Lord is full of bounty toward people, but most of them do not give thanks.﴾ ﴿Indeed your Lord knows what their breasts conceal and what they disclose.﴾ ﴿And there is no hidden thing in the heaven or the earth but that it is in a clear Book.﴾ ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an relates to the Children of Israel most of that over which they differ.﴾ ﴿And indeed it is a guidance and a mercy for the believers.﴾ ﴿Indeed your Lord will judge between them by His judgment, and He is the Mighty, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿So rely upon Allah. Indeed, you are upon the clear truth.﴾ ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear, nor can you make the deaf hear the call when they turn away, retreating.﴾ ﴿Nor can you guide the blind out of their error. You will not make hear except those who believe in Our verses, so they are Muslims [submitting].﴾ ﴿And when the word befalls them, We will bring forth for them a creature from the earth which will speak to them, [saying] that people were not certain of Our signs.﴾

When the Most High had mentioned that He alone has knowledge of the unseen, and that among it is the time of the Hour, and that they have no awareness of its time, and that the disbelievers are in doubt about it and blind to it, it was fitting to mention their statements in denying it, and that what they were promised of it is not true; rather, it is only what the ancients wrote down, without any report of it being a reality.

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read ﴿أئِذا، أئِنّا﴾ [a'idhā, a'innā] with the two interrogatives combined, the second being changed to a yā' (ya). Abu 'Amr separated the two with an alif. 'Asim and Hamzah read both with two hamzas. Nafi' read ﴿إذا﴾ with a kasrah-marked hamzah, and ﴿آينّا﴾ with the interrogative hamzah, the second changed to a yā', with a madd between them. The rest read ﴿آئِذا﴾ with a prolonged interrogative, and ﴿إنّنا﴾ with two nūns without an interrogative. The governing element (al-'amil) of ﴿إذا﴾ is omitted, indicated by the meaning of the second clause; its estimated form is "will come out." It is impossible for ﴿لَمُخْرَجُونَ﴾ to govern it, because each of ''inna'' and the lam of initiation (lam al-ibtida') and the interrogative prevents what follows them from governing what precedes them, except the lam that falls in the predicate of ''inna'', for the complement of the predicate may precede it and the predicate, as established in the science of grammar (ʿilm al-naḥw).

﴿وآباؤنا﴾ [and our fathers] is coordinated with the subject of ''kāna'' (kāna's noun), and that separation by the predicate of ''kāna'' is permissible. The bringing forth here is from the graves, alive, with their spirits returned to their bodies. Combining the interrogative in ''idhā'' and in ''innā'' is a denial upon a denial, and an emphasis on the impossibility of that occurring. The pronoun in ''a'innā'' refers to them and to their fathers, because their becoming dust is inclusive of all of them. Then they mentioned that they had been promised this, they and their fathers, but none of this promised thing had come to pass; then they affirmed and restricted that it was among the fabrications of those who came before. Here the object of the promise, which is ''hādhā'' [this], is placed first, while in another verse it is placed later, according to the context in which the speech was delivered. Where the report about them concerning the denial of resurrection and the Hereafter was emphasized, they gave it priority by placing it first out of concern; and where that was not the case, they aimed at denying the bringing into existence of the one who is resurrected, so they placed that first and delayed the object of the promise.

Then He commanded His Prophet to tell them to travel through the earth. The discussion of this verse has preceded in the beginning of al-An'am. By "the criminals" he meant the disbelievers. Then He consoled His Prophet, saying: ﴿Do not grieve over them﴾, meaning, regarding their not having submitted or yielded to what you have brought. ﴿And do not be in distress﴾, meaning, in a hardship and a matter that is difficult for you, ﴿because of what they plot﴾, for their plotting returns upon them, not upon you, and Allah protects you from them. The reading ''ḍīq'' (ضِيقٍ) has been mentioned, with a kasrah and a fatḥah on the ḍād, and both are verbal nouns (maṣdar). Abu 'Ali (al-Farisi) disliked that the one with the fatḥah on the ḍād should be the original ''ḍayyiq'', with the yā' doubled, then lightened, like ''layn'' from ''layyin'', because that requires deleting the modified noun and setting the adjective in its place, and it is not among the adjectives that stand in for the modified noun in a regular manner. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that, saying: "It may also be intended as: in a narrow matter of their plotting."

When the Quraysh hastened [to ask] about the matter of the Hour, or about the punishment promised to them, and asked about the time of what was promised, mockingly, it was said to him: ﴿Say: "Perhaps some of it has drawn close to you."﴾ That is, it has followed you soon, and some of what you hastened for has become like a rider that follows you. This was the punishment of the Day of Badr. It was also said: the punishment of the grave. The majority read ''radifa'' (رَدِفَ) with a kasrah on the dāl. Ibn Hurmuz read it with a fatḥah, and both are dialects. Its original form is transitive, in the sense of "followed" and "overtook," so it may be understood as implying the intransitive meaning, and therefore Ibn 'Abbas and others interpreted it as ''azifa'' and ''qariba'' (drew near and approached), since what comes after a thing is near to it, within its meaning, or with an extension. The lam in its object serves to emphasize the arrival of the verb to it, as the ba' was added in ﴿and do not cast yourselves by your own hands [into destruction]﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:195], as al-Zamakhshari said. It has also been construed with ''min'' by way of implicit meaning (taḍmīn) for what is transitive with it. The poet said:

*"So when we followed closely upon ʿUmayr and his companions, they turned back swiftly, while death was driving them on."*

meaning, they approached ʿUmayr. It was also said: ''radifahu'' and ''radifa lahu'' are two dialects. It was also said: the verb is construed according to the verbal noun, meaning "the following for you." And ''baʿḍ'' [some] is according to the estimate of "the following of some of what you hasten for," and this involves a strain from which the Qur'an is to be exempted. It was also said: the lam in ''lakum'' is attached to the object for which (the causal), and the direct object is omitted, its estimate being: "He caused the creation to follow for your sake," and this is weak. It was also said: the subject of ''radifa'' is a pronoun referring to the promise, then He said: ''lakum baʿḍu mā tastaʿjilūn'' [some of what you hasten for is for you], as a subject and predicate. This involves a disjointing of the speech and a departure from the apparent sense without any need that calls for it.

﴿Indeed, your Lord is full of bounty﴾, meaning, bounties upon them by delaying their punishment for their sins and their disbelief. The object of ''yashkurūn'' [they give thanks] is omitted, meaning: they do not thank Him for His blessings upon them; or ''lā yashkurūn'' means "they do not know the right of the blessing," and the absence of their knowledge of the blessing is expressed by the absence of what follows from knowing it, which is gratitude.

Then the Most High informed of the breadth of His knowledge, beginning with what concerns humankind, then generalizing to every hidden thing. He expressed it by ''ṣudūr'' [breasts/chests], which is the locus of the hearts, in which thought and reasoning reside, as He said: ﴿But it is the hearts within the breasts that go blind﴾ [al-Hajj 22:46], regarding the state within them, namely the hearts. He attributed the disclosure to their persons, because disclosure is among the actions of the limbs. Since what is concealed in the breast is what prompts what appears on the limbs, and the cause of its manifestation is that concealing precedes informing. The majority read ﴿ما تُكِنُّ﴾ [what they conceal], from ''akanna al-shay'' [he hid the thing]. Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd, and Ibn al-Sumayfa' read it with a fatḥah on the tā' and a ḍammah on the kāf, from ''kanna al-shay'' [he covered the thing]. The meaning: what they hide and what they disclose of enmity toward the Messenger and their schemes.

The apparent generality of His saying ''min ghā'ibah'' [any hidden thing] is: there is no thing in the utmost state of concealment and obscurity but that it is in a Book with Allah and in the hidden store of His knowledge. It was also said: what was hidden from them of the punishment of heaven and earth. It was also said: it is the Day of Resurrection and its terrors; this was reported by al-Hasan. The "Book" is the Preserved Tablet (al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ). It was also said: the deeds of the servants have been recorded in order that they be recompensed for them. The author of al-Ghunyan (Ṣāḥib al-Ghunyān) said: meaning, an incident that is hidden, or a calamity that befalls. Ibn 'Abbas said: meaning, there is no secret thing in the heavens and the earth, nor an open one, so he sufficed with mentioning the secret instead of its opposite. Al-Zamakhshari said: that which is hidden and concealed is called ''ghā'ibah'' [hidden] and ''khāfiyah'' [concealed], and the tā' in both is like its role in ''ʿāqibah'' [outcome] and ''ʿāfiyah'' [well-being], and their parallels are ''naṭīḥah'' [the gored animal], ''dhabīḥah'' [the slaughtered animal], and ''ramiyyah'' [the shot animal], in that they are nouns and not adjectives. It is permissible that these two be adjectives, and the tā' in them is for intensification, like the ''riwāyah'' [transmission] in their saying: "Woe to the poet for the evil of his transmission," as if he said: "there is no thing of extreme hiddenness and obscurity but that Allah knows it, encompasses it, and has recorded it in the Clear Tablet, which is manifest to whoever among the angels looks into it." End of quote.

When the Most High mentioned the origin and the return, He mentioned what pertains to prophethood, and the major basis for establishing the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ is the Qur'an. Among its miraculous qualities is its report of the narratives it contains, which agree with what is in the Torah and the Gospel, together with the knowledge that he was unlettered, who had not mixed with scholars nor occupied himself with teaching. The Children of Israel are the Jews and the Christians. It relates to them most of what they differed about, in its proper form, and clarifies it for them; had they been fair, they would have submitted. Among what they differed about is the matter of the Messiah: they formed factions concerning it; some said he is Allah, some said he is the son of Allah, some said he is the third of three, and some said he is a prophet like the other prophets. They held councils for this and diverged in their creeds, and they disputed about matters until some of them cursed others.

The apparent sense is the generality of the believers, and it was also said: it refers to those among the Children of Israel who believed. As for ''al-qaḍāʾ'' [judgment] and ''al-ḥukm'' [ruling]: although it becomes apparent that they are synonyms, it was said that what is meant here is justice, meaning, by His justice, because He judges only with justice. It was also said: what is meant by His wisdom (ḥikmah) is judgment. It was said: this is indicated by the reading of one who read ''biḥikamihi'' with a kasrah on the ḥā' and a fatḥah on the kāf, the plural of ''ḥikmah'', and that is the reading of Junāḥ ibn Jaysh. Since judgment requires the execution of what is judged and knowledge of what is ruled upon, these two attributes came after it, namely: the Mighty, that is, the Dominant, the Powerful, and the All-Knowing. Then the Most High commanded him to rely upon Him, and informed him that he is upon the clear truth that has no doubt in it. This is like a reasoning for trusting in Him, and in it is evidence that whoever is upon the truth is entitled to trust in Allah, for He will support him and not forsake him.

Since the Qur'an and what Allah related in it is hardly beneficial to them, the Most High informed about them that they are dead of heart, or they were likened to the dead, even though they were living with sound sight; for when it is recited to them their ears do not retain it, so their state, due to the lack of benefit from hearing, was like the state of the dead. The majority read ﴿ولا تَسْمَعُ الصُّمُّ﴾ [nor can the deaf hear] here and in al-Rūm with a ḍammah on the tā' and a kasrah on the mīm, with ''al-ṣummu'' in the nominative. Since the dead cannot hear, no complement was mentioned for him, but rather the causing to hear was negated, meaning: no causing of hearing from you can ever reach them, due to their lack of receptivity. As for the deaf person, he may at times be in a state in which he can be made to hear and can hear, so the complement of the verb, which is the call, was mentioned. The word ''idhā'' [when] governs ''tasmaʿu'' [you hear], and the negation of causing to hear or of hearing was restricted by this temporal clause and what follows it, for emphasis regarding the state of the deaf person; because when he turns away from the caller, retreating, he is further from perceiving his voice.

He likened them first to the dead, then to the deaf in a certain state, then to the blind, saying: ﴿Nor can you guide the blind﴾ [out of their error], since they lose the way, and no one can remove that from them and turn them into guided, seeing people except Allah, the Most High. The majority read ''bihādī al-ʿum'' [guide the blind] as an active participle with its object in the genitive; Yaḥyā ibn al-Ḥārith and Abū Ḥaywah read ''bihādin'' with tanwīn, and ''al-ʿumya'' [the blind] in the accusative; al-A'mash, Ṭalḥah, Ibn Wathhāb, Ibn Ya'mur, and Ḥamzah read ''tahdī'' [you guide], the present tense of ''hadā'', with ''al-ʿumya'' in the accusative; Ibn Mas'ūd read ''wa-mā anta tahtadī'', with ''an'' added after ''mā'', and ''yahtadī'' is the present of ''ihtadā'', and ''al-ʿumyu'' in the nominative. The meaning: it is not within your capacity to introduce guidance into the heart of one who is blind to the truth and has not looked at it with the eye of his heart.

﴿You will not make hear except those who believe in Our verses﴾, and they are those whom Allah knows will affirm His signs.

﴿So they are Muslims﴾, submitting to the truth. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Muslims" means sincere, from His saying: ﴿Yes, whoever submits his face to Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:112], meaning He made it wholly and purely for Allah. End of quote.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 27, verses 67–82 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And when the word comes due against them﴾, i.e., when the promise of their punishment, which the eternal decree from Allah contains, is fulfilled, as in His saying: ﴿the word of punishment has come due against the disbelievers﴾ [al-Zumar: 71]. The meaning is: when Allah wills to carry out upon the disbelievers the punishment that His prior knowledge concerning them determined, He will bring forth for them a beast (dabbah) that emerges from the earth. "Waqa'a" (came due, took place) is an expression for being established and necessary. As for "al-qawl" (the word), it is either by eliding a modifier, meaning "the content of the word," or the word "qawl" is used for "maqul" (what is said), since what is said is conveyed through speech, namely what they were promised of the Hour and the punishment. Ibn Mas'ud said: ﴿the word comes due against them﴾ happens through the death of the scholars, the departure of knowledge, and the lifting of the Qur'an. End. It is narrated that its emergence will be when goodness ceases, when no one is commanded to do right, when no one is forbidden from wrong, and when no one repentant or penitent remains. In a hadith: "That the beast and the rising of the sun from the west are among the first of the signs" (al-ashrat, the major portents), but it does not specify which is first. Likewise the Dajjal (the Antichrist). The apparent sense of the hadiths is that the rising of the sun is the last of them, and the apparent sense is that the beast that emerges is one. It is also narrated that in every land a beast will emerge of the kind whose species is established on the earth, and that it is not one, so that His saying "dabbah" (a beast) is a generic noun (ism jins, a noun denoting a whole category). They differed concerning its nature, its form, the place of its emergence, the number of its emergences, the extent of what emerges from it, what it does to people, and what it emerges with, in a confused disagreement, some of it contradicting other parts and some of it refuting others; so we have set aside mention of it, because transmitting it is blackening paper with what is not authentic and wasting the time of its transmission.

The apparent reading of His saying ﴿tukallimuhum﴾ (speaks to them) is with the doubled letter (tashdid), which is the reading of the majority, from "kalam" (speech). This is supported by Ubayy's reading: tunabbi'uhum (informs them), and in some readings: tuhaddithuhum (tells them), which is the reading of Yahya ibn Sallam. Abdullah's reading is: "bi-anna al-nas" (that the people). Al-Suddi said: it speaks to them about the falsehood of all religions except Islam. It is said: it addresses them, saying to the believer: "This is a believer," and to the disbeliever: "This is a disbeliever." It is also said that the meaning of "tukallimuhum" is: it wounds them, from "kalm" (wound), and the doubling is for intensity. This is supported by the reading of Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, Abu Zur'a, al-Jahdari, Abu Haywa, and Ibn Abi Abla: "tuklimuhum," with a fatha on the ta', a sukun on the kaf, and a light lam. Also the reading of one who read "tajrahuhum" (wounds them) in place of "tukallimuhum." Abu al-Hawra asked Ibn Abbas: "Does it say tukallimu or tuklimu?" He said: "It does all of that: it speaks to the believer and wounds the disbeliever." End. It is narrated that it brands the disbeliever on his forehead and darkens him, and wipes over the face of the believer so that it whitens him.

The Kufans and Zayd ibn Ali read "anna al-nas" with a fatha on the hamza, and Ibn Mas'ud read "bi-anna" (and this has been mentioned). The rest of the seven readers read "inna," with a kasra on the hamza. The kasra allows that it is part of Allah's speech, which is the apparent sense given His saying "bi-ayatina" (by Our signs), and it allows that it is part of the speech of the beast. This is narrated from Ibn Abbas. The kasra of "inna" here is according to the saying (al-qawl), either by supposing an implied "qal" (said), or by treating "tukallimuhum" as if it were "taqulu lahum" (says to them). His saying ﴿bi-ayatina﴾ (by Our signs) is either by eliding a modifier, or because they are particular to Allah, as when some intimates of a king say: "our horses and our lands." On the reading with the fatha, the estimate is "bi-anna" like the reading of Abdullah. The apparent sense is that it is connected to "tukallimuhum," meaning: it addresses them with this speech. It is permissible that the ba' (bi), whether pronounced or implied, is causal, meaning: it addresses them or wounds them because of their failure to have certainty in Our signs.

Since what is concealed in the breast is what prompts what appears on the limbs, and the cause of its manifestation is that concealing precedes informing. The majority read ﴿ما تُكِنُّ﴾ [what they conceal], from ''akanna al-shay'' [he hid the thing]. Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd, and Ibn al-Sumayfa' read it with a fatḥah on the tā' and a ḍammah on the kāf, from ''kanna al-shay'' [he covered the thing]. The meaning: what they hide and what they disclose of enmity toward the Messenger and their schemes.

The apparent generality of His saying ''min ghā'ibah'' [any hidden thing] is: there is no thing in the utmost state of concealment and obscurity but that it is in a Book with Allah and in the hidden store of His knowledge. It was also said: what was hidden from them of the punishment of heaven and earth. It was also said: it is the Day of Resurrection and its terrors; this was reported by al-Hasan. The "Book" is the Preserved Tablet (al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ). It was also said: the deeds of the servants have been recorded in order that they be recompensed for them. Ibn 'Abbas said: meaning, there is no secret thing in the heavens and the earth, nor an open one, so he sufficed with mentioning the secret instead of its opposite. Al-Zamakhshari said: that which is hidden and concealed is called ''ghā'ibah'' [hidden] and ''khāfiyah'' [concealed], and the tā' in both is like its role in ''ʿāqibah'' [outcome] and ''ʿāfiyah'' [well-being], and their parallels are ''naṭīḥah'' [the gored animal], ''dhabīḥah'' [the slaughtered animal], and ''ramiyyah'' [the shot animal], in that they are nouns and not adjectives. It is permissible that these two be adjectives, and the tā' in them is for intensification, like the ''riwāyah'' [transmission] in their saying: "Woe to the poet for the evil of his transmission," as if he said: "there is no thing of extreme hiddenness and obscurity but that Allah knows it, encompasses it, and has recorded it in the Clear Tablet, which is manifest to whoever among the angels looks into it." End of quote.

The Children of Israel are the Jews and the Christians. It relates to them most of what they differed about, in its proper form, and clarifies it for them; had they been fair, they would have submitted. Among what they differed about is the matter of the Messiah: they formed factions concerning it; some said he is Allah, some said he is the son of Allah, some said he is the third of three, and some said he is a prophet like the other prophets. They held councils for this and diverged in their creeds, and they disputed about matters until some of them cursed others.

The apparent sense is the generality of the believers, and it was also said: it refers to those among the Children of Israel who believed. As for ''al-qaḍāʾ'' [judgment] and ''al-ḥukm'' [ruling]: although it becomes apparent that they are synonyms, it was said that what is meant here is justice, meaning, by His justice, because He judges only with justice. It was also said: what is meant by His wisdom (ḥikmah) is judgment. It was said: this is indicated by the reading of one who read ''biḥikamihi'' with a kasrah on the ḥā' and a fatḥah on the kāf, the plural of ''ḥikmah'', and that is the reading of Junāḥ ibn Jaysh. Since judgment requires the execution of what is judged and knowledge of what is ruled upon, these two attributes came after it, namely: the Mighty, that is, the Dominant, the Powerful, and the All-Knowing. Then the Most High commanded him to rely upon Him, and informed him that he is upon the clear truth that has no doubt in it. This is like a reasoning for trusting in Him, and in it is evidence that whoever is upon the truth is entitled to trust in Allah, for He will support him and not forsake him.

Since the Qur'an and what Allah related in it is hardly beneficial to them, the Most High informed about them that they are dead of heart, or they were likened to the dead, even though they were living with sound sight; for when it is recited to them their ears do not retain it, so their state, due to the lack of benefit from hearing, was like the state of the dead. The majority read ﴿ولا تَسْمَعُ الصُّمُّ﴾ [nor can the deaf hear] here and in al-Rūm with a ḍammah on the tā' and a kasrah on the mīm, with ''al-ṣummu'' in the nominative. Since the dead cannot hear, no complement was mentioned for him, but rather the causing to hear was negated, meaning: no causing of hearing from you can ever reach them, due to their lack of receptivity. As for the deaf person, he may at times be in a state in which he can be made to hear and can hear, so the complement of the verb, which is the call, was mentioned. The word ''idhā'' [when] governs ''tasmaʿu'' [you hear], and the negation of causing to hear or of hearing was restricted by this temporal clause and what follows it, for emphasis regarding the state of the deaf person; because when he turns away from the caller, retreating, he is further from perceiving his voice.

He likened them first to the dead, then to the deaf in a certain state, then to the blind, saying: ﴿Nor can you guide the blind﴾ [out of their error], since they lose the way, and no one can remove that from them and turn them into guided, seeing people except Allah, the Most High. The majority read ''bihādī al-ʿum'' [guide the blind] as an active participle with its object in the genitive; Yaḥyā ibn al-Ḥārith and Abū Ḥaywah read ''bihādin'' with tanwīn, and ''al-ʿumya'' [the blind] in the accusative; al-A'mash, Ṭalḥah, Ibn Wathhāb, Ibn Ya'mur, and Ḥamzah read ''tahdī'' [you guide], the present tense of ''hadā'', with ''al-ʿumya'' in the accusative; Ibn Mas'ūd read ''wa-mā anta tahtadī'', with ''an'' added after ''mā'', and ''yahtadī'' is the present of ''ihtadā'', and ''al-ʿumyu'' in the nominative. The meaning: it is not within your capacity to introduce guidance into the heart of one who is blind to the truth and has not looked at it with the eye of his heart.

﴿You will not make hear except those who believe in Our verses﴾, and they are those whom Allah knows will affirm His signs.

﴿So they are Muslims﴾, submitting to the truth. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Muslims" means sincere, from His saying: ﴿Yes, whoever submits his face to Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:112], meaning He made it wholly and purely for Allah. End of quote.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 27, verses 67–82 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And when the word comes due against them﴾, i.e., when the promise of their punishment, which the eternal decree from Allah contains, is fulfilled, as in His saying: ﴿the word of punishment has come due against the disbelievers﴾ [al-Zumar: 71]. The meaning is: when Allah wills to carry out upon the disbelievers the punishment that His prior knowledge concerning them determined, He will bring forth for them a beast (dabbah) that emerges from the earth. "Waqa'a" (came due, took place) is an expression for being established and necessary. As for "al-qawl" (the word), it is either by eliding a modifier, meaning "the content of the word," or the word "qawl" is used for "maqul" (what is said), since what is said is conveyed through speech, namely what they were promised of the Hour and the punishment. Ibn Mas'ud said: ﴿the word comes due against them﴾ happens through the death of the scholars, the departure of knowledge, and the lifting of the Qur'an. End. It is narrated that its emergence will be when goodness ceases, when no one is commanded to do right, when no one is forbidden from wrong, and when no one repentant or penitent remains. In a hadith: "That the beast and the rising of the sun from the west are among the first of the signs" (al-ashrat, the major portents), but it does not specify which is first. Likewise the Dajjal (the Antichrist). The apparent sense of the hadiths is that the rising of the sun is the last of them, and the apparent sense is that the beast that emerges is one. It is also narrated that in every land a beast will emerge of the kind whose species is established on the earth, and that it is not one, so that His saying "dabbah" (a beast) is a generic noun (ism jins, a noun denoting a whole category). They differed concerning its nature, its form, the place of its emergence, the number of its emergences, the extent of what emerges from it, what it does to people, and what it emerges with, in a confused disagreement, some of it contradicting other parts and some of it refuting others; so we have set aside mention of it, because transmitting it is blackening paper with what is not authentic and wasting the time of its transmission.

The apparent reading of His saying ﴿tukallimuhum﴾ (speaks to them) is with the doubled letter (tashdid), which is the reading of the majority, from "kalam" (speech). This is supported by Ubayy's reading: tunabbi'uhum (informs them), and in some readings: tuhaddithuhum (tells them), which is the reading of Yahya ibn Sallam. Abdullah's reading is: "bi-anna al-nas" (that the people). Al-Suddi said: it speaks to them about the falsehood of all religions except Islam. It is said: it addresses them, saying to the believer: "This is a believer," and to the disbeliever: "This is a disbeliever." It is also said that the meaning of "tukallimuhum" is: it wounds them, from "kalm" (wound), and the doubling is for intensity. This is supported by the reading of Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, Abu Zur'a, al-Jahdari, Abu Haywa, and Ibn Abi Abla: "tuklimuhum," with a fatha on the ta', a sukun on the kaf, and a light lam. Also the reading of one who read "tajrahuhum" (wounds them) in place of "tukallimuhum." Abu al-Hawra asked Ibn Abbas: "Does it say tukallimu or tuklimu?" He said: "It does all of that: it speaks to the believer and wounds the disbeliever." End. It is narrated that it brands the disbeliever on his forehead and darkens him, and wipes over the face of the believer so that it whitens him.

The Kufans and Zayd ibn Ali read "anna al-nas" with a fatha on the hamza, and Ibn Mas'ud read "bi-anna" (and this has been mentioned). The rest of the seven readers read "inna," with a kasra on the hamza. The kasra allows that it is part of Allah's speech, which is the apparent sense given His saying "bi-ayatina" (by Our signs), and it allows that it is part of the speech of the beast. This is narrated from Ibn Abbas. The kasra of "inna" here is according to the saying (al-qawl), either by supposing an implied "qal" (said), or by treating "tukallimuhum" as if it were "taqulu lahum" (says to them). His saying ﴿bi-ayatina﴾ (by Our signs) is either by eliding a modifier, or because they are particular to Allah, as when some intimates of a king say: "our horses and our lands." On the reading with the fatha, the estimate is "bi-anna" like the reading of Abdullah. The apparent sense is that it is connected to "tukallimuhum," meaning: it addresses them with this speech. It is permissible that the ba' (bi), whether pronounced or implied, is causal, meaning: it addresses them or wounds them because of their failure to have certainty in Our signs.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 27, verses 67–82 (part 1 of 2):**

(p. 94) ﴿The disbelievers say: "When we have become dust, and our fathers too, shall we really be brought forth?"﴾ ﴿"We and our fathers were certainly promised this before. This is nothing but the fables of the ancients."﴾ ﴿Say: "Travel through the earth and see what was the end of the criminals."﴾ ﴿Do not grieve over them, and do not be distressed by what they plot.﴾ ﴿They say: "When will this promise be, if you are truthful?"﴾ ﴿Say: "Perhaps some of what you are hastening for has drawn close to you."﴾ ﴿Indeed your Lord is full of bounty toward people, but most of them do not give thanks.﴾ ﴿Indeed your Lord knows what their breasts conceal and what they disclose.﴾ ﴿And there is no hidden thing in the heaven or the earth but that it is in a clear Book.﴾ ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an relates to the Children of Israel most of that over which they differ.﴾ ﴿And indeed it is a guidance and a mercy for the believers.﴾ ﴿Indeed your Lord will judge between them by His judgment, and He is the Mighty, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿So rely upon Allah. Indeed, you are upon the clear truth.﴾ ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear, nor can you make the deaf hear the call when they turn away, retreating.﴾ ﴿Nor can you guide the blind out of their error. You will not make hear except those who believe in Our verses, so they are Muslims [submitting].﴾ ﴿And when the word befalls them, We will bring forth for them a creature from the earth which will speak to them, [saying] that people were not certain of Our signs.﴾

When the Most High had mentioned that He alone has knowledge of the unseen, and that among it is the time of the Hour, and that they have no awareness of its time, and that the disbelievers are in doubt about it and blind to it, it was fitting to mention their statements in denying it, and that what they were promised of it is not true; rather, it is only what the ancients wrote down, without any report of it being a reality.

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read ﴿أئِذا، أئِنّا﴾ [a'idhā, a'innā] with the two interrogatives combined, the second being changed to a yā' (ya). Abu 'Amr separated the two with an alif. 'Asim and Hamzah read both with two hamzas. Nafi' read ﴿إذا﴾ with a kasrah-marked hamzah, and ﴿آينّا﴾ with the interrogative hamzah, the second changed to a yā', with a madd between them. The rest read ﴿آئِذا﴾ with a prolonged interrogative, and ﴿إنّنا﴾ with two nūns without an interrogative. The governing element (al-'amil) of ﴿إذا﴾ is omitted, indicated by the meaning of the second clause; its estimated form is "will come out." It is impossible for ﴿لَمُخْرَجُونَ﴾ to govern it, because each of ''inna'' and the lam of initiation (lam al-ibtida') and the interrogative prevents what follows them from governing what precedes them, except the lam that falls in the predicate of ''inna'', for the complement of the predicate may precede it and the predicate, as established in the science of grammar (ʿilm al-naḥw).

﴿وآباؤنا﴾ [and our fathers] is coordinated with the subject of ''kāna'' (kāna's noun), and that separation by the predicate of ''kāna'' is permissible. The bringing forth here is from the graves, alive, with their spirits returned to their bodies. Combining the interrogative in ''idhā'' and in ''innā'' is a denial upon a denial, and an emphasis on the impossibility of that occurring. The pronoun in ''a'innā'' refers to them and to their fathers, because their becoming dust is inclusive of all of them. Then they mentioned that they had been promised this, they and their fathers, but none of this promised thing had come to pass; then they affirmed and restricted that it was among the fabrications of those who came before. Here the object of the promise, which is ''hādhā'' [this], is placed first, while in another verse it is placed later, according to the context in which the speech was delivered. Where the report about them concerning the denial of resurrection and the Hereafter was emphasized, they gave it priority by placing it first out of concern; and where that was not the case, they aimed at denying the bringing into existence of the one who is resurrected, so they placed that first and delayed the object of the promise.

Then He commanded His Prophet to tell them to travel through the earth. The discussion of this verse has preceded in the beginning of al-An'am. By "the criminals" he meant the disbelievers. Then He consoled His Prophet, saying: ﴿Do not grieve over them﴾, meaning, regarding their not having submitted or yielded to what you have brought. ﴿And do not be in distress﴾, meaning, in a hardship and a matter that is difficult for you, ﴿because of what they plot﴾, for their plotting returns upon them, not upon you, and Allah protects you from them. The reading ''ḍīq'' (ضِيقٍ) has been mentioned, with a kasrah and a fatḥah on the ḍād, and both are verbal nouns (maṣdar). Abu 'Ali (al-Farisi) disliked that the one with the fatḥah on the ḍād should be the original ''ḍayyiq'', with the yā' doubled, then lightened, like ''layn'' from ''layyin'', because that requires deleting the modified noun and setting the adjective in its place, and it is not among the adjectives that stand in for the modified noun in a regular manner. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that, saying: "It may also be intended as: in a narrow matter of their plotting."

When the Quraysh hastened [to ask] about the matter of the Hour, or about the punishment promised to them, and asked about the time of what was promised, mockingly, it was said to him: ﴿Say: "Perhaps some of it has drawn close to you."﴾ That is, it has followed you soon, and some of what you hastened for has become like a rider that follows you. This was the punishment of the Day of Badr. It was also said: the punishment of the grave. The majority read ''radifa'' (رَدِفَ) with a kasrah on the dāl. Ibn Hurmuz read it with a fatḥah, and both are dialects. Its original form is transitive, in the sense of "followed" and "overtook," so it may be understood as implying the intransitive meaning, and therefore Ibn 'Abbas and others interpreted it as ''azifa'' and ''qariba'' (drew near and approached), since what comes after a thing is near to it, within its meaning, or with an extension. The lam in its object serves to emphasize the arrival of the verb to it, as the ba' was added in ﴿and do not cast yourselves by your own hands [into destruction]﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:195], as al-Zamakhshari said. It has also been construed with ''min'' by way of implicit meaning (taḍmīn) for what is transitive with it. The poet said:

*"So when we followed closely upon ʿUmayr and his companions, they turned back swiftly, while death was driving them on."*

meaning, they approached ʿUmayr. It was also said: ''radifahu'' and ''radifa lahu'' are two dialects. It was also said: the verb is construed according to the verbal noun, meaning "the following for you." And ''baʿḍ'' [some] is according to the estimate of "the following of some of what you hasten for," and this involves a strain from which the Qur'an is to be exempted. It was also said: the lam in ''lakum'' is attached to the object for which (the causal), and the direct object is omitted, its estimate being: "He caused the creation to follow for your sake," and this is weak. It is narrated that its emergence will be when goodness ceases, when no one is commanded to do right, when no one is forbidden from wrong, and when no one repentant or penitent remains. In a hadith: "That the beast and the rising of the sun from the west are among the first of the signs" (al-ashrat, the major portents), but it does not specify which is first. Likewise the Dajjal (the Antichrist). The apparent sense of the hadiths is that the rising of the sun is the last of them, and the apparent sense is that the beast that emerges is one. It is also narrated that in every land a beast will emerge of the kind whose species is established on the earth, and that it is not one, so that His saying "dabbah" (a beast) is a generic noun (ism jins, a noun denoting a whole category). They differed concerning its nature, its form, the place of its emergence, the number of its emergences, the extent of what emerges from it, what it does to people, and what it emerges with, in a confused disagreement, some of it contradicting other parts and some of it refuting others; so we have set aside mention of it, because transmitting it is blackening paper with what is not authentic and wasting the time of its transmission.

The apparent reading of His saying ﴿tukallimuhum﴾ (speaks to them) is with the doubled letter (tashdid), which is the reading of the majority, from "kalam" (speech). This is supported by Ubayy's reading: tunabbi'uhum (informs them), and in some readings: tuhaddithuhum (tells them), which is the reading of Yahya ibn Sallam. Abdullah's reading is: "bi-anna al-nas" (that the people). Al-Suddi said: it speaks to them about the falsehood of all religions except Islam. It is said: it addresses them, saying to the believer: "This is a believer," and to the disbeliever: "This is a disbeliever." It is also said that the meaning of "tukallimuhum" is: it wounds them, from "kalm" (wound), and the doubling is for intensity. This is supported by the reading of Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, Abu Zur'a, al-Jahdari, Abu Haywa, and Ibn Abi Abla: "tuklimuhum," with a fatha on the ta', a sukun on the kaf, and a light lam. Also the reading of one who read "tajrahuhum" (wounds them) in place of "tukallimuhum." Abu al-Hawra asked Ibn Abbas: "Does it say tukallimu or tuklimu?" He said: "It does all of that: it speaks to the believer and wounds the disbeliever." End. It is narrated that it brands the disbeliever on his forehead and darkens him, and wipes over the face of the believer so that it whitens him.

The Kufans and Zayd ibn Ali read "anna al-nas" with a fatha on the hamza, and Ibn Mas'ud read "bi-anna" (and this has been mentioned). The rest of the seven readers read "inna," with a kasra on the hamza. The kasra allows that it is part of Allah's speech, which is the apparent sense given His saying "bi-ayatina" (by Our signs), and it allows that it is part of the speech of the beast. This is narrated from Ibn Abbas. The kasra of "inna" here is according to the saying (al-qawl), either by supposing an implied "qal" (said), or by treating "tukallimuhum" as if it were "taqulu lahum" (says to them). His saying ﴿bi-ayatina﴾ (by Our signs) is either by eliding a modifier, or because they are particular to Allah, as when some intimates of a king say: "our horses and our lands." On the reading with the fatha, the estimate is "bi-anna" like the reading of Abdullah. The apparent sense is that it is connected to "tukallimuhum," meaning: it addresses them with this speech. It is permissible that the ba' (bi), whether pronounced or implied, is causal, meaning: it addresses them or wounds them because of their failure to have certainty in Our signs.

[p. 98] That is: remember the Day when We gather from every nation a multitude (fawj) of those who denied Our signs, and they are driven on. Al-hashr means gathering by force.

*"From every nation"*: min here means "from among the nations," and min is partitive (lil-tab'id).

*"A multitude"*: meaning a large group.

*"Of those who deny Our signs"*: min here is explanatory (lil-bayan), meaning "those who deny." The "signs" (al-ayat) are said to be the prophets, or the Qur'an, or the proofs; these are the views reported.

*"Then they are driven on"*: its explanation was already given at the beginning of the story of Sulayman in this surah. It is reported from Ibn Mas'ud that Abu Jahl, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and Shayba ibn Rabi'a were said to be "in front of the people of Makkah." In the same way, the leaders of all the other nations will be driven before them into the Fire.

*"Until, when they come"*: that is, to the place of standing (al-mawqif). *"He will say: Did you deny My signs"*: this is an interrogative of rebuke, reproach and humiliation. *"And you did not encompass them in knowledge"*: the apparent reading is that the waw is for the circumstantial state (lil-hal), meaning: did you deny them without reflecting upon them and without having encompassed knowledge of their reality? It is also permissible for the waw to be conjunctive (lil-atf), meaning: did you reject them, and along with their rejection you did not apply your minds to verify and perceive them. For the one to whom a writing is sent may deny that it came from the one who wrote it to him, yet he does not refrain from reading it and comprehending its meanings. It has also been said: "and you did not encompass them in knowledge" means that you did not know their falsehood so as to turn away from them; rather, you denied them in ignorance, without seeking evidence. Here *am* is disjunctive (munqati'ah), and it should be estimated as equivalent to *bal* alone. The speech moves from the interrogation that implies rebuke to an interrogation about their deeds, also in the manner of rebuke: *"What was it that you used to do?"* The meaning is: if you had any deed or proof, then produce it; but they have no deed or proof regarding what they did except disbelief and denial. *Madha* as a whole may be understood as an interrogative in the accusative, governed as the predicate of *kana*, which is *ta'malun*; or *ma* may be the interrogative and *dha* a relative pronoun meaning "that which," so that the two form a subject and predicate, with *kana* as a relative clause for *dha*, and the returning pronoun omitted, meaning "you used to do it." Abu Haywa read *amadha*, with the mim lightened, placing the interrogative particle before the interrogative noun for emphasis.

*"And the word has come due against them"*: that is, the promised punishment, because of their wrongdoing, which is their denial of the signs of God.

*"So they cannot speak"*: that is, they have no proof and no excuse, because they are occupied with the punishment of God. It has also been said: their mouths will be sealed, so they will not speak; and the absence of their speech may be at one station of the Resurrection, or it may apply to one group of people, because the Qur'an implies that at other stations they speak with proofs.

When He had mentioned some of the conditions of the Day of Resurrection, so that whoever God wills to be restrained may be restrained by hearing them, He drew their attention to what is evidence for the oneness of God (tawhid), for the gathering, and for prophethood, through something they witness in their own lives: the alternation of night and day from light to darkness and from darkness to light. The one who does this is one, and He is God Most High, so He must be singled out for worship and divinity. In this alternation there is also evidence for the turning of the heart from life to death and from death to another life. There is also evidence here for prophethood, because this alternation serves the benefits of those who are responsible (mukallafun); for this reason He gave the reason for that arrangement in His words: *"that you may rest therein"*. And the sending of prophets is for achieving the benefits of creation. He attributed seeing (al-ibsar) to the day as a figurative usage (majaz), since it occurs in the day; he attributed it to it as you would say, "your night is sleeping." He gave as the reason for the making of the night His words *"that you may rest therein"*, meaning so that their rest may take place in it, from the fatigue they suffer during the day, and so that their souls may be refreshed. One of the rajaz poets said:

Sleep is the rest of the sensory powers from their movements, and of the psychic powers.

The opposition was not stated explicitly in the making of the day with a mention of its reason, so the construction would have been "and the day so that you may see in it." Instead He said *"seeing"* (mubsiran) as a qualifier in the making of the day, not as a reason for the making. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is considered in terms of meaning, and this is the natural, uncontrived arrangement, because the meaning of *mubsiran* is: that you may see in it the way of moving about in pursuits of gain. End of quotation. What appears to be the case is that this is one of those forms in which what is omitted from the first part is what is affirmed in its counterpart, and what is omitted from the second part is what is affirmed in the first. The estimate therefore is: We made the night dark so that you may rest in it, and the day seeing so that you may go about in it. Darkness results in rest, and seeing results in disposing oneself in matters of benefit. This is shown by His words: *"And We made the sign of the day a seeing one, that you may seek bounty from your Lord"* (17:12). Rest is the reason for making the night dark, and going about is the reason for making the day seeing. We have previously discussed these two omissions at length in al-Baqarah, in His words: *"And the likeness of those who disbelieve is like one who shouts..."* (2:171).

*"Indeed in that"*: that is, in this making, *"are signs for a people who believe."* Since only believers benefit from reflection on these signs, they were singled out for mention, even though the signs are for them and for others.

*"And the Day the Horn is blown"*: the discussion of the Horn (al-sur) was given earlier in Surat al-An'am. This blast is the blast of terror. Abu Hurayrah reported that the angel has three blasts on the Horn: the blast of terror, which is the terror of the life of this world and is not the greatest terror; the blast of swooning; and the blast of rising from the graves. It has also been said there are two blasts: they took the terror and the swooning as one blast, and they took as evidence His words: *"Then it will be blown again"* (39:68). The discussion of that will come, God willing. The author of al-Ghunyan said: *"And the Day the Horn is blown"* is for the resurrection from the graves and the gathering. The past tense is used here in His words *"so there is terror"*, even though it has not yet happened, to signal that it is certain to occur and that it is inevitable. This is the purpose of putting the past tense in place of the future, as in His words: *"Then He will lead them into the Fire"* (11:98), after His words: *"He will precede his people on the Day of Resurrection"* (11:98).

*"Except whom God wills"*: that is, this terror will not reach them, because God strengthens their hearts. Muqatil said: they are Jibril, Mika'il, Israfil and the Angel of Death, peace be upon them. Since the greatest terror will not reach them, they are most fitting that this lesser one will not reach them either. Al-Dahhak said: they are the wide-eyed maidens of paradise (al-hur al-'in), the keepers of the Fire, and the bearers of the Throne. From Jabir: among them is Musa, because he swooned once. Abu Hurayrah said: they are the martyrs; and Abu Hurayrah narrated it as a hadith, which is: "They are the martyrs, with their Lord, who are provided for." This is also the view of Ibn Jubayr, who said: they are the martyrs, girded with swords around the Throne. It has also been said: they are the believers, because of His words: *"and they will be secure from terror on that Day."* Some scholars said: no sound report has come concerning their identity, and all of these are possibilities. Al-Qurtubi said: Abu Hurayrah's hadith escaped his notice; Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi authenticated it, so it is relied upon for identification, while the rest are ijtihad (personal judgement). This blowing is literal, whether into the trumpet or into the Horn; this is the view of the majority. It has also been said it may be a figure of speech for calling the dead, since their emergence from their graves is like the army's emergence at the sound of a call, and so it would be figurative. The first view is that of the majority, and it is the correct one, because of the frequency with which the blowing into the Horn occurs in the Qur'an and in the sound hadith. It has also been said that *"fa-faza'a"* is not from fear in the sense of dread, but its meaning is: responded and hastened to remain.

*"And all come to Him"*: the genitive pronoun of *kullun* is omitted; its estimate is: "and all of them." Al-Jumhur read *atuhu* as an active participle (ism fa'il); Abdullah, Hamzah and Hafs read *atawhu* as a past-tense verb. In both readings the meaning of *kull* as plural has been observed. Qatada read *ataha* as a past-tense verb with the pronoun referring to *kull* in its singular form, and he made *dakhirin* plural according to its meaning. Al-Hasan and al-A'mash read *dakhirin* without the alif. It has been said that the meaning of *atuhu* is: present at the place of standing after the second blast; it may also be meant that they return to His command and submit to Him.

*"And you see the mountains"*: this is from sight by the eye. *"You think them"* is a circumstantial state (hal) of the subject of *tara*, or of *al-jibal*. *"Solid"* (jamidah): one who has become solid in his place when he has not moved from it. This state of the mountains comes after the blast of the Horn, and it is the first of the mountains' conditions: they shake and move; then God blows them away so they become like carded wool; then they become scattered dust in the end.

*"While they pass by as clouds pass by"*: this is a circumstantial clause, meaning: you think them, in the view of the eye, to be firmly fixed in their places while they are moving. Their passing is compared to the passing of clouds. It has been said: in their passing swiftly, as the clouds pass, and in the same way large bodies that are numerous, when they move, their movement is hardly discernible, as al-Nabigha al-Ja'di said describing an army:

A fire from a mass like a mountain, you think them standing still for a pilgrimage, while the riding-camels are trotting.

It has been said: their passing is compared to the passing of clouds in that they move at a middling pace, as al-A'sha said:

Her walk from her neighbour's house is like the passing of a cloud, neither hesitant nor hasty.

The observer's supposition that the mountains are solid while they pass is said to be due to the terror of that day, so that his mind does not have the firm grasp necessary in thought to verify that they are not solid. Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: the reason for their supposing them to be solid is that large bodies, when they move swiftly in a single direction, the observer thinks they are standing still, while they are passing swiftly. End of quotation. It has been said: He described the mountains with different attributes, which return to the emptying of the earth of them and the exposure of what they used to cover. The first of these attributes is their quaking; then their becoming like carded wool; then like dust, by being broken up after having been like carded wool; then their being blown away. With the preceding conditions they remain fixed in their places, and the earth is not exposed; by the blowing away, it is exposed. Their blowing away is by sending winds upon them, then their being carried by the wind in the air like dust; then their becoming a mirage, so that when you look at their places you will find nothing of them there, like a mirage. Muqatil said: rather, they fall upon the earth and are levelled with it.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 27, verses 83–93 (part 2 of 3):

The phrase ﴿ṣun'a Allāh﴾ (the handiwork of God) is in the accusative because it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) that emphasises the meaning of the clause that follows it, so its governing verb is implied and drawn from its own root. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿ṣun'a Allāh﴾ is one of the emphatic verbal nouns, like His saying ﴿waʿd Allāh﴾ (the promise of God) [Luqman: 9] and ﴿ṣibgha Allāh﴾ (the colouring of God) [al-Baqarah: 138], except that the clause it emphasises (p. 101) is omitted, and it is the verb governing "the day when the Trumpet is blown". The meaning is: "And on the day when the Trumpet is blown, such-and-such happens: God rewards the good-doers and punishes the wrongdoers." Then He said: ﴿ṣun'a Allāh﴾, meaning by it the reward and the punishment. This handiwork is counted among the things He perfected and carried out in wisdom and rightness, since He said: ﴿ṣun'a Allāh alladhī atqana kulla shay'﴾ (the handiwork of God, who perfected everything). That is, His answering a good deed with reward and an evil deed with punishment is part of His firm ordering of things, His perfecting them, and His running them according to the dictates of wisdom, and that He knows what the servants do and what they deserve, and so He recompenses them according to that. Then He summed this up in His saying: ﴿man jāʾa bil-ḥasanati fa-lahu﴾ (whoever comes with a good deed, for him there is), to the end of the two verses. So consider the eloquence of this discourse, the excellence of its arrangement and order, the solidity of its structure and the soundness of its explanation, and how one part takes hold of another, as though it were poured out in a single casting. How marvellous a matter, which overpowers faculties and silences the boastful! A verbal noun of this kind, when it comes after a statement, comes as a witness to its truth and a herald of its soundness, and it shows that it could not have been other than what it is. Do you not see His saying: ﴿ṣun'a Allāh﴾, and ﴿ṣibgha Allāh﴾ [al-Baqarah: 138], and ﴿waʿd Allāh﴾ [Yunus: 4], and ﴿fiṭrata Allāh﴾ (the nature of God) [al-Rum: 30]? After He had marked them by attributing them to Himself, as a name of exalting, how did He follow them with His saying: "﴿alladhī atqana kulla shay'﴾", "﴿wa-man aḥsanu mina Allāh ṣibghatan﴾ (and who is better than God in colouring?) [al-Baqarah: 138]", "﴿inna Allāha lā yukhlifu al-mīʿād﴾ (surely God does not fail the promise) [Al ʿImran: 9]", "﴿lā tabdīla li-khalq Allāh﴾ (there is no changing of the creation of God) [al-Rum: 30]"? End of quotation. What has been mentioned of his boastfulness and his excess in speech, and his contrivance in bending the words of the Qur'an to what he holds, is from the doctrines of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist school of theology).

What appears to me is that ﴿ṣun'a Allāh﴾ is an emphatic verbal noun for the meaning of the preceding clause, which is the clause of circumstance: God did that to them, namely uprooting them from the earth and making them pass like the passing of clouds. As for his statement that its emphasised element is omitted, and that it is the verb governing "the day when the Trumpet is blown" up to His saying "﴿ṣun'a Allāh﴾", meaning by it reward and punishment, this is not valid. The emphatic verbal noun for the meaning of a clause may not have its clause omitted, because it is governed by a verb of its own root, so the omission of the governing verb and the omission of the clause whose meaning is emphasised by the verbal noun would coincide, and that is a frequent and damaging omission. Whoever surveys the context of these verbal nouns that emphasise the meaning of a clause will find the clauses stated explicitly, and no omission occurs in any of them. The principle is that the emphasised element should not be omitted, since omission contradicts emphasis: from the standpoint of its being emphasised it is given importance, and from the standpoint of its being omitted it is not given importance. It has been said that ﴿ṣun'a Allāh﴾ is in the accusative as an incitement (ighrāʾ) with the sense of "Look at the handiwork of God." The two Iraqi readers (al-ʿArabiyyān, i.e. Abu ʿAmr and ʿAsim?) and Ibn Kathir read ﴿yaf'alūna﴾ with the yāʾ (third person); the rest of the seven read it with the tāʾ of address.

When He mentioned the signs of the Resurrection, He mentioned the conditions of the responsible persons after the Hour has come. The good deed (ḥasanah) is faith. Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Nakhaʿi and Qatadah said: it is "There is no god but God." He placed two things as consequences of the responsible person coming with a good deed. The first: that he has from it something better, and it appears that "khayr" (better) is not an elative (af'al al-tafḍīl, comparative form), and "min" (from) is for the beginning of the limit (ibtidāʾ al-ghāyah), meaning: he has a good from among the goods whose origin and rise is from it, that is, from the direction of this good deed. The "khayr" here is the reward. This is the view of al-Hasan, Ibn Jurayj and ʿIkrimah. ʿIkrimah said: nothing is better than "There is no god but God," meaning that it is not an elative. It has been said that it is an elative. Al-Zamakhshari said: "﴿fa-lahu khayrun minhā﴾" means multiplication (al-ibḍāʿ), and that the action ends while the reward endures, and how far apart are the act of the servant and the act of the master! End of quotation. His saying "how far apart are the act of the servant and the act of the master" is a construction that is disputed: some scholars prohibited it, and the correct view is that it is permissible. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: it may be that it is for comparison, and that in His saying "minhā" (from it) there is an omitted noun, its estimate being: better than its measure and its deserving, meaning that God bestowed upon him beyond what his good deed merits. Ibn Zayd said: he is given ten for one. What calls for this estimate is that between the good deed and the reward no comparison can be conceived. End of quotation. It has been said: the reward for the knowledge acquired in this world is the knowledge that is necessary and attained in the Hereafter, and the pleasure of gazing upon His noble Face. Indications have shown that the noblest of felicities is this pleasure, and if the verse is not taken in that sense, it would follow that eating and drinking are better than knowing God, and that is not possible.

The Kufans read ﴿min faza'in﴾ with tanwīn, and ﴿yawma'idhin﴾ is in the accusative as an adverb of time, governed either by His saying "āminūn" (safe) or by "faza'in". What shows that it is governed by it is the reading of the one who made it an annexed noun (iḍāfah) to it, or it is in the position of an adjective to "faza'in", meaning: occurring at that time. The rest of the seven read "faza'in" annexed to "yawma'idhin"; the two Iraqi readers, Ibn Kathir, Isma'il ibn Ja'far from Nafi', read the mīm with a kasrah, and Nafi' (in other than the transmission of Isma'il) read it with a fatḥah, on the basis that it is annexed to a non-declinable word (ghayr mutamakkin). The tanwīn in "yawma'idhin" is the tanwīn of replacement (tanwīn al-ʿiwaḍ): the clause has been omitted and replaced by it. The preferable view is that the omitted clause is what is nearest to the adverb, that is, "the day when he came with the good deed." It is also possible that the estimate is: "the day when you see the mountains," and it is possible that the estimate is: "the day when the Trumpet is blown," especially if it is interpreted as the blast of rising from the graves for reckoning, and the fear will then be one thing. Abu ʿAli said, in substance: "min faza'in" may be with tanwīn or with annexation; it may mean one single fear, and it may mean abundance, since it is a verbal noun. If abundance is meant, it includes every fear that occurs on the Day of Resurrection; if the single fear is meant, it is the one indicated by His saying: "lā yaḥzunuhumu al-faza' al-akbar" (the greatest terror shall not grieve them). Al-Zamakhshari said: "(If you say) what is the difference between the two fears? (I say) the first fear is that from which no one is free when he senses a severe event that befalls him; it startles him out of terror and awe, even if the doer of good is safe from harm reaching him. The second is fear of punishment." End of quotation.

The evil deed (sayyi'ah) is disbelief and sins committed by those upon whom God has set a seal from among the people of the Will, by their entering the Fire. The faces are singled out, since they are the noblest of the limbs, and their being cast into the Fire entails the casting of the whole body; or the face is used to express the whole human being, as the head and the neck are used to express it, as He said: ﴿fa-kubkibū fīhā﴾ (so they will be flung into it) [al-Shuʿara: 94]; it is as if it were said: "so they will be cast into the Fire." The apparent meaning of "kubbat" is that they are thrown into the Fire upside down, as Abu al-ʿAliyah said, its top before its bottom. It is also possible that this is a metaphor for their being cast into the Fire, as al-Dahhak said. "Hal tujzawna" (Are you being recompensed?) is addressed to them with an implied saying, meaning: it is said to them at the time of the casting: "Are you being recompensed?"

Then God, exalted is He, commanded His Prophet to say: ﴿innamā umirtu﴾ (I have only been commanded), and the one who commands is God, exalted is He, through the tongue of Jibril, or it is the proof of reason for the unity of God, exalted is He. ﴿an aʿbuda﴾ (that I should worship): that is, that I single Him out for worship, and not take a partner with Him as the Quraysh did. This is an expression of exaltation, like His saying: ﴿wa-hādhā kitābun anzalnāhu﴾ (and this is a Book We have sent down) [al-Anʿam: 92]. "This" refers to the one who is with me, insofar as he is the place of residence of His Prophet and the descent-point of His revelation. The land (al-baldah) is Makkah, and the making sacred is attributed to Him to honour it and single it out. There is no contradiction between His saying ﴿alladhī ḥarramahā﴾ (who has made it sacred) and his peace be upon him saying: "Indeed Ibrahim made Makkah sacred, and I have made Madinah sacred." This is because the attribution of that to God is insofar as it was by His decree and prior knowledge, and its attribution to Ibrahim is insofar as its manifestation came through his supplication, his desire, and his conveying it to his community. In His saying "ḥarramahā" (made it sacred) there is an admonition to the Quraysh of His blessing upon them, since He made their land secure from raids and the strife that occurs in the lands of the Arabs, and destroyed whoever intended it with evil. The majority read ﴿alladhī﴾ as an adjective of the Lord. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn ʿAbbas read ﴿allatī ḥarramahā﴾ as an adjective of "the land". When He informed that He is the owner of this land, He informed that He possesses everything, so He said: ﴿wa-lahu kullu shay'﴾ (and to Him belongs everything), that is, all things are included in His lordship; thus the land was honoured by the mention of its being included under His lordship in particular and in general. ﴿wa-umirtu an akūna mina al-muslimīn﴾ (and I have been commanded to be of the Muslims): that is, of those who submit and are obedient to the command of God, so that I worship Him as He commanded me; or of the ḥunafāʾ (upright in faith), who stand firm on the religion of Islam, referred to in His saying: "He named you the Muslims" [al-Hajj: 78]. ﴿wa-an atlūa al-Qurʾān﴾ (and that I should recite the Qur'an): either from recitation (tilāwah), that is, "and that I recite the Qur'an to you," and this is the apparent meaning, since after it comes the division appropriate to recitation; or from what is recited (al-matluww), that is, "and that I follow the Qur'an," as in His saying: "follow what is revealed to you" [Yunus: 109]. The majority read "wa-an atlūa". ʿAbd Allah read "wa-ani-tlu" without the waw, as an imperative from talā, so "an" may be a verbal (maṣdariyyah) particle connected to the imperative, and it may be an explanatory "an" with an implied "wa-umirtu an atlu", meaning: recite. Ubayy read "wa-tlu hādhā al-Qurʾān", making it an imperative without "an". "So whoever is guided" by it, and affirms the oneness of God and of His Prophet, and believes in what he brought, then the fruit of his guidance belongs to him alone. "And whoever goes astray," then the burden of his misguidance is his alone.
