After He had marked them by attributing them to Himself, as a name of exalting, how did He follow them with His saying: "﴿alladhī atqana kulla shay'﴾", "﴿wa-man aḥsanu mina Allāh ṣibghatan﴾ (and who is better than God in colouring?) [al-Baqarah: 138]", "﴿inna Allāha lā yukhlifu al-mīʿād﴾ (surely God does not fail the promise) [Al ʿImran: 9]", "﴿lā tabdīla li-khalq Allāh﴾ (there is no changing of the creation of God) [al-Rum: 30]"? End of quotation. What has been mentioned of his boastfulness and his excess in speech, and his contrivance in bending the words of the Qur'an to what he holds, is from the doctrines of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist school of theology).

What appears to me is that ﴿ṣun'a Allāh﴾ is an emphatic verbal noun for the meaning of the preceding clause, which is the clause of circumstance: God did that to them, namely uprooting them from the earth and making them pass like the passing of clouds. As for his statement that its emphasised element is omitted, and that it is the verb governing "the day when the Trumpet is blown" up to His saying "﴿ṣun'a Allāh﴾", meaning by it reward and punishment, this is not valid. The emphatic verbal noun for the meaning of a clause may not have its clause omitted, because it is governed by a verb of its own root, so the omission of the governing verb and the omission of the clause whose meaning is emphasised by the verbal noun would coincide, and that is a frequent and damaging omission. Whoever surveys the context of these verbal nouns that emphasise the meaning of a clause will find the clauses stated explicitly, and no omission occurs in any of them. The principle is that the emphasised element should not be omitted, since omission contradicts emphasis: from the standpoint of its being emphasised it is given importance, and from the standpoint of its being omitted it is not given importance. It has been said that ﴿ṣun'a Allāh﴾ is in the accusative as an incitement (ighrāʾ) with the sense of "Look at the handiwork of God." The two Iraqi readers (al-ʿArabiyyān, i.e. Abu ʿAmr and ʿAsim?) and Ibn Kathir read ﴿yaf'alūna﴾ with the yāʾ (third person); the rest of the seven read it with the tāʾ of address.

When He mentioned the signs of the Resurrection, He mentioned the conditions of the responsible persons after the Hour has come. The good deed (ḥasanah) is faith. Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Nakhaʿi and Qatadah said: it is "There is no god but God." He placed two things as consequences of the responsible person coming with a good deed. The first: that he has from it something better, and it appears that "khayr" (better) is not an elative (af'al al-tafḍīl, comparative form), and "min" (from) is for the beginning of the limit (ibtidāʾ al-ghāyah), meaning: he has a good from among the goods whose origin and rise is from it, that is, from the direction of this good deed. The "khayr" here is the reward. This is the view of al-Hasan, Ibn Jurayj and ʿIkrimah. ʿIkrimah said: nothing is better than "There is no god but God," meaning that it is not an elative. It has been said that it is an elative. Al-Zamakhshari said: "﴿fa-lahu khayrun minhā﴾" means multiplication (al-ibḍāʿ), and that the action ends while the reward endures, and how far apart are the act of the servant and the act of the master! End of quotation. His saying "how far apart are the act of the servant and the act of the master" is a construction that is disputed: some scholars prohibited it, and the correct view is that it is permissible. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: it may be that it is for comparison, and that in His saying "minhā" (from it) there is an omitted noun, its estimate being: better than its measure and its deserving, meaning that God bestowed upon him beyond what his good deed merits. Ibn Zayd said: he is given ten for one. What calls for this estimate is that between the good deed and the reward no comparison can be conceived. End of quotation. It has been said: the reward for the knowledge acquired in this world is the knowledge that is necessary and attained in the Hereafter, and the pleasure of gazing upon His noble Face. Indications have shown that the noblest of felicities is this pleasure, and if the verse is not taken in that sense, it would follow that eating and drinking are better than knowing God, and that is not possible.

The Kufans read ﴿min faza'in﴾ with tanwīn, and ﴿yawma'idhin﴾ is in the accusative as an adverb of time, governed either by His saying "āminūn" (safe) or by "faza'in". What shows that it is governed by it is the reading of the one who made it an annexed noun (iḍāfah) to it, or it is in the position of an adjective to "faza'in", meaning: occurring at that time. The rest of the seven read "faza'in" annexed to "yawma'idhin"; the two Iraqi readers, Ibn Kathir, Isma'il ibn Ja'far from Nafi', read the mīm with a kasrah, and Nafi' (in other than the transmission of Isma'il) read it with a fatḥah, on the basis that it is annexed to a non-declinable word (ghayr mutamakkin). The tanwīn in "yawma'idhin" is the tanwīn of replacement (tanwīn al-ʿiwaḍ): the clause has been omitted and replaced by it. The preferable view is that the omitted clause is what is nearest to the adverb, that is, "the day when he came with the good deed." It is also possible that the estimate is: "the day when you see the mountains," and it is possible that the estimate is: "the day when the Trumpet is blown," especially if it is interpreted as the blast of rising from the graves for reckoning, and the fear will then be one thing. Abu ʿAli said, in substance: "min faza'in" may be with tanwīn or with annexation; it may mean one single fear, and it may mean abundance, since it is a verbal noun. If abundance is meant, it includes every fear that occurs on the Day of Resurrection; if the single fear is meant, it is the one indicated by His saying: "lā yaḥzunuhumu al-faza' al-akbar" (the greatest terror shall not grieve them). Al-Zamakhshari said: "(If you say) what is the difference between the two fears? (I say) the first fear is that from which no one is free when he senses a severe event that befalls him; it startles him out of terror and awe, even if the doer of good is safe from harm reaching him. The second is fear of punishment." End of quotation.

The evil deed (sayyi'ah) is disbelief and sins committed by those upon whom God has set a seal from among the people of the Will, by their entering the Fire. The faces are singled out, since they are the noblest of the limbs, and their being cast into the Fire entails the casting of the whole body; or the face is used to express the whole human being, as the head and the neck are used to express it, as He said: ﴿fa-kubkibū fīhā﴾ (so they will be flung into it) [al-Shuʿara: 94]; it is as if it were said: "so they will be cast into the Fire." The apparent meaning of "kubbat" is that they are thrown into the Fire upside down, as Abu al-ʿAliyah said, its top before its bottom. It is also possible that this is a metaphor for their being cast into the Fire, as al-Dahhak said. "Hal tujzawna" (Are you being recompensed?) is addressed to them with an implied saying, meaning: it is said to them at the time of the casting: "Are you being recompensed?"

Then God, exalted is He, commanded His Prophet to say: ﴿innamā umirtu﴾ (I have only been commanded), and the one who commands is God, exalted is He, through the tongue of Jibril, or it is the proof of reason for the unity of God, exalted is He. ﴿an aʿbuda﴾ (that I should worship): that is, that I single Him out for worship, and not take a partner with Him as the Quraysh did. This is an expression of exaltation, like His saying: ﴿wa-hādhā kitābun anzalnāhu﴾ (and this is a Book We have sent down) [al-Anʿam: 92]. "This" refers to the one who is with me, insofar as he is the place of residence of His Prophet and the descent-point of His revelation. The land (al-baldah) is Makkah, and the making sacred is attributed to Him to honour it and single it out. There is no contradiction between His saying ﴿alladhī ḥarramahā﴾ (who has made it sacred) and his peace be upon him saying: "Indeed Ibrahim made Makkah sacred, and I have made Madinah sacred." This is because the attribution of that to God is insofar as it was by His decree and prior knowledge, and its attribution to Ibrahim is insofar as its manifestation came through his supplication, his desire, and his conveying it to his community. In His saying "ḥarramahā" (made it sacred) there is an admonition to the Quraysh of His blessing upon them, since He made their land secure from raids and the strife that occurs in the lands of the Arabs, and destroyed whoever intended it with evil. The majority read ﴿alladhī﴾ as an adjective of the Lord. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn ʿAbbas read ﴿allatī ḥarramahā﴾ as an adjective of "the land". When He informed that He is the owner of this land, He informed that He possesses everything, so He said: ﴿wa-lahu kullu shay'﴾ (and to Him belongs everything), that is, all things are included in His lordship; thus the land was honoured by the mention of its being included under His lordship in particular and in general. ﴿wa-umirtu an akūna mina al-muslimīn﴾ (and I have been commanded to be of the Muslims): that is, of those who submit and are obedient to the command of God, so that I worship Him as He commanded me; or of the ḥunafāʾ (upright in faith), who stand firm on the religion of Islam, referred to in His saying: "He named you the Muslims" [al-Hajj: 78]. ﴿wa-an atlūa al-Qurʾān﴾ (and that I should recite the Qur'an): either from recitation (tilāwah), that is, "and that I recite the Qur'an to you," and this is the apparent meaning, since after it comes the division appropriate to recitation; or from what is recited (al-matluww), that is, "and that I follow the Qur'an," as in His saying: "follow what is revealed to you" [Yunus: 109]. The majority read "wa-an atlūa". ʿAbd Allah read "wa-ani-tlu" without the waw, as an imperative from talā, so "an" may be a verbal (maṣdariyyah) particle connected to the imperative, and it may be an explanatory "an" with an implied "wa-umirtu an atlu", meaning: recite. Ubayy read "wa-tlu hādhā al-Qurʾān", making it an imperative without "an". "So whoever is guided" by it, and affirms the oneness of God and of His Prophet, and believes in what he brought, then the fruit of his guidance belongs to him alone. "And whoever goes astray," then the burden of his misguidance is his alone. The answer to "whoever goes astray" is omitted because the answer to its counterpart indicates it; or a pronoun is to be estimated in His saying: ﴿fa-qul innamā anā mina al-mundhirīn﴾ (say: I am only one of the warners), so that the recompense is linked to the condition, since the particle of condition is a noun and not an adverb, so there must be in the answer clause (p. 103) a reference returning to it, either spoken or estimated, so that this clause becomes the answer of the condition; and the pronoun is estimated as: "of the warners to him," that is, I have only to warn him, and as for his guidance, it is to God.

"And say: Praise belongs to God": he was commanded to say this, so that he praises his Lord for what He has specified him with of the nobility of prophethood and messengership, and singled him out with an exalted station. ﴿sa-yurīkum āyātihi﴾ (He will show you His signs): a threat to His enemies, with what God shows them of His signs, which will compel them to know them and to acknowledge that they are the signs of God. Al-Hasan said: this is in the Hereafter, so that knowledge will not benefit them. Al-Kalbi said: it is in this world, namely the smoke, the splitting of the moon, and what befell them of the vengeance of God. It has been said: the Day of Badr. It has been said: the emergence of the beast, even if after a time. It has been said: His signs are in yourselves and in all that He created, like His saying: ﴿sa-nurīhim āyātinā fī al-āfāqi wa-fī anfusihim﴾ (We shall show them Our signs on the horizons and in themselves) [Fussilat: 53]. It has been said: they are the miracles of the Messenger, and He attributed them to Himself because He is the one who brings them about through the hands of His Messenger, and manifests them from His side. ﴿fa-taʿrifūnahā﴾ (and you will recognise them): that is, their reality, and it is not possible for you to deny them. The majority read ﴿ʿammā yaʿmalūn﴾ (of what they do) with the yāʾ of the third person, a shift (iltifāt) from the pronoun of address to the pronoun of absence; Nafi' and Ibn ʿAmir read it with the tāʾ of address, in line with His saying: "He will show you." When He divided them into the guided and the astray, He informed, exalted is He, that He encompasses their deeds, and is not heedless of them.

* *

(Vocabulary of Surah al-Qasas)

al-Wakz: striking with the hand closed, like the closing of the fingers to make seventy-three (a gesture of counting). It has been said: gathering the palm. It has been said: wakz, nakz, lahz and lakz are all pushing with the fingertips. It has been said: wakz is on the heart, and lakz is on the jaw. It has been said: wakz is with the fingertips. Dhaʿada (he drove away), and drove back, and pushed. Al-Farra' said: he restrained. Jadhawtu al-shay' jadhwan: I cut it. And al-jadhwah is a stick in which there is fire without flame. Ibn Muqbil said:

They spent the night, the gatherers of wood for Layla, seeking for her firm firewood, neither crumbling nor brittle.

Al-Khawwar is that which crumbles, and al-Dhaʿir is that which has weariness in it. Another said:

And he cast upon a brand of fire a burning ember, its ash and its glow around it.

It is said: *al-jadhwah* (the *jim* may carry three vowels) is a thick piece of wood, whether or not there was fire on its end.

Al-Sulami said, describing the fire:

*The love of this fire has kindled the love of my beloved,*
*and the love of the young women, though it falls short of the beloved.*

*After musk and ben-tree perfume, I was given in exchange misery:*
*the smoke of al-Judhafi, a gray-haired, pale-faced old man.*

*Al-shati'* and *al-shatt* are the edge of a valley. *Al-fasahah* (eloquence) is the free use of the tongue in clarifying the intended meaning; its opposite is *al-lukn* (a faltering, unclear speech).

*Al-ridʾ* is the helper through whom one is strengthened in a matter. It is a verb in the sense of a passive participle (*fiʿl bi-maʿna maful*), so it is a noun for that by which one is aided, just as *al-difʾ* is a noun for that by which one is warmed. Salamah ibn Jandal said:

*And a helper for every white, Indian-sworded (blade),*
*sharpened at the edge, keen, with notches.*

It is said: *radaʾtu al-ha'it arduʾuhu*, meaning when you prop up a wall with a piece of wood so that it does not fall. Abu Ubaydah said: *al-ʿawn* (help). It is also said: *radaʾtuhu ʿala ʿaduwwihi*, meaning I aided him against his enemy.

*Al-maqbuh* is the one who is rejected and driven away. The poet said:

*Surely God has disfigured all the Baraajim tribes,*
*and cut off the nose of Yarbuʿ and abased Darim.*

*Thawa yathwi thawaʾan* means he stayed or resided. The poet said:

*Indeed there was a stay I made in a year,*
*when the milk-camels were consumed and the herding camels were wearied.*

Al-Ajjaj said:

*So he spent the night where the sojourner (al-thawiyy) enters,*

that is, the guest who stays. *Al-batar* is insolence. *Al-sarmad* is that which is everlasting and never ceases.

[p. 98] That is: remember the Day when We gather from every nation a multitude (fawj) of those who denied Our signs, and they are driven on. Al-hashr means gathering by force.

*"From every nation"*: min here means "from among the nations," and min is partitive (lil-tab'id).

*"A multitude"*: meaning a large group.

*"Of those who deny Our signs"*: min here is explanatory (lil-bayan), meaning "those who deny." The "signs" (al-ayat) are said to be the prophets, or the Qur'an, or the proofs; these are the views reported.

*"Then they are driven on"*: its explanation was already given at the beginning of the story of Sulayman in this surah. It is reported from Ibn Mas'ud that Abu Jahl, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and Shayba ibn Rabi'a were said to be "in front of the people of Makkah." In the same way, the leaders of all the other nations will be driven before them into the Fire.

*"Until, when they come"*: that is, to the place of standing (al-mawqif). *"He will say: Did you deny My signs"*: this is an interrogative of rebuke, reproach and humiliation. *"And you did not encompass them in knowledge"*: the apparent reading is that the waw is for the circumstantial state (lil-hal), meaning: did you deny them without reflecting upon them and without having encompassed knowledge of their reality? It is also permissible for the waw to be conjunctive (lil-atf), meaning: did you reject them, and along with their rejection you did not apply your minds to verify and perceive them. For the one to whom a writing is sent may deny that it came from the one who wrote it to him, yet he does not refrain from reading it and comprehending its meanings. It has also been said: "and you did not encompass them in knowledge" means that you did not know their falsehood so as to turn away from them; rather, you denied them in ignorance, without seeking evidence. Here *am* is disjunctive (munqati'ah), and it should be estimated as equivalent to *bal* alone. The speech moves from the interrogation that implies rebuke to an interrogation about their deeds, also in the manner of rebuke: *"What was it that you used to do?"* The meaning is: if you had any deed or proof, then produce it; but they have no deed or proof regarding what they did except disbelief and denial. *Madha* as a whole may be understood as an interrogative in the accusative, governed as the predicate of *kana*, which is *ta'malun*; or *ma* may be the interrogative and *dha* a relative pronoun meaning "that which," so that the two form a subject and predicate, with *kana* as a relative clause for *dha*, and the returning pronoun omitted, meaning "you used to do it." Abu Haywa read *amadha*, with the mim lightened, placing the interrogative particle before the interrogative noun for emphasis.

*"And the word has come due against them"*: that is, the promised punishment, because of their wrongdoing, which is their denial of the signs of God.

*"So they cannot speak"*: that is, they have no proof and no excuse, because they are occupied with the punishment of God. It has also been said: their mouths will be sealed, so they will not speak; and the absence of their speech may be at one station of the Resurrection, or it may apply to one group of people, because the Qur'an implies that at other stations they speak with proofs.

When He had mentioned some of the conditions of the Day of Resurrection, so that whoever God wills to be restrained may be restrained by hearing them, He drew their attention to what is evidence for the oneness of God (tawhid), for the gathering, and for prophethood, through something they witness in their own lives: the alternation of night and day from light to darkness and from darkness to light. The one who does this is one, and He is God Most High, so He must be singled out for worship and divinity. In this alternation there is also evidence for the turning of the heart from life to death and from death to another life. There is also evidence here for prophethood, because this alternation serves the benefits of those who are responsible (mukallafun); for this reason He gave the reason for that arrangement in His words: *"that you may rest therein"*. And the sending of prophets is for achieving the benefits of creation. He attributed seeing (al-ibsar) to the day as a figurative usage (majaz), since it occurs in the day; he attributed it to it as you would say, "your night is sleeping." He gave as the reason for the making of the night His words *"that you may rest therein"*, meaning so that their rest may take place in it, from the fatigue they suffer during the day, and so that their souls may be refreshed. One of the rajaz poets said:

Sleep is the rest of the sensory powers from their movements, and of the psychic powers.

The opposition was not stated explicitly in the making of the day with a mention of its reason, so the construction would have been "and the day so that you may see in it." Instead He said *"seeing"* (mubsiran) as a qualifier in the making of the day, not as a reason for the making. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is considered in terms of meaning, and this is the natural, uncontrived arrangement, because the meaning of *mubsiran* is: that you may see in it the way of moving about in pursuits of gain. End of quotation. What appears to be the case is that this is one of those forms in which what is omitted from the first part is what is affirmed in its counterpart, and what is omitted from the second part is what is affirmed in the first. The estimate therefore is: We made the night dark so that you may rest in it, and the day seeing so that you may go about in it. Darkness results in rest, and seeing results in disposing oneself in matters of benefit. This is shown by His words: *"And We made the sign of the day a seeing one, that you may seek bounty from your Lord"* (17:12). Rest is the reason for making the night dark, and going about is the reason for making the day seeing. We have previously discussed these two omissions at length in al-Baqarah, in His words: *"And the likeness of those who disbelieve is like one who shouts..."* (2:171).

*"Indeed in that"*: that is, in this making, *"are signs for a people who believe."* Since only believers benefit from reflection on these signs, they were singled out for mention, even though the signs are for them and for others.

*"And the Day the Horn is blown"*: the discussion of the Horn (al-sur) was given earlier in Surat al-An'am. This blast is the blast of terror. Abu Hurayrah reported that the angel has three blasts on the Horn: the blast of terror, which is the terror of the life of this world and is not the greatest terror; the blast of swooning; and the blast of rising from the graves. It has also been said there are two blasts: they took the terror and the swooning as one blast, and they took as evidence His words: *"Then it will be blown again"* (39:68). The discussion of that will come, God willing. The author of al-Ghunyan said: *"And the Day the Horn is blown"* is for the resurrection from the graves and the gathering. The past tense is used here in His words *"so there is terror"*, even though it has not yet happened, to signal that it is certain to occur and that it is inevitable. This is the purpose of putting the past tense in place of the future, as in His words: *"Then He will lead them into the Fire"* (11:98), after His words: *"He will precede his people on the Day of Resurrection"* (11:98).

*"Except whom God wills"*: that is, this terror will not reach them, because God strengthens their hearts. Muqatil said: they are Jibril, Mika'il, Israfil and the Angel of Death, peace be upon them. Since the greatest terror will not reach them, they are most fitting that this lesser one will not reach them either. Al-Dahhak said: they are the wide-eyed maidens of paradise (al-hur al-'in), the keepers of the Fire, and the bearers of the Throne. From Jabir: among them is Musa, because he swooned once. Abu Hurayrah said: they are the martyrs; and Abu Hurayrah narrated it as a hadith, which is: "They are the martyrs, with their Lord, who are provided for." This is also the view of Ibn Jubayr, who said: they are the martyrs, girded with swords around the Throne. It has also been said: they are the believers, because of His words: *"and they will be secure from terror on that Day."* Some scholars said: no sound report has come concerning their identity, and all of these are possibilities. Al-Qurtubi said: Abu Hurayrah's hadith escaped his notice; Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi authenticated it, so it is relied upon for identification, while the rest are ijtihad (personal judgement). This blowing is literal, whether into the trumpet or into the Horn; this is the view of the majority. It has also been said it may be a figure of speech for calling the dead, since their emergence from their graves is like the army's emergence at the sound of a call, and so it would be figurative. The first view is that of the majority, and it is the correct one, because of the frequency with which the blowing into the Horn occurs in the Qur'an and in the sound hadith. It has also been said that *"fa-faza'a"* is not from fear in the sense of dread, but its meaning is: responded and hastened to remain.

*"And all come to Him"*: the genitive pronoun of *kullun* is omitted; its estimate is: "and all of them." Al-Jumhur read *atuhu* as an active participle (ism fa'il); Abdullah, Hamzah and Hafs read *atawhu* as a past-tense verb. In both readings the meaning of *kull* as plural has been observed. Qatada read *ataha* as a past-tense verb with the pronoun referring to *kull* in its singular form, and he made *dakhirin* plural according to its meaning. Al-Hasan and al-A'mash read *dakhirin* without the alif. It has been said that the meaning of *atuhu* is: present at the place of standing after the second blast; it may also be meant that they return to His command and submit to Him.

*"And you see the mountains"*: this is from sight by the eye. *"You think them"* is a circumstantial state (hal) of the subject of *tara*, or of *al-jibal*. *"Solid"* (jamidah): one who has become solid in his place when he has not moved from it. This state of the mountains comes after the blast of the Horn, and it is the first of the mountains' conditions: they shake and move; then God blows them away so they become like carded wool; then they become scattered dust in the end.

*"While they pass by as clouds pass by"*: this is a circumstantial clause, meaning: you think them, in the view of the eye, to be firmly fixed in their places while they are moving. Their passing is compared to the passing of clouds. It has been said: in their passing swiftly, as the clouds pass, and in the same way large bodies that are numerous, when they move, their movement is hardly discernible, as al-Nabigha al-Ja'di said describing an army:

A fire from a mass like a mountain, you think them standing still for a pilgrimage, while the riding-camels are trotting.

It has been said: their passing is compared to the passing of clouds in that they move at a middling pace, as al-A'sha said:

Her walk from her neighbour's house is like the passing of a cloud, neither hesitant nor hasty.

The observer's supposition that the mountains are solid while they pass is said to be due to the terror of that day, so that his mind does not have the firm grasp necessary in thought to verify that they are not solid. Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: the reason for their supposing them to be solid is that large bodies, when they move swiftly in a single direction, the observer thinks they are standing still, while they are passing swiftly. End of quotation. It has been said: He described the mountains with different attributes, which return to the emptying of the earth of them and the exposure of what they used to cover. The first of these attributes is their quaking; then their becoming like carded wool; then like dust, by being broken up after having been like carded wool; then their being blown away. With the preceding conditions they remain fixed in their places, and the earth is not exposed; by the blowing away, it is exposed. Their blowing away is by sending winds upon them, then their being carried by the wind in the air like dust; then their becoming a mirage, so that when you look at their places you will find nothing of them there, like a mirage. Muqatil said: rather, they fall upon the earth and are levelled with it.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 27, verses 83–93 (part 2 of 3):

The phrase ﴿ṣun'a Allāh﴾ (the handiwork of God) is in the accusative because it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) that emphasises the meaning of the clause that follows it, so its governing verb is implied and drawn from its own root. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿ṣun'a Allāh﴾ is one of the emphatic verbal nouns, like His saying ﴿waʿd Allāh﴾ (the promise of God) [Luqman: 9] and ﴿ṣibgha Allāh﴾ (the colouring of God) [al-Baqarah: 138], except that the clause it emphasises (p. 101) is omitted, and it is the verb governing "the day when the Trumpet is blown". The meaning is: "And on the day when the Trumpet is blown, such-and-such happens: God rewards the good-doers and punishes the wrongdoers." Then He said: ﴿ṣun'a Allāh﴾, meaning by it the reward and the punishment. This handiwork is counted among the things He perfected and carried out in wisdom and rightness, since He said: ﴿ṣun'a Allāh alladhī atqana kulla shay'﴾ (the handiwork of God, who perfected everything). That is, His answering a good deed with reward and an evil deed with punishment is part of His firm ordering of things, His perfecting them, and His running them according to the dictates of wisdom, and that He knows what the servants do and what they deserve, and so He recompenses them according to that. Then He summed this up in His saying: ﴿man jāʾa bil-ḥasanati fa-lahu﴾ (whoever comes with a good deed, for him there is), to the end of the two verses. So consider the eloquence of this discourse, the excellence of its arrangement and order, the solidity of its structure and the soundness of its explanation, and how one part takes hold of another, as though it were poured out in a single casting. How marvellous a matter, which overpowers faculties and silences the boastful! A verbal noun of this kind, when it comes after a statement, comes as a witness to its truth and a herald of its soundness, and it shows that it could not have been other than what it is. Do you not see His saying: ﴿ṣun'a Allāh﴾, and ﴿ṣibgha Allāh﴾ [al-Baqarah: 138], and ﴿waʿd Allāh﴾ [Yunus: 4], and ﴿fiṭrata Allāh﴾ (the nature of God) [al-Rum: 30]? After He had marked them by attributing them to Himself, as a name of exalting, how did He follow them with His saying: "﴿alladhī atqana kulla shay'﴾", "﴿wa-man aḥsanu mina Allāh ṣibghatan﴾ (and who is better than God in colouring?) [al-Baqarah: 138]", "﴿inna Allāha lā yukhlifu al-mīʿād﴾ (surely God does not fail the promise) [Al ʿImran: 9]", "﴿lā tabdīla li-khalq Allāh﴾ (there is no changing of the creation of God) [al-Rum: 30]"? End of quotation. What has been mentioned of his boastfulness and his excess in speech, and his contrivance in bending the words of the Qur'an to what he holds, is from the doctrines of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist school of theology).

What appears to me is that ﴿ṣun'a Allāh﴾ is an emphatic verbal noun for the meaning of the preceding clause, which is the clause of circumstance: God did that to them, namely uprooting them from the earth and making them pass like the passing of clouds. As for his statement that its emphasised element is omitted, and that it is the verb governing "the day when the Trumpet is blown" up to His saying "﴿ṣun'a Allāh﴾", meaning by it reward and punishment, this is not valid. The emphatic verbal noun for the meaning of a clause may not have its clause omitted, because it is governed by a verb of its own root, so the omission of the governing verb and the omission of the clause whose meaning is emphasised by the verbal noun would coincide, and that is a frequent and damaging omission. Whoever surveys the context of these verbal nouns that emphasise the meaning of a clause will find the clauses stated explicitly, and no omission occurs in any of them. The principle is that the emphasised element should not be omitted, since omission contradicts emphasis: from the standpoint of its being emphasised it is given importance, and from the standpoint of its being omitted it is not given importance. It has been said that ﴿ṣun'a Allāh﴾ is in the accusative as an incitement (ighrāʾ) with the sense of "Look at the handiwork of God." The two Iraqi readers (al-ʿArabiyyān, i.e. Abu ʿAmr and ʿAsim?) and Ibn Kathir read ﴿yaf'alūna﴾ with the yāʾ (third person); the rest of the seven read it with the tāʾ of address.

When He mentioned the signs of the Resurrection, He mentioned the conditions of the responsible persons after the Hour has come. The good deed (ḥasanah) is faith. Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Nakhaʿi and Qatadah said: it is "There is no god but God." He placed two things as consequences of the responsible person coming with a good deed. The first: that he has from it something better, and it appears that "khayr" (better) is not an elative (af'al al-tafḍīl, comparative form), and "min" (from) is for the beginning of the limit (ibtidāʾ al-ghāyah), meaning: he has a good from among the goods whose origin and rise is from it, that is, from the direction of this good deed. The "khayr" here is the reward. This is the view of al-Hasan, Ibn Jurayj and ʿIkrimah. ʿIkrimah said: nothing is better than "There is no god but God," meaning that it is not an elative. It has been said that it is an elative. Al-Zamakhshari said: "﴿fa-lahu khayrun minhā﴾" means multiplication (al-ibḍāʿ), and that the action ends while the reward endures, and how far apart are the act of the servant and the act of the master! End of quotation. His saying "how far apart are the act of the servant and the act of the master" is a construction that is disputed: some scholars prohibited it, and the correct view is that it is permissible. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: it may be that it is for comparison, and that in His saying "minhā" (from it) there is an omitted noun, its estimate being: better than its measure and its deserving, meaning that God bestowed upon him beyond what his good deed merits. Ibn Zayd said: he is given ten for one. What calls for this estimate is that between the good deed and the reward no comparison can be conceived. End of quotation. It has been said: the reward for the knowledge acquired in this world is the knowledge that is necessary and attained in the Hereafter, and the pleasure of gazing upon His noble Face. Indications have shown that the noblest of felicities is this pleasure, and if the verse is not taken in that sense, it would follow that eating and drinking are better than knowing God, and that is not possible.

The Kufans read ﴿min faza'in﴾ with tanwīn, and ﴿yawma'idhin﴾ is in the accusative as an adverb of time, governed either by His saying "āminūn" (safe) or by "faza'in". What shows that it is governed by it is the reading of the one who made it an annexed noun (iḍāfah) to it, or it is in the position of an adjective to "faza'in", meaning: occurring at that time. The rest of the seven read "faza'in" annexed to "yawma'idhin"; the two Iraqi readers, Ibn Kathir, Isma'il ibn Ja'far from Nafi', read the mīm with a kasrah, and Nafi' (in other than the transmission of Isma'il) read it with a fatḥah, on the basis that it is annexed to a non-declinable word (ghayr mutamakkin). The tanwīn in "yawma'idhin" is the tanwīn of replacement (tanwīn al-ʿiwaḍ): the clause has been omitted and replaced by it. The preferable view is that the omitted clause is what is nearest to the adverb, that is, "the day when he came with the good deed." It is also possible that the estimate is: "the day when you see the mountains," and it is possible that the estimate is: "the day when the Trumpet is blown," especially if it is interpreted as the blast of rising from the graves for reckoning, and the fear will then be one thing. Abu ʿAli said, in substance: "min faza'in" may be with tanwīn or with annexation; it may mean one single fear, and it may mean abundance, since it is a verbal noun. If abundance is meant, it includes every fear that occurs on the Day of Resurrection; if the single fear is meant, it is the one indicated by His saying: "lā yaḥzunuhumu al-faza' al-akbar" (the greatest terror shall not grieve them). Al-Zamakhshari said: "(If you say) what is the difference between the two fears? (I say) the first fear is that from which no one is free when he senses a severe event that befalls him; it startles him out of terror and awe, even if the doer of good is safe from harm reaching him. The second is fear of punishment." End of quotation.

The evil deed (sayyi'ah) is disbelief and sins committed by those upon whom God has set a seal from among the people of the Will, by their entering the Fire. The faces are singled out, since they are the noblest of the limbs, and their being cast into the Fire entails the casting of the whole body; or the face is used to express the whole human being, as the head and the neck are used to express it, as He said: ﴿fa-kubkibū fīhā﴾ (so they will be flung into it) [al-Shuʿara: 94]; it is as if it were said: "so they will be cast into the Fire." The apparent meaning of "kubbat" is that they are thrown into the Fire upside down, as Abu al-ʿAliyah said, its top before its bottom. It is also possible that this is a metaphor for their being cast into the Fire, as al-Dahhak said. "Hal tujzawna" (Are you being recompensed?) is addressed to them with an implied saying, meaning: it is said to them at the time of the casting: "Are you being recompensed?"

Then God, exalted is He, commanded His Prophet to say: ﴿innamā umirtu﴾ (I have only been commanded), and the one who commands is God, exalted is He, through the tongue of Jibril, or it is the proof of reason for the unity of God, exalted is He. ﴿an aʿbuda﴾ (that I should worship): that is, that I single Him out for worship, and not take a partner with Him as the Quraysh did. This is an expression of exaltation, like His saying: ﴿wa-hādhā kitābun anzalnāhu﴾ (and this is a Book We have sent down) [al-Anʿam: 92]. "This" refers to the one who is with me, insofar as he is the place of residence of His Prophet and the descent-point of His revelation. The land (al-baldah) is Makkah, and the making sacred is attributed to Him to honour it and single it out. There is no contradiction between His saying ﴿alladhī ḥarramahā﴾ (who has made it sacred) and his peace be upon him saying: "Indeed Ibrahim made Makkah sacred, and I have made Madinah sacred." This is because the attribution of that to God is insofar as it was by His decree and prior knowledge, and its attribution to Ibrahim is insofar as its manifestation came through his supplication, his desire, and his conveying it to his community. In His saying "ḥarramahā" (made it sacred) there is an admonition to the Quraysh of His blessing upon them, since He made their land secure from raids and the strife that occurs in the lands of the Arabs, and destroyed whoever intended it with evil. The majority read ﴿alladhī﴾ as an adjective of the Lord. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn ʿAbbas read ﴿allatī ḥarramahā﴾ as an adjective of "the land". When He informed that He is the owner of this land, He informed that He possesses everything, so He said: ﴿wa-lahu kullu shay'﴾ (and to Him belongs everything), that is, all things are included in His lordship; thus the land was honoured by the mention of its being included under His lordship in particular and in general. ﴿wa-umirtu an akūna mina al-muslimīn﴾ (and I have been commanded to be of the Muslims): that is, of those who submit and are obedient to the command of God, so that I worship Him as He commanded me; or of the ḥunafāʾ (upright in faith), who stand firm on the religion of Islam, referred to in His saying: "He named you the Muslims" [al-Hajj: 78]. ﴿wa-an atlūa al-Qurʾān﴾ (and that I should recite the Qur'an): either from recitation (tilāwah), that is, "and that I recite the Qur'an to you," and this is the apparent meaning, since after it comes the division appropriate to recitation; or from what is recited (al-matluww), that is, "and that I follow the Qur'an," as in His saying: "follow what is revealed to you" [Yunus: 109]. The majority read "wa-an atlūa". ʿAbd Allah read "wa-ani-tlu" without the waw, as an imperative from talā, so "an" may be a verbal (maṣdariyyah) particle connected to the imperative, and it may be an explanatory "an" with an implied "wa-umirtu an atlu", meaning: recite. Ubayy read "wa-tlu hādhā al-Qurʾān", making it an imperative without "an". "So whoever is guided" by it, and affirms the oneness of God and of His Prophet, and believes in what he brought, then the fruit of his guidance belongs to him alone. "And whoever goes astray," then the burden of his misguidance is his alone. The answer to "whoever goes astray" is omitted because the answer to its counterpart indicates it; or a pronoun is to be estimated in His saying: ﴿fa-qul innamā anā mina al-mundhirīn﴾ (say: I am only one of the warners), so that the recompense is linked to the condition, since the particle of condition is a noun and not an adverb, so there must be in the answer clause (p. 103) a reference returning to it, either spoken or estimated, so that this clause becomes the answer of the condition; and the pronoun is estimated as: "of the warners to him," that is, I have only to warn him, and as for his guidance, it is to God.

"And say: Praise belongs to God": he was commanded to say this, so that he praises his Lord for what He has specified him with of the nobility of prophethood and messengership, and singled him out with an exalted station. ﴿sa-yurīkum āyātihi﴾ (He will show you His signs): a threat to His enemies, with what God shows them of His signs, which will compel them to know them and to acknowledge that they are the signs of God. Al-Hasan said: this is in the Hereafter, so that knowledge will not benefit them. Al-Kalbi said: it is in this world, namely the smoke, the splitting of the moon, and what befell them of the vengeance of God. It has been said: the Day of Badr. It has been said: the emergence of the beast, even if after a time. It has been said: His signs are in yourselves and in all that He created, like His saying: ﴿sa-nurīhim āyātinā fī al-āfāqi wa-fī anfusihim﴾ (We shall show them Our signs on the horizons and in themselves) [Fussilat: 53]. It has been said: they are the miracles of the Messenger, and He attributed them to Himself because He is the one who brings them about through the hands of His Messenger, and manifests them from His side. ﴿fa-taʿrifūnahā﴾ (and you will recognise them): that is, their reality, and it is not possible for you to deny them. The majority read ﴿ʿammā yaʿmalūn﴾ (of what they do) with the yāʾ of the third person, a shift (iltifāt) from the pronoun of address to the pronoun of absence; Nafi' and Ibn ʿAmir read it with the tāʾ of address, in line with His saying: "He will show you." When He divided them into the guided and the astray, He informed, exalted is He, that He encompasses their deeds, and is not heedless of them.

* *

(Vocabulary of Surah al-Qasas)

al-Wakz: striking with the hand closed, like the closing of the fingers to make seventy-three (a gesture of counting). It has been said: gathering the palm. It has been said: wakz, nakz, lahz and lakz are all pushing with the fingertips. It has been said: wakz is on the heart, and lakz is on the jaw. It has been said: wakz is with the fingertips. Dhaʿada (he drove away), and drove back, and pushed. Al-Farra' said: he restrained. Jadhawtu al-shay' jadhwan: I cut it. And al-jadhwah is a stick in which there is fire without flame. Ibn Muqbil said:

They spent the night, the gatherers of wood for Layla, seeking for her firm firewood, neither crumbling nor brittle.

Al-Khawwar is that which crumbles, and al-Dhaʿir is that which has weariness in it. Another said:

And he cast upon a brand of fire a burning ember, its ash and its glow around it.

It is said: *al-jadhwah* (the *jim* may carry three vowels) is a thick piece of wood, whether or not there was fire on its end.

Al-Sulami said, describing the fire:

*The love of this fire has kindled the love of my beloved,*
*and the love of the young women, though it falls short of the beloved.*

*After musk and ben-tree perfume, I was given in exchange misery:*
*the smoke of al-Judhafi, a gray-haired, pale-faced old man.*

*Al-shati'* and *al-shatt* are the edge of a valley. *Al-fasahah* (eloquence) is the free use of the tongue in clarifying the intended meaning; its opposite is *al-lukn* (a faltering, unclear speech).

*Al-ridʾ* is the helper through whom one is strengthened in a matter. It is a verb in the sense of a passive participle (*fiʿl bi-maʿna maful*), so it is a noun for that by which one is aided, just as *al-difʾ* is a noun for that by which one is warmed. Salamah ibn Jandal said:

*And a helper for every white, Indian-sworded (blade),*
*sharpened at the edge, keen, with notches.*

It is said: *radaʾtu al-ha'it arduʾuhu*, meaning when you prop up a wall with a piece of wood so that it does not fall. Abu Ubaydah said: *al-ʿawn* (help). It is also said: *radaʾtuhu ʿala ʿaduwwihi*, meaning I aided him against his enemy.

*Al-maqbuh* is the one who is rejected and driven away. The poet said:

*Surely God has disfigured all the Baraajim tribes,*
*and cut off the nose of Yarbuʿ and abased Darim.*

*Thawa yathwi thawaʾan* means he stayed or resided. The poet said:

*Indeed there was a stay I made in a year,*
*when the milk-camels were consumed and the herding camels were wearied.*

Al-Ajjaj said:

*So he spent the night where the sojourner (al-thawiyy) enters,*

that is, the guest who stays. *Al-batar* is insolence. *Al-sarmad* is that which is everlasting and never ceases.

[p. 98] That is: remember the Day when We gather from every nation a multitude (fawj) of those who denied Our signs, and they are driven on. Al-hashr means gathering by force.

*"From every nation"*: min here means "from among the nations," and min is partitive (lil-tab'id).

*"A multitude"*: meaning a large group.

*"Of those who deny Our signs"*: min here is explanatory (lil-bayan), meaning "those who deny." The "signs" (al-ayat) are said to be the prophets, or the Qur'an, or the proofs; these are the views reported.

*"Then they are driven on"*: its explanation was already given at the beginning of the story of Sulayman in this surah. It is reported from Ibn Mas'ud that Abu Jahl, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and Shayba ibn Rabi'a were said to be "in front of the people of Makkah." In the same way, the leaders of all the other nations will be driven before them into the Fire.

*"Until, when they come"*: that is, to the place of standing (al-mawqif). *"He will say: Did you deny My signs"*: this is an interrogative of rebuke, reproach and humiliation. *"And you did not encompass them in knowledge"*: the apparent reading is that the waw is for the circumstantial state (lil-hal), meaning: did you deny them without reflecting upon them and without having encompassed knowledge of their reality? It is also permissible for the waw to be conjunctive (lil-atf), meaning: did you reject them, and along with their rejection you did not apply your minds to verify and perceive them. For the one to whom a writing is sent may deny that it came from the one who wrote it to him, yet he does not refrain from reading it and comprehending its meanings. It has also been said: "and you did not encompass them in knowledge" means that you did not know their falsehood so as to turn away from them; rather, you denied them in ignorance, without seeking evidence. Here *am* is disjunctive (munqati'ah), and it should be estimated as equivalent to *bal* alone. The speech moves from the interrogation that implies rebuke to an interrogation about their deeds, also in the manner of rebuke: *"What was it that you used to do?"* The meaning is: if you had any deed or proof, then produce it; but they have no deed or proof regarding what they did except disbelief and denial. *Madha* as a whole may be understood as an interrogative in the accusative, governed as the predicate of *kana*, which is *ta'malun*; or *ma* may be the interrogative and *dha* a relative pronoun meaning "that which," so that the two form a subject and predicate, with *kana* as a relative clause for *dha*, and the returning pronoun omitted, meaning "you used to do it." Abu Haywa read *amadha*, with the mim lightened, placing the interrogative particle before the interrogative noun for emphasis.

*"And the word has come due against them"*: that is, the promised punishment, because of their wrongdoing, which is their denial of the signs of God.

*"So they cannot speak"*: that is, they have no proof and no excuse, because they are occupied with the punishment of God. It has also been said: their mouths will be sealed, so they will not speak; and the absence of their speech may be at one station of the Resurrection, or it may apply to one group of people, because the Qur'an implies that at other stations they speak with proofs.

When He had mentioned some of the conditions of the Day of Resurrection, so that whoever God wills to be restrained may be restrained by hearing them, He drew their attention to what is evidence for the oneness of God (tawhid), for the gathering, and for prophethood, through something they witness in their own lives: the alternation of night and day from light to darkness and from darkness to light. The one who does this is one, and He is God Most High, so He must be singled out for worship and divinity. In this alternation there is also evidence for the turning of the heart from life to death and from death to another life. There is also evidence here for prophethood, because this alternation serves the benefits of those who are responsible (mukallafun); for this reason He gave the reason for that arrangement in His words: *"that you may rest therein"*. And the sending of prophets is for achieving the benefits of creation. He attributed seeing (al-ibsar) to the day as a figurative usage (majaz), since it occurs in the day; he attributed it to it as you would say, "your night is sleeping." He gave as the reason for the making of the night His words *"that you may rest therein"*, meaning so that their rest may take place in it, from the fatigue they suffer during the day, and so that their souls may be refreshed. One of the rajaz poets said:

Sleep is the rest of the sensory powers from their movements, and of the psychic powers.

The opposition was not stated explicitly in the making of the day with a mention of its reason, so the construction would have been "and the day so that you may see in it." Instead He said *"seeing"* (mubsiran) as a qualifier in the making of the day, not as a reason for the making. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is considered in terms of meaning, and this is the natural, uncontrived arrangement, because the meaning of *mubsiran* is: that you may see in it the way of moving about in pursuits of gain. End of quotation. What appears to be the case is that this is one of those forms in which what is omitted from the first part is what is affirmed in its counterpart, and what is omitted from the second part is what is affirmed in the first. The estimate therefore is: We made the night dark so that you may rest in it, and the day seeing so that you may go about in it. Darkness results in rest, and seeing results in disposing oneself in matters of benefit. This is shown by His words: *"And We made the sign of the day a seeing one, that you may seek bounty from your Lord"* (17:12). Rest is the reason for making the night dark, and going about is the reason for making the day seeing. We have previously discussed these two omissions at length in al-Baqarah, in His words: *"And the likeness of those who disbelieve is like one who shouts..."* (2:171).

*"Indeed in that"*: that is, in this making, *"are signs for a people who believe."* Since only believers benefit from reflection on these signs, they were singled out for mention, even though the signs are for them and for others.

*"And the Day the Horn is blown"*: the discussion of the Horn (al-sur) was given earlier in Surat al-An'am. This blast is the blast of terror. Abu Hurayrah reported that the angel has three blasts on the Horn: the blast of terror, which is the terror of the life of this world and is not the greatest terror; the blast of swooning; and the blast of rising from the graves. It has also been said there are two blasts: they took the terror and the swooning as one blast, and they took as evidence His words: *"Then it will be blown again"* (39:68). The discussion of that will come, God willing. The author of al-Ghunyan said: *"And the Day the Horn is blown"* is for the resurrection from the graves and the gathering. The past tense is used here in His words *"so there is terror"*, even though it has not yet happened, to signal that it is certain to occur and that it is inevitable. This is the purpose of putting the past tense in place of the future, as in His words: *"Then He will lead them into the Fire"* (11:98), after His words: *"He will precede his people on the Day of Resurrection"* (11:98).

*"Except whom God wills"*: that is, this terror will not reach them, because God strengthens their hearts. Muqatil said: they are Jibril, Mika'il, Israfil and the Angel of Death, peace be upon them. Since the greatest terror will not reach them, they are most fitting that this lesser one will not reach them either. Al-Dahhak said: they are the wide-eyed maidens of paradise (al-hur al-'in), the keepers of the Fire, and the bearers of the Throne. From Jabir: among them is Musa, because he swooned once. Abu Hurayrah said: they are the martyrs; and Abu Hurayrah narrated it as a hadith, which is: "They are the martyrs, with their Lord, who are provided for." This is also the view of Ibn Jubayr, who said: they are the martyrs, girded with swords around the Throne. It has also been said: they are the believers, because of His words: *"and they will be secure from terror on that Day."* Some scholars said: no sound report has come concerning their identity, and all of these are possibilities. Al-Qurtubi said: Abu Hurayrah's hadith escaped his notice; Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi authenticated it, so it is relied upon for identification, while the rest are ijtihad (personal judgement). This blowing is literal, whether into the trumpet or into the Horn; this is the view of the majority. It has also been said it may be a figure of speech for calling the dead, since their emergence from their graves is like the army's emergence at the sound of a call, and so it would be figurative. The first view is that of the majority, and it is the correct one, because of the frequency with which the blowing into the Horn occurs in the Qur'an and in the sound hadith. It has also been said that *"fa-faza'a"* is not from fear in the sense of dread, but its meaning is: responded and hastened to remain.

*"And all come to Him"*: the genitive pronoun of *kullun* is omitted; its estimate is: "and all of them." Al-Jumhur read *atuhu* as an active participle (ism fa'il); Abdullah, Hamzah and Hafs read *atawhu* as a past-tense verb. In both readings the meaning of *kull* as plural has been observed. Qatada read *ataha* as a past-tense verb with the pronoun referring to *kull* in its singular form, and he made *dakhirin* plural according to its meaning. Al-Hasan and al-A'mash read *dakhirin* without the alif. It has been said that the meaning of *atuhu* is: present at the place of standing after the second blast; it may also be meant that they return to His command and submit to Him.

*"And you see the mountains"*: this is from sight by the eye. *"You think them"* is a circumstantial state (hal) of the subject of *tara*, or of *al-jibal*. *"Solid"* (jamidah): one who has become solid in his place when he has not moved from it. This state of the mountains comes after the blast of the Horn, and it is the first of the mountains' conditions: they shake and move; then God blows them away so they become like carded wool; then they become scattered dust in the end.

*"While they pass by as clouds pass by"*: this is a circumstantial clause, meaning: you think them, in the view of the eye, to be firmly fixed in their places while they are moving. Their passing is compared to the passing of clouds. It has been said: in their passing swiftly, as the clouds pass, and in the same way large bodies that are numerous, when they move, their movement is hardly discernible, as al-Nabigha al-Ja'di said describing an army:

A fire from a mass like a mountain, you think them standing still for a pilgrimage, while the riding-camels are trotting.

It has been said: their passing is compared to the passing of clouds in that they move at a middling pace, as al-A'sha said:

Her walk from her neighbour's house is like the passing of a cloud, neither hesitant nor hasty.

The observer's supposition that the mountains are solid while they pass is said to be due to the terror of that day, so that his mind does not have the firm grasp necessary in thought to verify that they are not solid. Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: the reason for their supposing them to be solid is that large bodies, when they move swiftly in a single direction, the observer thinks they are standing still, while they are passing swiftly. End of quotation. It has been said: He described the mountains with different attributes, which return to the emptying of the earth of them and the exposure of what they used to cover. The first of these attributes is their quaking; then their becoming like carded wool; then like dust, by being broken up after having been like carded wool; then their being blown away. With the preceding conditions they remain fixed in their places, and the earth is not exposed; by the blowing away, it is exposed. Their blowing away is by sending winds upon them, then their being carried by the wind in the air like dust; then their becoming a mirage, so that when you look at their places you will find nothing of them there, like a mirage. Muqatil said: rather, they fall upon the earth and are levelled with it.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 27, verses 83–93 (part 2 of 3):

The phrase ﴿ṣun'a Allāh﴾ (the handiwork of God) is in the accusative because it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) that emphasises the meaning of the clause that follows it, so its governing verb is implied and drawn from its own root. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿ṣun'a Allāh﴾ is one of the emphatic verbal nouns, like His saying ﴿waʿd Allāh﴾ (the promise of God) [Luqman: 9] and ﴿ṣibgha Allāh﴾ (the colouring of God) [al-Baqarah: 138], except that the clause it emphasises (p. 101) is omitted, and it is the verb governing "the day when the Trumpet is blown". The meaning is: "And on the day when the Trumpet is blown, such-and-such happens: God rewards the good-doers and punishes the wrongdoers." Then He said: ﴿ṣun'a Allāh﴾, meaning by it the reward and the punishment. This handiwork is counted among the things He perfected and carried out in wisdom and rightness, since He said: ﴿ṣun'a Allāh alladhī atqana kulla shay'﴾ (the handiwork of God, who perfected everything). That is, His answering a good deed with reward and an evil deed with punishment is part of His firm ordering of things, His perfecting them, and His running them according to the dictates of wisdom, and that He knows what the servants do and what they deserve, and so He recompenses them according to that. Then He summed this up in His saying: ﴿man jāʾa bil-ḥasanati fa-lahu﴾ (whoever comes with a good deed, for him there is), to the end of the two verses. So consider the eloquence of this discourse, the excellence of its arrangement and order, the solidity of its structure and the soundness of its explanation, and how one part takes hold of another, as though it were poured out in a single casting. How marvellous a matter, which overpowers faculties and silences the boastful! A verbal noun of this kind, when it comes after a statement, comes as a witness to its truth and a herald of its soundness, and it shows that it could not have been other than what it is. Do you not see His saying: ﴿ṣun'a Allāh﴾, and ﴿ṣibgha Allāh﴾ [al-Baqarah: 138], and ﴿waʿd Allāh﴾ [Yunus: 4], and ﴿fiṭrata Allāh﴾ (the nature of God) [al-Rum: 30]? After He had marked them by attributing them to Himself, as a name of exalting, how did He follow them with His saying: "﴿alladhī atqana kulla shay'﴾", "﴿wa-man aḥsanu mina Allāh ṣibghatan﴾ (and who is better than God in colouring?) [al-Baqarah: 138]", "﴿inna Allāha lā yukhlifu al-mīʿād﴾ (surely God does not fail the promise) [Al ʿImran: 9]", "﴿lā tabdīla li-khalq Allāh﴾ (there is no changing of the creation of God) [al-Rum: 30]"? End of quotation. What has been mentioned of his boastfulness and his excess in speech, and his contrivance in bending the words of the Qur'an to what he holds, is from the doctrines of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist school of theology).

What appears to me is that ﴿ṣun'a Allāh﴾ is an emphatic verbal noun for the meaning of the preceding clause, which is the clause of circumstance: God did that to them, namely uprooting them from the earth and making them pass like the passing of clouds. As for his statement that its emphasised element is omitted, and that it is the verb governing "the day when the Trumpet is blown" up to His saying "﴿ṣun'a Allāh﴾", meaning by it reward and punishment, this is not valid. The emphatic verbal noun for the meaning of a clause may not have its clause omitted, because it is governed by a verb of its own root, so the omission of the governing verb and the omission of the clause whose meaning is emphasised by the verbal noun would coincide, and that is a frequent and damaging omission. Whoever surveys the context of these verbal nouns that emphasise the meaning of a clause will find the clauses stated explicitly, and no omission occurs in any of them. The principle is that the emphasised element should not be omitted, since omission contradicts emphasis: from the standpoint of its being emphasised it is given importance, and from the standpoint of its being omitted it is not given importance. It has been said that ﴿ṣun'a Allāh﴾ is in the accusative as an incitement (ighrāʾ) with the sense of "Look at the handiwork of God." The two Iraqi readers (al-ʿArabiyyān, i.e. Abu ʿAmr and ʿAsim?) and Ibn Kathir read ﴿yaf'alūna﴾ with the yāʾ (third person); the rest of the seven read it with the tāʾ of address.

When He mentioned the signs of the Resurrection, He mentioned the conditions of the responsible persons after the Hour has come. The good deed (ḥasanah) is faith. Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Nakhaʿi and Qatadah said: it is "There is no god but God." He placed two things as consequences of the responsible person coming with a good deed. The first: that he has from it something better, and it appears that "khayr" (better) is not an elative (af'al al-tafḍīl, comparative form), and "min" (from) is for the beginning of the limit (ibtidāʾ al-ghāyah), meaning: he has a good from among the goods whose origin and rise is from it, that is, from the direction of this good deed. The "khayr" here is the reward. This is the view of al-Hasan, Ibn Jurayj and ʿIkrimah. ʿIkrimah said: nothing is better than "There is no god but God," meaning that it is not an elative. It has been said that it is an elative. Al-Zamakhshari said: "﴿fa-lahu khayrun minhā﴾" means multiplication (al-ibḍāʿ), and that the action ends while the reward endures, and how far apart are the act of the servant and the act of the master! End of quotation. His saying "how far apart are the act of the servant and the act of the master" is a construction that is disputed: some scholars prohibited it, and the correct view is that it is permissible. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: it may be that it is for comparison, and that in His saying "minhā" (from it) there is an omitted noun, its estimate being: better than its measure and its deserving, meaning that God bestowed upon him beyond what his good deed merits. Ibn Zayd said: he is given ten for one. What calls for this estimate is that between the good deed and the reward no comparison can be conceived. End of quotation. It has been said: the reward for the knowledge acquired in this world is the knowledge that is necessary and attained in the Hereafter, and the pleasure of gazing upon His noble Face. Indications have shown that the noblest of felicities is this pleasure, and if the verse is not taken in that sense, it would follow that eating and drinking are better than knowing God, and that is not possible.

The Kufans read ﴿min faza'in﴾ with tanwīn, and ﴿yawma'idhin﴾ is in the accusative as an adverb of time, governed either by His saying "āminūn" (safe) or by "faza'in". What shows that it is governed by it is the reading of the one who made it an annexed noun (iḍāfah) to it, or it is in the position of an adjective to "faza'in", meaning: occurring at that time. The rest of the seven read "faza'in" annexed to "yawma'idhin"; the two Iraqi readers, Ibn Kathir, Isma'il ibn Ja'far from Nafi', read the mīm with a kasrah, and Nafi' (in other than the transmission of Isma'il) read it with a fatḥah, on the basis that it is annexed to a non-declinable word (ghayr mutamakkin). The tanwīn in "yawma'idhin" is the tanwīn of replacement (tanwīn al-ʿiwaḍ): the clause has been omitted and replaced by it. The preferable view is that the omitted clause is what is nearest to the adverb, that is, "the day when he came with the good deed." It is also possible that the estimate is: "the day when you see the mountains," and it is possible that the estimate is: "the day when the Trumpet is blown," especially if it is interpreted as the blast of rising from the graves for reckoning, and the fear will then be one thing. Abu ʿAli said, in substance: "min faza'in" may be with tanwīn or with annexation; it may mean one single fear, and it may mean abundance, since it is a verbal noun. If abundance is meant, it includes every fear that occurs on the Day of Resurrection; if the single fear is meant, it is the one indicated by His saying: "lā yaḥzunuhumu al-faza' al-akbar" (the greatest terror shall not grieve them). Al-Zamakhshari said: "(If you say) what is the difference between the two fears? (I say) the first fear is that from which no one is free when he senses a severe event that befalls him; it startles him out of terror and awe, even if the doer of good is safe from harm reaching him. The second is fear of punishment." End of quotation.

The evil deed (sayyi'ah) is disbelief and sins committed by those upon whom God has set a seal from among the people of the Will, by their entering the Fire. The faces are singled out, since they are the noblest of the limbs, and their being cast into the Fire entails the casting of the whole body; or the face is used to express the whole human being, as the head and the neck are used to express it, as He said: ﴿fa-kubkibū fīhā﴾ (so they will be flung into it) [al-Shuʿara: 94]; it is as if it were said: "so they will be cast into the Fire." The apparent meaning of "kubbat" is that they are thrown into the Fire upside down, as Abu al-ʿAliyah said, its top before its bottom. It is also possible that this is a metaphor for their being cast into the Fire, as al-Dahhak said. "Hal tujzawna" (Are you being recompensed?) is addressed to them with an implied saying, meaning: it is said to them at the time of the casting: "Are you being recompensed?"

Then God, exalted is He, commanded His Prophet to say: ﴿innamā umirtu﴾ (I have only been commanded), and the one who commands is God, exalted is He, through the tongue of Jibril, or it is the proof of reason for the unity of God, exalted is He. ﴿an aʿbuda﴾ (that I should worship): that is, that I single Him out for worship, and not take a partner with Him as the Quraysh did. This is an expression of exaltation, like His saying: ﴿wa-hādhā kitābun anzalnāhu﴾ (and this is a Book We have sent down) [al-Anʿam: 92]. "This" refers to the one who is with me, insofar as he is the place of residence of His Prophet and the descent-point of His revelation. The land (al-baldah) is Makkah, and the making sacred is attributed to Him to honour it and single it out. There is no contradiction between His saying ﴿alladhī ḥarramahā﴾ (who has made it sacred) and his peace be upon him saying: "Indeed Ibrahim made Makkah sacred, and I have made Madinah sacred." This is because the attribution of that to God is insofar as it was by His decree and prior knowledge, and its attribution to Ibrahim is insofar as its manifestation came through his supplication, his desire, and his conveying it to his community. In His saying "ḥarramahā" (made it sacred) there is an admonition to the Quraysh of His blessing upon them, since He made their land secure from raids and the strife that occurs in the lands of the Arabs, and destroyed whoever intended it with evil. The majority read ﴿alladhī﴾ as an adjective of the Lord. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn ʿAbbas read ﴿allatī ḥarramahā﴾ as an adjective of "the land". When He informed that He is the owner of this land, He informed that He possesses everything, so He said: ﴿wa-lahu kullu shay'﴾ (and to Him belongs everything), that is, all things are included in His lordship; thus the land was honoured by the mention of its being included under His lordship in particular and in general. ﴿wa-umirtu an akūna mina al-muslimīn﴾ (and I have been commanded to be of the Muslims): that is, of those who submit and are obedient to the command of God, so that I worship Him as He commanded me; or of the ḥunafāʾ (upright in faith), who stand firm on the religion of Islam, referred to in His saying: "He named you the Muslims" [al-Hajj: 78]. ﴿wa-an atlūa al-Qurʾān﴾ (and that I should recite the Qur'an): either from recitation (tilāwah), that is, "and that I recite the Qur'an to you," and this is the apparent meaning, since after it comes the division appropriate to recitation; or from what is recited (al-matluww), that is, "and that I follow the Qur'an," as in His saying: "follow what is revealed to you" [Yunus: 109]. The majority read "wa-an atlūa". ʿAbd Allah read "wa-ani-tlu" without the waw, as an imperative from talā, so "an" may be a verbal (maṣdariyyah) particle connected to the imperative, and it may be an explanatory "an" with an implied "wa-umirtu an atlu", meaning: recite. Ubayy read "wa-tlu hādhā al-Qurʾān", making it an imperative without "an". "So whoever is guided" by it, and affirms the oneness of God and of His Prophet, and believes in what he brought, then the fruit of his guidance belongs to him alone. "And whoever goes astray," then the burden of his misguidance is his alone. The answer to "whoever goes astray" is omitted because the answer to its counterpart indicates it; or a pronoun is to be estimated in His saying: ﴿fa-qul innamā anā mina al-mundhirīn﴾ (say: I am only one of the warners), so that the recompense is linked to the condition, since the particle of condition is a noun and not an adverb, so there must be in the answer clause (p. 103) a reference returning to it, either spoken or estimated, so that this clause becomes the answer of the condition; and the pronoun is estimated as: "of the warners to him," that is, I have only to warn him, and as for his guidance, it is to God.

"And say: Praise belongs to God": he was commanded to say this, so that he praises his Lord for what He has specified him with of the nobility of prophethood and messengership, and singled him out with an exalted station. ﴿sa-yurīkum āyātihi﴾ (He will show you His signs): a threat to His enemies, with what God shows them of His signs, which will compel them to know them and to acknowledge that they are the signs of God. Al-Hasan said: this is in the Hereafter, so that knowledge will not benefit them. Al-Kalbi said: it is in this world, namely the smoke, the splitting of the moon, and what befell them of the vengeance of God. It has been said: the Day of Badr. It has been said: the emergence of the beast, even if after a time. It has been said: His signs are in yourselves and in all that He created, like His saying: ﴿sa-nurīhim āyātinā fī al-āfāqi wa-fī anfusihim﴾ (We shall show them Our signs on the horizons and in themselves) [Fussilat: 53]. It has been said: they are the miracles of the Messenger, and He attributed them to Himself because He is the one who brings them about through the hands of His Messenger, and manifests them from His side. ﴿fa-taʿrifūnahā﴾ (and you will recognise them): that is, their reality, and it is not possible for you to deny them. The majority read ﴿ʿammā yaʿmalūn﴾ (of what they do) with the yāʾ of the third person, a shift (iltifāt) from the pronoun of address to the pronoun of absence; Nafi' and Ibn ʿAmir read it with the tāʾ of address, in line with His saying: "He will show you." When He divided them into the guided and the astray, He informed, exalted is He, that He encompasses their deeds, and is not heedless of them.

* *

(Vocabulary of Surah al-Qasas)

al-Wakz: striking with the hand closed, like the closing of the fingers to make seventy-three (a gesture of counting). It has been said: gathering the palm. It has been said: wakz, nakz, lahz and lakz are all pushing with the fingertips. It has been said: wakz is on the heart, and lakz is on the jaw. It has been said: wakz is with the fingertips. Dhaʿada (he drove away), and drove back, and pushed. Al-Farra' said: he restrained. Jadhawtu al-shay' jadhwan: I cut it. And al-jadhwah is a stick in which there is fire without flame. Ibn Muqbil said:

They spent the night, the gatherers of wood for Layla, seeking for her firm firewood, neither crumbling nor brittle.

Al-Khawwar is that which crumbles, and al-Dhaʿir is that which has weariness in it. Another said:

And he cast upon a brand of fire a burning ember, its ash and its glow around it.

It is said: *al-jadhwah* (the *jim* may carry three vowels) is a thick piece of wood, whether or not there was fire on its end.

Al-Sulami said, describing the fire:

*The love of this fire has kindled the love of my beloved,*
*and the love of the young women, though it falls short of the beloved.*

*After musk and ben-tree perfume, I was given in exchange misery:*
*the smoke of al-Judhafi, a gray-haired, pale-faced old man.*

*Al-shati'* and *al-shatt* are the edge of a valley. *Al-fasahah* (eloquence) is the free use of the tongue in clarifying the intended meaning; its opposite is *al-lukn* (a faltering, unclear speech).

*Al-ridʾ* is the helper through whom one is strengthened in a matter. It is a verb in the sense of a passive participle (*fiʿl bi-maʿna maful*), so it is a noun for that by which one is aided, just as *al-difʾ* is a noun for that by which one is warmed. Salamah ibn Jandal said:

*And a helper for every white, Indian-sworded (blade),*
*sharpened at the edge, keen, with notches.*

It is said: *radaʾtu al-ha'it arduʾuhu*, meaning when you prop up a wall with a piece of wood so that it does not fall. Abu Ubaydah said: *al-ʿawn* (help). It is also said: *radaʾtuhu ʿala ʿaduwwihi*, meaning I aided him against his enemy.

*Al-maqbuh* is the one who is rejected and driven away. The poet said:

*Surely God has disfigured all the Baraajim tribes,*
*and cut off the nose of Yarbuʿ and abased Darim.*

*Thawa yathwi thawaʾan* means he stayed or resided. The poet said:

*Indeed there was a stay I made in a year,*
*when the milk-camels were consumed and the herding camels were wearied.*

Al-Ajjaj said:

*So he spent the night where the sojourner (al-thawiyy) enters,*

that is, the guest who stays. *Al-batar* is insolence. *Al-sarmad* is that which is everlasting and never ceases.

[p. 98] That is: remember the Day when We gather from every nation a multitude (fawj) of those who denied Our signs, and they are driven on. Al-hashr means gathering by force.

*"From every nation"*: min here means "from among the nations," and min is partitive (lil-tab'id).

*"A multitude"*: meaning a large group.

*"Of those who deny Our signs"*: min here is explanatory (lil-bayan), meaning "those who deny." The "signs" (al-ayat) are said to be the prophets, or the Qur'an, or the proofs; these are the views reported.

*"Then they are driven on"*: its explanation was already given at the beginning of the story of Sulayman in this surah. It is reported from Ibn Mas'ud that Abu Jahl, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and Shayba ibn Rabi'a were said to be "in front of the people of Makkah." In the same way, the leaders of all the other nations will be driven before them into the Fire.

*"Until, when they come"*: that is, to the place of standing (al-mawqif). *"He will say: Did you deny My signs"*: this is an interrogative of rebuke, reproach and humiliation. *"And you did not encompass them in knowledge"*: the apparent reading is that the waw is for the circumstantial state (lil-hal), meaning: did you deny them without reflecting upon them and without having encompassed knowledge of their reality? It is also permissible for the waw to be conjunctive (lil-atf), meaning: did you reject them, and along with their rejection you did not apply your minds to verify and perceive them. For the one to whom a writing is sent may deny that it came from the one who wrote it to him, yet he does not refrain from reading it and comprehending its meanings. It has also been said: "and you did not encompass them in knowledge" means that you did not know their falsehood so as to turn away from them; rather, you denied them in ignorance, without seeking evidence. Here *am* is disjunctive (munqati'ah), and it should be estimated as equivalent to *bal* alone. The speech moves from the interrogation that implies rebuke to an interrogation about their deeds, also in the manner of rebuke: *"What was it that you used to do?"* The meaning is: if you had any deed or proof, then produce it; but they have no deed or proof regarding what they did except disbelief and denial. *Madha* as a whole may be understood as an interrogative in the accusative, governed as the predicate of *kana*, which is *ta'malun*; or *ma* may be the interrogative and *dha* a relative pronoun meaning "that which," so that the two form a subject and predicate, with *kana* as a relative clause for *dha*, and the returning pronoun omitted, meaning "you used to do it." Abu Haywa read *amadha*, with the mim lightened, placing the interrogative particle before the interrogative noun for emphasis.

*"And the word has come due against them"*: that is, the promised punishment, because of their wrongdoing, which is their denial of the signs of God.

*"So they cannot speak"*: that is, they have no proof and no excuse, because they are occupied with the punishment of God. It has also been said: their mouths will be sealed, so they will not speak; and the absence of their speech may be at one station of the Resurrection, or it may apply to one group of people, because the Qur'an implies that at other stations they speak with proofs.

When He had mentioned some of the conditions of the Day of Resurrection, so that whoever God wills to be restrained may be restrained by hearing them, He drew their attention to what is evidence for the oneness of God (tawhid), for the gathering, and for prophethood, through something they witness in their own lives: the alternation of night and day from light to darkness and from darkness to light. The one who does this is one, and He is God Most High, so He must be singled out for worship and divinity. In this alternation there is also evidence for the turning of the heart from life to death and from death to another life. There is also evidence here for prophethood, because this alternation serves the benefits of those who are responsible (mukallafun); for this reason He gave the reason for that arrangement in His words: *"that you may rest therein"*. And the sending of prophets is for achieving the benefits of creation.
